parts.overview: Ostra is a local workspace that runs an engineering pipeline: research, spec, plan, build, review, test, and docs. A person starts a session in a browser console. The engine runs each stage as an event-sourced state machine and spawns leaf agents. Each agent runs on the native API loop or inside an installed CLI harness (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity). Every tool call passes the policy engine, and the sandbox limits what agent commands can reach. The Rust server in `crates/ostra-server` serves a REST and WebSocket API and the React console in `web/`. The workspace can include many projects, and each project can have a documentation book that agents search before they read code.

sections.title: What Ostra is and its core concepts
sections.summary: Defines the core terms of Ostra, follows one session from request to completion report, and links to every other page of the book.
sections.body:
Ostra runs a request through a fixed pipeline of stages with approval gates. This page defines the core terms, follows one session from request to completion report, and links to every other page.

## The problem Ostra solves

Ostra is a local workspace that runs the engineering pipeline. A user writes a request in plain text: a change, a question, or a documentation job. Ostra moves the request through fixed stages and asks the user to approve at set points.

A single long conversation with one agent fails in known ways. Each lane of the Ostra pipeline exists to prevent one failure:

- Code that an agent writes before it understands the problem carries wrong assumptions. The Research lane reads the code and the current documentation first.
- A requirement that exists only in a person's head never reaches the plan. The Requirements lane writes one spec with testable requirements.
- A spec or plan that its author approves can hold a false claim. The Verification lane fact-checks each concrete claim before Ostra asks the user to approve.
- Without a design step, the architecture drifts. The Design lane turns the spec into phases with dependencies, risks, and a test policy.
- The author of code cannot review it with fresh eyes. The Review lane uses a separate reviewer agent, and the loop repeats until the findings are fixed.
- Tests and documentation are the first work that a team drops. The Test and Docs lanes run when the user asks for them.
- A stage that did not run looks like a bug later. The completion report names each stage that did not run.

Two design choices follow from these failures. First, code decides the order of the stages. The planner `next_steps` is a pure function from the session state to the next steps, so a model never decides which stage runs next. A model decides only inside a judge call, and Ostra records each judge call as a decision. Second, a session is an append-only event log. The state is a fold of the events, so a restart replays the log and continues. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for the replay.

## How the engine drives a session

The engine repeats one loop for each session. The runner performs the steps that the planner returns, appends the resulting events to the log, and then calls the planner again.

### The planner and runner loop

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Event log"] -->|"fold"| B["SessionState"]
    B -->|"next_steps"| C["Step values"]
    C -->|"runner performs"| D["Judge, agent, gate, command"]
    D -->|"appends events"| A
```

The loop has these parts:

- `SessionState` (in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`) is the fold of the session events.
- `next_steps` (in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`) reads the state and a `PlanCtx`. It does no input or output.
- `Step` has 13 values: `Judge`, `Spawn`, `OpenGate`, `YoloAnswer`, `Command`, `Autofix`, `AnnounceBlocked`, `FinishInit`, `RecordInitProblem`, `Deliver`, `WriteBook`, `Complete`, and `Fail`.
- `Step::key` gives each step an identity. The runner uses it so that a step already in flight does not start twice.
- `Engine` (in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`) is the runner. It performs each step and appends events.

The planner returns no step when the session is paused or ended. Because the planner is pure, the conformance fixtures test it directly: an event history goes in, and the expected next steps come out. See [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) for the planner rules and [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for the runner.

## Workspace, project, and session

A workspace is a folder that Ostra opens. It holds one or more projects and the state of every session that works on them. A project is one code repository in a workspace, named by a project key. A session is one request that moves through the pipeline.

### Workspace

The runtime folder of a workspace is `.ostra/` in the workspace root. Among other items, it holds these:

- `workspace.toml`: the settings of the workspace.
- `workspace.db`: the SQLite database of the workspace.
- `sessions/`: one folder for each session.
- `uploads/`: the files that the user uploaded and that wait for a session to claim them. The function `upload_staging` in `crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs` gives this path.
- `.gitignore`: a file that lists `workspace.db*`, `sessions/`, and `uploads/`. `WorkspaceDb::open` in `crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs` writes it when it does not exist. The event log keeps every tool output, so a `git add -A` in the workspace root must not publish it.

The global config file is `config.toml` in the config folder of the user. The `OSTRA_CONFIG` variable overrides its path. The registry database `registry.db` is in the data folder, and the `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` variable overrides that folder. The workspace has an ID with the prefix `ws_`. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) and [Storage](storage.md).

### Project

A project has its own `.ostra/` folder. The folder holds `INVENTORY.md` and `project.toml`. Every agent routes its work by these two files, so a project must have them before an agent works in it. A session can touch many projects. The Classify judge names the projects in scope, and the user can pin projects, which then become the whole scope.

### Session

A session has an ID with the prefix `s_`. Its kind is `Pipeline` or `Init`. A `Pipeline` session runs a user request. An `Init` session sets up one project: it detects the stack, scouts exemplar files, proposes skills, asks the user to approve them, generates the skills, and generates the inventory.

The user sets these options when the session starts (`SessionOptions`):

- `tests`: ask for the test stage.
- `docs`: ask for the docs stage.
- `yolo`: let Ostra answer the gates.
- `track`: force the `light` or `full` track for an `IMPLEMENT` request.

The user can add text, files, or uploads after the session starts (`RequestAmended`). The default delivery is `queue`: running executions finish on the old request, and the next step sees the new context. The delivery `now` interrupts the running executions and runs them again with the new context.

The session folder is `.ostra/sessions/<session id>/`. The spec and the plan are in its root. The reports of each project are in the subfolder `<project key>/`. Uploaded files are in `uploads/`. The folder `.state/` belongs to the engine, and no agent can write in it.

### Session status

`SessionStatus` has six values:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `running` | An execution or a judge call is in progress. |
| `waiting` | At least one gate is open. |
| `completed` | The session wrote its completion report. |
| `failed` | The session ended with an error. |
| `stalled` | Nothing runs and no gate is open, but the session is not done. |
| `paused` | The user paused the session, or containment signals paused it. Nothing starts until the user continues it. |

> The command `ostra sessions` does not list pipeline sessions. It lists browser sign-ins, and `ostra sessions revoke` revokes them. See [Running Ostra](running-ostra.md).

## Agents, executions, executors, and harnesses

An agent is a leaf worker with one job. An execution is one run of one agent. An executor is the program that runs the execution. A harness is an installed command-line tool that one kind of executor uses.

### Agents

`AgentName` has 14 values. Their prompts are in `assets/agents/<name>/`:

`explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`, and `advisor`.

Each agent ends its work with one typed call, `submit_<agent>` (for example `submit_code_reviewer`). The call returns structured data to the engine. See [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md).

### Executions

An execution has an ID with the prefix `x_`. Its purpose is an `ExecPurpose` value, for example `Implement { phase, work }`. The events `ExecutionStarted` and `ExecutionFinished` bound it. `ExecutionStatus` has nine values:

- `running`: the execution is in progress.
- `ok`: the execution finished with a result.
- `stuck`: the agent reported that it cannot continue and gave a diagnostic.
- `handoff`: the agent asked a specialist to do part of the work.
- `waiting`: the agent asked another subagent and waits for the answer.
- `error`, `denied`, `interrupted`, and `cancelled`: the execution ended without a result.

The setting `limits.max_parallel_executions` sets how many executions run at the same time in one workspace. The default is `3`. The setting `limits.session_budget_usd` sets the dollars that one session can spend before it pauses for a decision. The default is `25.0`, and `0` means no limit. See [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md).

### Executors and harnesses

`ExecutorKind` has two forms. The text form is `native` or `harness:<name>`.

| Executor | What runs the agent | What the console shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | The agent loop inside Ostra, on an API key | The Activity feed |
| `harness:claude` | Claude Code under a PTY | A terminal |
| `harness:codex` | Codex under a PTY | A terminal |
| `harness:grok` | Grok Build under a PTY | A terminal |
| `harness:agy` | Antigravity under a PTY | A terminal |

`HarnessKind` names the four harnesses. The text `antigravity` also parses as `agy`. A harness is a CLI that the user installed. Ostra starts it in a pseudo-terminal, routes each tool call through the policy engine with a hook bridge, and serves the Ostra tools through an MCP stdio shim.

The workspace settings route the executor, the model, the effort, and the tier for each agent. `Tier` has four values: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, and `frontier`. `Effort` has five values: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`. The agents `implementer` and `write-test` route by the `Complexity` of the phase (`low`, `medium`, or `high`). Every tool call from every executor passes the policy engine before it runs. See [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md), [Harness executors](harness-executors.md), and [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).

## Categories, stages, lanes, and tracks

The Classify judge gives each request a category. The category selects which stages run. A stage is one kind of node in the pipeline. A lane is a group of stages that the console shows as one column.

### Category

`Category` has 10 values:

| Category | What the session does |
| --- | --- |
| `RESEARCH` | Runs the research tasks and reports. |
| `SPEC` | Runs research, then writes a spec that passes the fact-check. |
| `PLAN` | Runs research and the spec with approval, then writes a plan. |
| `IMPLEMENT` | Builds the change in reviewed phases. The track decides how much comes before. |
| `VERIFY` | Runs the project test command and reports. |
| `TEST` | Runs the test stage alone on existing code. |
| `DOCS` | Runs the docs stage alone on existing code. It writes a documentation book and changes no code. |
| `PROMPT` | Writes instruction files to the prompt authoring standard. |
| `QUICK_CHANGE` | Makes a small edit that the request fully describes, with one implementer pass on the native executor. |
| `QUICK_ANSWER` | Gives a direct, read-only answer. |

### Stage and lane

`StageKind` has 38 values. One value is one kind of node. A stage instance carries a project key, a phase, and a round. Each stage belongs to one lane through `StageKind::lane`. `Lane::ALL` lists the nine lanes in the order of the software development life cycle:

| Lane | Stages |
| --- | --- |
| Research | `intake`, `classify`, `explore`, `sufficiency`, `track`, `quick-answer`, `detect`, `scout` |
| Requirements | `spec`, `open-questions`, `propose`, `skill-approval` |
| Verification | `fact-check-spec`, `fact-check-plan`, `spec-approval` |
| Design | `stakes`, `plan`, `plan-approval` |
| Build | `implement`, `autofix`, `handoff`, `rescue`, `verify`, `prompt-gen`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory` |
| Review | `review`, `staging`, `format`, `implementation-review` |
| Test | `closing-gate`, `epa`, `write-test`, `test-review` |
| Docs | `documentation`, `architecture`, `book-write` |
| Done | `completion` |

The stage `epa` is the execution path analysis. The console labels it Verification plan. The stage `staging` adds the files of a phase to the git index. See [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) for each stage.

### Track, stakes, and phase

An `IMPLEMENT` request runs on one of two tracks (`Track`). The `light` track goes from research straight to reviewed phases. The `full` track adds the spec, its fact-check, the plan, and the approvals. The Track judge chooses `light` by default and escalates to `full` on evidence. The user can force a track with the `track` option.

On the full track, the Stakes judge gives `Stakes` of `low`, `medium`, or `high`. Low stakes skip the plan stage. A phase is one entry of the plan. It has a complexity and a `TestPolicy` of `Required` (the default) or `Skip`. Ostra builds one phase at a time for each project.

## Gates, judges, and decisions

A gate stops the session until the user answers. A judge is a model call that makes one orchestration decision. A decision is the stored record of one judge call.

### Gates

A gate has an ID with the prefix `g_`. The events `GateOpened` and `GateAnswered` bound it. When a gate is open, the session status is `waiting`. `GatePayload` has 14 kinds:

| Kind | The user decides |
| --- | --- |
| `open_questions` | The answers to the open questions of a spec or plan. |
| `spec_approval` | Whether to approve the spec. |
| `plan_approval` | Whether to approve the plan. |
| `fact_check_recurring` | Whether to run another round when the fact-check keeps failing. |
| `review_cap` | Whether to run another review pass when the review loop hits its cap. |
| `stuck` | A fact for a stuck agent, or whether to block the phase. |
| `phase_blocked` | Whether to retry a blocked phase or leave it. |
| `closing_gate` | Which optional stages to run: tests and documentation. |
| `permission` | Whether to allow one tool call that the policy asks about. |
| `harness_failure` | Whether to retry the harness or switch to `native`. |
| `skill_approval` | The choice for each proposed skill: generate, regenerate, reuse, or drop. |
| `execution_failed` | Whether to `retry` or `abandon` a failed or cancelled execution. |
| `implementation_review` | Feedback for a revision, or `done` to accept the implementation. |
| `budget_reached` | Whether to `raise` the session budget or `stop`. |

See [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) for the gates of each stage and [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for retries and caps.

### Judges

A judge call returns JSON that matches a schema. It is the only place where a model makes an orchestration decision. `JudgeKind` has 10 values: `classify`, `sufficiency`, `track`, `stakes`, `route-answer`, `feedback`, `rescue`, `resolve-review`, `yolo-answer`, and `completion`. The judge prompts are in `assets/judges/`.

### Decisions

A decision has an ID with the prefix `d_`. The event `DecisionMade` stores the judge, the subject, a summary of the input, the output, and the reason. The user can change a decision later. The event `DecisionOverridden` stores the new output and the reason.

A judge also decides where an answer goes (`Disposition`). The value `Deliver` makes the current stage act on the answer now. The value `Remember` keeps the answer for later stages. The value `Discard` drops the answer, but the gate answer stays in the log. See [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

### YOLO mode

YOLO mode is a session option. When it is on, the planner returns a `YoloAnswer` step for most open gates, and the runner answers each one without a wait. The event `GateAnswered` records the source as `AnswerSource::Yolo`. The other sources are `User` and `Engine`. The setting `yolo.default` is `false` unless the user changes it.

YOLO leaves these gates open:

- `budget_reached`: YOLO never raises a budget, because spending more is the decision of the user.
- `execution_failed` of an execution that the user stopped (Rule P4): YOLO does not retry work that the user stopped.
- `permission`: the planner skips these gates because the runner answers each one at once with `AllowOnce`.

A fixed answer or the YOLO judge gives the answer for each other gate. Some answers are fixed choices (`YoloPlan::Fixed`) with a fixed reason. Examples are `another-pass` for `review_cap`, `native` for `harness_failure`, and `done` for `implementation_review`. The YOLO judge writes the reason only for `YoloPlan::Judge`. These gates use the judge: `open_questions`, `spec_approval`, `plan_approval`, and `stuck`. Under YOLO, the completion report lists every decision that Ostra made for the user. See [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md) for each answer.

## Tour of one session

This tour follows an `IMPLEMENT` request on the `full` track. Other categories use a part of the same path.

### Path of an IMPLEMENT request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Request"] -->|"SessionCreated"| B["Classify judge"]
    B -->|"category, projects, research tasks"| C["Explore agents"]
    C -->|"research documents"| D["Sufficiency judge"]
    D --> E["Track judge"]
    E -->|"light"| K["Phases: implement and review"]
    E -->|"full"| F["Spec and fact-check"]
    F -->|"spec_approval gate"| H["Stakes judge"]
    H -->|"medium or high"| I["Plan and fact-check"]
    H -->|"low"| K
    I -->|"plan_approval gate"| K
    K -->|"implementation_review gate"| L["Format command"]
    L --> M["Closing gate, tests, docs"]
    M --> N["Completion judge and report"]
```

The steps in order:

1. The user submits the request in the console. The engine appends `SessionCreated` with the request, the options, and the projects.
2. The Classify judge returns the category, the projects in scope, the research tasks, and a title of 2 to 5 words.
3. The engine starts one `explore` execution for each research task. These read-only executions run at the same time. Each one writes a research document.
4. The Sufficiency judge decides, for each item that the research did not cover, whether the item is needed. A needed item starts more research.
5. The Track judge chooses `light` or `full`.
6. On the full track, `generate-spec` writes the spec. If the spec has open questions, an `open_questions` gate asks the user first. Then `fact-check` verifies the spec.
7. After a fact-check pass, the `spec_approval` gate asks the user to approve the spec. Ostra records the approval only after the pass.
8. The Stakes judge rates the change. If the stakes are `low`, the plan stage is skipped.
9. Otherwise `plan` writes a master plan and one file for each phase. `fact-check` verifies it, and the `plan_approval` gate asks the user to approve it.
10. For each phase, `implementer` writes the code and runs the build command of the project. `code-reviewer` reviews the change. The loop repeats until the findings are fixed or the review cap opens a `review_cap` gate. The engine applies mechanical fixes without an agent (`autofix`), and it stages the files of the phase.
11. After the last phase, the `implementation_review` gate asks the user to accept the result or to send feedback. Feedback becomes new revision phases. The gate text tells the user that acceptance moves on to formatting, tests, documentation, and the completion report (Rule F1).
12. After the user accepts, `closing_stages()` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` runs. First, the engine runs the format command of the project once, without a gate (Rule D8).
13. Next, the `closing_gate` asks which optional stages to run. If the request asked for both tests and docs, the engine skips the gate (Rule T3). If the request asked for only one of them, the gate still opens and asks for the other. The test stages are `epa`, `write-test`, and `test-review`. The docs stages are `documentation`, `architecture`, and `book-write`. The docs stages start after the test stages finish.
14. When nothing runs and no gate is open, the Completion judge writes the completion report. The engine appends `SessionCompleted` with the path of the report.

The completion report states what Ostra did, what did not run and how to run it later, and every decision that Ostra made for the user. Ostra writes it so that a skipped stage is never hidden.

### What happens when something goes wrong

- **An agent reports that it is stuck.** A `stuck` gate shows the diagnostic and the need. The user answers `fact` with the missing fact, or `block`.
- **An execution fails or the user cancels it.** An `execution_failed` gate opens. The user answers `retry` or `abandon`.
- **A harness fails.** A `harness_failure` gate opens. The user answers `retry` or `native`.
- **The review loop reaches its cap.** A `review_cap` gate opens. The user answers `another-pass` or `stop`.
- **The fact-check keeps failing.** A `fact_check_recurring` gate opens. The user answers `another-round` or `stop`.
- **The session reaches its budget.** No new execution starts, and running executions finish. A `budget_reached` gate opens. The user answers `raise` with the extra dollars, or `stop`.
- **The user pauses the session.** The planner returns no step, not even a YOLO answer. Executions that the pause interrupted run again under their own IDs when the user continues.
- **The server restarts.** The engine replays the event log. An execution that was running starts again with `WorkKind::Rerun`.
- **Every research task fails or is abandoned.** The session fails, because no research document exists to write a spec from.

## Identifiers

Each ID is a prefix and a time-ordered UUID version 7, so the lexical order of IDs is the creation order. The types are in `crates/ostra-core/src/ids.rs`.

| Type | Prefix | Names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WorkspaceId` | `ws_` | A workspace |
| `SessionId` | `s_` | A session |
| `ExecutionId` | `x_` | An execution |
| `GateId` | `g_` | A gate |
| `DecisionId` | `d_` | A decision |
| `MessageId` | `m_` | A message between agents |

## Layout of the repository

The Cargo workspace (`Cargo.toml`) has the members `crates/*`. It uses edition `2024`, `rust-version` `1.98`, and the license MIT. The folder `tests/windows-probes` is outside the workspace on purpose. The server binary is `ostra`. It listens on `127.0.0.1` at port `7878` by default.

| Crate | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Shared types: IDs, agents, settings, pipeline enums, events, and contracts |
| `ostra-engine` | The event-sourced session, the planner, the judges, and the runner |
| `ostra-agents` | Agent definitions, prompts, and the spawn contract |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The native agent loop |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | The harness executors |
| `ostra-providers` | The model providers |
| `ostra-tools` | The native tools |
| `ostra-policy` | Guards and permissions |
| `ostra-sandbox` | Kernel enforcement under agent commands |
| `ostra-store` | The SQLite stores and the lesson memory |
| `ostra-workspace` | Workspaces, projects, and settings |
| `ostra-code` | The code index, the graph, and LSP |
| `ostra-mcp` | The MCP client |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push |
| `ostra-server` | The HTTP and WebSocket server and the `ostra` binary |

Other folders: `web/` holds the React console, `design/` holds the design system, `assets/` holds the agent prompts, the judge prompts, the skills, and `tool-mapping.toml`, and `tests/` holds the browser, conformance, eval, and Windows probe tests. The commands are `cargo build --workspace`, `cargo test --workspace`, and `cargo fmt --all`. See [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) for the dependency direction.

sections.title: Install, run, and configure the server
sections.summary: How to build the `ostra` binary, start it, sign in, keep it running as a service or in Docker, set the machine config file, and finish first-run onboarding.
sections.body:
Ostra is one binary named `ostra`. It serves the web console, runs the engine for each workspace, and bridges harness CLIs. Without a fixed start procedure, a new user cannot build the binary, choose a port, sign in, or keep the server alive after a restart of the machine. This page explains each step and the reason for each rule.

The page covers:

- the toolchain and the build commands
- the scripts `build.sh`, `run.sh`, `install.sh`, and `install.ps1`
- the Docker files
- the `ostra` subcommands and the serve flags
- the machine config file and the data folder
- the start sequence of the server
- first-run onboarding and the harness setup terminals

The page stops before workspace settings. For those, read [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md). For the sign-in token, the cookie, and the host checks, read [Server security](server-security.md).

## Toolchain and build commands

The repository pins its tools, so every machine compiles the same code.

| Item | Value | Where it is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust toolchain | `1.98.1`, with the components `rustfmt` and `clippy` | `rust-toolchain.toml` |
| Rust edition | `2024` | `Cargo.toml`, `[workspace.package]` |
| Minimum Rust version | `1.98` | `Cargo.toml`, `rust-version` |
| Node.js | 24 | `Dockerfile` (NodeSource `setup_24.x`) and `install.ps1` |
| npm workspaces | `design`, `web`, `site` | root `package.json` |

The `.cargo/config.toml` file sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen` and `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` to `number`. The Rust types that carry `#[ts(export)]` write their TypeScript types to that folder.

Use these commands:

- Compile every crate: `cargo build --workspace`
- Run every Rust test: `cargo test --workspace`
- Format every crate: `cargo fmt --all`
- Compile the release binary only: `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`

The `ostra-server` crate defines the binary `ostra` (`[[bin]]` in `crates/ostra-server/Cargo.toml`). The release binary is `target/release/ostra`. On Windows it is `target\release\ostra.exe`.

The binary embeds the folder `web/dist` at compile time (`#[derive(RustEmbed)]` in `crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs`). Build the web UI before you compile the binary. The script `build.sh` does both steps. For the test layout, read [Testing and verification](testing.md).

## Build with build.sh

The script `build.sh` builds the web UI only when it changed, then compiles the release binary. It runs these steps from the repository root:

1. If the folder `node_modules` is missing, run `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`.
2. If `web/dist/index.html` is missing, or a file in `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, or `design/package.json` is newer than it, run `npm run -s build` in `web`.
3. Run `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`.

The script skips the web build when no input file is newer than `web/dist/index.html`. This check saves the time of a full web build on each start.

The Dockerfile and `install.ps1` copy this logic. `install.ps1` compares file times with `LastWriteTimeUtc`.

## Start from source with run.sh

The script `run.sh` builds, loads credentials, and starts the server in the foreground. Pass any `ostra` flag after the script name, for example `./run.sh --bind 0.0.0.0`.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `SKIP_BUILD=1` | Starts the existing `target/release/ostra` and skips `build.sh`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | Names a credentials file. The script applies its `export NAME=value` lines before it starts the server. |

The script applies only lines that match `export NAME=value`, so other lines in the file do not run. It runs each matching line with `eval`.

Caution: Do not put shell commands on an `export` line of the credentials file. The script runs the whole matching line as shell code.

After these steps, the script replaces itself with `./target/release/ostra` and your flags (`exec`).

## The ostra commands

The command `ostra` with no subcommand starts the server. Each other subcommand does one task and exits.

| Command | What it does | Needs a running server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra` or `ostra serve` | Starts the server. Both accept the flags in the next part. | n/a |
| `ostra config` | Prints the path of the global config file. It writes the default file first if none exists. | No |
| `ostra url` | Prints a fresh sign-in URL. | Yes |
| `ostra sessions` | Lists the browsers that are signed in. | No |
| `ostra sessions revoke <id>` | Revokes one sign-in by the id that `ostra sessions` lists. | No |
| `ostra sessions revoke --all` | Revokes every sign-in. | No |
| `ostra signout` | Revokes every sign-in. It does the same as `ostra sessions revoke --all`. | No |
| `ostra stop <session>` | Stops a pipeline session when no server runs. | No, and it refuses if one runs |
| `ostra hook` | Hook bridge for harness executions. A harness calls it. | Yes, inside an execution |
| `ostra mcp-stdio` | MCP stdio shim for harness executions. A harness calls it. | Yes, inside an execution |

The word "sessions" has two meanings in these commands. The command `ostra sessions` lists browser sign-ins. The command `ostra stop` ends a pipeline session. A pipeline session is one request that runs through the pipeline. The page [Overview](overview.md) defines it.

The binary also has a hidden first argument, `sandbox-init`. The sandbox backends use it inside a sandbox. It runs before the runtime and the logger start, and it does not appear in `--help`. Do not call it yourself.

### The commands that users run

- `ostra url` reads `server.json` in the data folder, then creates a new sign-in token in the registry. It prints `http://<host>/#token=<token>`. If `server.json` is missing, it prints the error `No Ostra server is running. Start one with ` followed by `ostra`.
- `ostra sessions` prints one line for each sign-in: the id, the sign-in time, the last-seen time, the address, and the browser. If no browser is signed in, it prints `No browser is signed in.`
- `ostra sessions revoke <id>` prints `Revoked <id>. That browser is signed out within 5 seconds.` The running server checks sign-ins again every 5 seconds (`RECHECK` in `crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`). If the id does not exist, the command fails and tells you to run `ostra sessions`.
- `ostra signout` and `ostra sessions revoke --all` print the count of revoked browsers. After either command, run `ostra url` to sign in again.
- `ostra stop <session>` looks in every registered workspace for the session id. It cancels the running executions of the session, so the next start does not recover and run them again. If a server runs, the command fails. Then use the session board in the console, or send `POST /api/sessions/<session>/stop`.

The commands `sessions`, `signout`, and `stop` open the registry directly. They work when the server is off.

### The commands that harnesses run

A harness is an installed agent CLI that Ostra runs under a pseudo terminal. The harness calls `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio`, and Ostra gives each call the environment variables `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`.

- `ostra hook` takes `--execution <id> --harness <name> --event <event>`. It reads the hook payload on standard input, asks the server for a decision, and prints the answer. If `--execution` and `OSTRA_EXECUTION` are both empty, it does nothing and exits with 0. The reason: the Antigravity integration is installed globally, so the command also runs outside Ostra executions.
- If the server is not reachable inside an execution, a `PreToolUse` event gets a deny answer. This rule stops a harness from running a tool that Ostra cannot check.
- `ostra mcp-stdio` is the shim that gives harness tools to a harness over MCP.

For the full bridge, read [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

## Serve flags

The flags below belong to `ostra` and to `ostra serve`.

| Flag | Type | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--port <n>` | `u16` | Sets the port. It overrides `server.port` in the config. |
| `--no-open` | switch | Does not open a browser. |
| `--dev` | switch | Also accepts the Vite dev server hosts `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`. Use it for work on the web UI. |
| `--bind <address>` | text | Sets the listen address. It overrides `server.bind` in the config. |
| `--allow-host <name>` | text, repeatable | Adds a host name that the browser can use, for example the domain of a reverse proxy. |

The server adds each `--allow-host` value to the list `server.allowed_hosts` of the config. A name without a port is allowed with the server port and without a port, because a reverse proxy on its default port sends the bare name. A name with a port is allowed as written.

The server always allows `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, and `[::1]:<port>`. If the address is `0.0.0.0` or `::`, it also allows every interface address and the machine host name, with and without the suffix `.local`. The page [Server security](server-security.md) explains the host check.

For web work, run `npm run dev` in `web`, or `npm run dev:mock` for the mock API, and start the server with `--dev`.

## Choose the port and the address

The server resolves the port and the address before it builds any other state. It reads the config file first, and a broken config file gives the default values at this point. The later build step then fails with the parse error.

### Port choice

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Start"] --> B{"--port given?"}
  B -- yes --> E["Bind exactly that port"]
  B -- no --> C{"server.port set?"}
  C -- yes --> E
  C -- no --> D["Try ports 7878 to 7897 in order"]
  D --> F{"A port is free?"}
  F -- yes --> G["Use the first free port"]
  F -- no --> H["Bind port 0 and let the OS choose"]
  E --> I{"Bind works?"}
  I -- no --> J["Exit with the error"]
```

The rules:

- A port that you set (`--port` or `server.port`) is exact. If it is busy, the server exits with the bind error. It does not try another port, because a script that expects a fixed port must fail loudly.
- With no port set, the server starts at `DEFAULT_PORT` (`7878`) and tries 20 ports in a row (`7878` to `7897`).
- If all 20 ports are busy, the server binds port `0`, and the OS gives a free port.
- The server prints the real port after it binds, and writes it to `server.json`.

### Address choice

The server takes the first value that exists: the flag `--bind`, then `server.bind` in the config, then `127.0.0.1`. The function `bind_addr` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` parses the value.

| Value | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `localhost` | `127.0.0.1` |
| `all` or `*` | `0.0.0.0` (every IPv4 interface) |
| An IP address, with or without `[` `]` | That address. Use `::` for every interface in IPv6. |
| Anything else | The server exits with an error that asks for an IP address. |

The default `127.0.0.1` keeps the server on the local machine. A non-loopback address serves plain HTTP to the network. The server then prints this warning: anyone who reaches the port with a sign-in link can run commands as you, and the traffic is not encrypted. Use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy, and add its host name with `--allow-host`. Push notifications need HTTPS or `localhost`.

## Machine config file and data folder

Ostra keeps machine-wide settings in the global config file, and its state in the data folder. Workspace settings live in the workspace and are a different topic.

| Item | Default path | Override |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global config file | `<config dir>/ostra/config.toml` | environment variable `OSTRA_CONFIG` (the full file path) |
| Data folder | `<local data dir>/ostra` | environment variable `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` |

The `<config dir>` and `<local data dir>` values come from the `dirs` crate. On Linux they are `~/.config` and `~/.local/share`. On macOS the data folder is `~/Library/Application Support/ostra`. On Windows the data folder is under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ostra`.

Run `ostra config` to print the path. If the file does not exist, the command writes `GlobalConfig::default()` as TOML first. The server does the same at start.

### The data folder

The server creates the data folder with owner-only mode `0700` on Unix. The folder holds:

- `registry.db` and its side files `registry.db-wal` and `registry.db-shm`. The server sets them to mode `0600` on Unix, because the registry holds provider keys, git credentials, and the push signing key. The page [Storage](storage.md) describes the tables.
- `server.json`, with the keys `port`, `url_host`, and `pid`. The server writes it at start and deletes it at a clean stop.
- `server.log`, which the server appends to. The server writes each log line to standard output and to this file, so you can read problems back later.
- `assets/`, the agent assets that the binary embeds. The server writes them again at each start.

The service installers also write `service.err.log` in this folder on macOS.

### Keys of the server table

The `[server]` table of the global config has four keys.

| Key | Type and default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `port` | integer, none | Fixed port. If unset, the server tries `7878` to `7897`. |
| `bind` | text, `127.0.0.1` | Listen address, with the values in the table above. |
| `allowed_hosts` | list of text, empty | Extra host names that the browser can use. |
| `use_ip_host` | boolean, `false` | Applies only to a loopback bind. If `true`, the sign-in URL uses `127.0.0.1`. If `false`, it uses a private `ostra-<hex>.localhost` name. With a non-loopback bind, the sign-in URL uses the first LAN address, whatever `use_ip_host` says. |

The private name applies only when `access.private_host && !access.is_remote()`, that is, when the bind address is loopback (`Auth::new` in `crates/ostra-server/src/auth.rs`). The private name exists because a cookie is not scoped to a port. A cookie on `127.0.0.1` reaches every other port on the machine. A cookie on the private name does not. Set `use_ip_host` to `true` only for a browser that cannot resolve `*.localhost`.

The global config also holds `tool_enforcement`, `providers`, `tiers`, `harness`, `permissions`, and `sandbox`. The page [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md) lists them.

### When a change takes effect

The server reads the global config again each time code calls `Shared::global()`. An edit applies without a restart. These rules protect a running server from a bad edit:

- If the file does not parse, the server logs a warning and keeps the last good copy.
- If the `[sandbox]` table is invalid, the server also keeps the last good copy. A `[sandbox]` path must be absolute or start with `~/`.

The server reads `server.port`, `server.bind`, `server.allowed_hosts`, and `server.use_ip_host` only at start. Restart the server after you change them.

At start, an invalid `[sandbox]` table stops the server. The error names the key, the problem, and the config path.

### Other environment variables

| Variable | Used by | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_LOG` | `ostra serve` | A `tracing` filter. The default is `info`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | `run.sh`, `install.sh` | Credentials file with `export` lines. |
| `OSTRA_PREFIX` | `install.sh`, `install.ps1` | Install prefix. The default is `~/.local`. |
| `SKIP_BUILD=1` | `run.sh`, `install.sh`, `install.ps1` | Skips the build step. |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | the server | Path of a master key file. Read [Server security](server-security.md). |

## What the server does at start

The function `run` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` runs the start sequence. The function `main` in `main.rs` does three things before it: it scrubs the startup environment, records the path of the binary for the sandbox helper, and appends the install folders of the harness CLIs to `PATH`.

### The start sequence

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Read config, resolve address and port"] --> B["Bind the listener"]
  B --> C{"Another server runs?"}
  C -- no --> D["Clean up leftovers of an earlier server"]
  C -- yes --> E
  D --> E["Validate the sandbox table, unlock the registry"]
  E --> F["Write the agent assets to the data folder"]
  F --> G["Build providers, executors, and the harness runtime"]
  G --> H["Detect installed harnesses"]
  H --> I["Attach each registered workspace and recover its sessions"]
  I --> J["Write server.json, print the sign-in URL"]
  J --> K["Open the browser unless --no-open"]
  K --> L["Serve until Ctrl+C"]
  L --> M["Remove the hook socket and server.json"]
```

The details of each step:

1. **Address and port.** The server reads the config, resolves the address (`bind_addr`), and binds the listener (`bind`).
2. **Leftover cleanup.** If `server.json` does not name a live process, the server stops processes that sandboxes of an earlier server left running. It removes stale egress sockets and stale decoy files. It does this before recovery, so recovery cannot start an execution next to an old process.
3. **Sandbox check.** The server validates `[sandbox]` and logs one of three results. If the sandbox is active, it logs the backend and any gaps. If the sandbox cannot start, it logs the reason and prints a warning to standard error, because with `mode = "auto"` the server still starts and the log is easy to miss. If `mode = "off"`, it logs that agent commands run with your full user rights. The page [Sandbox](sandbox.md) explains the modes.
4. **Registry and master key.** The server opens `registry.db` and unlocks it with the master key. It then encrypts any credential that an older version stored as plaintext.
5. **Assets.** The server writes the embedded agent assets to `<data folder>/assets`.
6. **Executors.** The server builds the providers from the config and the saved credentials. It builds the native executor, the MCP gateway, the code tools, and the harness runtime. It creates the push signing key (VAPID) if the registry has none.
7. **Harness detection.** The server checks each harness CLI. The part "Detect installed harnesses" explains how.
8. **Hook callback address.** Harness hooks call the server back. If the bind address is loopback or unspecified, the callback is `127.0.0.1:<port>`. Otherwise it is the bind address and the port. On Unix, the server also creates a bridge socket for sandboxed hooks. Windows has no sandbox backend, so hooks there use loopback HTTP on `/internal/*`.
9. **Workspaces.** For each registered workspace, the server opens it and calls `recover` on its engine. A workspace whose `workspace.toml` is missing is logged and skipped. A workspace that fails to open is logged as an error, and the other workspaces still open.
10. **Cache sweep.** The server removes the tool caches of completed and failed sessions that an earlier run left behind.
11. **Sign-in URL.** The server writes `server.json`, then prints `Ostra is running on <address>. Open this URL to sign in:` and the URL. It opens the browser unless you pass `--no-open`. If it cannot open a browser, it prints `Could not open a browser; copy the URL above.`
12. **Stop.** The server stops its listener on Ctrl+C (SIGINT) and finishes open requests. It then removes the bridge socket and `server.json`.

The server forwards the notices of each workspace engine to the browser sockets through the broadcast channels `hub` and `push`. The page [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md) owns the channel capacities and the lag behavior.

## Sign in and manage sign-ins

The server prints a sign-in URL at start. Open it in a browser. The URL carries a one-time token in the fragment (`#token=`). The browser exchanges the token for a session cookie.

- If you lose the URL, run `ostra url` on the same machine. Each call creates a new token.
- If the address is not loopback, the server prints the other addresses of the machine. The link works once, from any of them.
- To list and remove sign-ins, use `ostra sessions`, `ostra sessions revoke`, and `ostra signout`.

The token lifetime, the cookie lifetime, the failure limit, and the cookie flags are in [Server security](server-security.md) and [Reference: server, code, store, and notify limits](reference-server-limits.md).

A crash can leave `server.json` behind. `ostra url` does not check that the process runs, so it then prints a URL for a server that is not there. The server checks the recorded pid with a signal-0 probe on Unix, and by opening the process on Windows. It uses that check before it cleans up leftovers.

## Install as a per-user service

The scripts `install.sh` and `install.ps1` build Ostra, copy the binary, and register a per-user service. The service starts at login. Neither script needs administrator rights.

Both scripts take the same subcommands:

| Subcommand | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `install` (default) | Builds, installs, and starts or restarts the service. |
| `restart` | Restarts the service with the installed binary. |
| `status` | Shows whether the service runs. |
| `url` | Prints a fresh sign-in URL (`ostra url`). |
| `uninstall` | Stops the service and removes it and the binary. |

If the first argument starts with `-`, the script runs `install` and passes all arguments to `ostra serve`. Example: `./install.sh --port 8080`.

The service listens on `127.0.0.1` unless you pass `--bind`. If the bind address is not loopback, the script prints the plain-HTTP warning. To go back, install again with `--bind 127.0.0.1`.

### install.sh on macOS and Linux

The script supports macOS (`Darwin`) and Linux. On another system it exits and tells you to use `./run.sh`.

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Install prefix | `$OSTRA_PREFIX`, default `~/.local` |
| Binary | `<prefix>/bin/ostra` |
| Launcher | `<prefix>/bin/ostra-service` |
| Service name | `dev.ostra.server` (macOS launchd agent in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`) or `ostra.service` (Linux systemd user unit in `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/systemd/user`) |
| Data folder | `$OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, else the default data folder of the system |

The install steps:

1. Run `build.sh`, unless `SKIP_BUILD=1`.
2. Copy `target/release/ostra` to a temporary file and rename it over `<prefix>/bin/ostra`. A running server keeps its old file, and macOS does not kill it for a changed image.
3. Write the launcher. It exports the `PATH` of the installing shell, because service managers start with a short `PATH` and the harness CLIs must resolve. It exports `OSTRA_CONFIG` and `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` if you set them. It applies the `export` lines of `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` at each start, so a changed key needs only a restart, and the secrets stay out of the plist and the unit file. It then runs `ostra serve --no-open --bind 127.0.0.1` and your flags.
4. Write the plist or the unit and start the service.
5. Wait up to 15 seconds for a `server.json` that is newer than a marker file, then print the sign-in URL. If none appears, the script prints where to look: `service.err.log` and `server.log` on macOS, or `journalctl --user -u ostra` and `server.log` on Linux.

The restart rules differ by system:

- **launchd:** `KeepAlive` restarts the server after a failed exit (`SuccessfulExit` is `false`), with a 10 second throttle.
- **systemd:** `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=5`. The unit sends `SIGINT` and waits up to 20 seconds (`TimeoutStopSec=20`), because the server shuts down cleanly on `SIGINT`. `SIGTERM` stops the server in the middle of a write.

On Linux, the service runs only when you are logged in. To keep it after logout, run `loginctl enable-linger <user>`. The script prints this hint if linger is off. If `<prefix>/bin` is not on `PATH`, it also tells you to add it, so that `ostra url` and `ostra stop` work.

`./install.sh uninstall` stops the service and removes the launcher and the binary. It keeps the config file and the data folder.

### install.ps1 on Windows

Run `.\install.ps1` in PowerShell. It registers a Task Scheduler task named `dev.ostra.server`. The task runs at logon with limited rights.

- The script needs `npm` (Node.js 24) and `cargo` (Rust with rustup) on `PATH`. It first adds the saved user and machine `PATH` entries, because an old terminal keeps its old `PATH`.
- The binary goes to `<prefix>\bin\ostra.exe`. The default prefix is `~\.local`. The data folder is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ostra` unless `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` says otherwise.
- The task runs `conhost.exe --headless ostra.exe serve --no-open --bind 127.0.0.1` and your flags. The `--headless` flag gives the server a console without a window.
- The task repeats every 5 minutes with the rule `IgnoreNew`. `conhost` exits with 0 in every case, so Task Scheduler never sees a failure. The repetition starts a server that stopped, and `IgnoreNew` skips the start when a server runs.
- A running `.exe` cannot be overwritten, but it can be renamed. The script renames the old file to `ostra.exe.old`, copies the new file, and deletes the old one.
- The script refuses to run if `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` is set, because the task runs `ostra.exe` directly and applies no credentials file. Save provider keys in the setup screen or as user environment variables.
- `OSTRA_CONFIG` and `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` must be saved as user environment variables (`setx`), because the task starts with the saved environment and not the environment of your shell. The script refuses if your shell value differs from the saved value.
- The script refuses to continue if the recorded server process is not the installed binary, because two servers must not share one data folder.

The script waits up to 15 seconds for the new `server.json`, then prints the sign-in URL. `status` prints the task state, the last run time, the last result, and the server pid.

## Run in Docker

The `Dockerfile` builds the web UI, compiles the binary, and makes a small runtime image. The file `docker-compose.yml` runs it.

| Stage | Base | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs Node.js 24 from NodeSource, runs `npm ci`, and builds `web/dist`. |
| `rust` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs rustup, installs the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`, and runs `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`. |
| `runtime` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs `ca-certificates`, `git`, `openssh-client`, `curl`, and `bubblewrap`, and copies the binary. |

BuildKit cache mounts keep the cargo registry, the target folder, and the npm cache between builds. The `target` folder is a cache mount and vanishes after the step, so the build copies the binary out of it.

The runtime image uses these settings:

- User `ostra` with UID and GID `1000`. A bind-mounted host folder that the first normal Linux user (UID 1000) owns is then writable without a `chown`.
- Folders `/data` and `/config`, with `OSTRA_DATA_DIR=/data` and `OSTRA_CONFIG=/config/config.toml`.
- `EXPOSE 7878` and `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT`. The server shuts down cleanly on `SIGINT`.
- `ENTRYPOINT ["ostra"]` and `CMD ["--bind", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "7878", "--no-open"]`. The container must listen on every interface, because the host reaches it through the Docker network.

The compose file publishes the port as `127.0.0.1:7878:7878`. It is loopback only because Ostra serves plain HTTP. Reach it from another machine through an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy. Do not publish the port on every interface.

The compose file mounts these volumes:

| Mount | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-data:/data` | The data folder. |
| `ostra-home:/home/ostra` | The home folder. Harness CLIs that the setup check installs go to `~/.local/bin` or `~/.grok/bin`, and their logins go to dot folders, so the home folder must outlive the container. |
| `./config:/config` | The global config file. |
| `/srv/ostra/projects:/srv/ostra/projects` | The projects and workspaces. |

Do these steps before the first `docker compose up -d`:

1. Create `./config` and give it to UID 1000 and GID 1000: `mkdir -p config` and `sudo chown 1000:1000 config`. A folder that the Docker daemon creates is owned by root, and Ostra then cannot write `/config/config.toml` and exits at start.
2. Replace `/srv/ostra/projects` on both sides of the projects mount with one absolute host folder. UID 1000 must be able to write to it. Both sides must be the same path, because Ostra stores workspace and project paths literally.
3. Run `docker compose up -d`, then read the sign-in URL from the log: `docker compose logs ostra`.

Because the bind address is `0.0.0.0`, the printed URL names the first non-loopback address of the container. The server also accepts the host names `127.0.0.1:7878` and `localhost:7878`.

The `Dockerfile` copies `site/package.json`. This checkout has no `site/` folder, so that copy step fails until the folder exists.

## First-run onboarding

Onboarding is the first-run setup in the console. The server only stores one flag and answers two checks. The setup wizard itself is part of the [Web console](web-console.md).

The registry stores the flag under the key `onboarded_at` in its `kv` table. The server treats the first run as `onboarded_at` empty and `workspaces` equal to 0.

| Route | Handler | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/onboarding` | `setup::onboarding` | `OnboardingState`: `onboarded_at` and the count of registered `workspaces`. |
| `POST /api/onboarding/complete` | `complete_onboarding` | Sets the flag, then returns `OnboardingState`. |
| `GET /api/environment` | `setup::environment` | `EnvironmentStatus`: `providers`, `harnesses`, `stacks`, `sandbox`, and `shell`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces` | `create_workspace` | Creates and registers the workspace, opens it, and sets the flag. |
| `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup` | `harness_setup` | Starts a setup terminal. |

The call `mark_onboarded` uses `INSERT OR IGNORE`. A second call keeps the first time. A user can leave the wizard with `POST /api/onboarding/complete`, or finish it when the first workspace is created.

`GET /api/environment` is the machine check. It refreshes the harness status first if the last check is older than 60 seconds. It returns:

- the status of each provider, including whether it has a key
- the status of each harness
- the names of the stacks that have a seed reference
- the sandbox status
- the status of the shell that the Bash tool uses

For the full route table, read [Server API](server-api.md).

## Detect installed harnesses

The server checks each harness CLI at start, and again when the last check is older than 60 seconds and a route needs it. The routes that refresh are `GET /api/environment`, `POST /api/workspaces`, and `POST /api/workspaces/validate`. The check keeps its result in `EnvStatus` with the time of the check (`stale` after 60 seconds).

For each harness (`claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`), the check does this:

1. Get the command name. It is `harness.<name>.command` from the global config, or else the harness name.
2. Look for the command on `PATH` (`which`). The field `installed` is the result.
3. If installed, run `<command> --version` with a time limit of 8 seconds. The field `version` is the first non-empty line of its output.
4. Set `logged_in`.

The rules for `logged_in`:

| Harness | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Not installed | `false` |
| `claude` | `true` if `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is set, or if `~/.claude/.credentials.json` exists, or if `~/.claude.json` contains `"oauthAccount"`. Otherwise unknown. |
| `codex` | `true` if `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set. Otherwise `true` if `auth.json` exists in `$CODEX_HOME` (default `~/.codex`), else `false`. |
| `grok`, `agy` | Unknown (`None`). |

Unknown is not the same as logged out. Claude Code can keep its credentials in the OS keychain, which Ostra does not read. For that reason, no marker means "unknown".

The server also appends the install folders of the official installers to its own `PATH` at start, when they are missing. On Unix these are `~/.local/bin` and `~/.grok/bin`. On Windows they are `~\.local\bin`, `~\AppData\Roaming\npm`, and `~\.grok\bin`. The reason: a harness that you install when the server runs then resolves by name without a restart, because a running server does not see the `PATH` change of a shell profile. The function `extend_path` writes the environment, so `main` calls it before the runtime starts any thread.

## Setup terminals for harness install and login

A setup terminal runs a harness installer or login in a pseudo terminal on the server machine. The browser streams its output and sends keystrokes, in the same way as for a harness execution. The route is `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup` with the body `{"action": "install"}` or `{"action": "login"}`.

The module `crates/ostra-server/src/harness_setup.rs` owns this flow:

1. The terminal id is `setup_<harness>_<action>`, for example `setup_agy_login`. The id is fixed for each harness and action. A second click attaches to the terminal that still runs, and does not start another.
2. For `login`, if the command is not on `PATH`, the route answers 409 with ``Install <name> first, because `<command>` is not on this machine's PATH.`` The `<name>` is the display name of the harness, and `<command>` is the configured command.
3. The server starts the command in a pseudo terminal of 100 columns and 30 rows. The working folder is your home folder.
4. When the process exits, the server runs the harness check again, stores the result, and sends a `HarnessStatus` message on the channel `home`. The console then shows the new state.

The route returns 404 for an unknown harness name. It returns 409 for any start failure.

### The install commands

On Linux and macOS the install command runs with `sh -c`. A prefix first checks that `curl` exists. If it does not, the terminal prints `Install curl on the machine that runs Ostra, then try again, because the installer downloads with it.` and exits with 127. The prefix stops the shell from showing a bare "not found" in the middle of a pipeline.

| Harness | Linux and macOS command | Windows command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude` | `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh \| bash` | `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 \| iex` |
| `codex` | `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh \| sh` | `npm install -g @openai/codex` |
| `grok` | `curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh \| bash` | none: the terminal prints a message and exits with 1 |
| `agy` | `curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh \| bash` | none: the terminal prints a message and exits with 1 |

On Windows the terminal runs the command in PowerShell with `-NoProfile`. For `codex`, a prefix checks that `npm` exists first.

### The login commands

| Harness | Login command |
| --- | --- |
| `claude` | `claude auth login` |
| `codex` | `codex login` |
| `grok` | `grok login` |
| `agy` | the command alone, with no arguments |

The program name is the configured harness command. The terminal shows the command line with shell quoting.

## What happens when

- **The port is busy and you set it.** The server exits with the bind error. Free the port or choose another one.
- **The port is busy and you did not set it.** The server tries the next port, up to `7897`, then lets the OS choose.
- **`--bind` is not an IP address.** The server exits with `` `<value>` is not an IP address to listen on ``.
- **The config file has a syntax error at start.** The port and address use their defaults for the bind step, then `build` fails with `reading <path>` and the parse error.
- **The config file breaks when the server runs.** The server logs a warning and keeps the last good copy.
- **The sandbox cannot start and `mode` is `auto`.** The server starts, logs the reason, and prints a warning to standard error. Agent commands then run with your full user rights.
- **A workspace folder is gone.** The server logs `workspace <name> is missing at <path>` and skips it.
- **A second server uses the same data folder.** Do not do this. `server.json` and the registry belong to one server.
- **You press Ctrl+C.** The server finishes open requests, removes the bridge socket and `server.json`, and exits.
- **The browser cannot be opened.** The server prints `Could not open a browser; copy the URL above.` and keeps running.
- **You run `ostra stop` and a server runs.** The command fails, because the running server owns the session.
- **You install a harness when the server runs.** The server finds it by name without a restart, and the next check updates the status.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_PORT` (`app.rs`) | `7878` | First port that the server tries when you set none. |
| Port scan range | 20 ports (`7878` to `7897`) | Ports tried before the server asks the OS for a port. |
| Default bind address | `127.0.0.1` | Listen address when neither the flag nor the config sets it. |
| `RECHECK` (`auth.rs`) | 5 seconds | How soon a running server refuses a revoked sign-in. |
| Harness `--version` limit | 8 seconds | Time that the server waits for the version of one harness. |
| `EnvStatus::stale` | 60 seconds | Age at which the harness status is checked again. |
| `hub` channel | 8192 slots | Capacity of the broadcast channel to the browser sockets. See [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md). |
| `push` channel | 1024 slots | Capacity of the channel for messages that the server starts. See [Architecture and crate map](architecture.md). |
| Setup terminal size | 100 columns, 30 rows | Size of the pseudo terminal of an install or login. |
| Service start wait | 15 seconds | Time that the install scripts wait for `server.json`. |
| Windows task repetition | 5 minutes | Interval at which Task Scheduler starts a stopped server. |
| Docker UID and GID | `1000` | Owner of `/data` and `/config` in the image. |

For the constants of the other server files, read [Reference: server, code, store, and notify limits](reference-server-limits.md).
