sections.title: Architecture and crate map
sections.summary: The 15 Rust crates and their dependency direction, the non-Rust folders, the layers a tool call passes, the data on disk, the three notice channels, and the flows that start a session, spawn an execution, and answer a gate.
sections.body:
Ostra splits one local server into 15 Rust crates so that each part has one job and one direction of dependency. Without a fixed direction, the engine depends on the executors, the executors depend on the server, and no part can run in a test without the whole system. This page shows which crate owns what, how the crates connect, where data lives, and how three main flows move through the code. Each crate has its own page, and this page links to it.

## Crate map and owning pages

The workspace in `Cargo.toml` has the member list `crates/*`. That glob matches 15 crates. The binary is named `ostra` and comes from `crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs`. The other 14 crates are libraries.

| Crate | Job | Page that owns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Shared types: ids, agents, settings, pipeline enums, events, API shapes, paths, and the traits `Executor` and `ExecutionHost`. | [Session pipeline](session-pipeline.md), [Artifacts and structured documents](artifacts-and-documents.md), [Reference: settings](reference-settings.md) |
| `ostra-engine` | Event-sourced session state, the pure planner `next_steps`, judge calls, and the `Engine` runner. | [Session pipeline](session-pipeline.md), [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md), [Judges and YOLO](judges-and-yolo.md) |
| `ostra-agents` | Agent assets, prompt rendering, the repo brief, and the typed spawn contract. | [Agents and prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The native agent loop on an API key. | [Native executor](native-executor.md) |
| `ostra-providers` | Anthropic and OpenAI chat clients behind one interface, plus a mock provider. | [Native executor](native-executor.md) |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | Runs an installed CLI under a PTY with a hook bridge and an MCP stdio shim. | [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) |
| `ostra-tools` | The native tool implementations. | [Tools](tools.md) |
| `ostra-policy` | The policy engine: guards, then permissions. | [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) |
| `ostra-sandbox` | Kernel enforcement under agent commands. | [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `ostra-store` | SQLite storage: the workspace database, the registry, and lesson memory. | [Storage](storage.md) |
| `ostra-code` | Code index, dependency graph, LSP clients, and editor hints. | [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) |
| `ostra-mcp` | The client for the MCP servers of a workspace. | [Integrations](integrations.md) |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push with RFC 8291 encryption and VAPID authentication. | [Integrations](integrations.md) |
| `ostra-workspace` | Workspace settings, projects, trust approvals, create and delete, and the runtime of an open workspace. | [Workspaces and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) |
| `ostra-server` | Start-up, sign-in, the REST and WebSocket API, the embedded web build, and the glue that gives each workspace its engine. | [Server API](server-api.md), [Server security](server-security.md), [Project files and git](project-files-and-git.md) |

The agent tools for coordination and the project management tools are not separate crates. Their definitions live in `ostra-core` and `ostra-tools`, and the server implements them. [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md) owns that topic.

## Dependency direction between crates

Each crate depends only on crates in a lower tier. A tier here is a group of crates that use no other crate of the same group. The direction is fixed by the `[dependencies]` tables of the crate manifests, and a Cargo cycle is not possible.

### Tiers

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T4["Tier 4: ostra-server"]
  T3["Tier 3: ostra-exec-native, ostra-workspace"]
  T2["Tier 2: ostra-engine, ostra-tools, ostra-code, ostra-exec-harness"]
  T1["Tier 1: ostra-agents, ostra-store, ostra-policy, ostra-providers, ostra-sandbox, ostra-mcp, ostra-notify"]
  T0["Tier 0: ostra-core"]
  T4 -->|depends on| T3
  T3 -->|depends on| T2
  T2 -->|depends on| T1
  T1 -->|depends on| T0
```

A crate can use any lower tier, not only the tier next to it. For example, `ostra-server` uses all 14 other crates, and `ostra-engine` uses `ostra-core`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, and `ostra-agents`.

### Direct dependencies and users

| Crate | Tier | Direct `ostra-*` dependencies | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | 0 | none | all 14 other crates |
| `ostra-sandbox` | 1 | core | code, engine, exec-harness, exec-native, tools, workspace, server |
| `ostra-store` | 1 | core | engine, exec-native, tools, workspace, server |
| `ostra-agents` | 1 | core | engine, workspace, server |
| `ostra-policy` | 1 | core | exec-native, workspace, server |
| `ostra-providers` | 1 | core | exec-native, server |
| `ostra-mcp` | 1 | core | server |
| `ostra-notify` | 1 | core | server |
| `ostra-tools` | 2 | core, sandbox, store | exec-native, server |
| `ostra-code` | 2 | core, sandbox | server |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | 2 | core, sandbox | server |
| `ostra-engine` | 2 | core, sandbox, store, agents | workspace, server |
| `ostra-exec-native` | 3 | core, sandbox, providers, tools, policy, store | server |
| `ostra-workspace` | 3 | core, sandbox, store, engine, agents, policy | server |
| `ostra-server` | 4 | all 14 other crates | none (the `ostra` binary) |

The dev-dependencies of `ostra-exec-harness` add `ostra-code` and `ostra-tools` for tests only. Tests of `ostra-core`, `ostra-exec-harness`, `ostra-exec-native`, and `ostra-providers` use the `test-prices` feature of `ostra-core`.

## Traits that connect crates without a dependency

The engine, the executors, and the workspace never name the server. Each crate states what it needs as a trait, and `ostra-server` implements the trait. This rule is the reason that the engine runs in tests with fakes, as the comment in `crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs` says.

| Trait | Defined in | Implemented by | What it carries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Executor` | `ostra-core` (`exec.rs`) | `NativeExecutor`, `HarnessExecutor` | `run(spec, host, cancel)` returns an `ExecutionResult`. |
| `ExecutionHost` | `ostra-core` (`exec.rs`) | `EngineHost` in `ostra-engine` | The executor calls `emit`, `ask_permission`, `record_message`, `transcript`, and `yolo`. |
| `Services` | `ostra-engine` (`services.rs`) | `ServerServices` in `ostra-server` | Settings, executors, the spawn factory, judge calls, push notices, protected paths, format-command approval, and allow rules. |
| `SpawnFactory` | `ostra-engine` (`services.rs`) | `AgentsFactory` in `ostra-engine` (`factory.rs`) | `agent_meta`, `build`, and `judge_prompt`. |
| `WorkspaceHost` | `ostra-workspace` (`host.rs`) | `Shared` in `ostra-server` | The registry, the global config, environment facts, and the `Services` of a workspace. |
| `CodeNav`, `McpConnector`, `ManageConnector`, `CoordConnector` | `ostra-tools` | `CodeTools`, `Connector`, `Management`, `Coordination` in `ostra-server` | Code navigation, MCP tool calls, project management, and subagent coordination for native tools. |
| `BridgeServices` | `ostra-exec-harness` | `ServerBridge` in `ostra-server` | Policy checks, permission asks, and MCP calls from a harness CLI. |

Two details follow from this design. First, `ServerServices` reads the global config and the workspace settings again on every call, so an edit applies to the next execution without a restart. A broken global file keeps the last good copy, and `Shared::global` logs a warning. Second, `ServerServices::judge` resolves the provider with `Providers::for_model` and calls `ostra_providers::structured`. The engine never sees a provider type.

## Folders outside the crates

Four folders hold the non-Rust parts. The root `package.json` lists the npm workspaces `design`, `web`, and `site`. This checkout has no `site/` folder, so only `design` and `web` exist.

- **`web/`** holds the React console. It imports the `@ostra/design` package. `build.sh` builds `web/dist` first, because `crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs` embeds `web/dist` into the binary with `rust-embed`. See [Web console](web-console.md).
- **`design/`** holds the component package: tokens, core, data, feedback, forms, navigation, and pipeline components, plus the brand mark and the gallery. See [Design system](design-system.md).
- **`assets/`** holds the agent folders (14 folders under `assets/agents`), the 10 judge prompts under `assets/judges`, the stack references under `assets/refs`, the skill `meta-author`, and the files `code-tools.md`, `coordination.md`, `output-rules.md`, and `tool-mapping.toml`. `ostra-agents` embeds the folder with `rust-embed`. At start-up the server writes a copy to `<data dir>/assets` and marks that path as protected. See [Agents and prompts](agents-and-prompts.md).
- **`tests/`** holds `browser` (the browser security suite), `conformance` (`main.rs`), `evals`, and `windows-probes`. The probe program is listed in `exclude` in `Cargo.toml`, so `cargo build --workspace` does not compile it. See [Testing](testing.md).

The root also holds `build.sh`, `run.sh`, `install.sh`, `install.ps1`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, and `biome.json`. [Running Ostra](running-ostra.md) owns them.

## Server start-up sequence

`ostra serve` (or `ostra` with no subcommand) runs `serve` in `main.rs`, which opens `server.log` in the data dir and then calls `app::run`. The steps run in this order:

1. `main` calls `ostra_sandbox::scrub_startup_env` before any thread starts, and it handles the hidden `sandbox-init` argument first.
2. `run` reads the global config and binds a port. If no port is set, it tries the 20 ports from `DEFAULT_PORT` (`7878`) upward, and then it asks the OS for a free port.
3. If no other server runs, `run` stops processes that earlier sandboxes left, and it removes stale egress sockets and decoys.
4. `build` validates the sandbox section of the global config. It stops with an error if the section is invalid.
5. `build` opens the registry with owner-only modes and unlocks it with the master key. See [Server security](server-security.md).
6. `build` writes the embedded assets to `<data dir>/assets` and creates `Providers`, `NativeExecutor`, `Notifier`, `HarnessRuntime`, and the `Shared` value.
7. `build` creates `App`, binds `CodeTools`, `Management`, and `Coordination` to it, and starts the hook bridge socket on Unix.
8. `build` calls `App::attach` for each registered workspace whose `workspace.toml` exists. `attach` opens a `WorkspaceRt`, runs `Engine::recover`, and forwards the engine notices to the hub.
9. `run` writes `server.json`, prints the sign-in URL, and serves `api::router` until `ctrl_c`.

### Notice channels and their capacities

Three `tokio` broadcast channels carry data from the engines to the browser. Each has its own capacity and its own lag rule. This page owns these capacities.

- **Engine channel, capacity `4096` notices.** `Engine::new` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` creates one for each workspace engine. The task in `App::attach` (`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`) receives from it with `rt.engine.subscribe()`. If that task falls behind, it gets a `Lagged` error, logs `hub lagged by N notices`, and calls `nav.lagged` for the workspace.
- **Hub, capacity `8192` notices.** `build` creates `hub`. The `attach` task sends each notice to it as a `HubMsg` that holds the workspace id and the notice. Each `/ws` socket subscribes to the hub. If a socket falls behind, it gets a `Lagged` error. The server does not log this error. `crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs` sends the browser the error `lagged`, and the page refetches its REST snapshot.
- **Push channel, capacity `1024` messages.** `build` creates `push`. It carries `Pushed` values: messages that the server itself starts, with the channels that receive them. Files, git, code, and navigation code send them. Each `/ws` socket subscribes to it. A socket that falls behind on this channel also gets the error `lagged`.

The log line `hub lagged by N notices` shows that the engine channel overflowed, not the hub. To debug that log line, check the engine channel capacity of `4096`. A slow browser socket shows only as the `lagged` error on the socket. See [Server API](server-api.md) for the socket behavior.

## Layers a tool call passes

Every tool call of every executor passes the policy engine before it runs, and the sandbox limits what a command can reach after it starts. The policy judges a call by the paths it names, and a shell can hide a path. The sandbox is what the kernel enforces below the policy. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) and [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

### Native executor path

The native loop in `Run::tool_end` (`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`) runs one call in these layers.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Model returns a tool call"] --> B["Run::tool_end: canonical_call"]
  B --> C{"ExecutionPolicy::check"}
  C -->|Deny| D["Error result to the model"]
  C -->|Ask| E["ExecutionHost::ask_permission: Permission gate"]
  E -->|Deny| D
  E -->|AllowOnce or AlwaysInWorkspace| F["ostra_tools::execute"]
  C -->|Allow| F
  F --> G["Bash runs under the sandbox Backend"]
  F --> H["policy.observe: notes and lessons"]
  G --> H
  H --> I["ToolResult to the model"]
```

- **Canonical call.** `env.canonical_call` resolves relative paths and the Bash working directory once. The policy check, the user approval, and the tool then name the same target.
- **Layer 1, guards.** `ExecutionPolicy::check` runs the guards first. Nothing overrides a guard denial, not even YOLO.
- **Layer 2, permissions.** If no guard denies the call, the permission mode and the allow, ask, and deny rules decide. Under YOLO every `Ask` becomes an `Allow`, and denials stand.
- **Ask.** The `EngineHost` opens a `Permission` gate and waits for the answer. A session under YOLO answers `AllowOnce` at once and records the answer with source `Yolo`.
- **Execute.** `ostra_tools::execute` runs the tool. The tools crate does not check permissions or guards, as its module comment says.
- **Sandbox.** Only Bash and the programs that Ostra starts for a project run under the kernel sandbox. After a Bash call, `repair_git_dirs` repairs git metadata that the command changed, and the repair counts as a containment signal.
- **Observe.** `policy.observe` can append a note to the result or recall lessons from the project memory when a build fails.

### Harness executor path

A harness CLI runs its own tools, so Ostra checks each call through a bridge instead of running it.

1. The CLI starts under a PTY and inside the sandbox profile of the execution. The CLI's own Bash tool and every child process inherit the sandbox.
2. A hook of the CLI runs `ostra hook`. The hook posts the call to the policy route under `/internal`, with a bearer token for the execution.
3. `ServerBridge::policy_check` finds the running execution and calls the same `ExecutionPolicy::check` as the native path. If the execution is unknown, it denies the call.
4. For an `Ask` decision, `ServerBridge::resolve_ask` calls `ExecutionHost::ask_permission`, so the user sees the same gate.
5. Ostra's own tools reach the CLI through the `ostra mcp-stdio` shim, which posts to the MCP route under `/internal`.

A workspace MCP tool and a project management tool skip `ServerBridge::policy_check` (`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`) only when the execution is not in inspect mode (`!r.inspect`). For a workspace MCP tool, the MCP handler checks and logs the call when it runs it, so the hook passes the call unchecked. A project management tool skips the check because its ask then reaches the user once and not twice. If the execution is in inspect mode, both kinds of tool go through the full policy check. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

## Data on disk

Ostra keeps state at four levels: the machine, the workspace, the session, and the project. The event log in the workspace database is the source of truth for sessions. See [Storage](storage.md) for the tables.

### Machine level

The data dir is the value of `OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, or the `ostra` folder under the local data folder of the user. On Unix, `ensure_data_dir` sets the folder to mode `0700`. The global config is the file in `OSTRA_CONFIG`, or `config.toml` in the `ostra` folder under the config folder of the user.

| Path in the data dir | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `registry.db` with `-wal` and `-shm` | The tables `workspaces`, `push_subscriptions`, and `kv`. Mode `0600` on Unix. The registry also holds trust approvals, the permission mode, the YOLO default, and sealed secrets. |
| `master.key` | The master key, only when the OS keychain is not used. |
| `server.json` | The port, the URL host, and the pid of the running server. `server_running` reads it. |
| `server.log` | The server log. |
| `assets/` | The copy of the repo `assets/` folder that agents read. |
| `decoys/`, `egress/`, `tmp/` | Sandbox decoys, egress proxy sockets, and temporary git files. |
| `models-dev.json` | The cached model price table. |

No agent can read the data dir, the master key file named by `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`, or the credential stores under the home folder. `paths::secret_paths` lists them, the policy refuses calls that name them, and the sandbox hides them.

### Workspace level

The folder `<workspace>/.ostra/` holds `workspace.toml` (the settings), `workspace.db` (the event log and the materialized tables), `sessions/`, `uploads/` (files that wait for a session to claim them), `artifacts/`, and `docs/<book id>/book.json` for the documentation books. `workspace.db` has the tables `meta`, `projects`, `sessions`, `events`, `executions`, `messages`, `activity`, `gates`, `decisions`, `tool_calls`, and `search_docs`. The engine adds the file `sessions/.gitignore` with the content `*`, so git ignores all session files.

### Session level

The folder `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>/` is the session root. It holds the cross-project artifacts (spec and plan), one folder per project key for the reports, `uploads/`, `ostra-session-context.md`, and `.state/`. The engine owns `.state/`, and no agent can write there. A harness execution keeps its hook config, its MCP registration, and its `terminal.log` transcript in `.state/harness/<execution id>/`.

### Project level

The folder `<project>/.ostra/` holds `INVENTORY.md`, `project.toml`, and `memory/knowledge.sqlite3` (the lesson memory). Project skills live in `<project>/.agents/skills`, and Ostra still reads the older `.ostra/skills` folder but never writes to it. Ostra also reads the instruction files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` at the project root.

## Flow: start a session

A session starts when the browser posts a request to `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions`. The handler `create_session` in `api.rs` takes the shared work lock of the workspace and calls `Engine::create_session`. [Session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) explains the stages that follow.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant API as api.rs handler
  participant Engine
  participant Store as WorkspaceDb
  participant Planner as next_steps
  participant Services as ServerServices
  Browser->>API: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions
  API->>Engine: create_session(CreateSession)
  Engine->>Store: create_session(NewSession)
  Engine->>Store: append_event(SessionCreated)
  Engine-->>API: SessionSummary
  API-->>Browser: 200 SessionSummary
  Engine->>Planner: next_steps(state, ctx)
  Planner-->>Engine: Step Judge Classify
  Engine->>Services: judge(route, system, user, schema, effort)
  Services-->>Engine: value and usage
  Engine->>Store: append_event(DecisionMade)
  Engine-->>Browser: EngineNotice, then ServerMsg over /ws
```

The steps in `start_session` run in this order:

1. `create_session` refuses an empty request with `Describe the task first.` It also refuses a documentation book id that is not lowercase letters, digits, dashes, and underscores.
2. `start_session` reads the workspace settings. If `yolo.default` is set, the session starts with YOLO on.
3. For a pipeline session, it keeps only the projects that have an `INVENTORY.md`. If none remain, it returns an error, because every agent routes its work by the inventory.
4. If the request pins project keys, the session keeps only those projects. An unknown or uninitialized key returns an error.
5. It validates the context files and the uploads, creates the session root and one folder for each project, and claims the uploads.
6. It inserts the session row, creates the in-memory `Live` state, and appends the `SessionCreated` event.
7. `ensure_driver` starts the driver task, and the call returns the stored `SessionSummary`.

The driver is one `tokio` task for each session. In each round it locks the folded `SessionState`, calls the pure planner `next_steps`, and starts each new step as its own task. A set of in-flight step keys stops the driver from starting the same step twice. The driver then waits for `live.wake`, and it stops when the session is terminal. A new session has no category, so the first step is the `Classify` judge.

`Inner::append` is the one write path for every event. It does these things in this order, under the state lock of the session, so that the order of `seq` equals the order of the fold:

1. Store the event with `append_event`.
2. Materialize gates and decisions into their tables.
3. Apply the event to the in-memory state.
4. Update the session row with category, status, lane, stage label, cost, and title.
5. Broadcast `SessionUpdated` and `Event` notices.
6. Send a push notice when the event needs the user.
7. Wake the driver.

## Flow: spawn an execution

An execution is one run of one agent. The planner returns a `Step::Spawn` value with a `SpawnRequest`, and `Inner::perform_spawn` runs it. [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) owns the retries, pause, and resume rules, and [Agents and prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) owns the prompt rendering.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Driver
  participant Spawn as perform_spawn
  participant Services as ServerServices
  participant Factory as AgentsFactory
  participant Store as WorkspaceDb
  participant Executor
  participant Host as EngineHost
  Driver->>Spawn: perform(Step Spawn)
  Spawn->>Spawn: acquire_slot
  Spawn->>Services: global, workspace, executor(kind)
  Spawn->>Factory: agent_meta, build(SpawnRequest, SpawnEnv)
  Factory-->>Spawn: BuiltSpawn
  Spawn->>Store: append_event(ExecutionStarted), insert_execution
  Spawn->>Executor: run(ExecutionSpec, host, token)
  Executor->>Host: emit(ExecutionDelta)
  Host->>Store: append_activity
  Executor->>Host: ask_permission(call, reason, rule)
  Executor-->>Spawn: ExecutionResult
  Spawn->>Store: finish_execution
  Spawn->>Store: append_event(ExecutionFinished)
```

The steps run in this order:

1. `acquire_slot` waits for a free slot. The limit is `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default `3`, minimum `1`), and the code reads it again on each check. A waiting spawn checks at least every 2 seconds.
2. The spawn reads a snapshot of the state. If the session is terminal or paused, it returns without an event.
3. `resolve_route` picks the executor, model, and effort from the global config, the workspace settings, the agent default tier, and the complexity of the phase. If the route fails, `record_denied` records the failure and the spawn ends.
4. If the run continues an earlier run, the new run keeps the executor and the model of the earlier run. This also keeps the prompt cache.
5. `Services::executor` returns the executor. If it is not available, `record_denied` records `The <executor> executor is not available.`
6. `SpawnFactory::build` renders the system prompt, the first message, the spawn block, and the parameters for the chosen executor.
7. The engine appends `ExecutionStarted` and inserts the execution row. A resumed run appends `ExecutionResumed` instead, and it keeps its id.
8. The engine builds an `ExecContext` with the repo root, the permission mode, the merged permission rules, the protected paths, and the sandbox settings. It builds an `ExecutionSpec` and calls `Executor::run` with an `EngineHost` and a cancellation token.
9. During the run, `EngineHost::emit` stores each `ExecutionDelta` in the `activity` table and broadcasts it. It also updates the usage and cost of the execution and classifies containment signals.
10. When the executor returns, the engine adds the earlier usage, finishes the execution row, and appends `ExecutionFinished`. A run that the user cancelled for a pause becomes `Interrupted`.
11. The `Slot` value drops, which frees the slot and wakes the waiting spawns.

### What happens when

- **The server restarts during a run.** `Engine::recover` marks each running execution `Interrupted` with the error `The server restarted while this execution ran.` The driver then spawns it again. A harness run that waited for a message keeps the status `Waiting`.
- **A permission gate is open at restart.** `recover` answers it with `Deny` and source `Engine`, because the execution that asked is gone.
- **A stop arrives while a spawn is set up.** `append` returns `EngineError::Ended` for `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, and `CommandStarted` on a terminal session. The driver ignores that error.
- **A step fails.** The driver logs the error and appends a `Note` event with the text `A step failed:` and the error. Then it removes the step key, so the planner can return the step again.
- **A judge call fails.** `call_judge` tries 3 times and waits `500 ms` times the attempt number between tries. If all tries fail, it returns an error. The `Completion` judge is the exception: the engine writes a state-only report instead.
- **The limit of parallel executions changes.** The next check reads the new value. Ostra cancels no running execution.

## Flow: answer a gate

A gate is a point where the pipeline waits for a decision. A `Permission` gate waits inside a running tool call, and the other gates wait in the planner. The browser answers both kinds with `POST /api/gates/{id}/answer`. [Session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) lists the gates, and [Judges and YOLO](judges-and-yolo.md) owns the YOLO answers.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant API as api.rs handler
  participant Engine
  participant Store as WorkspaceDb
  participant Waiter as permission waiter
  participant Planner as next_steps
  Browser->>API: POST /api/gates/{id}/answer
  API->>Engine: answer_gate(gate, answer)
  Engine->>Store: get_gate(gate)
  Engine->>Engine: validate_answer
  Engine->>Store: append_event(GateAnswered, source User)
  Engine-->>Waiter: send(PermissionAnswer)
  Engine->>Planner: wake driver, next_steps
  Engine-->>API: GateView
  API-->>Browser: 200 GateView
```

`Engine::answer_gate` does these things in this order:

1. It loads the gate. It returns `NotFound` for an unknown gate, and it returns `This gate was already answered.` for a gate that has an answer.
2. `validate_answer` checks that the answer fits the gate payload.
3. For a `SpecApproval` or `PlanApproval` gate, it refuses an approval unless the current version has a fact-check pass. The error text is `Approval requires a fact-check PASS on this version.`
4. For a `Permission` gate with the answer `AlwaysInWorkspace`, it calls `suggest_rule` and `Services::add_allow_rule`. `ServerServices` saves the rule in the workspace allow list.
5. It appends `GateAnswered` with source `User`. The `routed` field is true when the answer carries free text or content that a judge must route before the engine applies it. A bare choice such as approve, stop, retry, or a budget raise is applied as it is.
6. For a `Permission` gate, it removes the waiter from `permission_waiters` and sends the answer. The tool call that waited then runs, or returns an error to the model.
7. For all gates, the append wakes the driver. The next `next_steps` call reads the folded state, which no longer holds the open gate, and returns the next steps.

Under YOLO, the engine answers for the user. An `Ask` from the policy becomes an `Allow` in `ExecutionPolicy::check`. For a permission gate that still opens, `ask_permission` appends `GateOpened` and `GateAnswered` with source `Yolo` and answers `AllowOnce`. For other gates, the planner returns `Step::YoloAnswer`, which uses a fixed answer or a `YoloAnswer` judge call. If the judge fails or its answer is refused, the engine appends a `Note` event and the gate waits for the user.

A gate that needs the user also sends a push notice, unless the session is under YOLO. A `HarnessFailure` gate always sends one, because the harness needs a login. The server sends the notice only when `notifications.push` is on. See [Integrations](integrations.md).

## How notices reach the browser

The engine does not know about sockets. It sends `EngineNotice` values on its own broadcast channel, and `App::attach` forwards each notice to the hub with the workspace id. The socket handler in `ws.rs` maps each notice to a `ServerMsg` and sends it on the channels of the notice. The section on notice channels above gives the capacity and the lag rule of each channel.

| Notice | Channels |
| --- | --- |
| `Event` | `session:<id>` |
| `Delta`, `ExecutionStatus` | `execution:<id>` |
| `SessionUpdated` | `session:<id>`, `workspace:<id>`, `home` |
| `ProjectsChanged` | `workspace:<id>` |

The `attach` task also gives each notice to `Files::observe` and `Nav::observe`, so the Files view and the Sessions tree stay current. [Server API](server-api.md) owns the socket protocol.

## Limits named on this page

| Name | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_PORT` | `7878` | The first port that `ostra serve` tries. |
| Port search range | 20 ports | The number of ports from `DEFAULT_PORT` that `bind` tries before it asks the OS. |
| Engine channel | `4096` notices | The capacity of the broadcast channel that `Engine::new` creates for each workspace engine. The `attach` task reads it. Overflow logs `hub lagged by N notices`. |
| Hub channel | `8192` notices | The capacity of the `hub` broadcast channel from the `attach` tasks to the `/ws` sockets. Overflow sends the browser the error `lagged`. |
| Push channel | `1024` messages | The capacity of the `push` broadcast channel for messages that the server starts. Overflow sends the browser the error `lagged`. |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | `3` | The workspace limit of running executions. The minimum used is `1`. |
| Slot wait | 2 seconds | The longest time a waiting spawn sleeps before it checks the limit again. |
| Judge tries | 3 | The tries of one judge call, with `500 ms` times the attempt number between them. |
| `MAX_MESSAGE` in `ws.rs` | `1048576` bytes | The largest client message on `/ws`. |
| `MAX_TERM_INPUT` in `ws.rs` | `65536` bytes | The largest `term_input` message. |
| `MAX_CHANNELS` in `ws.rs` | `256` | The channels of one socket. |
| `TERM_QUEUE` in `ws.rs` | `64` frames | The binary frames queued for one socket. |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | `25.0` | The dollars one session can spend before it pauses. `0` means no limit. |

The other pages own the full catalogs. See [Reference: server limits](reference-server-limits.md), [Reference: engine limits](reference-engine-limits.md), and [Reference: settings](reference-settings.md).

## What this architecture does not guarantee

- The tiers stop Cargo cycles between crates. They do not stop a cycle between modules inside one crate. `CodeMap` reports such cycles, for example between `runner.rs`, `uploads.rs`, and `view.rs` in `ostra-engine`, and between `app.rs` and `services.rs` in `ostra-server`.
- The policy and the sandbox are two separate layers. The policy does not prove that a shell command is safe, and the sandbox does not cover a platform where no backend works. In that case the server prints a warning and agent commands run with the full rights of the user. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).
- The event log is the source of truth for a session. The materialized tables can be rebuilt from it, but a file that an agent wrote in a project is not part of the log.
- The notice channels drop notices when a receiver falls behind. The browser recovers because it refetches its REST snapshot after the `lagged` error.

code_refs.note: Workspace members (`crates/*`), the excluded `tests/windows-probes`, package metadata, the `ostra-*` path dependencies, the third-party versions, and the dev and release profiles.
The trait that lists everything the engine needs from the server, with `SpawnFactory`, `BuiltSpawn`, and `Notice`.
The server implementation of `Services`: settings, executors, judge calls, push, protected paths, allow rules.

Opens a workspace, recovers sessions, and forwards engine notices to the hub. Logs `hub lagged by N notices`.
`Engine::new` creates the engine broadcast channel with capacity 4096.
The socket loop. It subscribes to `hub` and `push` and sends the error `lagged` when a receiver falls behind.
The spawn flow from slot to `ExecutionFinished`.
The gate answer flow and its validation.
The single write path for events: store, materialize, fold, broadcast, wake.

The module list of the shared types crate.

sections.title: The session pipeline: lanes, stages, tracks, and gates
sections.summary: Explains the categories, lanes, stage kinds, light and full tracks, stakes, test policy, gates, review loops, phases, and the completion report. Also explains the pure planner `next_steps` and its `Step` values.
sections.body:
## Why the session pipeline exists

An agent that gets a free-form request can skip the research, build on a false claim, or stop without a report. Ostra prevents this with a fixed pipeline. The pipeline splits one request into stages. Each stage has one owner: an agent, a judge, a shell command, a gate that waits for the user, or the engine itself.

The engine keeps no pointer to the current stage. The planner function `next_steps` reads the session state and returns the steps that are ready now. The session state is a fold of the event log, so a restart or a replay gives the same steps.

This page covers:

- the 10 categories, the 9 lanes, and the 38 stage kinds,
- the light track, the full track, stakes, and the test policy,
- the explore, spec, plan, phase, review, closing, and completion stages,
- the 14 gate kinds,
- the planner and its 13 `Step` values.

The page stops before the runner, which performs the steps ([Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md)). It also stops before the judge prompts ([Judges and YOLO](judges-and-yolo.md)).

## The planner: next_steps and Step

`next_steps(state, ctx)` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs) is a pure function. It takes a `SessionState` and a `PlanCtx`, and it returns a `Vec<Step>`. It does no I/O and writes no event. The runner performs each step and appends the resulting events. Then the planner runs again. Conformance fixtures call the function directly: an event history goes in, and the expected step summaries come out.

`PlanCtx` holds two facts that are not in the event log:

- `format_commands`: the format command of each project, or `None`.
- `budget_usd`: the session budget from workspace settings. `None` means no limit.

### The planner and runner loop

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Runner
    participant P as Planner
    participant W as Worker
    participant L as Event log
    R->>P: next_steps(state, ctx)
    P-->>R: Vec of Step
    R->>R: skip each step whose key is in flight
    R->>W: run judge, agent, command, or gate
    W-->>R: result
    R->>L: append SessionEvent
    L-->>R: fold into SessionState
    R->>P: next_steps(state, ctx)
```

### The 13 step values

`Step` is serialized with the tag `step` in snake case. Each step has a `key()`. The runner uses the key to avoid starting a step that is already in flight. The key of a gate step is `gate:<kind>:<owner>`, so the planner can return the same gate on every pass without opening it twice.

| Step | Fields | What the runner does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Judge` | `judge`, `subject` | Calls one judge. The key is `judge:<kind>:<subject>`. |
| `Spawn` | `SpawnRequest` | Starts an agent execution. The key comes from the execution purpose. |
| `OpenGate` | `title`, `explanation`, `payload` | Opens a gate and waits for an answer. |
| `YoloAnswer` | `gate` | Answers an open gate in YOLO mode. |
| `Command` | `purpose`, `project`, `command`, `files` | Runs the `Format` or `Stage` command in one project. |
| `Autofix` | `project`, `phase`, `tests`, `findings` | Applies the replacement text of auto-fixable findings. |
| `AnnounceBlocked` | `project`, `phase`, `tests`, `reason` | Records a `PhaseBlocked` event. |
| `FinishInit` | `project` | Ends the init of a created project (Rule O4). |
| `RecordInitProblem` | `project`, `execution`, `error` | Records an init step that left nothing usable (Rule O5). |
| `Deliver` | `execution`, `ask`, `kind` | Hands a message to a harness run that waits with its process alive (Rule H2). |
| `WriteBook` | `book` | Writes the session documentation into the workspace book (Rule B5). |
| `Complete` | `report_markdown` | Ends the session with the completion report. |
| `Fail` | `error` | Ends the session with an error. |

`Step::summary()` gives the compact text that fixtures compare, for example `spawn implementer phase 1 initial`, `gate closing_gate`, `command format p`, `judge track`, `write-book p`, `autofix phase 1`, and `blocked phase 1`.

### What a spawn carries

`SpawnRequest` has the fields `agent`, `purpose` (an `ExecPurpose`), `stage` (from `stage_of(purpose)`), `project`, `session_dir`, `inputs`, `resumes`, and `continues`. `SpawnInputs` holds everything that a spawn needs besides its agent and purpose, such as the task, research documents, answers, findings, the phase, and the report paths. The spawn factory turns it into the agent parameters (see [Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md)). `SpawnRequest::complexity()` returns the phase complexity that routes use. A phase without a plan file counts as `Low`.

### The order of the planner checks

The planner runs `flows` and then `coordination`. `flows` does these checks in order:

1. If the session is not created, is finished, or is paused, it returns no step (Rule P1). A paused session starts nothing, not even a YOLO answer.
2. In YOLO mode, it returns one `YoloAnswer` for each open gate. It skips `Permission` gates, because the live execution answers them. It also skips gates that `yolo_leaves_open` names: the budget gate, and a failed execution that the user stopped.
3. For an init session, it runs the init flow and stops.
4. If the session has no category, it returns a `Classify` judge one time and stops.
5. For each held spec or plan answer, it returns a `RouteAnswer` judge (Rule J1). For each pending context amendment, it returns a `RouteAnswer` judge and stops, because nothing starts before the judge decides (Rule C2).
6. It spawns each research task that is ready. Rescue research can arrive in the middle of a build, so this check does not depend on the category.
7. It runs the flow of the category.

`coordination` then adds two kinds of step: `Consult` spawns for questions to a subagent that ended its run, and `Deliver` steps for harness runs that wait. See [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md).

### What push does before it keeps a step

Every step passes through `Planner::push`. These filters can drop or change a step:

- **Init hold (Rule O4).** A created project that has not finished its init accepts only spawns of the `Initializer` and `Advisor` agents. The planner drops every other spawn, `Command`, and `Autofix` in that project, because each other agent routes its work by the project inventory and profile.
- **Waiting run (Rule H2).** If a native run waits for a message under the same purpose key, the planner drops the spawn when no message is ready. When a message is ready, it sets `resumes` to wake the run in place.
- **Paused run (Rule P2).** A spawn that replaces a paused run gets `resumes` from `resume_from`.
- **Pair loop (Rules H5 and H6).** A spawn in a pair loop gets `continues`, which names the earlier run whose conversation it continues.
- **Busy conversation (Rule H7).** The planner drops a spawn when the conversation to continue has a live run.
- **Budget guard.** See the next list.
- **Duplicate key.** The planner keeps the first step of each key in one pass.

### What happens when

- **The session budget is spent.** The limit is `budget_usd` plus the dollars the user added. The spent amount is the sum of the cost of finished executions. When spent is equal to or more than the limit, the planner drops every `Spawn` and returns one `budget_reached` gate. Running executions finish. YOLO never answers this gate, because spending more is the user's decision.
- **The user answers `raise` on the budget gate.** The text is the extra dollars. Without a valid number, the raise is the budget again (at least 1 dollar). The session also adds any overspend, so it can spend the extra amount in full.
- **The user answers `stop` on the budget gate.** The session fails with the text `Stopped at the session budget after spending` and the amount.
- **The session is paused.** The planner returns nothing until the session resumes.
- **A step is already in flight.** The runner skips it, because its key matches a running step.

## Categories

The Classify judge puts each request in one `Category`. The category chooses the flow. In JSON the names are `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`. A log that has `UNIT_TEST` folds as `TEST`.

| Category | Research tasks | What the planner runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RESEARCH` | Yes | Research tasks and the Sufficiency judge. Then the completion report. No spec. |
| `SPEC` | Yes | Research, then the spec flow without an approval gate. Then the completion report. |
| `PLAN` | Yes | Research, the spec flow with approval, then the plan flow with approval. No build. |
| `IMPLEMENT` | Yes | Research, the Track judge, the light or full track, phases, implementation review, closing stages, completion. |
| `VERIFY` | No | One inline phase for each project. It runs the project test command with no review and no staging. |
| `TEST` | No | The test stage alone on existing code. No closing gate. No format command. |
| `DOCS` | No | The docs stage alone on existing code. No closing gate. No format command. |
| `PROMPT` | No | One inline phase in the first project, run by the `PromptGeneration` agent. |
| `QUICK_CHANGE` | No | One inline phase for each project on the native executor, with no review. |
| `QUICK_ANSWER` | No | One read-only `QuickAnswer` run on the native executor. Its answer is the report. |

The planner code that chooses a flow has this shape:

```rust
match category {
    Category::QuickAnswer => self.quick_answer(),
    Category::Research => { if self.explore_complete() { self.completion(); } }
    Category::Spec => { if self.explore_complete() && self.spec_flow(false) { self.completion(); } }
    Category::Plan => {
        if self.explore_complete() && self.spec_flow(true) && self.plan_flow() { self.completion(); }
    }
    Category::Implement => { /* track, spec, stakes, plan, phases, review, closing */ }
    Category::Verify | Category::Prompt | Category::QuickChange => { self.phases(); ... }
    Category::Test | Category::Docs => { self.closing_stages(); ... }
}
```

### How each category sets up its phases

The fold builds the phases when the Classify decision arrives (`apply_classify`).

- `VERIFY`: one inline phase titled `Verification` for each project. The review mode is `Never` and staging is off. The task text is `Verification request:` plus the request.
- `TEST`: one inline phase that is already `Done`. The project closing choice is set to tests only, and the format step counts as skipped.
- `DOCS`: the same set-up, with the closing choice set to docs only.
- `QUICK_CHANGE`: one inline phase titled `Quick change` for each project. The review mode is `Never`. After the pass, the engine stages the files if any changed.
- `PROMPT`: one inline phase for the first project only. The work agent is `PromptGeneration` and the fix agent is `Implementer`. The loop reviews only when a changed file is not an instruction file.

The engine forces the native executor for `QUICK_CHANGE`, for the `QuickAnswer` agent, and for an agent that fell back to native after a harness failure (`forced_executor`).

### What happens when

- **The Classify judge returns no research task** for a category that researches. The engine makes one task for each project in scope, with the full request, because the spec derives its criteria from research (Rule D1).
- **Every research task fails or is abandoned.** The planner returns `Fail` with the text `Every research task failed or was abandoned, so there is no research document to write a spec from.` This applies to `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, and `IMPLEMENT`.
- **The user pinned projects on the New task form.** The pinned projects are the whole scope, whatever the judge picked (Rule O6).
- **The user overrides the Classify decision.** The override takes effect only before any research task or phase work starts.

## Lanes

A lane is a column on the session board. `Lane` has 9 values in this order: `research`, `requirements`, `verification`, `design`, `build`, `review`, `test`, `docs`, `done`. `Lane::ALL` lists them. `StageKind::lane()` maps each stage kind to one lane.

| Lane | Stage kinds in the lane | Why the lane exists (from `web/src/content/stages.ts`) |
| --- | --- | --- |

## Light and full tracks

A `Track` decides how much of the pipeline an `IMPLEMENT` request runs. The light track goes from research straight to reviewed phases. The full track adds the spec, its fact-check, the stakes judge, the plan, and the approvals.

The pipeline is light by default. After the research, the Track judge returns `light` or `full`. The judge escalates to `full` on evidence, for example when a contract or a schema changes. The reason for two tracks: a contained change does not need three approval rounds, and a change to a contract or a schema must not skip them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Classify judge"] --> B["Research tasks and Sufficiency judge"]
    B --> C{"Track judge"}
    C -->|light| H["Phases: implement, review, stage"]
    C -->|full| D["Spec, fact-check, approval"]
    D --> E{"Stakes judge"}
    E -->|low| H
    E -->|"medium or high"| F["Plan, fact-check, approval"]
    F --> H
    H --> I["Implementation review gate"]
    I --> J["Format command"]
    J --> K["Closing gate"]
    K --> L["Tests: EPA, write-test, test review"]
    L --> M["Docs, architecture, book write"]
    M --> N["Completion judge and report"]
```

| Part | Light track | Full track |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who decides | The Track judge, or the user on the New task form | The Track judge, or the user on the New task form |
| Spec and spec approval | None | Yes |
| Stakes judge | None | Yes, after the spec approval |
| Plan and plan approval | None | When stakes are `medium` or `high` |
| Phases | One inline phase for each project, titled `Implementation` | The phases of the plan, or inline phases when stakes are `low` |
| Input of the implementer | The request and the research documents | The phase file of the plan |

### What happens when

- **The user sets a track on the New task form.** `SessionOptions.track` holds it. The planner then does not call the Track judge.
- **The user overrides the Track decision.** This works until the spec has run or a phase has started (`can_override`). The fold clears the phases, so the new track builds them again.
- **The track is `full` and the spec changes after approval.** The planner returns no phase until the revised spec and plan are ready (`plan.invalidated` or `spec.needs_run`).
- **Several projects are in scope.** Inline phases depend on the phase before them, so the projects build in order. There is no graph to read (Rule M5).

## Stakes

`Stakes` has the values `low`, `medium`, and `high`. The Stakes judge runs only in the full track of an `IMPLEMENT` request, after the spec approval. `Low` stakes skip the plan stage. The phases become inline phases with no plan file, one for each project, and the implementer works from the request (Hard rule 13). `Medium` and `high` stakes run the plan flow.

The reason for the judge: it stops a full plan for a one-line change, and it stops a skipped plan for a risky change. The `PLAN` category has no Stakes judge, because the user asked for a plan.

The user can override the Stakes decision while no plan has run and no phase has started. An override clears the phases.

## Spec and plan stages

The spec and plan stages share one pattern: generate, ask the open questions, fact-check, and approve. The state of each stage is one `ArtifactTrack`.

### The spec flow

`spec_flow(needs_approval)` returns true when the spec is done for the category. `SPEC` needs no approval. `PLAN` and the full track of `IMPLEMENT` need it.

1. If the user stopped the stage, the planner returns `Fail` with `The spec stage was stopped.`
2. If a run, a gate, or an answer routing is open, the planner waits.
3. If the last run failed, the planner opens an `execution_failed` gate.
4. If no spec exists or the spec needs a run, the planner spawns `GenerateSpec` with the next round number. A revision gets only the input that the spec does not reflect yet: new answers, new changes, and new research documents. The agent edits the spec in place, and the file name stays the same.
5. If the spec has open questions that the user has not seen for this version, the planner opens an `open_questions` gate. The questions come before any fact-check (Rule D3).
6. If no fact-check covers this version, the planner spawns `FactCheck` with the next pass number.
7. A FAIL sends the findings back to the spec agent. A PASS ends the stage, or opens a `spec_approval` gate when approval is required.

The fact-check source mode is `refetch` on the first pass of a spec that has External Evidence rows. In all other cases it is `citations` (Rule D3b). A plan fact-check always uses `citations` and gets the approved spec (Rules D3b and D5). A second pass gets `Prior findings:` from the earlier pass. The text is `no findings on the previous pass` (`NO_PRIOR_FINDINGS`) when the earlier pass found nothing, so the agent knows that this is a re-pass (Rule D3a).

### The plan flow

`plan_flow` follows the same steps with these differences:

- The plan agent reads the spec and its own earlier plan, and nothing else (Rule D4). The fact-check findings are the one addition, on a FAIL re-run (Rule D5).
- Clarifying questions open an `open_questions` gate with the artifact `plan`. The answers go into the spec first, and then the planner writes a new plan (Rule D10).
- The approval gate `plan_approval` lists the phases of the plan with the `PhaseInfo` fields.

### Why a change restarts at the spec

A requirement change after the spec exists restarts the work at the spec (Rule D10). The fold adds the text to `spec.changes`, sets `needs_run`, and revokes the spec approval. If a plan exists, it revokes the plan approval and sets `invalidated`. The planner then revises the earlier plan in place against the spec diff. This keeps one source of truth: the plan never holds a requirement that the spec lacks.

### What happens when

- **The fact-check fails in a row up to the limit.** `FACTCHECK_RECURRING_LIMIT` is 3. The first `fact_check_recurring` gate opens when the count of consecutive FAIL verdicts reaches 3. The planner opens the gate with the findings. The answer `another-round` sets `fail_limit_extra` to the count of consecutive FAIL verdicts at that time. A later gate then opens at `FACTCHECK_RECURRING_LIMIT + fail_limit_extra`, which is a higher count. The formula is in [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md). The answer `stop` stops the stage, and the planner then returns `Fail`. An answer with text becomes a change to the spec.
- **A fact-check run ends with an error or the verdict `Error`.** The fold does not count it as a FAIL. It retries one time (`ERROR_RETRIES`). Then it records a failure and the planner opens an `execution_failed` gate.
- **The user approves a version that a change replaced.** The fold ignores the approval, because a PASS covers only the version that it checked. A conformance test, `approval_without_pass_is_ignored_by_the_fold`, checks this.
- **The user answers with free text.** The answer waits for the Route answer judge before any agent sees it (Rule J1). See [Judges and YOLO](judges-and-yolo.md).

## Phases and the scheduler

A phase is one unit of build work. `PhaseInfo` has these fields: `id`, `deliverable`, `project`, `title`, `complexity` (`Low`, `Medium`, or `High`), `test_policy`, `depends_on`, `file`, and `test_rationale`. A phase from the plan has a `file`. An inline phase, made when the plan is skipped, has no `file`.

The scheduler in `Planner::phases` follows these rules:

- **One pipeline for each project (Rule M2).** A project has at most one phase in work at a time.
- **Dependencies (Rules D6 and M3).** A phase starts when each phase that it depends on is done and passed its review.
- **Unreadable dependencies (Rule M5).** If `depends_on` is `None`, the phase depends on every earlier phase.
- **Different projects run in parallel.** Ready phases in different projects start in the same planner pass.
- **A blocked phase (Rule D9).** The planner removes each phase that depends on it, directly or through other phases. Independent phases continue.

The complexity of a phase routes the executor, model, effort, and tier. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## The work loop and the review loop

Each phase has two loops: `impl_loop` for the build and `test_loop` for the tests. Each loop is a `WorkLoop`. Its `next` field is a `LoopNext` value. The planner reads `next` and returns the matching step.

| `LoopNext` | Step that the planner returns |
| --- | --- |
| `Idle` | None. The scheduler starts the loop when the phase is ready. |
| `Work` | A `Spawn` of the work agent. The kinds are `Initial`, `Fix`, `BlockerFix`, `Resume`, `Rescue`, and `Rerun`. |
| `Review` | A `Spawn` of `CodeReviewer`. |
| `Autofix` | An `Autofix` step. |
| `Rescue` | A `Rescue` judge for the stuck execution. |
| `RescueExplore`, `AnswerResearch` | None. The loop waits for research tasks. |
| `RescueGate` | A `stuck` gate. |
| `AwaitRoute` | A `RouteAnswer` judge for the free text of a gate answer. |
| `Handoff` | A `Spawn` of `PromptGeneration` with `handoff_for`. |
| `CapReached` | A `review_cap` gate, or a `ResolveReview` judge in YOLO mode. |
| `Resolve` | A `ResolveReview` judge. |
| `Stage` | A `Command` Stage with the changed files. |
| `Failed` | An `execution_failed` or `harness_failure` gate. |
| `Blocked` | An `AnnounceBlocked` step, then a `phase_blocked` gate. |
| `Done` | None. |

A work pass ends in one of three submit states. `ok` goes to review. `stuck` goes to the Rescue judge and never to a plain retry. `handoff` runs `PromptGeneration` and then resumes the work agent with the resume instructions.

### The review loop

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    W["Work pass"] --> R["Review pass"]
    R --> B{"Findings"}
    B -->|"BLOCKER or security block"| BF["BlockerFix pass, no cap"]
    BF --> R
    B -->|"auto-fixable rule"| AF["Autofix step"]
    AF --> C{"Passes at the cap"}
    B -->|"HIGH or MEDIUM"| C
    B -->|"none, or LOW only"| S["Stage step, then Done"]
    C -->|no| F["Fix pass"]
    F --> R
    C -->|"yes, not YOLO"| G["review_cap gate"]
    C -->|"yes, YOLO"| RJ["resolve-review judge"]
```

The fold sorts each review into groups (`loop_finished`):

- **BLOCKER, or `security_block` on the submit.** The loop sets `blocker_open` and starts a `BlockerFix` pass. The pass gets only the BLOCKER findings and an instruction to remove the dangerous code, not to rewrite it with the same effect. This path has no cap (Hard rule 21). An open BLOCKER also blocks the docs stage.
- **Auto-fixable.** A finding is auto-fixable when its severity is not BLOCKER, its rule ID does not start with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ`, and the rule ID is in the project list `auto_fixable_ids` (`AUTO_FIXABLE_PARAM`). The engine records that list in the review execution parameters at spawn, so the fold stays a pure function of the event log. The `Autofix` step applies the fixes. Each fix that fails and has severity HIGH or MEDIUM goes back to the remaining findings.
- **HIGH or MEDIUM.** These go to the fix agent, word for word, with the path of the review ledger. The agent records a `FIXED` or `WONTFIX` line with a reason for each finding, and the reviewer reads the ledger on the next pass.
- **LOW.** These stay in `leftover_low` and do not start another pass. A review with only LOW findings ends the loop.

After the findings are clear, the loop goes to `Stage`: the `Command` step runs `git add` for the changed files of the phase. Later reviews then look only at unstaged changes, so the reviewer does not read the same lines twice. A loop with staging off goes straight to `Done`.

### Review caps

```rust
pub fn effective_cap(&self, yolo: bool) -> u32 {
    (if yolo { YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET } else { REVIEW_CAP }) + self.extra_cap
}
```

- **Not YOLO.** After 3 review passes (`REVIEW_CAP`) with HIGH or MEDIUM findings open, the planner opens a `review_cap` gate. The answer `another-pass` adds 1 to `extra_cap` and starts a fix pass. The answer `stop` blocks the phase. Text in the answer goes through the Route answer judge.
- **YOLO.** The cap is 10 passes (`YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET`). At the cap, the planner calls the `ResolveReview` judge. If it returns `fix`, the loop adds 1 to `extra_cap` for one verification pass. The loop repeats the resolution while the count of open findings falls. If the count does not fall, or the judge returns `block`, the phase is blocked with no gate.

### What happens when

- **An execution ends with an error.** The loop retries it one time (`ERROR_RETRIES`). A harness error, with the prefix `harness-`, does not retry. It opens a `harness_failure` gate. The answer `retry` runs it again. The answer `native` moves that agent to the native executor for the rest of the session.
- **An execution ends in another way, or the submit is missing.** The loop moves to `Failed`, and the planner opens an `execution_failed` gate with the answers `retry` and `abandon`.
- **The user stopped the execution.** The error text is `You stopped this execution.` (`STOPPED_EXECUTION`). The planner opens the gate with the title `You stopped <agent>`. YOLO leaves this gate to the user.
- **The server restarts while an execution runs.** The execution ends as `Interrupted`. The loop re-runs the same step with the work kind `Rerun`.
- **The agent reports `stuck`.** The Rescue judge picks `Explore` (research first), `Rerun` (run again with a stated fact), or `Gate`. The `Gate` action opens a `stuck` gate. The answer `fact` with text sends the text through the Route answer judge and re-runs the work. The answer `block` blocks the phase.
- **A phase is blocked.** The planner returns `AnnounceBlocked` first. Then, if the session is not in YOLO mode, it opens a `phase_blocked` gate. The answer `retry` gives the loop a new full cap, with optional instructions. The answer `leave` keeps the phase blocked. The planner writes no completion report until each blocked phase is announced.

## Implementation review

After every phase is finished or removed, nothing runs, and the build is not yet accepted, the planner opens an `implementation_review` gate (Rule F1). This gate exists only in the `IMPLEMENT` category and only when phases exist. The gate says: try the change, then describe what to change, or accept it. Accepting moves on to the closing stages. The reason: tests and docs written for a result that you have not tried are wasted if you then ask for a change.

- **The answer `feedback` with text.** The Feedback judge routes the text to one or more projects. The fold adds one revision phase for each target. A revision phase has the title `Revision <round>`, complexity `Low`, test policy `Required`, and no plan file. It reads the session context file, not a conversation, and it gets the implementer reports of the other phases in its project (Rule F2).
- **A requirement change.** If a spec exists, the text goes into the spec first (Rule D10). The revision phases start after the new spec approval.
- **The answer `done`.** The fold marks the implementation accepted. In YOLO mode, the engine answers `done`, because only the user can say what they want changed.
- **A new round.** After the revision phases finish, the planner opens the gate again with the round number plus 1.

## Closing stages: format, closing gate, tests, and docs

The closing stages run for each project after its last phase passes. Each project has a `ProjectTrack` with the fields `format`, `closing_gate`, `closing`, and `docs`.

### Format

The planner returns one `Command` with the purpose `Format` for each project, one time, after its last phase. The step has no gate (Rule D8). The reason: formatting between phases adds noise to reviews, and a formatter fights with later phases.

The runner runs the format command only after the user approved it (Rule A1). If the format command in `project.toml` changed outside Ostra, the runner skips the command. In that case it records the constant `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED` ([`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs), line 128) as the output of the step, with exit code `None`. The text is: `The format command in project.toml changed outside Ostra, so format was skipped. Approve it in the project's settings to run it next time.` The planner does not ask again.

If the project has no format command, the runner records `No format command in project.toml, so format was skipped.` with exit code `None`.

### The closing gate

The tests and the docs are optional. The `closing_gate` gate asks for each project whether to run them.

- **An explicit request replaces the gate (Rule T3).** The user can turn on `tests` or `docs` on the New task form, or the Classify judge can set `opts_in`. If both are on, the project closing choice is set with no gate. If one is on, the gate asks only about the other (`ask_tests`, `ask_docs` in `ClosingItem`).
- **One gate for all projects (Rule T6).** Projects that reach the gate in the same planner pass share one gate.
- **Neither stage changes the requirements (Rule T5).** The gate text says so.
- **The answer.** `GateAnswer::Closing` holds one `ClosingChoice` with `tests` and `docs` for each project. An item that the gate did not ask uses the explicit request.
- **YOLO.** The engine answers with no tests and no docs, unless the request already asked for them (Rules T2 and T3).

The reason for the gate: it prevents token spend on stages that you did not ask for.

### The test stage and the test policy

`TestPolicy` has the values `Required` and `Skip`. The default is `Required`, so any doubt resolves to covering the phase (Rule T4). The plan sets the policy for each phase and gives a reason in `test_rationale` for each `Skip`. A phase without a plan file always counts as covered.

The test stage of a project (`test_stage`) works in this order:

1. The planner spawns one `ExecutionPathAnalyzer` (EPA) run for each covered phase. These runs go in parallel, because they only read.
2. A failed EPA run opens an `execution_failed` gate. An abandoned EPA run removes its phase from the stage.
3. When every EPA run is done, the planner starts the test loops one phase at a time, in phase order (Rule T4). The loop spawns `WriteTest` with the EPA report. Then it spawns `CodeReviewer` with `tests` true and the phase value `<phase>-tests`. The same review rules as the build loop apply. Then the test files are staged.
4. The stage is finished when each covered test loop is terminal.

Tests run only after the build is accepted. No EPA run starts between phases (Rule T1). The reason: no later phase changes the code under test.

### The docs stage and the book

The docs stage of a project starts after its tests are done, or immediately if the project has no tests.

- **Writers.** The planner spawns one `Documentation` run for each project. The input is the implementer reports of the passed phases and the notes of the user. At most 4 writers run in one session (`MAX_DOCS_WRITERS`, Rule B7). The planner counts both running writers and writers that it already queued in the same pass.
- **Open BLOCKER.** A project with an open BLOCKER gets no docs run (Hard rule 21).
- **Architecture (Rule B4).** After every part is written, a book of 2 or more projects gets one `SystemArchitecture` run. A book of one project has no architecture.
- **The write (Rule B5).** The planner then returns `WriteBook`. The book ID is the book that the user picked on the New task form, or an ID built from the names of the parts that were written (Rule B6). An abandoned part does not name the book.
- **A failed docs run.** The planner opens an `execution_failed` gate for it.

The docs stage itself is in [Documentation books](documentation-books.md).

## Approval gates

A gate is a stop that waits for an answer from the user, or from YOLO mode. The planner returns it as `OpenGate` with a `GatePayload`. The payload has 14 kinds. The console shows one card for each kind.

| Gate kind | `kind_str` | Stage | Answers | Opens when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OpenQuestions` | `open_questions` | `open-questions` | `Questions` | The spec or the plan has open questions for this version. |
| `SpecApproval` | `spec_approval` | `spec-approval` | `Approval` | The spec passed its fact-check. |
| `PlanApproval` | `plan_approval` | `plan-approval` | `Approval` | The plan passed its fact-check. |
| `FactCheckRecurring` | `fact_check_recurring` | `fact-check-spec` or `fact-check-plan` | `another-round`, `stop` | The consecutive FAIL verdicts reach the limit: 3 for the first gate, and a higher count for a later gate. |
| `ReviewCap` | `review_cap` | `review` or `test-review` | `another-pass`, `stop` | A review loop reached its cap with findings open. |
| `Stuck` | `stuck` | `rescue` | `fact`, `block` | The Rescue judge needs a fact only the user has. |
| `PhaseBlocked` | `phase_blocked` | `implement` | `retry`, `leave` | A phase is blocked and announced. |
| `ClosingGate` | `closing_gate` | `closing-gate` | `Closing` | A project finished its format step and its tests or docs are not chosen. |
| `Permission` | `permission` | `implement` | `Permission` | A live execution needs a decision on a tool call. |
| `HarnessFailure` | `harness_failure` | `implement` | `retry`, `native` | A harness CLI failed to start or is not logged in. |
| `SkillApproval` | `skill_approval` | `skill-approval` | `Skills` | The init flow proposed skills. |
| `ExecutionFailed` | `execution_failed` | `implement` | `retry`, `abandon` | An execution ended without a usable result. |
| `ImplementationReview` | `implementation_review` | `implementation-review` | `feedback`, `done` | Every phase is finished. |
| `BudgetReached` | `budget_reached` | `intake` | `raise`, `stop` | The session spent its budget. |

These rules apply to all gates:

- **One gate for each owner.** The key is `gate:<kind>:<owner>`. The owner is the artifact, the phase, the execution, or the project that the gate is about. Because of this, the planner does not open a second gate for the same owner.
- **Approval needs a PASS.** The fold records a spec or plan approval only when `passed_current` is true for the version that the gate showed. A change after the gate opened revokes the approval, and its answer is stale. The YOLO answer check gives the message `approval requires a fact-check PASS`.
- **A rejection needs text.** A YOLO answer that rejects without feedback fails with `a rejection needs feedback saying what to change`.
- **Free text is routed.** For a spec or plan answer, a stuck fact, a review cap answer, and a feedback text, the Route answer judge decides where the text goes before any agent reads it (Rule J1). It can keep the text as a note, drop it, or queue research first.
- **YOLO.** In YOLO mode the engine answers the gates. `Permission`, `BudgetReached`, and a failure that the user caused by stopping an execution stay open. See [Judges and YOLO](judges-and-yolo.md).
- **The answer source.** The log records `AnswerSource` as `User`, `Yolo`, or `Engine`. `Engine` means that no judgment was needed.

## Completion and the completion report

The planner ends a session in the `completion` method. It checks these conditions first:

- No execution runs, and each open gate is a `Permission` gate.
- Each blocked phase is announced.
- Each created project finished its init.
- No subagent waits for an answer (Rule H9).

If the conditions hold and no completion decision exists, the planner returns a `Completion` judge. After the decision exists, the planner returns `Complete`. The report text is the `report_markdown` field of the decision. If agents created projects, the engine adds a `## Projects created` section. It lists the key, path, and stack of each project, and says `initialized` or `not initialized` with the reason (Rule O3).

The report names what was done, each stage that did not run and how to run it later, and each decision that Ostra made for the user in YOLO mode. The reason: silent omissions look like bugs later. A `QUICK_ANSWER` session skips the judge, and its answer is the report.

For `IMPLEMENT`, `TEST`, and `DOCS`, the planner finishes only when `all_implement_done` is true:

1. Nothing runs.
2. Each project has finished its code and recorded its format step.
3. The closing choice for each project is known.
4. Each covered test loop is terminal.
5. The docs stage is settled for each project, unless an open BLOCKER blocks it.
6. The book is written, when any part exists.

## Constants of the pipeline

| Constant | File | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `FACTCHECK_RECURRING_LIMIT` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | 3 | Consecutive FAIL verdicts before the first `fact_check_recurring` gate. A later gate opens at this value plus `fail_limit_extra`. |
| `REVIEW_CAP` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | 3 | Review passes in one loop before the `review_cap` gate. |
| `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | 10 | Review passes in one loop in YOLO mode before the `ResolveReview` judge. |
| `ERROR_RETRIES` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | 1 | Automatic retries of an execution that ended with an error. |
| `SUFFICIENCY_ROUNDS` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | 3 | Sufficiency judge rounds. After 3, the spec starts with the research that exists. |
| `AUTO_FIXABLE_PARAM` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | `auto_fixable_ids` | Key in the review execution parameters. It holds the auto-fixable rule IDs. |
| `NO_PRIOR_FINDINGS` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | `no findings on the previous pass` | Value of `Prior findings:` after a pass with no findings. |
| `STOPPED_EXECUTION` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | `You stopped this execution.` | Error text of a cancelled execution that has no error. |
| `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` | 4 | Documentation writers in one session at the same time. |
| `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | `The format command in project.toml changed outside Ostra, so format was skipped. Approve it in the project's settings to run it next time.` | Output of a skipped format step. The exit code is `None`. |

The other engine constants are in [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md).

## How the console shows the pipeline

The session board has one column for each lane. `web/src/content/stages.ts` holds the text that the console shows. `LANES` maps each `Lane` to a title and a reason. `STAGES` maps each `StageKind` to a label, a `produces` text, and a `protects` text. Both are `Record` types, so the TypeScript compiler requires an entry for each lane and each stage kind. If you add a stage kind in `pipeline.rs`, add its entry in `stages.ts` too, because the web build fails without it.

The session screen shows phases in the lanes `design`, `build`, `review`, and `test` (`PHASE_LANES` in `web/src/screens/SessionScreen.tsx`). The read model in `crates/ostra-engine/src/view.rs` builds the stage cards. It shows format and staging commands, the book write, and the completion report as cards.

`EARS_NOTE` is the note that the console shows the first time a spec or plan is opened. It explains the sentence forms of the requirements in a spec:

- **Ubiquitous:** `The system shall ...` holds all the time.
- **Event-driven:** `When <trigger>, the system shall ...` holds after the trigger.
- **State-driven:** `While <state>, the system shall ...` holds during the state.
- **Unwanted behavior:** `If <condition>, then the system shall ...` covers errors and edge cases.
- **Optional feature:** `Where <feature is present>, the system shall ...`

Acceptance criteria use Given, When, Then. Each criterion becomes at least one test, and the reviewer checks the code against it.

## Tests of the planner

`tests/conformance/main.rs` tests `next_steps` directly. The helper `H` holds an event history and a `PlanCtx`. A test adds events with `h.ev`, `h.decide`, `h.run`, `h.answer`, and `h.command`. Then it compares `h.summaries()` with the expected step text. Test names carry the rule ID that they check, for example `d5_plan_fact_check_and_approval`, `t4_epa_fans_out_and_write_test_is_serial`, `hard21_blocker_has_no_cap`, and `b7_docs_writers_fan_out_under_a_cap`.

To add a rule, write a fixture that builds the event history before the rule applies. Then assert the steps that the planner must return. Run `cargo test --workspace`. See [Testing and verification](testing.md).
