sections.title: Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode
sections.summary: How the ten judge calls decide routing questions, how the engine builds their input and stores their decisions, how a user overrides a decision, and what YOLO mode answers for the user.
sections.body:
A session needs some decisions that no fixed rule can make. Examples are the category of a request, whether research is complete, and where a typed answer goes. Ostra asks a model for each of these decisions. The model call is a judge call. A judge call is the only place where a model makes an orchestration decision. The engine stores each result as a decision with a reason, so the user can read it and, for four judges, change it.

This page covers the ten judges, the input that the engine builds for each, the stored decision records, the `Disposition` of an answer, the override rules, YOLO mode, and the judge evals. It stops before the pipeline stages. For the stages and the planner, read [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md). For the runner, retries, and the event fold, read [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md).

## The ten judges

The `JudgeKind` enum in `crates/ostra-core/src/event.rs` has ten values. Each value has one prompt file in `assets/judges/` and one output type in `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs`. The prompt file name is the value of `JudgeKind::as_str`.

| Judge (`JudgeKind`) | Prompt file | The planner asks when | Output type | What the engine does with the output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Classify` | `classify.md` | The session has no category and no Classify decision. | `ClassifyOut` | Sets the category, the projects in scope, the first research tasks, the opt-ins, and the title. |
| `Sufficiency` | `sufficiency.md` | Research tasks finished and some have `Not covered` items that no judge has read. | `SufficiencyOut` | Queues one more research task for each needed item. |
| `Track` | `track.md` | An `IMPLEMENT` session finished research and has no track. | `TrackOut` | Sets the light track or the full track. |
| `Stakes` | `stakes.md` | A full-track session has a finished spec and no stakes. | `StakesOut` | `low` skips the plan stage. `medium` and `high` run it. |
| `RouteAnswer` | `route-answer.md` | A spec or plan answer is held, a phase gate waits for a route, or the user added context. | `RouteAnswerOut` | Decides the route, the `Disposition`, the research, and the notes to forget. |
| `Feedback` | `feedback.md` | A feedback round after the implementation review has no route. | `FeedbackOut` | Picks the route and the projects that get a revision phase. |
| `Rescue` | `rescue.md` | An agent returned `STUCK`. | `RescueOut` | Re-runs the agent, queues research first, or opens a gate. |
| `ResolveReview` | `resolve-review.md` | A review loop reached its budget under YOLO. | `ResolveReviewOut` | Runs one fix pass with exact instructions, or blocks the phase. |
| `Completion` | `completion.md` | Nothing runs and the session has no completion decision. | `CompletionOut` | Stores the Markdown completion report. |
| `YoloAnswer` | `yolo-answer.md` | YOLO is on and an open gate is of a kind that needs judgment. | `YoloAnswerOut` | The engine turns the answer into a gate answer. |

Each prompt starts with the role of the judge, then lists its input, the rules for its decision, and its output. Each prompt ends with the same instruction: call `decide` once. The tool `decide` is the forced tool call of `ostra_providers::structured` (`DECIDE_TOOL`).

### Classify

The Classify judge picks one category from `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, `IMPLEMENT`, `VERIFY`, `TEST`, `DOCS`, `PROMPT`, `QUICK_CHANGE`, and `QUICK_ANSWER`. It also picks the projects in scope, one research task for each project, the `opts_in` flags for tests and docs, and a title of 2 to 5 words.

These rules from the prompt decide the hard cases:

- Judge by what the request asks Ostra to produce, not by its first verb. A request that asks for changed files is a changing category.
- If two categories fit, pick the one that runs more of the pipeline. A stage that the request did not need costs one round. A stage that the request needed but skipped gives a wrong result.
- `QUICK_CHANGE` is only for an edit that the request spells out in full. An edit to a prompt, a `SKILL.md`, an agent file, or a judge prompt under `assets/` is `PROMPT`.
- `DOCS` is for a documentation book about code that exists. A change to a docs page or a README inside a project is `IMPLEMENT`.
- When the user pinned projects, return exactly those projects. The engine also forces this: `apply_classify` uses the pinned projects as the scope, whatever the judge returned (Rule O6).

The engine cleans the title with `clean_title`. The function joins the words on one line, removes wrapping quotes and a final period, and cuts the result to `TITLE_CHARS` (60) characters. A title with nothing left is dropped.

### Sufficiency

Each research pass lists what it could not investigate under `Not covered`. The Sufficiency judge answers one question for each item: does the request depend on it? A needed item carries a `task` for one more research pass. When the judge cannot tell, it marks the item needed. The reason is the cost: a wasted research pass costs one round, and a missed dependency gives a wrong spec after approval.

The engine asks this judge at most `SUFFICIENCY_ROUNDS` (3) times for a session. After that, the spec stage starts with the research that exists. When the output maps several items to one task, the engine queues the task once. An item with no valid project goes to the primary project, with the item text as the task.

### Track

An `IMPLEMENT` request starts on the light track: research, then reviewed phases. The Track judge moves it to the full track only when the research shows one of six things: an open behavior that the user must settle, a changed contract, a schema or stored data change, ordered changes across modules, security or data deletion, or a new codebase that no project holds. Thin evidence gives `light`, because the user can ask for changes after the build and a spec round costs several approvals.

If the user forced a track in the New task form, `SessionOptions.track` sets the track at creation. The planner then does not ask the Track judge.

### Stakes

The Stakes judge classifies an approved spec as `low`, `medium`, or `high`. A `low` result needs one deliverable in one project, an isolated change, no schema change, and no contract change. Any doubt resolves upward, because skipping the plan removes the phase review that catches a wrong sequence. For a `low` result on an `IMPLEMENT` session, the engine skips the plan stage and creates one inline phase named `Implementation` for each project in scope.

### Route answer

The Route answer judge decides what happens to a user answer before any agent reads it (Rule J1). It gives one item for each answer, a route, research tasks, and the IDs of notes to forget. The parts [Disposition and answer items](#disposition-and-answer-items) and [Routes](#routes) give the full rules.

### Feedback

The Feedback judge routes one round of feedback that the user typed at the implementation review gate. It gives a route (`requirement_change` or `implementation_detail`), one target for each project whose files the revision must edit, and exactly one item with the ID `answer`. Each target has an `instruction` that the implementer of that project reads. The engine rejects an output with no targets, because `perform_judge` validates `FeedbackOut` with a non-empty `targets` list.

A `requirement_change` needs a spec. With no spec, the judge always picks `implementation_detail`. When a requirement addresses the subject and the judge is not sure, it picks `requirement_change`, because a spec that disagrees with the code misleads every later stage.

### Rescue

An agent that returned `STUCK` hit its retry ceiling on one failure. A plain retry reproduces the failure, so the Rescue judge picks one of three actions:

- `rerun`: the missing fact is already in the lessons, the phase file, the spec, or the diagnostic. The judge writes it in `fact`. The engine re-runs the agent with the fact in its task.
- `explore`: the fact is findable in code or documentation. The judge writes an `explore_task`. The engine runs that research and then re-runs the agent.
- `gate`: only the user has the fact. The engine opens a `Stuck` gate. Under YOLO the YoloAnswer judge answers that gate (see [What YOLO answers](#what-yolo-answers)).

After two rescues of the same phase with the same diagnostic, the prompt tells the judge to choose `gate`. Neither rescue changed the failure, so the user is the remaining source of the fact. The input lists the earlier Rescue decisions of the session, so the judge can apply this rule.

### Resolve review

The review loop repeats fix and review until no HIGH or MEDIUM finding is open. Under YOLO the loop has a budget of `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` (10) passes. At the budget, the loop goes to the ResolveReview judge and not to the user. The judge reads the ledger and finds why the findings recur. It then picks one of two actions:

- `fix`: the judge writes one exact instruction for each open finding. The engine adds 1 to `resolve_rounds` and 1 to `extra_cap`, runs one fix pass with only these instructions, and then runs one verification review.
- `block`: the findings do not converge, they need a fact only the user has, or the fix contradicts the phase file. The engine marks the phase blocked with the reason and the ledger path.

After a `fix` round, the loop returns to the judge only if findings remain and their count fell below `open_before_resolve`. Otherwise the phase is blocked. `BLOCKER` security findings never reach this judge. They loop without a cap until removed.

### Completion

The Completion judge writes the report that the user reads at the end. The report has these sections in this order: `## Summary`, `## Phases`, `## Checks`, `## Not run`, `## Blocked` (only when something was blocked), and `## Decided for you` (only under YOLO). The prompt requires the judge to report every stage that did not run, because a silent omission reads as a bug (Rule T7). It also forbids praise and says that a command which the input does not show did not run.

If the Completion call fails after all attempts, the engine still stores a decision. Its report starts with `# Session complete`, states that the judge failed, and then lists the same input that the judge reads in a successful call. The session work is done, and a report without prose is better than no report.

## How one judge call runs

The planner (`next_steps`) is a pure function. It returns `Step::Judge` with a judge and a subject when a judgment is due. The runner (`perform_judge` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`) does the call. The diagram shows one call.

### Sequence of one judge call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Planner
    participant Runner
    participant Input as judge_input
    participant Services
    participant Provider as structured
    participant Log as Event log
    participant State as SessionState
    Planner->>Runner: Step::Judge with judge and subject
    Runner->>Input: judge_input(state, kind, subject, project_facts)
    Input-->>Runner: user message and input_summary
    Runner->>Runner: output_schema(kind) and judge_prompt(kind)
    Runner->>Services: judge(route, system, input, schema, Effort::Low)
    Services->>Provider: forced decide tool call
    Provider-->>Services: JSON value and usage
    Services-->>Runner: value and usage
    Runner->>Runner: validate(value)
    Runner->>Log: append DecisionMade
    Log->>State: fold calls on_decision
```

These steps run in order:

1. The runner takes a snapshot of the session state and calls `judge_input` to build the user message and a short `input_summary`.
2. The runner builds the output schema with `output_schema(kind, None)` and reads the system prompt with `judge_prompt`. The prompt comes from `assets/judges/<name>.md`.
3. The runner resolves the route with the key `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`) and the tier `Advanced`. The judge always runs on the native executor, because it is an engine call and not an agent execution. The effort is `Effort::Low`.
4. `Services::judge` finds the provider for the model and calls `ostra_providers::structured`. The call forces the `decide` tool, so the model must return JSON that matches the schema.
5. The runner adds the cost of the call to the judge cost of the session. The session cost in the summary includes this value.
6. The runner validates the value by parsing it into the output type of the judge. If the value is valid, the runner appends `SessionEvent::DecisionMade` with a new `DecisionId`, the judge, the subject, the `input_summary`, the output, and the `reason`.
7. The fold of the event log calls `on_decision` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`. This function applies the decision to the session state.

Because the state is a fold of events, a restart replays each `DecisionMade` event and applies the decision again. The judge is not called again for a decision that the log already holds.

### What happens when

- **The call fails or the output is invalid.** The runner makes up to 3 attempts. After each failed attempt it waits 500, then 1,000, then 1,500 milliseconds. The runner counts the cost of every call that returned a value, also when the value was invalid.
- **All 3 attempts fail for a judge other than Completion or YoloAnswer.** The runner appends `SessionFailed` with the error and this advice: check that the judge route has a provider with a working API key.
- **All 3 attempts fail for the Completion judge.** The runner stores the fallback report that the part on Completion describes.
- **All 3 attempts fail for the YoloAnswer judge.** The runner appends a `Note` event. The gate stays open for the user.
- **The prompt for a judge is missing.** The runner returns the error `No prompt for the <name> judge.`
- **The route has no usable model.** The runner returns the routing error. Set the `judge` model route in the workspace settings. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).
- **Many executions run at the same time.** A judge call is an engine call and not an execution (`resolve_executor` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`). Thus it takes no execution slot, and `call_judge` never calls `acquire_slot`.

## What the engine puts in judge input

`judge_input` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs` builds the user message for each judge from the session state. It returns the message and a one-line summary. The engine stores the summary with the decision, and the console shows it as the basis of the decision.

Every message starts with the full request. The full request is the request text, the attached files and folders with absolute paths, the uploads, and each context addition that a judge delivered (`SessionState::full_request`). The judge reads this text only. It never reads the repository.

| Judge | The message holds | `input_summary` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classify | The request, the New task toggles (`tests`, `docs`, `yolo`), the pinned projects, and each project with its path, stack, and module map areas. A project with no inventory is marked as not initialized, or as created in this session. | `Request: ` and the first line of the request |
| Sufficiency | The request, each finished research task with its scope, findings, and research document path, the `Not covered` items of the tasks in the subject, and the project keys it can target. | The count of `Not covered` items and of research documents |
| Track | The request, the projects in scope, and each research document with its excerpt. | `Research for: ` and the first line of the request |
| Stakes | The request, the approved spec counts and summary, an excerpt of the spec file, and the projects in scope. | `Approved spec and request` |
| Feedback | The request, the track, the spec excerpt (or a note that there is no spec), the phases with their implementer reports, the research, the kept notes, and the feedback text. | `Feedback: ` and the first line of the feedback |
| RouteAnswer, gate | The request, the category, the track, the projects, the research, the spec summary, the plan phases, the kept notes, and the gate with the user answer. | `Answer: ` and the first line of the answer |
| RouteAnswer, added context | The same session facts, the added text, and the list of work that the user interrupted. | `Added context: ` and the first line |
| Rescue | The request, the stuck agent, its phase, the verbatim diagnostic, what it needs, and the earlier Rescue decisions. | `STUCK: ` and the first line of the need |
| ResolveReview | The phase and the pass counts, the open findings, an excerpt of the review ledger, and an excerpt of the phase file. | `Open findings and the review ledger` |
| YoloAnswer | The request, the gate title and explanation, the gate payload as JSON, and the context that the gate kind needs. | The gate title |
| Completion | The state at completion, as the part [Completion input](#completion-input) lists. | `Session state at completion` |

The YoloAnswer message adds context by gate kind. An `OpenQuestions` gate adds the findings of each research document. A `SpecApproval` gate adds an excerpt of the spec. A `PlanApproval` gate adds an excerpt of the master plan.

### Excerpts and truncation

The engine reads files into the message with `excerpt_n`. A file longer than the limit is cut at the limit, rounded down to a character boundary, and the engine adds the line `(truncated at N characters)`. A file that the engine cannot read becomes the text `(could not read <path>)`. The summary line comes from `first_line`. It keeps the first line and cuts a line of more than 160 bytes to 157 characters plus `...`.

- `FILE_EXCERPT` is 24,000. It limits the spec, the plan, the review ledger, and the phase file in one message.
- `TRACK_EXCERPT` is 12,000. It limits each research document in the Track message. The Track judge reads every research document of the session, so the limit for each document is half of `FILE_EXCERPT`.

### Route answer input by gate kind

For a gate with questions (`OpenQuestions`), the message lists each question with its options numbered as the user saw them. It marks the option that the agent recommended. It shows the answer of the user for each question and asks for one item for each question ID. For every other gate, the message holds the facts of the payload and the user answer, and asks for one item with the ID `answer`. The facts depend on the payload:

- `SpecApproval`: the spec summary.
- `PlanApproval`: the plan summary and the list of phases.
- `FactCheckRecurring`: the target, the number of failed passes, and the number of findings.
- `ReviewCap`: the phase, the pass count, and at most 20 findings.
- `Stuck`: the agent, the phase, the need, and the diagnostic.
- `PhaseBlocked`: the phase and the reason.

If the user approved or did not approve, the message says so. If the user chose an option, the message names it.

### Completion input

The Completion message lists the category, the YOLO flag, and the track. For `IMPLEMENT`, a light track adds a note that the spec, fact-check, and plan stages did not run. The message then lists the feedback rounds, the research documents and abandoned research tasks, the spec, and the plan (or a note that the stakes skipped the plan).

For each phase the message gives the status: passed after N review passes, `BLOCKED` with the reason, or removed because a dependency failed. It also gives the test policy with its rationale, each LOW finding left open, and the state of the test stage. For each project it gives the format result, the closing gate choices, and the docs state. A `QuickAnswer` session sends only the request, the category, and the YOLO flag.

Under YOLO the message also lists each gate that YOLO answered, with its title, gate ID, and reason, under the heading `Decided for you under YOLO`. The Completion prompt turns this list into the `## Decided for you` section.

## Disposition and answer items

The Route answer and Feedback judges decide what happens to each answer. They return a list of `AnswerItem` values. Each item has an `id`, a `disposition`, a `note`, and a list of `stages`. The `id` is the ID of an open question, or `answer` (the constant `ANSWER_ITEM`) for a gate with one text.

### The three dispositions

The `Disposition` enum in `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs` has three values. `Deliver` is the default.

| `Disposition` | When the judge picks it | What the engine does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Deliver` | The answer settles what the stage asked, or changes what the agent must do now. | The agent that asked receives the answer as written. |
| `Remember` | The whole answer is about a later stage, such as how to test or document. | The current stage receives no text. The note reaches the stages in `stages`. |
| `Discard` | The user tells Ostra to ignore the answer, drop the question, or disregard the text. | No agent reads the answer. The gate answer stays in the session log. |

These rules from the prompts apply to the choice:

- Pick `Discard` only when the user says so in their own words. A wrong `Discard` loses a decision that the user meant to give.
- Pick `Remember` only when the whole answer is for a later stage. An answer that also settles something now is `Deliver`.
- Words that repeat the choice that the user made on the gate, such as "retry" with the option `retry`, settle nothing new. The engine applies the choice itself, so the judge reads the rest of the answer.
- Follow the user. When the answer and the recommendation of the agent disagree, the answer wins. A typed answer that names several options of a single-choice question is read as the combination and is delivered.
- Ostra rules still apply: guards, the session budget, the fact-check `PASS` before approval, the review cap count, the removal of `BLOCKER` findings, and the rule that a plan is built only from an approved spec. The judge delivers such an answer as written and names the rule in its reason.

The Feedback judge uses the same three values with these meanings. `Deliver` builds the revision from the targets. `Remember` accepts the implementation and keeps the note. `Discard` builds nothing and asks for review again. A change to a page that people read, such as a README or a docs site, is a revision to build now, so it is `Deliver` even when the user says the work looks good.

### How the engine merges items

A model can split one answer into several items. The function `item_for` merges the items for one ID in this order. `Deliver` wins when any part is `Deliver`, because the user gave the answer. Otherwise `Remember` wins when any part is `Remember`. Otherwise the result is `Discard`.

The note and the stages come from the first part that has stages. An answer that the judge did not name is delivered. On a gate with one text, every item counts as an item about that text, whatever ID it carries. The prompts still tell the judge to give exactly one item for each answer.

### Notes and stages

The `stages` list names the later stages that also receive `note`. The values of `NoteStage` are `implement`, `tests`, and `docs`. The judge names only the stages that the words of the user address. An instruction about tests is `tests`, never `implement`. The stage `docs` means the documentation writers that write the workspace book, never a page inside a project. Nothing can be kept for the plan agent, because it reads only the spec. An answer that the plan needs is `Deliver`, and Ostra writes it into the spec.

When an item has stages, the fold keeps a `UserNote` with the ID `N1`, `N2`, and so on, in the order that the notes are kept. The text is the `note`, or the answer text when the note is empty. A later judge call sees the notes that are not forgotten, in the section `Notes already kept for later stages`.

The list `forget` holds the IDs of kept notes that the answer takes back or replaces. A forgotten note stays in the log and reaches no agent. A remembered note never changes a requirement. An answer that changes what the system must do is `Deliver`, so the spec records it.

### Research from an answer

The `research` list holds research tasks that run before the engine applies the answer. The judge adds a task when the answer asks for research, picks an option that runs research, or needs a fact that no research document has. The engine keeps at most `MAX_ANSWER_RESEARCH` (3) tasks. It drops a task with empty text. It uses the primary project when the project key is not valid. Each task carries the user request for context. For a gate at a phase, the phase loop waits for this research and then adds the new documents to the instructions of the agent.

### Which answers need the judge

A bare choice has one meaning, so the engine applies it as is. The function `answer_needs_route` decides whether a gate answer is routed. The `GateAnswered` event stores the result in `routed`.

| Gate kind | The answer is routed when |
| --- | --- |
| `OpenQuestions` | The answer list is not empty. |
| `SpecApproval`, `PlanApproval` | The approval has feedback text. |
| `FactCheckRecurring` | The option is not `stop` and the answer has text. |
| `ReviewCap` | The option is `another-pass` and the answer has text. |
| `Stuck` | The option is `fact` and the answer has text. |
| `PhaseBlocked` | The option is `retry` and the answer has text. |
| `ImplementationReview` | The option is `feedback` and the answer has text. |

The `ImplementationReview` answer goes to the Feedback judge. Every other routed answer goes to the Route answer judge. Answers recorded before Rule J1 have `routed` set to `false` and fold as they always did.

## Routes

The Route answer judge picks one route for the delivered part of an answer. The `AnswerRoute` enum has three values.

| Route | When | What the engine does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `requirement_change` | The answer changes, adds, or removes what the system must do. | At a phase gate, stops the phase, runs generate-spec again with the answer, asks for spec approval again, then plans again (Rule D10). |
| `implementation_detail` | The answer is about how to build something that the spec already settles. | Passes the answer to the implementer as an instruction. The spec does not change. |
| `stage_choice` | The answer only chooses which optional stages run, such as tests or docs at the closing gate. | Runs the chosen stages. The spec does not change (Rule T5). |

Doubt resolves to `requirement_change`. A stale spec silently corrupts every later stage, and an extra spec round costs one round trip. At the spec questions and the spec approval, every delivered answer goes into the spec, whatever the route. So the route matters most at a phase gate.

With no spec in the session, the judge picks `implementation_detail`, and the engine sends a delivered answer to the agent that asked. The Feedback judge cannot pick `stage_choice`, because its schema allows only the first two routes.

### Context that the user adds during a session

The user can add text, files, or uploads to a running session. This is not a gate answer. The engine marks the amendment as pending and starts nothing until the Route answer judge decides (Rule C2). The subject of the call is the amendment index. The message says whether the user sent the context now or queued it, and lists the work that the user interrupted. The judge gives one item with the ID `answer`.

- `Deliver` adds the text to the request that every later agent reads. The interrupted work runs again with it. With `requirement_change` after a spec exists, the engine also writes it into the spec and asks for approval again.
- `Remember` keeps the text as a note for the named stages. It does not join the request.
- `Discard` drops the text. The interrupted work runs again without it.

The judge also names the project for research. When the user names a project, the research runs in that project, even when another project is first in scope. A project that the session created holds its new code.

## Decision records and events

The engine stores each judge result as an event in the append-only session log. Two events carry decisions. Both are variants of `SessionEvent` in `crates/ostra-core/src/event.rs`.

| Event | Fields | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DecisionMade` | `id`, `judge`, `subject`, `input_summary`, `output`, `reason` | A judge call returned a valid value. |
| `DecisionOverridden` | `id`, `output`, `reason` | The user replaced the output of a decision. |

The `subject` says what the decision is about. It is a gate ID for RouteAnswer and YoloAnswer, an execution ID for Rescue, a loop key for ResolveReview, a round index for Feedback, and a comma list of research task indexes for Sufficiency. It is empty for Classify, Track, Stakes, and Completion.

The fold turns each `DecisionMade` event into a `DecisionRecord` with the fields `id`, `judge`, `subject`, `input_summary`, `output`, `reason`, `overridden`, and `at`. The runner also writes the row to the `decisions` table. See [Storage](storage.md). The read model in `view.rs` sends each record to the console as a `DecisionView`, with `overridden` and `can_override`. The console shows the records in the panel `Decisions Ostra made` on the session screen.

Every output has a `reason`: one or two sentences that the user reads. The function `reason_of` reads it from the output. The Classify prompt requires the reason to name the words of the request that decided the category. The console shows it as "Ostra chose X because Y".

A YOLO answer has a second record. The `GateAnswered` event stores `source: AnswerSource::Yolo` and the reason of the judge. `AnswerSource` has three values: `User`, `Yolo`, and `Engine`. `Engine` marks an answer that needs no judgment, such as a closing gate where the request already asked for every stage.

## Override a decision

A user can replace the output of a decision before the work that depends on it starts. Only four judges allow this: Classify, Sufficiency, Track, and Stakes. The other six judges have no override. Their decisions act on a loop or a gate at the moment that the engine makes them.

### How to override

1. Open the session screen and find the decision in the panel `Decisions Ostra made`.
2. Choose the override button. The button shows only when `can_override` is true.
3. Edit the JSON of the output in the same shape as the judge output.
4. Write the reason in the field `Why`. The dialog refuses an empty reason, so the record explains the change.
5. Choose `Save the override`.

The dialog calls `POST /api/decisions/{id}/override` with the body `{ output, reason }`. The route is in [Server API](server-api.md). The engine method `override_decision` does these checks:

- The decision must exist. If it does not, the engine returns `NotFound`.
- `can_override` must be true. If it is not, the error is `Work that depends on this decision has already started, so it can no longer be overridden.` The same error shows for a judge that has no override.
- The output must parse into the output type of the judge. If it does not, the error is `The override does not match the decision's output shape.`

After the checks, the engine marks the row in the `decisions` table and appends `DecisionOverridden`. The fold replaces the output and the reason in the record, sets `overridden`, and applies the new output.

### When an override is still possible

The function `can_override` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` returns false for a finished session. For an active session, the rule depends on the judge:

| Judge | The override is possible when | What the new output does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classify | No research task has started and no phase has started work. | Replaces the category, scope, opt-ins, and title. Removes the research tasks that Classify queued and queues the new ones. Clears the phases and builds the phases of the new category. |
| Sufficiency | The spec stage has no run. | Removes the research tasks that Sufficiency queued and that have not started. Queues the needed items of the new output. The round count does not change. |
| Track | The spec stage has no run and no phase has started. | Sets the new track. Clears the phases. A light track creates one inline phase for each project. |
| Stakes | The plan stage has no run and no phase has started. | Sets the new stakes and clears the phases. A `low` value on an `IMPLEMENT` session creates one inline phase for each project. |

For Classify, Stakes, and Track, the fold checks the same rule again when it applies an override, so a replay of the log gives the same state. If the rule fails at that point, the fold keeps the old state. The record still shows the override.

### What an override does not do

An override does not stop an agent that already runs and does not undo started work. It does not change the pins of the user: a pinned scope stays the scope. It also does not change a RouteAnswer, Feedback, Rescue, ResolveReview, Completion, or YoloAnswer decision. To change the effect of a YOLO answer, switch YOLO off before the next gate and answer that gate yourself.

## What YOLO answers

YOLO mode tells Ostra to decide for the user. Without YOLO, a gate waits until the user answers. With YOLO, the planner pushes `Step::YoloAnswer` for each open gate, and the engine answers it. YOLO changes who answers and never what must be true. Guards still apply, an approval still needs a fact-check `PASS`, `BLOCKER` security findings are still removed, and the deny rules of the user still apply.

YOLO leaves three gates open for the user: `BudgetReached`, `ExecutionFailed` of an execution that the user stopped (Rule P4), and `Permission`. The planner never pushes `Step::YoloAnswer` for these three gates. The part [Gates that YOLO leaves open](#gates-that-yolo-leaves-open) gives the reason for each.

### Turn YOLO on or off

- **For one session at creation:** set the `yolo` toggle in the New task form. The engine stores it in `SessionOptions.yolo`.
- **For every new session of a workspace:** set `yolo.default` to `true` in the workspace settings. The engine sets `options.yolo` when it creates a session. See [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md).
- **For a running session:** call `POST /api/sessions/{id}/yolo` with `{ "enabled": true }`. The engine appends `YoloSet`.

When the user switches YOLO on in a running session, the engine answers every open `Permission` gate at once with `AllowOnce` and the reason `YOLO was switched on, so every permission ask is allowed.` The planner answers other open gates in its next pass. When the user switches YOLO off, gates that open later wait for the user. A paused session starts nothing, and that includes each YOLO answer (Rule P1).

### Answer for each gate kind

The function `yolo_plan` returns `YoloPlan::Fixed` for a gate that needs no judgment and `YoloPlan::Judge` with an answer schema for a gate that does. It returns nothing for a gate that YOLO leaves open.

| Gate kind | YOLO answer | Source of the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OpenQuestions` | Each question gets an answer. The judge takes the recommended option unless the research gives a specific reason for another option. | YoloAnswer judge |
| `SpecApproval`, `PlanApproval` | Approve when the latest fact-check verdict is `PASS` and the artifact does not omit something that the request asked for. Otherwise reject with feedback. | YoloAnswer judge |
| `Stuck` | Choose `fact` with the missing fact, or `block`. | YoloAnswer judge |
| `ImplementationReview` | Choose `done`. Only the user can say what to change. | Fixed |
| `ClosingGate` | For each project, no tests and no docs, unless the request already asked for them (Rules T2, T3). | Fixed |
| `FactCheckRecurring` | Choose `another-round` when `passes` is less than 6. Choose `stop` from 6 passes on. The reason of `stop` is: "The fact-check failed six times in a row, so the engine stopped rather than guess." | Fixed |
| `ReviewCap` | Choose `another-pass`. | Fixed |
| `PhaseBlocked` | Choose `leave`. Independent work continues (Rule D9). | Fixed |
| `ExecutionFailed` | Choose `retry` while fewer than 2 earlier `ExecutionFailed` gates for the same agent have an answer. Then choose `abandon`. The reason of `abandon` is: "This agent failed three times, so the engine abandoned the step instead of retrying again." | Fixed |
| `HarnessFailure` | Choose `native`, which re-routes the execution to the native executor. | Fixed |
| `SkillApproval` | Use the default disposition of each proposed skill. | Fixed |
| `Permission` | Allow once. The runner answers it at once, not the planner. | Runner |
| `BudgetReached` | No answer. The gate stays open. | None |

The two cutoffs stop a loop that no answer can fix. The fact-check cutoff is 6 passes. The execution cutoff is the third failure of the same agent, after 2 earlier answered gates. At each cutoff the engine ends the loop and does not guess.

The judge prompt `yolo-answer.md` also lists rules for gate kinds that the engine answers by itself. The judge never sees those gates, so the table above is what the engine does. For example, the engine always picks `another-pass` for a `ReviewCap` gate. Under YOLO a review loop goes to the ResolveReview judge at its budget, so that gate rarely opens.

### Gates that YOLO leaves open

Three gates get no `Step::YoloAnswer` from the planner. The planner skips `Permission`, and the function `yolo_leaves_open` names the other two.

- **`BudgetReached`:** spending more is the decision of the user, so YOLO never raises a budget.
- **`ExecutionFailed` for an execution that the user stopped:** the execution has the status `Cancelled`, so nothing retries it without the user, YOLO included (Rule P4).
- **`Permission`:** the planner skips it because the runner answers each `Permission` gate at once with `AllowOnce`. The execution that asks owns its permission gate. When YOLO is on, the gate opens and the runner answers it in the same moment.

The policy engine applies deny rules before it asks, so YOLO does not override a deny rule. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).

### Flow of a YOLO answer

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Open gate and YOLO on"] --> B{"Budget gate, or failed run that the user stopped?"}
    B -- yes --> C["Gate stays open for the user"]
    B -- no --> D{"Which plan?"}
    D -- "Judge" --> E["Call the YoloAnswer judge"]
    D -- "Fixed" --> J["Append GateAnswered, source Yolo"]
    E --> G{"Call succeeded?"}
    G -- no --> H["Append Note, gate waits for the user"]
    G -- yes --> I{"yolo_answer_from_judge accepts?"}
    I -- no --> H
    I -- yes --> J
    J --> K{"answer_needs_route?"}
    K -- yes --> L["Route answer judge runs next"]
    K -- no --> M["Planner applies the answer"]
```

The diagram starts after the planner skips `Permission` gates. The runner answers those gates outside this flow.

### What the engine checks in a judge answer

The function `yolo_answer_from_judge` turns the `answer` value into a `GateAnswer`. It enforces what must stay true, whatever the model wrote:

- **Open questions:** the engine fills each missing answer with the label of the recommended option. The result always has one answer for each question.
- **Approval:** an approval needs a fact-check `PASS` of the current spec or plan. Without it the engine refuses with `approval requires a fact-check PASS`. A rejection needs feedback text. Without it the engine refuses with `a rejection needs feedback saying what to change`.
- **Stuck:** the option `fact` without text becomes `block`. The schema also tells the judge never to guess a fact that only the user has.
- **Any other gate:** the engine refuses with `this gate is answered without the judge`.

If the engine refuses an answer, it appends a `Note` event: `The YOLO answer was refused: <error>. The gate waits for you.` If the judge call fails, the note is `YOLO could not answer "<title>": <error>. The gate waits for you.` Before it appends the answer, the engine reads the state again. If the user answered the gate in the meantime, the engine drops the YOLO answer.

A YOLO answer that carries text goes through the same routing as a user answer. For example, a rejection with feedback gives `routed: true`, and the Route answer judge decides where the feedback goes.

### What YOLO changes for the review loop

Under YOLO a review loop has `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` (10) passes before its cap. Without YOLO the cap is `REVIEW_CAP` (3). At the cap, a loop without YOLO opens a `ReviewCap` gate. A YOLO loop goes to the ResolveReview judge. If the user switches YOLO on when a loop waits at its cap, the planner sends the loop to the judge at once. Each `fix` round adds 1 to the cap of that loop for the verification pass.

### What the user sees

YOLO sessions send no push notification for a gate, because the engine answers it. The exception is `HarnessFailure`, because it needs the user to sign in to the harness. The completion report lists each YOLO decision with its reason and ID in the section `## Decided for you`. Each answered gate also keeps its reason in the `GateAnswered` event.

## Judge evals

The file `tests/evals/judges.toml` holds 83 cases that score the judges against the answer that a careful engineer picks. Every request is about the source of Ostra. The test is `judge_routing_evals` in `crates/ostra-server/tests/judge_evals.rs`. It builds the session state with the same fold and the same `judge_input` that the engine uses. It calls the judge several times for each model and scores the answers.

| Judge | Cases |
| --- | --- |
| `classify` | 23 |
| `track` | 14 |
| `stakes` | 3 |
| `sufficiency` | 2 |
| `feedback` | 16 |
| `route_answer` | 25 |

The eval file has no cases for Rescue, ResolveReview, Completion, and YoloAnswer. A case sets `judge`, `workspace`, `request`, and an `expect` table. The `workspace` field names one of three workspaces, and the function `projects()` in `judge_evals.rs` builds each one:

| Workspace | Projects | Cases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `one` | Ostra as one project. | 52 |
| `split` | A `server` project and a `web` project. | 28 |
| `triple` | A `server` project, a `web` project, and a `site` project. | 3 |

The `expect` table can hold `category`, `projects`, `track`, `route`, `targets`, `stakes`, `needed`, `not_needed`, `dispositions`, `stages`, `research`, `research_projects`, and `forget`.

The Route answer cases follow one pairing rule. Every case that must queue research has a counter-case that must not. Every case that must `Remember` or `Discard` has a counter-case that must `Deliver`.

The test is live, costs money, and is ignored by default. Run it with these variables:

```text
OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS=anthropic:claude-opus-5-5,anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS=3 \
  cargo test -p ostra-server --test judge_evals -- --ignored --nocapture
```

- `OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS`: a comma list of models. The default is `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`.
- `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS`: the number of calls for each case and model. The default is 3.
- `OSTRA_EVAL_CASES`: a comma list of substrings. The test runs only cases whose ID contains one of them.

The report goes to `target/evals/` and lists pass counts, the spread of answers, and the cost. Model results vary from run to run, so `judge_routing_evals` does not fail on a wrong answer. It fails only when every judge call failed, with the message `every judge call failed; check the provider credentials`. One failed call does not fail the test.

The test `eval_cases_build_their_sessions` runs offline without a model. It folds each case into the state that its judge expects, so a broken case fails in a normal test run. For the other test suites, read [Testing and verification](testing.md).

## Limits and constants

| Name | Value | File | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ANSWER_ITEM` | `answer` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs` | The ID of the item for an answer with one text. |
| `MAX_ANSWER_RESEARCH` | 3 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs` | Research tasks that one answer can queue. Also the `maxItems` of the `research` schema. |
| `TITLE_CHARS` | 60 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge.rs` | The longest session title, in characters. |
| `FILE_EXCERPT` | 24,000 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs` | The longest excerpt of a spec, plan, ledger, or phase file in judge input. |
| `TRACK_EXCERPT` | 12,000 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs` | The longest excerpt of one research document in Track input. |
| `JUDGE_ROUTE` | `judge` | `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs` | The routing key of the judge model, beside the agent names. |
| Judge attempts | 3 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | Calls to the provider for one decision. The waits are 500, 1,000, and 1,500 ms. |
| Judge effort and tier | `Low`, `Advanced` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | The effort and the model tier of every judge call. |
| `SUFFICIENCY_ROUNDS` | 3 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | Sufficiency calls before the spec starts with the research that exists. |
| `REVIEW_CAP` | 3 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | Review passes in a loop without YOLO. |
| `YOLO_REVIEW_BUDGET` | 10 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | Review passes in a loop under YOLO. |
| `FACTCHECK_RECURRING_LIMIT` | 3 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` | Failed fact-checks in a row before the first `FactCheckRecurring` gate opens. A later gate opens at `3 + fail_limit_extra`. The fold sets `fail_limit_extra` to `consecutive_fails` after the user chooses another round. YOLO stops at 6 passes. The page [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md) owns this constant. |
| Findings listed for a `ReviewCap` gate | 20 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs` | The most findings that Route answer input lists. |
| `first_line` cut | 160 bytes | `crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs` | The engine cuts a longer first line to 157 characters and `...`. |

For the other engine constants, read [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md).

sections.title: Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract
sections.summary: How Ostra defines the 14 agents, renders each prompt for an executor, builds the repo brief, loads skills, turns a SpawnRequest into a spawn block, and validates the submit result.
sections.body:
Every agent run needs three inputs that Ostra builds for each spawn. The first is a system prompt that names the tools of the executor. The second is a first message with typed parameters and project facts. The third is a typed result that the engine can read. Without one source for these inputs, a prompt names the wrong tools on a harness, an agent spends its first tool calls to find the build command, and the engine scrapes free text for results.

This page covers the `ostra-agents` crate, the agent types in `ostra-core`, and the skill code in `ostra-server`. It explains the agent names, the `assets/agents` folders, prompt rendering, `tool-mapping.toml`, the repo brief, skills, instruction files, the spawn block, and the submit contracts. It stops before agent coordination. For the `subagent_*` tools, read [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md). For the pipeline that decides which agent runs next, read [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md).

## The 14 agent names

`AgentName` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs) lists every leaf agent that Ostra runs. A leaf agent is an agent that does one step and ends with one submit call. `AgentName::ALL` holds the 14 values in this order. The kebab-case name is also the folder name under `assets/agents/`.

| Name | Role | Default tier | Timeout (seconds) | Effort | Session-only | Result type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | Researches one task and writes one research document | advanced | 1800 | high | yes | `ExploreSubmit` |
| `generate-spec` | Writes one spec file from all research documents | advanced | 1800 | high | yes | `GenerateSpecSubmit` |
| `fact-check` | Checks a spec or a plan for claims that break the implementer | advanced | 1800 | high | yes | `FactCheckSubmit` |
| `plan` | Turns an approved spec into a master plan and phase files | advanced | 1800 | high | yes | `PlanSubmit` |
| `implementer` | Writes the code of one phase or one inline change | balanced | 2400 | high | no | `ImplementerSubmit` |
| `code-reviewer` | Reviews the unstaged changes of one review loop | balanced | 1200 | high | yes | `CodeReviewerSubmit` |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Plans the verification of a phase and writes the EPA report | balanced | 1200 | high | yes | `ReportSubmit` |
| `write-test` | Writes the tests that the EPA report assigns | balanced | 2400 | high | no | `ReportSubmit` |
| `documentation` | Writes one project's part of a documentation book | advanced | 2400 | high | yes | `DocumentationSubmit` |
| `system-architecture` | Writes the architecture of a book with two or more projects | advanced | 1800 | high | yes | `ArchitectureSubmit` |
| `prompt-generation` | Writes instruction files to the meta-author standard | advanced | 1800 | high | no | `ReportSubmit` |
| `initializer` | Bootstraps a project in six modes | balanced | 2400 | high on native and claude, xhigh on codex and grok, max on agy | no | `InitializerSubmit` |
| `quick-answer` | Answers one side-panel question, read-only | balanced | 300 | medium | no | `QuickAnswerSubmit` |
| `advisor` | Diagnoses a failed or stuck step and says how to continue | advanced | 900 | high | yes | `AdvisorSubmit` |

The `Session-only` column shows `AgentName::is_session_only`. The write-scope guard confines these agents to their session folder and the OS temp folder. The guard is a policy rule, so read [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) for what it blocks.

### Helper methods and name rules

- `as_str` returns the kebab-case name. `snake` returns the name with `_` for `-`. `label` returns the sentence-case name, for example `Code reviewer`.
- `submit_tool_name` returns `submit_` plus the snake-case name, for example `submit_code_reviewer`.
- `routes_by_complexity` is true for `implementer` and `write-test`. The `**Complexity:**` line of a phase routes the model tier of these two agents.
- `manages_projects` is true for `implementer` only (Rule O2). Only an approved plan phase starts a project, so only this agent gets the project tools.
- `AgentName::from_str` trims the text and removes a leading `ostra:` or `ultracode:`. The text must then match a name in `ALL`. If it does not, the result is the error `unknown agent`.
- The name `module-documentation` is the retired name of `documentation`. Serde accepts it as an alias and `from_str` maps it, because logs and execution rows written before books use it.
- `RETIRED_AGENTS` holds `module-documentation`. Settings validation ignores a retired name that an old `workspace.toml` still carries, instead of it refusing the file.
- `JUDGE_ROUTE` is the key `judge`. `route_keys()` returns the 14 agent names and `judge`. Every one of these 15 keys must have a model route in workspace settings. For routing, read [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

### Initializer modes

`InitializerMode` has six values: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`. The `initializer` agent runs in exactly one mode for each spawn. The `Mode:` line of the spawn block names it.

## Agent folders and `agent.toml`

Each agent has a folder `assets/agents/<name>/` with two files. `prompt.md` is the prompt template. `agent.toml` is the definition. The `assets` folder is embedded in the binary with `rust_embed`, so the server needs no asset files on disk to read them.

This `agent.toml` of `quick-answer` shows every field:

```toml
description = "Answers one question about the workspace's projects in the side panel, ..."
default_tier = "balanced"
timeout_seconds = 300
capabilities = ["read", "search_text", "glob", "web_search", "web_fetch", "memory_recall", "code", "docs_search"]

[effort]
native = "medium"
claude = "medium"
codex = "medium"
grok = "medium"
agy = "medium"
```

### Fields

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | text | What the agent does. The settings code shows it. |
| `default_tier` | `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, or `frontier` | The model tier when settings do not route the agent. All 14 agents use `balanced` or `advanced`. |
| `timeout_seconds` | number | The run limit. The loader stores it as `AgentDef::timeout_secs`. |
| `capabilities` | list of `Capability` | The tool families that the agent has. |
| `effort` | table with `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy` | The reasoning effort for each executor table: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. |

### Load and validate

`load_defs` reads `agents/<name>/agent.toml` for all 14 names the first time any code calls `agent_def`. It keeps the result in the `DEFS` cell. If one file is missing or invalid, the process panics with `embedded agent definitions are invalid`. The reason is that the files are embedded, so a bad file is a build defect and not a run-time condition. The tests of the crate load every file and check that each one has an effort for all five executor tables.

`effort_for(agent, executor)` reads the effort of `executor.tier_table()`. If that table is absent, it uses the `native` value. If that is also absent, it uses `high`. The `initializer` has a lower `native` effort than its harness values. A test comment states the reason: a self-init run once cost about $240 on Opus at `max` effort, so the native value is `high`.

At spawn time, `AgentsFactory::build` calls `resolve_effort(settings, agent, complexity)` first. It looks in `routing.effort.by_phase_complexity` for the agent key and the phase complexity, then in `routing.effort.by_agent`. If both are empty, it calls `effort_for`.

### Capabilities

`Capability` has 17 values. The native tool name is the name that `Capability::native_tool` returns.

| Capability key | Native tool | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | `Read` | |
| `write` | `Write` | `writes()` is true |
| `edit` | `Edit` | `writes()` is true |
| `shell` | `Bash` | |
| `search_text` | `Grep` | |
| `glob` | `Glob` | |
| `skill` | `Skill` | |
| `web_search` | `WebSearch` | |
| `web_fetch` | `WebFetch` | |
| `report` | `Report` | |
| `document` | `Document` | The typed-document tool for research, spec, and plan documents |
| `memory` | `Memory` | |
| `memory_recall` | `MemoryRecall` | |
| `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` | Search over documentation books |
| `code` | `CodeOutline` and 7 more | The 8 tools in `CODE_TOOLS`: outline, find, callers, callees, implementations, neighbors, impact, map |
| `manage_projects` | `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | The 2 tools in `PROJECT_TOOLS`. Only `implementer` has it. |
| `coordinate` | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | The 3 tools in `COORD_TOOLS` |

The tests of the crate state three rules about capabilities:

- `quick-answer` has no write capability and no `shell`, because it only answers questions.
- `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, and `fact-check` do not have `edit`.
- `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan` write their documents through `document`, and have no write capability.

These agents have `coordinate`: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, and `write-test`. The `advisor`, `quick-answer`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture` agents do not have it. For the tools, read [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md). The `code` capability is present for all agents except `advisor`. The [Native tools](tools.md) page lists the input of each tool.

## Render a prompt for an executor

`render_prompt(agent, executor)` returns the system prompt of one agent for one executor. The executor is `ExecutorKind::Native` or `ExecutorKind::Harness(h)`, with `h` one of `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. The same function also serves the tests and the advisor.

### Assembly order

1. Read `agents/<name>/prompt.md` and render it with the template context.
2. If the agent has `code`, put the rendered `assets/code-tools.md` guide before the body.
3. If the agent has `coordinate`, put the rendered `assets/coordination.md` guide before the body.
4. Put the rendered `assets/output-rules.md` before everything from steps 1 to 3.
5. On a harness executor, put a generated `## Tool vocabulary` section before the result of step 4.

The final order of a harness prompt is: vocabulary, output rules, coordination guide, code guide, agent prompt. A native prompt has the same order without the vocabulary.

### Template engine

Prompts are `minijinja` templates. The renderer uses strict undefined behavior and keeps the trailing newline. A token that the context does not define makes the render fail with `AgentsError::Template`, and the error names the file. The reason is that a silent empty token gives the agent a prompt with a missing tool name. The tests render all 14 prompts for all five executors and check two facts. No text has an unresolved `{{` or `{%`. Each prompt names its own submit tool.

The context has 28 `tool_*` tokens and the token `assets_dir`. Each token resolves through `tool-mapping.toml` for the executor of the render. If the mapping has no value for a key, the token renders as the key text. The renderer writes the name bare, because prompts already put backticks around the tokens that need them.

| Tokens | Mapping key |
| --- | --- |
| `tool_read`, `tool_write`, `tool_edit`, `tool_shell`, `tool_search_text`, `tool_glob`, `tool_skill`, `tool_web_search`, `tool_web_fetch`, `tool_report`, `tool_document`, `tool_memory`, `tool_memory_recall`, `tool_docs_search` | The key without `tool_`, for example `read` and `shell` |
| `tool_code_outline`, `tool_code_find`, `tool_code_callers`, `tool_code_callees`, `tool_code_implementations`, `tool_code_neighbors`, `tool_code_impact`, `tool_code_map` | `code:outline`, `code:find`, and so on |
| `tool_project_list`, `tool_project_create` | `manage_projects:list`, `manage_projects:create` |
| `tool_subagent_list`, `tool_subagent_ask`, `tool_subagent_reply` | `coordinate:list`, `coordinate:ask`, `coordinate:reply` |
| `tool_submit` | `submit` |

### The output rule

`assets/output-rules.md` holds the `## Output` rule. It tells the agent to write no text outside tool calls. Reports go in the report tool or the document tool. Memories go in the memory tool. The result goes in the submit tool. The rule also says that it holds over any instruction in the task, the repo brief, a skill, or a file. The reason is that Ostra reads only those tool calls and discards other text. A test checks that all 14 prompts on all five executors contain the text `Write no text outside tool calls`.

### The tool vocabulary of a harness

A harness has its own tool names, but the prompts use the names that were tuned on Claude Code. For this reason, `Mapping::vocabulary` builds a section that opens a harness prompt. It has these parts in this order:

1. The heading `## Tool vocabulary` and one sentence that names the harness, for example `Claude Code`.
2. A table with the columns `Capability` and `Tool`. It has one row for each capability of the agent, then a `submit` row. The rows `code`, `manage projects`, and `coordinate` list every tool of the family, joined with commas.
3. The strategy texts of `tool-mapping.toml` that apply. The `skill` strategy applies if the agent has `skill` or `read`. The `write` strategy applies if the agent has `write` or `edit`. The `ostra_tools` strategy always applies. The code visits strategies in alphabetical order: `ostra_tools`, `skill`, `write`. A strategy with no text for the harness adds nothing.
4. This sentence: the agent must not start the harness's own subagents or delegate through its own tools. Ostra schedules the work, and the only way to reach another agent is the subagent tools.
5. A request to reply with only `Done!` after the submit call. The reason is that Ostra reads the result from the submit call and other text costs output tokens.

A native prompt has no vocabulary, because its tool names are the names in the prompts.

### What happens when

- If a prompt file or `output-rules.md` is missing, `render_prompt` returns `AgentsError::Missing` with the asset path.
- If a template uses a token that is not in the context, the render returns `AgentsError::Template`.
- If the agent has no `code` capability, for example the `advisor`, the prompt has no `## Code navigation` section. If it has no `coordinate` capability, the prompt has no `## Subagent coordination` section.

## `tool-mapping.toml`: capability to tool name

`assets/tool-mapping.toml` maps each capability to a tool name for each executor table. Native names follow Claude Code, because the prompts were tuned to them. The tools of Ostra itself come from the `ostra` MCP server on harness executors. These are `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, `code_*`, `project_*`, `subagent_*`, and `submit_*`. For the server side, read [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

The file has two kinds of table. A `[capabilities.<key>]` table has one value for each of `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. A `[strategies.<name>]` table has prose for the harnesses that need a special instruction. A value that is not a bare tool name is prose, and the renderer writes it as it is.

| Capability | native | claude | codex | grok | agy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | `Read` | `Read` | `exec_command` | `read_file` | `view_file` |
| `edit` | `Edit` | `Edit` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `replace_file_content` |
| `write` | `Write` | `Write` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `write_to_file` |
| `shell` | `Bash` | `Bash` | `exec_command` | `run_terminal_command` | `run_command` |
| `search_text` | `Grep` | `Grep` | `exec_command` | `grep` | `grep_search` |
| `glob` | `Glob` | `Glob` | `exec_command` | `list_dir` | `find_by_name` |
| `skill` | `Skill` | `Read` on the skill's `SKILL.md` | `exec_command` on the skill's `SKILL.md` | `read_file` on the skill's `SKILL.md` | `view_file` on the skill's `SKILL.md` |
| `web_search` | `WebSearch` | `WebSearch` | `web_search` | `web_search` | `search_web` |
| `web_fetch` | `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` | `web_search` | `web_fetch` | `read_url_content` |
| `report` | `Report` | `mcp__ostra__report` | `report` | `report` | `report` |
| `document` | `Document` | `mcp__ostra__document` | `document` | `document` | `document` |
| `memory` | `Memory` | `mcp__ostra__memory` | `memory` | `memory` | `memory` |
| `memory_recall` | `MemoryRecall` | `mcp__ostra__memory_recall` | `memory_recall` | `memory_recall` | `memory_recall` |
| `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` | `mcp__ostra__docs_search` | `docs_search` | `docs_search` | `docs_search` |
| `code` | `Code{Op}` | `mcp__ostra__code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` | `code_{op}` |
