### Placeholders

`Mapping::tool(capability, executor, agent)` resolves one name. It splits the key at `:` into a family and an operation, for example `code:callers`. It reads the value for the family and the executor table. Then it fills three placeholders:

- `{agent}` becomes the snake-case agent name, for example `code_reviewer`.
- `{op}` becomes the operation, for example `callers`.
- `{Op}` becomes the operation with a capital first letter, for example `Callers`.

The public function `tool_name(capability, agent, executor)` wraps this call. The spawn factory uses it to find the docs search tool of an agent.

### Strategies

| Strategy | Harnesses with text | What the text tells the agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `skill` | `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy` | The harness has no tool for Ostra skills. Read the `SKILL.md` completely with the read tool before you act. |
| `ostra_tools` | `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy` | The Ostra tools come from the `ostra` MCP server. On Claude Code, load a missing tool with ToolSearch (`select:mcp__ostra__<tool>`). On Grok Build, find it with `search_tool` and call it with `use_tool`. |
| `write` | `codex` | Write and edit files with `apply_patch`. Create a file with an `*** Add File:` hunk and change one with an `*** Update File:` hunk. |

The `skill` text gives three paths. A skill that a task or brief names has its path there. Given only a name, the path is `{repo-root}/.agents/skills/{name}/SKILL.md`, or `{repo-root}/.ostra/skills/{name}/SKILL.md` in an older project. A skill that ships with Ostra, such as `meta-author`, is at `{{ assets_dir }}/skills/{name}/SKILL.md`. The Claude Code text exists because the skill catalog of Claude Code does not scan the Ostra skill folders. The Claude Code `ostra_tools` text exists because the MCP server connects after the session starts, so its tools arrive deferred.

To add a harness tool name, change the table of that harness in the file. The tests then check the new name in every prompt.

## The assets folder and `materialize_assets`

The `assets` folder at the repo root holds all text that Ostra gives to models. `rust_embed` puts it in the binary. The folder has these parts:

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `assets/agents/<name>/` | `agent.toml` and `prompt.md` of one agent. 14 folders. |
| `assets/judges/` | 10 judge prompts: `classify`, `completion`, `feedback`, `rescue`, `resolve-review`, `route-answer`, `stakes`, `sufficiency`, `track`, and `yolo-answer`. |
| `assets/refs/` | 7 reference files. Five are `_generic`, `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, and `typescript-node`. Two are `inventory-and-profile` and `skill-archetypes`. |
| `assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md` | The one skill that ships with Ostra. |
| `assets/code-tools.md`, `assets/coordination.md`, `assets/output-rules.md` | The guides that `render_prompt` puts before an agent prompt. |
| `assets/tool-mapping.toml` | The capability map. |

### Judge prompts

`judge_prompt(name)` returns the system prompt of a judge from `assets/judges/<name>.md`. It returns `None` for an unknown name. A test checks that each of the 10 judge prompts names the `decide` tool. The spawn factory also accepts a name with the prefix `__agent:`, for example `__agent:quick-answer`. It then renders the prompt of that agent on the native executor. The runner uses this form for the quick answer. For the judges, read [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

### Stack references

`reference(name)` returns `assets/refs/<name>.md` with `{{assets_dir}}` filled in. `reference_names()` lists all 7 names. `stack_names()` returns the names of the files whose first text is `# Stack Reference:`, without names that start with `_`. The result is sorted: `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, `typescript-node`. The `_generic` file is the fallback when no stack reference matches. If a project has an empty stack, the initializer detects the stack instead. The setup screen and the workspace runtime show the stack list.

`reference_path(name)` returns the absolute path of a materialized reference. The spawn block of an initializer scout uses it for the `Stack reference:` line.

### Write the assets to disk

Harness agents cannot read the embedded files, so Ostra writes some of them to disk. `materialize_assets(dir)` does these steps:

1. Collect every embedded file under `refs/` and `skills/`. Replace `{{assets_dir}}` and `{{ assets_dir }}` with `dir`.
2. For each of the 14 agents, render the prompt for the native executor and add it as `agents/<name>.md`.
3. Compare each file with the file on disk. Write only the files whose content changed, and create parent folders.
4. Return the list of paths that it wrote.

The second step exists because of Rule O5. The advisor reads the instructions of a failed agent to learn what that step can do and what it must return. `instructions_path(agent)` returns the path of that file.

The server calls `set_assets_dir(<data_dir>/assets)` and then `materialize_assets` at start. `set_assets_dir` sets a one-time cell. It returns `false` if the cell already holds a value. Call it before any prompt render, because `reference` and `embedded_skill` cache their text with the assets path of the first call. If code never calls `set_assets_dir`, `assets_dir()` returns `<data_dir>/assets`. If the write fails, the server stops with `writing assets`.

## The `meta-author` skill

`assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md` is the only skill that ships with Ostra. `embedded_skill("meta-author")` returns its text with the assets path filled in. The initializer loads it when it generates per-repo skills. The `prompt-generation` agent loads it when it writes prompts or agents. Both read the skill shapes in `refs/skill-archetypes.md`.

The skill sets 16 writing laws. Each law governs one unit: a term, a sentence, a rule, a step, or the whole file. The agent applies all 16 laws to every section.

1. Define before reference.
2. One instruction per sentence.
3. Explicit ALL and ANY.
4. Concrete over abstract.
5. Show both sides, with a PASS and a FAIL example.
6. Explicit stop and continue.
7. Exact error codes and strings.
8. No synonyms.
9. Anchor cross-references.
10. Exhaustive enumerations.
11. A fallback for every rule.
12. Priority on conflict.
13. Constrain output formats.
14. A self-check instruction.
15. Grounding over generation.
16. Plain statement over metaphor.

The skill also has a part for each file type that it writes: a `SKILL.md` (with creation, convention, and test shapes), a subagent markdown file, and an LLM system prompt. It ends with a 17-item self-review checklist that the agent runs against its own output, and a list of anti-patterns. Law 16 exists because a metaphor adds meaning that the writer did not choose, and the reader must translate it back before the reader acts.

## The repo brief

An agent that starts with no project facts spends its first tool calls to find the build command, the skill paths, and the module layout. The repo brief gives those facts in the first message. `brief::augment(first_message, input)` appends the brief to the spawn block, and `build_brief` builds it.

The first message has this form: the spawn block, a line `---`, and then the brief parts. The brief parts follow in this order. A part with nothing to say is left out.

| Order | Heading | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `## Repo brief for <agent>` | Facts from the project profile and the inventory |
| 2 | `## Project instructions` | The text of the project's instruction files |
| 3 | `## Projects created in this session` | Facts of projects that agents created (Rule O3) |
| 4 | `## Workspace artifacts` | The visible workspace artifacts (Rule W1) |
| 5 | `## Workspace documentation` | The documentation books of the workspace (Rules B5 and B8) |
| 6 | `## Workspace instructions` | The custom instructions from settings |

### Which sections each agent gets

`sections(agent)` decides which profile sections go in part 1. The `initializer` gets none, so it never gets part 1. If the profile is missing, no agent gets part 1, but the other parts still appear.

| Agent | Sections |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer` | Commands, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `write-test` | Commands, Testing, Skills, Conventions, Modules |
| `code-reviewer` | Commands, Review, Conventions, Skills |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Commands, Testing, Modules |
| `explore` | Stack, Skills, Modules |
| `plan` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `generate-spec` | Stack, Modules |
| `documentation` | Stack, Commands, Modules |
| `system-architecture` | Stack, Modules |
| `fact-check` | Stack, Modules |
| `prompt-generation` | Skills |
| `quick-answer` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `advisor` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Modules |
| `initializer` | none |

### What each section holds

- **Stack:** the profile fields `stack`, `build_tool`, and `test_framework`.
- **Commands:** the profile commands, each as `**name**: \`command\``. The text tells the agent to use these exact strings and to substitute the `{MODULE}`, `{TEST}`, and `{PATH}` placeholders.
- **Testing:** each test type with its level command. If the type also has a single-test command that differs, the row adds `one test:` and that command. The test stage runs a whole level for regression and single tests while it writes. The rows also show `applies to`, a note, and a report location when the inventory does not state them.
- **Skills:** at most 16 rows, each with the skill name, its absolute path, and `use for <component type>` (cut to 48 characters) when the inventory does not state the component type. The skill filter is described below.
- **Conventions:** naming, the immutability keyword, and the notes of the profile that the inventory does not state. Text is cut at 190 characters, and the immutability keyword at 90.
- **Review:** the full review rule set, each rule as `**id** (severity, auto-fixable): rule`, with the rule cut at 170 characters. The set is exempt from the containment test below. The reviewer judges only against this list, so a partial list narrows what the review checks without a sign.
- **Modules:** the module-map rows that cover a path of the task. At most 10 rows.

### The containment test

The brief must not state a fact twice and must not withhold a fact. A static list of fields cannot do both, because the same profile field repeats the inventory in one repository and is the only statement of a rule in another. So the code tests each value against the text of `INVENTORY.md`. `stated_in(haystack, value)` ignores white space, so a value that wraps across lines or has padding in a table cell still counts as stated. A value of fewer than 3 characters counts as stated, because it is too short to be distinctive. The brief leaves out a value that the inventory already states.

The brief never includes the routing settings. They mean nothing to an agent, and they add tier names to its context.

### Skill rows

`skill_rows` skips a skill with an empty path. It then applies the filter of the agent:

- A skill of kind `convention` is always included.
- For `write-test`, the skill name or kind must contain `test` or `spec`.
- For `code-reviewer`, only `convention` skills remain.
- For all other agents, every skill is included.

### Module rows

`scope_hints(prompt)` scans the spawn block and the task text with the pattern `[\w.-]+/[\w./-]+`. It removes a leading `./`. It drops a hint of 3 characters or fewer, a hint that contains `ostra-`, and a duplicate. It keeps at most 40 hints. A module row matches if its glob, without `*` and a trailing `/`, has at least 3 characters and the glob and a hint contain one another. If there are no hints, the brief leaves out the module map. The reason is that the full map of a large repository is bigger than the rest of the brief together.

### Limits of the brief

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` | 3600 characters | Cap of part 1 only. The code cuts the text and adds `(brief truncated; see the inventory for the rest)`. |
| `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` | 12000 characters | Cap for each instruction file. The code cuts the text and adds `(truncated; read the file for the rest)`. |
| `MAX_SKILL_ROWS` | 16 | Skill rows in the brief |
| `MAX_MODULE_ROWS` | 10 | Module rows in the brief |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Books that the brief names. The brief adds `and N more` and tells the agent to use Glob for the rest. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` (in `ostra-core`) | 40 | Artifacts that the brief lists. The brief adds `and N more`. |

The cap `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` does not apply to parts 2 to 6. A long set of instructions does not cut the facts of the profile.

### The other parts

- **Workspace artifacts.** The brief lists each visible artifact with its size in bytes. It tells the agent to read the relevant ones and not to write in the folder, because the folder belongs to the user. An artifact `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is a skill that the agent loads by path.
- **Workspace documentation.** The brief lists each book with its `index.md` path, its projects, its section count, and a note if it has the system architecture. If the agent has the `docs_search` capability, the brief names the search tool of the executor and tells the agent to search before it reads code. Otherwise it tells the agent to read the relevant sections. The agent must check what it finds against the code, because a book describes the code when it was written. The agent must not write in the books folder, because Ostra writes the books. For the books, read [Documentation books](documentation-books.md).
- **Projects created in this session.** A created project has no inventory until its init runs. The brief takes its key, path, stack, purpose, and base requirements from the call that created it.
- **Workspace instructions.** `WorkspaceSettings::instructions_for(agent)` returns `instructions.all` and then the entry of the agent. The factory adds the absolute paths of files and artifacts that an instruction tags (Rule W3), so every executor can read them. The brief tells the agent to follow the instructions unless they conflict with its own rules, and its own rules win. For the settings, read [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

### Idempotence

`augment` returns the message unchanged if it already contains one of five headings: `## Repo brief for `, `## Project instructions`, `## Workspace artifacts`, `## Workspace documentation`, or `## Workspace instructions`. A render that runs again never stacks two briefs.

```rust
pub fn augment(first_message: &str, input: &BriefInput<'_>) -> String {
    if [BRIEF_HEADING, PROJECT_DOCS_HEADING, ARTIFACTS_HEADING, BOOKS_HEADING, INSTRUCTIONS_HEADING]
        .iter()
        .any(|h| first_message.contains(h))
    {
        return first_message.to_string();
    }
    match build_brief(input) {
        Some(brief) => format!("{}\n\n---\n\n{brief}\n", first_message.trim_end()),
        None => first_message.to_string(),
    }
}
```

### What happens when

- If the project has no profile, part 1 is absent. `augment("Task: x", ...)` then returns the message as it is when no other part has content.
- If the agent is the `initializer`, only parts 2 to 6 can appear.
- If the brief exceeds 3600 characters, the code cuts it at that length. The cut can fall inside a section.
- If a hint names a path that no module row covers, the brief has no module section.

## Project instruction files

A project can carry its own rules for coding agents. Ostra reads these files at the project root and gives their text to every agent through the `## Project instructions` part of the brief.

`project_instruction_files` (in `ostra-core`, constant `INSTRUCTION_FILES`) finds `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md`. The match ignores letter case. The result is in that order. `project_docs(repo_root)` then reads them and drops three kinds of file:

- A file that cannot be read.
- A file with only white space.
- A file that is a link to a file that the code already read, or a copy of one, because repositories often ship `AGENTS.md` as a link to `CLAUDE.md`.

The brief shows each file as `### \`path\`` and its text. It cuts a text of more than 12000 characters (`MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS`) and tells the agent to read the file for the rest. The heading tells the agent to follow the files in this project unless they conflict with its own rules, and its own rules win. The runner reads the files when it builds a spawn and passes them in `SpawnEnv::project_docs`.

## Project skills

A skill is a `SKILL.md` file that tells an agent how to do one recurring job in a project. Ostra stores the skills of a project in three places, and `skills.rs` in `ostra-server` merges them.

| Source | Folder | Origin | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project profile | The `skills` list in `.ostra/project.toml` | `Ostra` | Each `SkillEntry` has `name`, `kind`, `path`, `component_type`, and `source` (`generated`, `reused`, `adopted`, or `user`). |
| Ostra folders | `.agents/skills/` (`SKILLS_DIR`) and `.ostra/skills/` (`LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR`) | `Ostra` | New skills go to `.agents/skills`, the cross-harness standard. The older folder is still read. |
| Harness folders | `.claude/skills`, `.codex/skills`, `.grok/skills`, `.gemini/skills`, `.ultracode/skills` (`HARNESS_DIRS`) | `Harness` | Not part of the project until the user adopts them. |

### Scan

`scan(root)` returns the skill views of a project in this order:

1. One view for each profile entry, with `exists` set to false if the file is missing.
2. Each skill folder under `.agents/skills` and `.ostra/skills` that holds a `SKILL.md`, if no earlier view has the same path or name. Sorted by name in each folder.
3. Each skill folder under the harness folders.

The description comes from the front matter of the file. `frontmatter_description` reads a plain value, a quoted value, a folded value (`>`), and a literal value (`|`). It returns nothing if the file has no front matter.

### Change rules

| Action | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Name | At most 64 characters. The first character is a letter or digit. The rest are letters, digits, `-`, or `_`. The name becomes a directory name, so a name like `../x` fails. |
| Kind | One of `convention`, `creation`, `test`, `other` (`KINDS`). |
| `save` | The content cannot be empty. It cannot exceed 512 KB (`MAX_SKILL_BYTES`, 524288 bytes). The reason is that agents read the file whole. A new skill goes to `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. An existing skill is written where it is. Then `upsert_entry` changes the profile. If the profile has no entry with that name, it adds an entry with `source` `user`. If an entry exists, it keeps the old `source`, updates only `kind` and `component_type`, and fills `path` only when `path` is empty. |
| `delete` | Removes the profile entry and the skill folder in both Ostra folders. If neither exists, it fails with not found. |
| `adopt` | Copies a harness skill folder to `.agents/skills/<name>` and adds a profile entry with `source` `adopted`. It fails if the name is taken. The copy skips symbolic links, so a copy cannot reach outside the skill. |
| `get_harness` | Reads a harness skill that the user has not adopted yet, by its path. |

A change fails with a conflict if the project folder is missing or an init session runs. The reason is that the initializer writes skills, and a user change races with it. The list shows a `blocked` message for such a project, and a missing folder gives an empty skill list.

The code contains each path in the project. `in_project` resolves symbolic links and returns nothing if the path leaves the project. The reason is that skill paths come from `project.toml`, and the repository itself can supply that file. `save` also refuses a file outside `.agents/skills` and `.ostra`, and the error tells the user to use the Files tab. For the HTTP routes, read [Server API](server-api.md).

The error classes are: bad request (name, kind, empty content, size), not found (no project or skill), conflict (blocked project, name taken, path leaves the project), and internal error (disk failure).

### How an agent loads a skill

A native agent calls the `Skill` tool. It gives a `path` or a `name` (also accepted as `skill`). If it gives a `path`, the tool passes the path through `env.resolve`. That call expands a leading `~/`, resolves a relative path against the working directory, and maps a sandbox path to a host path. For a name, the tool removes a leading `ostra:`, and it refuses a name that contains `/` or `..`. Then it looks in three places, in this order:

1. The project folders: `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, then `.ostra/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
2. A workspace artifact `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
3. The embedded skills, through the skill resolver. The result path is `<assets_dir>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.

If no place has the skill, the tool returns an error that lists the two project paths and tells the agent to use the paths of the repo brief and not to guess. A harness agent has no skill tool. It reads the `SKILL.md` with its own read tool, as the `skill` strategy of `tool-mapping.toml` says.

## The spawn block and `SpawnParams`

Each spawn starts with a block of lines of the form `Label: value`. The prompts name these lines as the required invocation parameters. `crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs` has one struct for each agent and one for each initializer mode. A required parameter is a field that is not an `Option`, so code that omits it does not compile. A test renders every struct and checks that the block passes the runtime contract of its own agent.

Every struct implements `SpawnParams`:

- `agent()` and `mode()` return the agent and the initializer mode, if any.
- `common()` returns the four common lines.
- `render()` returns the block.
- `to_json()` returns the struct as JSON. The initializer structs add the field `mode`.
- `report_file()` returns the report path for the agents that write one: `implementer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, and `prompt-generation`.

### The four common lines

`Common` holds `workspace_root`, `repo_root`, `session_dir`, and `repo_key`. They render as `Workspace root:`, `Repo root:`, `Session dir:`, and `Repo key:`. Every spawn has them.

### Render rules

- A value with a line break renders as the label and a colon, then each line indented by two spaces.
- A list renders as the label and a colon, then one indented line for each item. An empty list renders nothing.
- An absent `Option` or an empty text renders nothing.
- Required lines come first, then the four common lines, then the optional lines. The agents differ in the exact order. For example, `fact-check` puts `Target`, `Target type`, `Prior findings`, `Spec file`, and `Source check` before the common lines.

### Work source

Hard rule 13 says that an agent bound to a phase declares its phase file or states why there is none. `WorkSource` has two forms. `PhaseFile` renders `Phase file:`. `NoPlan` renders `No plan:` with a reason. The `implementer`, `write-test`, and `code-reviewer` carry one `WorkSource`. The factory chooses the reason text from the session state:

| Condition | `No plan:` text |
| --- | --- |
| A revision after the user reviewed the implementation | A revision the user asked for. The request and the session context file describe it. |
| Category `verify` | A verification request: no code change is planned. |
| Category `test` | The user asked for tests directly, so no plan exists. |
| Category `docs` | The user asked for documentation directly, so no plan exists. |
| Category `prompt` | A prompt change: the pipeline has no plan tier for it. |
| Category `quick_change` | A quick change: the request names the whole edit, so research, spec, plan, and review were skipped. |
| Category `implement` on the light track | The light track: research found a contained change, so the spec and plan stages were skipped. |
| Any other case | The stakes judge rated this request low, so the plan tier was skipped. |

### Optional lines (`Extras`)

| Label | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `Research docs` | Every research document, oldest first (Rule D2) |
| `Repos in scope` | Lines `key -> path` |
| `User answers` | Lines `id question: answer` |
| `Findings` | Fix instructions, review findings, or fact-check findings, verbatim |
| `Required skills` | Skill names, joined with commas |
| `Review ledger` | The ledger file that the fix agent records FIXED or WONTFIX in |
| `Rescue context` | The stuck diagnostic and the stated fact, never a plain retry |
| `Resume instructions` | What to do after a handoff specialist finished |
| `Prior phase reports` | Earlier implementer reports that a revision builds on |
| `Context files` | Files that the agent reads first |
| `User notes` | What the user said at an earlier gate for this stage (Rule J1) |
| `New project` | The key and the planned folder of a project that the phase must create first (Rule O2) |
| free text | A note below the lines, after a blank line |

## Map a `SpawnRequest` to spawn parameters

The planner returns `Step::Spawn(SpawnRequest)`. The runner then calls `SpawnFactory::build(&req, &env)`. `AgentsFactory` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs) implements it. This part states how the request becomes parameters. For the planner, read [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md). For the runner, read [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md).

### The request

`SpawnRequest` has eight fields: `agent`, `purpose` (`ExecPurpose`), `stage`, `project`, `session_dir`, `inputs` (`SpawnInputs`), `resumes`, and `continues`. `SpawnRequest::complexity()` returns the phase complexity that routes read. It returns nothing outside a phase, and `Low` for a phase without a file. `SpawnInputs` holds every value that a spawn can need. It is a plain data struct, and the factory reads only the fields that the agent needs.

`SpawnEnv` gives the factory what is not in the request: the session state, the executor, the workspace settings, the project profile, the text of `INVENTORY.md`, the repo root, and the project instruction files.

### Build steps

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Runner
    participant Factory as AgentsFactory
    participant Params as SpawnParams struct
    participant Brief as brief::augment
    participant Render as render_prompt
    participant Config as resolve_effort
    Runner->>Factory: build(req, env)
    Factory->>Factory: choose struct from req.agent and req.purpose
    Factory->>Params: render()
    Params-->>Factory: Label: value block
    Factory->>Brief: augment(block, BriefInput)
    Brief-->>Factory: first_message
    Factory->>Render: render_prompt(agent, env.executor)
    Render-->>Factory: system_prompt
    Factory->>Config: resolve_effort(settings, agent, complexity)
    Config-->>Factory: effort, or None then effort_for
    Factory-->>Runner: BuiltSpawn
```

`BuiltSpawn` has `system_prompt`, `first_message` (block plus brief plus instructions), `spawn_block` (the block alone), `params` (the JSON), `report_file`, and `effort`. The `SpawnFactory` trait also has `agent_meta(agent)`, which returns the default tier, the capabilities, and the timeout from the `agent.toml`, and `judge_prompt(name)`.

### Agent to struct

If `req.purpose` is `ExecPurpose::Consult`, the factory builds `ConsultParams` for any agent. It has the lines `Asked by` (from `inputs.task`), `Question`, and the common four. The block reaches the run as its resume message and not as a first spawn (Rule H3). For the message flow, read [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md). Otherwise, the agent chooses the struct.

| Agent | Struct | Required lines | Source in the request |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `ExploreParams` | `Task` | `inputs.task` |
| `generate-spec` | `GenerateSpecParams` | `Task` | `inputs.task`. Optional: `Spec file` from `spec_file`, `New research docs`, `Requirement changes` from `changes`, and the extras `research_docs`, `projects_in_scope`, `answers`, and `findings`. |
| `fact-check` | `FactCheckParams` | `Target`, `Target type`, `Prior findings`, `Spec file`, `Source check` | `target` and `spec_file` are required. `target_type` is `plan` for a plan target and `spec` for any other value. `prior_findings` defaults to `none`. `source_check` is `refetch` only when the input says `refetch`, otherwise `citations`. `Research docs` from `research_docs`. |
| `plan` | `PlanParams` | `Spec file` | `spec_file` is required. `projects_in_scope`, `findings`, and `Master plan` from `inputs.target`. |
| `implementer` | `ImplementerParams` | `Report file`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` | `report_file` is required. The work source, the extras of the work kind, and `New project` when the project does not exist yet. |
| `code-reviewer` | `CodeReviewerParams` | `Phase`, `Changed files`, `Change rationale`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` | `phase_value` is required. `Review scope` is always `unstaged`, because staging keeps each review on its own change. `Review context` is `Review test code` for a test review and `Review implementation code` otherwise. `EPA report` from `epa_report`. |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | `EpaParams` | `Implementer report`, `Report file` | Both required. `Phase file` from the phase. `User notes`. |
| `write-test` | `WriteTestParams` | `Implementer report`, `EPA report`, `Report file`, and one of `Phase file` or `No plan` | The three paths are required. The work source and the extras of the work kind. |
| `documentation` | `DocumentationParams` | `Implementer reports` | `implementer_reports`. `Existing book` when the `book.json` of the session book exists on disk. `User notes`. A note `The request:` with the full request. |
| `system-architecture` | `ArchitectureParams` | `Book parts`, `Repos in scope` | `inputs.target` is the book-parts file and is required. `projects_in_scope`. `Existing book`. `User notes`. |
| `prompt-generation` | `PromptGenParams` | `Task`, `Target files`, `Report file` | `task` and `report_file` are required. `target_files` splits into lines. |
| `quick-answer` | `QuickAnswerParams` | `Question` | `inputs.question`. `Repos in scope` lists all projects of the session. `Session artifacts` is empty. |
| `advisor` | `AdvisorParams` | `Failed step`, `Problem`, `Step inputs` | Read from the `inputs.init` map by these keys. Optional keys: `Step result`, `Step context`, and `Earlier guidance` (a JSON list of texts). |
| `initializer` | One of six structs | `Mode`, and the lines of the mode | `ExecPurpose::Init { mode }` chooses the struct. A spawn without a mode fails with `initializer without a mode`. |

### Work kinds and the task note

`work_extras` copies `ledger_file`, `research_docs`, `prior_reports`, `context_files`, and `user_notes` into the extras. It then maps the work kind:

- `Fix` and `BlockerFix` put `inputs.instructions` in `Findings`.
- `Rescue` puts them in `Rescue context`.
- `Resume` puts them in `Resume instructions`.
- `Rerun` writes a note that the earlier run ended before it finished, and it repeats the instructions if there are any. If there are none, the note tells the agent to check the progress log.
- `Initial` adds nothing.

If there is no note and `inputs.task` has a value, the note is `The request: <task>`.

### Initializer modes in the spawn block

| Mode | Lines after `Mode` | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `detect` | `User focus` (optional) | `inputs.init["User focus"]` |
| `adopt` | `Source harness`, `Source runtime dir`, `Source skills dir` | The factory sets `ultracode`, `.ultracode`, and `.ultracode/skills`. |
| `scout` | `Slice`, `Slice paths`, `Stack reference`, `Scout plan` | `Stack reference` is the absolute path from `reference_path`. |
| `propose` | `Scout findings`, `Scout plan` | |
| `generate-skill` | `Skill name`, `Skill kind` (`creation`, `convention`, or `test`), `Disposition` (`generate` or `regenerate`), `Proposal`, `Scout findings` | |
| `generate-inventory` | `Generated skills`, `Reused skills` (JSON lists of `{name, kind, component_type, path}`), `Proposal`, `Scout findings` | |

Every mode accepts `Advisor guidance`, the instructions of the advisor after an earlier run of the step failed (Rule O5). If no scout ran, `Scout findings` renders `none`, because the label is still required when existing skills already cover the project.

### What happens when

- If a required input is missing, `build` returns an error such as `missing task`, `missing target`, `missing spec file`, `missing report file`, or `missing phase`. The runner then does not start the execution.
- If the run is a consult, the struct does not depend on the agent, and no required-input check for the agent runs.
- If the system prompt fails to render, `build` returns the error text of `AgentsError`.
- If settings have no effort for the agent, the effort comes from the `agent.toml`.

## Validate a spawn block with `parse_block`

`parse_block(agent, text)` checks a block against the contract of the agent and returns the values by parameter ID. The contract is a port of `subagent-parameters.json` from Ultracode. In this version, only the tests call `parse_block`. They use it to check that each struct renders a block that its own contract accepts.

### Parse rules

- Parsing stops at a line `---` or at a line that starts with `## `. The brief starts there. The reason is that text in the brief must not inject a parameter. A test puts `Task: injected` in the brief and checks that the value stays `x`.
- A line that starts with a space or a tab continues the label above it.
- The text before the first `:` must be a known label. Other lines are ignored. The first value of a label wins.
- `Target files` and `Target file` are two labels for one parameter.

### Value kinds

`PARAMS` lists 47 parameters. Each has a kind, and `check` enforces it. An empty value always fails with the error ``` `<id>` is empty ```, with backticks around the ID.

| Kind | Rule | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AbsoluteDir`, `AbsolutePath` | The path must be absolute or have a root. A rooted path with no drive, such as `/ws`, counts as absolute, because real roots on Windows have a drive and this keeps prompts portable. | `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir`, `Report file` |
| `RepoKey` | A lowercase slug (`is_project_key`) | `Repo key` |
| `Phase` | `N`, `N-tests`, or `none`, with `N` digits | `Phase` |
| `Enum` | One of the listed values | `Mode`, `Target type` (`spec`, `plan`), `Source check` (`citations`, `refetch`) |
| `Path`, `Text` | Not empty | All others |

### Required lines

Every agent needs the common four (`COMMON`). The other required lines are the ones in the table of the previous part. In addition:

- `implementer`, `write-test`, and `code-reviewer` need exactly one of `Phase file` or `No plan`. If both are present, the error is `give exactly one of \`Phase file:\` or \`No plan:\`, not both`. If neither is present, the error is `missing required parameter: one of \`Phase file:\` or \`No plan:\``.
- `initializer` needs `Mode`, and then the lines of its mode. A missing mode gives `missing required parameter \`Mode:\``. An unknown mode gives `\`Mode: <value>\` is not an initializer mode`.
- A missing line gives `missing required parameter \`<Label>:\``.

## Submit contracts

Each agent ends its run with one call to its own submit tool. The engine then reads structured data and does not scrape a final message (Hard rule 4). The tool name is `AgentName::submit_tool_name`, for example `submit_fact_check`. On a harness executor, the MCP server shows the name with the `mcp__ostra__` prefix for Claude Code. The tool description says: call it exactly once, as the last action, after every file that the agent must write exists, because the engine reads only this call.

### Result types

`submit_schema(agent)` returns the JSON schema of the result type, made with `schemars`. A test checks that every agent has a schema with `properties`, and that the `result` field of the initializer is an object.

| Type | Agents | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ExploreSubmit` | `explore` | `research_path`, `scope_covered`, `findings_summary`, `sources_retrieved`, `open_questions` (counts), `not_covered` |
| `GenerateSpecSubmit` | `generate-spec` | `spec_path`, `open_questions` (a list of `Question`), `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, `requirements`, `summary` |
| `FactCheckSubmit` | `fact-check` | `verdict` (`PASS`, `FAIL`, or `ERROR`), `target` (`spec` or `plan`), `findings` |
| `PlanSubmit` | `plan` | `spec_path`, `master_plan_path`, `phases`, `stakes`, `summary`, `step_count`, `requirement_coverage`, `clarifying_questions`, `new_projects` |
| `ImplementerSubmit` | `implementer` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck`, `handoff` |
| `CodeReviewerSubmit` | `code-reviewer` | `findings`, `security_block`, `ledger_path`, `summary` |
| `ReportSubmit` | `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck` |
| `DocumentationSubmit` | `documentation` | See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md) |
| `ArchitectureSubmit` | `system-architecture` | See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md) |
| `InitializerSubmit` | `initializer` | `status`, `summary`, `files`, `result` (a JSON object that depends on the mode), `stuck` |
| `QuickAnswerSubmit` | `quick-answer` | `answer` (Markdown), `sources` |
| `AdvisorSubmit` | `advisor` | `action` (`retry` or `escalate`), `guidance`, `reason` |

### Shared parts

- `SubmitStatus` has three values: `ok` (the default), `stuck`, and `handoff`. `stuck` means the agent hit the retry ceiling on the same failure, and it carries `StuckInfo` with `diagnostic` (the exact failing output) and `need` (the fact or decision that the agent needs). `handoff` means the agent needs a specialist, and it carries `HandoffInfo` with `specialist` (always `prompt-generation` today), `request`, `target_files`, and `resume_instructions`.
- `Severity` has four values in this order: `BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, and `LOW`.
- `FactCheckFinding` has `severity`, `location`, `element` (the ID of the claim element, such as `R3`, `AC3.2`, or `phase 2`), `claim`, and `issue`. The field comment says that the verdict is `PASS` only when no finding is `HIGH` or `MEDIUM`. `validate_submit` does not enforce this rule. `findings_text()` renders the findings for the `Prior findings:` line of the next pass, one line each as `SEVERITY, location: claim issue`, or `none` if there are no findings (Rule D3a).
- `PlanPhaseSubmit` has `id`, `deliverable`, `project`, `title`, `complexity` (`Low`, `Medium`, or `High`), `test_policy` (`Required` or `Skip`), `test_rationale`, `depends_on`, and `file`. `PlanSubmit.new_projects` lists keys of projects that do not exist yet (Rule O2).
- `ReviewFinding` has `severity`, `file`, `rule` (`SEC-BLOCK-*`, `PHASE-REQ-*`, or a review rule ID), `description`, `fix`, and `guidance` (only for `BLOCKER`). `line()` renders `[SEVERITY] file (rule) - description Fix: fix`, and adds `Guidance:` for a blocker.
- `AdviceAction` has `retry` and `escalate`. `retry` runs the step again with the guidance. `escalate` asks the user, because the fix needs a decision or a fact that no agent has.

### Validate a result

`validate_submit(agent, input)` first parses the input into the type of the agent. A parse failure returns the serde message. Four agents have more checks:

- `code-reviewer`: `security_block` must be true exactly when a `BLOCKER` finding is present.
- `documentation`: `check_documentation` checks the book part. See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md).
- `system-architecture`: `check_architecture` checks the architecture.
- `advisor`: a `retry` needs a `guidance` that is not empty.

The native executor runs these steps for a submit call, in this order:

1. `coerce_json_strings` repairs the arguments (see below).
2. If the input was not valid JSON, return `The <tool> input was not valid JSON. Call <tool> again with a valid object.`
3. Run the policy check. A denial returns ``Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>``, with backticks around the rule. The `submit` function in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs` formats it. For the policy, read [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).
4. Run `validate_submit`. A failure returns `The <tool> input is invalid: <message>. Fix it and call <tool> again.`
5. Run `doc::check_submit`. It checks the research, spec, plan, or inventory document that the result names. A failure returns the message and `Nothing was recorded.` See [Artifacts and structured documents](artifacts-and-documents.md).
6. If the status is `ok` and the run has a declared report file, the file must exist, except for the `code-reviewer`. Otherwise the call fails with a request to write the report first, because the engine reads the report at that path.
7. Other tool calls in the same model turn return `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.`

The harness bridge does steps 1, 4, and 5 for an MCP submit call. A failed check returns an error and the text `Nothing was recorded.`. A run that owes a reply to a question must reply first. See [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md). After a good call, the bridge tells the agent that the run is complete and to end its turn. For the bridge, read [Harness executors](harness-executors.md). For the native loop, read [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md).

### Repair string arguments

A weaker model often sends an object or an array argument as a string that holds JSON. `coerce_json_strings(input, schema)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/args.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/args.rs) fixes this before validation. For each top-level argument that arrived as a string, it does these checks:

- If the schema allows a string for the argument (a `string` type, an `enum`, a string `const`, or an `anyOf` or `oneOf` branch with a string), the code keeps the string.
- If the trimmed text does not start with `{` or `[`, the code keeps the string.
- If the text parses as a JSON object or array, the code replaces the string with the parsed value.
- If the text does not parse, the code keeps the string. The validation then reports the error.

The function returns whether it changed anything. The native executor, the harness bridge, and the native tool dispatcher call it. The reason for the schema check is that a string field, such as `path`, can legitimately hold text that looks like JSON.

### What happens when

- If a result is invalid, the agent gets an error message and can call the submit tool again. The engine records nothing until a call passes.
- If an agent returns `stuck`, the engine reads `diagnostic` and `need`. For the retry and rescue flow, read [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md).
- If an agent returns `handoff`, the engine starts the `prompt-generation` agent with the `request` and `target_files`, and then resumes the first agent with `resume_instructions`.
- If a run ends without a submit call, the engine has no structured result for it. For the retry rules, read [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md).

| `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` | `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` | 3600 characters for the profile part of the brief |
| `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` | `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` | 12000 characters for each instruction file |
| `MAX_SKILL_ROWS` | `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` | 16 skill rows |

| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` | 20 books |
| `BRIEF_HEADING`, `INSTRUCTIONS_HEADING`, `PROJECT_DOCS_HEADING`, `ARTIFACTS_HEADING`, `BOOKS_HEADING`, `NEW_PROJECTS_HEADING` | `ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` | The six headings of the brief. The first five make `augment` idempotent. |
| `DEFS` | `ostra-agents/src/lib.rs` | The cell that holds the 14 `AgentDef` values |
| `ASSETS_DIR` | `ostra-agents/src/lib.rs` | The one-time cell for the assets path |
| `CACHE` | `ostra-agents/src/lib.rs` | One cache in each of `judge_prompt`, `reference`, and `embedded_skill` |
| `TOKENS` | `ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs` | The 28 template tokens and their mapping keys |
| `MAP` | `ostra-agents/src/mapping.rs` | The cell that holds the parsed `tool-mapping.toml` |
| `PARAMS` | `ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs` | The 47 parameter IDs with labels and kinds |
| `COMMON` | `ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs` | The four common parameter IDs |
| `JUDGE_ROUTE` | `ostra-core/src/agent.rs` | `judge` |
| `RETIRED_AGENTS` | `ostra-core/src/agent.rs` | `module-documentation` |
| `CODE_TOOLS` | `ostra-core/src/agent.rs` | The 8 code tools and their native names |

For the limits of the other crates, read [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md) and [Reference: server, code, store, and notify limits](reference-server-limits.md).

sections.title: Agent coordination: helpers, asks, and replies
sections.summary: How agents of one session ask each other questions with SubagentList, SubagentAsk, and SubagentReply. Covers helpers, the message model, routing, delivery, caps, and how a waiting run gives back its slot.
sections.body:
Without coordination, an agent that needs a fact from another agent reads that agent's report cold. The report does not hold the reasons, the data, or the dead ends of the other agent. Agent coordination lets one run ask another run a question. The receiver answers from its own conversation. This page covers the three coordination tools, helpers, the message and delivery model, the caps, and the way a waiting run gives back its slot. The tool input shapes of other tools are on [Native tools and their limits](tools.md).

## The three coordination tools

Ostra gives three tools to the agents that have the `Coordinate` capability. Each tool has a native name, a name on Ostra's MCP server, and a name that a harness executor shows.

| Native name | MCP name | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SubagentList` | `subagent_list` | Shows the caller's subagent ID and every subagent of the session. |
| `SubagentAsk` | `subagent_ask` | Sends a question to a new helper or to an existing subagent. The caller then waits. |
| `SubagentReply` | `subagent_reply` | Answers a question that another subagent asked the caller. |

The constants `SUBAGENT_LIST`, `SUBAGENT_ASK`, `SUBAGENT_REPLY`, and `COORD_TOOLS` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs) hold these names. The function `is_coord_tool` tells the native loop which tool calls are coordination calls. The function `reply_tool` gives the reply tool name for an executor: `SubagentReply` for the native executor, `mcp__ostra__subagent_reply` for Claude Code, and `subagent_reply` for the other harnesses.

These agents have `coordinate` in their `agent.toml` capabilities: `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `implementer`, `write-test`, `code-reviewer`, and `explore`. The other agents have no coordination tools. If a run has no capability, `ostra_tools::coord::run` returns this error: the tool "is not available to this run, because its agent does not coordinate with other subagents."

## Subagents and subagent IDs

A subagent is a conversation between Ostra and one agent. Its subagent ID is the execution ID of the first run of that conversation. A run (an execution) that continues an earlier conversation keeps the same subagent ID. The fold of the session log stores this link in `SessionState.subagents`, and `SessionState::subagent_of` reads it. An execution with no entry in the map is its own subagent.

The head of a subagent is its latest run. `SessionState::head` finds it by the highest execution ID. The status of the head decides where a question to that subagent goes. A subagent is live when any of its runs has no result yet.

The subagent ID stays the same for the whole conversation, because other agents must be able to address the same conversation in later calls. A new run that starts a fresh conversation gets a new subagent ID.

## What SubagentList returns

`SubagentList` runs `SessionState::subagent_list`. It never waits and never changes the session. The result is plain text with these parts:

- The line `Your subagent ID: <id>`.
- One line for each subagent, oldest first. The line shows the ID, the agent, the run label, the project, and the status.
- The report path of the head run, when the head has one.
- A role in parentheses for the subagents that the caller works with.
- A closing line that says how to ask a subagent or start a helper.

The status is one of these values:

- `running`: the head run is live.
- `waiting on <id>`: the head asked subagent `<id>` and waits.
- `waiting on a helper`: the head waits and no answerer is known yet.
- The lowercase execution status of a finished head, for example `ok` or `error`.

The role of a partner comes from `SessionState::partners`. The caller sees `(you)` on its own line. A spec author sees `(your fact checker)`. A fact checker sees `(the author of the document you check)`. An implementer sees `(the reviewer of your phase)`, and a reviewer sees `(the implementer of the phase you review)`. A run that owes an answer sees `(asked you the question you answer)` on the line of the asker.

## What SubagentAsk does

`SubagentAsk` sends one question. The input is `AskInput`: a `message`, and exactly one of `agent` or `subagent_id`, and an optional `project`. `AskInput::parse` trims every field and drops empty optional fields.

- `agent` starts a new helper of that agent. The only helper agent is `explore`, because `HELPER_AGENTS` lists only `AgentName::Explore`.
- `subagent_id` asks an existing subagent from `SubagentList`. The question goes to the conversation of that subagent.
- `project` names the project in which a new helper works. The default is the project of the asking run. It means nothing for a `subagent_id` ask.

The tool returns immediately with a text that says the question was sent. The asking run then waits for the answer. A native run ends with the status `Waiting`. A harness run ends its turn and the process stays alive. Both cases are in [Waiting and the execution slot](#waiting-and-the-execution-slot).

### Checks that reject an ask

`SessionState::ask_event` checks the call in this order. The first check that fails returns an error to the model, and Ostra records nothing.

1. The input must parse. A message must hold 1 to `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` characters (8000) after trimming. Exactly one of `agent` or `subagent_id` must be set.
2. The calling run must be running. Otherwise the error is "This run is not running in its session any more."
3. A consult run cannot ask. It must use `SubagentReply`.
4. A run that owes an answer must answer first, because its asker waits for it.
5. The session must hold fewer than `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` asks (24).
6. For `agent`: the agent must be in `HELPER_AGENTS`, the caller must not be a helper, the caller must have started fewer than `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` helpers (3), and `project` must be a project in the scope of the session.
7. For `subagent_id`: the ID must be an execution of this session, and its subagent must not be the caller's own subagent.

The error texts tell the model what to do next. For example, the helper cap error starts with "Continue with what you have". The session cap error starts with "Continue without asking". The reason: a capped agent must keep working, and it must not retry the same ask.

## Helpers

A helper is a new `explore` run that Ostra starts for one question. The asker waits for it. When the helper ends, its findings become the answer.

When the fold sees an `AgentAsked` event with an `AskTarget::Agent` target, it adds a research task with `push_explore` and the origin `ExploreOrigin::Ask`. The task text is: the asker (with its agent and run label) "asks for this research and waits for your findings", followed by the message. The planner then spawns an `explore` run for the task. This run is a normal research run with its own research document.

The rules for helpers are:

- A helper cannot start helpers. The error tells the helper to do the research itself.
- A helper can ask an existing subagent, for example the author who asked it.
- One run can start at most `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` helpers (3). The count is per run.
- A research task from an ask never holds the rest of the session. `ExploreOrigin::loop_bound` returns `true` for it.
- If a helper fails, its failure is the answer to its asker. The planner opens no gate for it.

When the helper ends with the status `Ok`, `SessionState::coord_finished` builds the answer from the research result: the findings summary, then `Research document: <path>`, then `Not covered: <items joined by "; ">` when the helper listed items it did not cover.

## What SubagentReply does

`SubagentReply` answers a question that another subagent asked the caller. The input is `ReplyInput`: one `message`, with the same limits as an ask message.

`SessionState::reply_event` finds the question with `owed_by`. That is the ask whose `answerer` is the caller, whose answer is not set, and whose target is a subagent. If no such ask exists, the error says that no question waits for an answer, so there is nothing to reply to. The reply records an `AgentReplied` event. The event fills `Ask.answer` only when no answer exists, so the first reply wins.

The call then returns one of two `RunEnd` values:

- `RunEnd::Finish`: the caller is a consult run. The run is complete and ends with the status `Ok`.
- `RunEnd::Wait`: the caller was woken in place with a question. It goes back to waiting for the answer to its own question.

The tool result tells the model which case applies. A consult run is told to end its turn with no more tool calls.

## The message model

Every question is an `Ask` in `SessionState.asks`. The map is keyed by `MessageId` and keeps the order of asking. All state of coordination is a pure function of the session log, so a restart rebuilds it from the events. Three events carry the data. Rule IDs `H8` in the code comments name them.

| Event | Recorded when | Effect in the fold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AgentAsked` | `SubagentAsk` passes its checks. | Inserts an `Ask`. For a helper target, it also adds the research task. |
| `AgentReplied` | `SubagentReply` passes its checks. | Sets `Ask.answer` if it is empty. |
| `MessageDelivered` | The engine hands a question or an answer to a run. | For a question, sets `Ask.answerer`. For an answer, marks `Ask.answer_delivered`. |

The fields of `Ask` are `id`, `from` (the asking execution), `target` (`AskTarget::Agent` or `AskTarget::Subagent`), `message`, `at`, `explore_task`, `answerer`, `answer`, and `answer_delivered`. The `DeliveryKind` of a delivered message is `Question` or `Answer`.

The fold also derives answers that no agent wrote. `SessionState::effective_answer` returns the stored answer. If the ask has no answerer and `route` returns `Route::Failed`, it returns the failure text as the answer. The reason: an asker must never wait for a subagent that cannot answer. `coord_finished` does the same for a run that ends without answering the question it owes.

The text `answer` that the asker receives also carries the user's amendments. `amended_since` appends a note that the user added to the request during the wait. The note tells the asker to take the addition into account. Then it lists the delivered amendments that came after the ask.

## Routing a question to a subagent

`SessionState::route` decides where a question to an existing subagent goes now. It returns a `Route` value. The planner and the delivery code call it again each time the log changes, so a `Pending` question moves on when the situation changes.

### Routing decision for one ask

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["route(ask)"] --> B{"target is a subagent?"}
    B -- "no, a helper" --> P1["Pending: the helper answers when it ends"]
    B -- "yes" --> C{"head run exists?"}
    C -- "no" --> F1["Failed: no such subagent"]
    C -- "yes" --> D{"head waits on the asker?"}
    D -- "yes" --> W["WakeInPlace"]
    D -- "no" --> E{"head running or waiting, or another run live?"}
    E -- "yes" --> P2["Pending"]
    E -- "no" --> G{"head status"}
    G -- "ok, stuck, handoff" --> CO["Consult"]
    G -- "error, denied, cancelled" --> F2["Failed"]
    G -- "other" --> P3["Pending"]
```

The four `Route` values are:

- `WakeInPlace(id)`: the subagent waits on the asker, for example because a helper asks back. Ostra wakes that run with the question. The run replies and goes back to waiting.
- `Consult(id)`: the subagent ended its run. A new consult run continues the conversation of `id` and answers.
- `Pending`: the subagent is busy, or the status does not allow an answer yet. The question waits.
- `Failed(text)`: no answer is possible. The text becomes the answer of the ask. Examples are "No subagent <id> exists in this session." and "<subagent> ended with status <status>, so it cannot answer. Continue without the answer, or ask another subagent."

The reason for `Consult`: a subagent that ended its run still holds its full conversation. A consult run continues that conversation, so the answer comes from what the agent read and decided, not from a summary. A consult run changes no file. The policy denies every write for a run with `answer_only` set, with the guard `answer-only`. The denial text says to name a change in the answer instead. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).

## How the engine delivers a message

Delivery has two parts: the planner decides what must happen, and the runner hands the message to the run. The planner is a pure function of the session state, so it reads the asks and returns steps. See [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) for `next_steps` and `Step`.

`SessionState::next_delivery` builds the message for one waiting run. It returns nothing when the run does not wait. For a waiting run it picks, in this order:

1. The answer to the run's own open question, when an effective answer exists. The note says: "The answer from <who> to your question arrived. Continue your task from here." It then repeats the question and the answer.
2. A question from the subagent that the run waits on, when `route` returns `WakeInPlace` for the run. The note names the asker and tells the run to answer with the reply tool and then end its turn.

The first rule has a reason: a run that waits needs its own answer first, and a question from the subagent it waits on is a second chance to make progress.

### Delivery to a native run

A native run that asked has ended with the status `Waiting`. The fold keeps its ID in `waiting_keys`, under the purpose key of its stage. The stage does not count a paused run as finished.

1. The planner wants to spawn the stage again. In `Planner::push`, `wake_for_key` checks `waiting_keys`.
2. If the run has no message yet, `wake_for_key` returns `Some(None)` and the planner drops the spawn. The stage waits.
3. If a message exists, the planner sets `req.resumes` to the waiting run.
4. `perform_spawn` takes a slot and finds the run with the status `Waiting`. It calls `next_delivery` again. If nothing is ready, it returns.
5. Otherwise it records `MessageDelivered` and `ExecutionResumed`, and the executor resumes the same execution ID with the note as the resume message.

A waiting run wakes only with its message. A pause, a restart, or a stage spawn does not wake it with other text.

### Delivery to a harness run

A harness run keeps its terminal process alive during its wait. `Planner::coordination` finds each running harness execution that has a delivery and pushes `Step::Deliver { execution, ask, kind }`. The runner then does these steps:

1. It reads the state and checks that `next_delivery` still returns the same ask and kind. If not, it does nothing.
2. It records `MessageDelivered`.
3. It calls `deliver_mail`. The mail box holds a `waiter` and a `pending` slot for each execution. If the run already waits, the note goes to the waiter. Otherwise the note stays in `pending` until the run starts to wait.
4. The harness executor wakes from `host.wait_for_wake`, sets `owes_reply` from the wake, and types the note into the terminal with `pty.type_line`.

The pending slot covers a race: the answer can arrive before the run reaches its wait. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) for the PTY and the hook bridge.

### Consult runs

`Planner::coordination` also looks for each ask that has no answerer and no answer, whose asker waits, and whose `route` is `Consult(head)`. It spawns a run with `ExecPurpose::Consult { subagent, ask }` that continues `head`. A consult run does not start if another spawn already continues the same subagent in this planning pass. The consult run gets the header from `consult_note`: another subagent asks a question, answer from the conversation, call the reply tool, end the turn, and change no file.

### One ask to a subagent that ended its run

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Asker as Asker run
    participant Coord as Engine.coordinate
    participant Log as Event log
    participant Planner as Planner
    participant Runner as Runner
    participant Consult as Consult run
    Asker->>Coord: SubagentAsk
    Coord->>Log: AgentAsked
    Coord-->>Asker: waiting text with RunEnd::Wait
    Planner->>Log: route gives Consult
    Planner->>Runner: Step::Spawn with ExecPurpose::Consult
    Runner->>Consult: resume with consult_note
    Consult->>Coord: SubagentReply
    Coord->>Log: AgentReplied
    Planner->>Runner: spawn resumes the asker
    Runner->>Log: MessageDelivered with Answer
    Runner->>Asker: resume with the answer note
```

## Waiting and the execution slot

A run that waits for a message gives back its execution slot. The slot count limits parallel runs for the workspace through `limits.max_parallel_executions` (default `3`). Without this rule, a limit of 1 stops the session. The waiting run holds the only slot, and the run that must answer it cannot start.

The two executors give back the slot in different ways:

- **Native run:** the run ends with the status `Waiting`. The runner drops its `Slot` when the result is recorded. The wake is a new spawn of the same execution ID. `perform_spawn` calls `acquire_slot` first, so the woken run takes a slot again before it gets its message.
- **Harness run:** the process stays alive. `wait_for_wake` in `EngineHost` drops the slot, waits on the mail box, and then calls `acquire_slot` before it returns the note.

A waiting spawn checks again when a slot becomes free, and at least every 2 seconds. Each time it reads `limits.max_parallel_executions`, so a changed setting applies to waiting spawns without a restart. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for the slot and the settings.

The wait of a harness run does not count against its time limit. The executor adds the waited time to the deadline. The reason: the run did no work during the wait, because the other agent did the work.

## Caps and limits

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_HELPERS_PER_RUN` | 3 | Helpers that one run can start. Counted from the asks of that execution with an `Agent` target. |
| `MAX_SESSION_ASKS` | 24 | Asks that one session can make. The count includes helper asks and subagent asks. |
| `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` | 6 | Runs that one conversation can have before a pair loop starts a fresh run. |
| `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` | 8000 | Characters in an ask or a reply. Longer material goes in a file, and the message names its path. |
| `HELPER_AGENTS` | `[explore]` | Agents that `SubagentAsk` can start as helpers. |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | 3 | Workspace setting for parallel runs. A waiting run gives back its slot. |
| slot recheck | 2 seconds | The longest time a waiting spawn sleeps before it checks the limit again. |
| `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` | 2 | Times a harness run that owes a reply is told to reply before Ostra stops it. |

The first five names are in [`crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/coord.rs). They are also in [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md). The setting is in [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md).

## A run that owes an answer

A run owes an answer when another subagent asked it a question and waits. This is the case for each consult run, and for each run that Ostra woke in place with a question. Such a run must call the reply tool before anything ends it.

- The policy denies the submit tool with the guard `reply-first`: "Call SubagentReply with your answer instead". The check is `ctx.owes_reply` and a tool name that starts with `submit_`.
- A native run that ends its turn with no tool call gets one reminder from `reply_instruction`. If it ends again with no tool call, the run ends with the status `Ok` and no reply.
- A harness run that tries to stop gets the same instruction as a stop nudge, up to `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` times (2). After that it gives up.
- The harness bridge also refuses the submit tool when `owes_reply` is set.

The reason is in the text: the asker reads only the reply call, so an answer given as plain text is lost. If the run still ends without a reply, `coord_finished` writes a failure answer for the asker: "<subagent> ended its run with status <status> without answering. Continue without the answer, or ask again."

## What happens when

- **The asked subagent failed.** If its head ended with `Error`, `Denied`, or `Cancelled`, `route` returns `Failed`. The asker gets a text that says to continue without the answer or ask another subagent.
- **The subagent does not exist.** The ask is rejected if the ID is not an execution of the session. If the ID is valid but its head is missing, the answer is "No subagent <id> exists in this session."
- **The subagent is busy.** The question stays `Pending`. The planner routes it again after each new event, so it moves to `WakeInPlace` or `Consult` when the subagent waits or ends.
- **A helper run is interrupted or waits.** The question stays with that run. An `Interrupted` or `Waiting` helper writes no answer.
- **A helper run errors.** Ostra retries the research once. After the research is marked failed, the asker gets the failure text as its answer.
- **A run is interrupted, not a consult run.** The owed question stays with the run. A consult run that is interrupted answers with the failure text.
- **The session pauses.** `Planner::coordination` returns immediately when the session is paused, so Ostra spawns no consult run and delivers no message. `perform_spawn` also returns for a paused session.
- **The server restarts.** `Engine::recover` marks each running execution with an open ask as `Waiting`. It marks other running executions as `Interrupted`. A harness answer then resumes the harness session. The state of all asks comes back from the log.
- **The server shuts down during a call.** The call returns "The Ostra server is shutting down."
- **The workspace is not open.** The call returns "This run's workspace is not open in Ostra."
- **Two asks wait on each other.** An ask to a subagent that waits on the asker routes as `WakeInPlace`, so the two runs trade messages in place.
- **The user amends the request during a wait.** The delivered answer carries the amendment text.
- **A run makes more tool calls in the same turn as its ask.** Native runs end the turn at the ask. Other calls of that turn return "Not run: the run stopped to wait for another subagent."
- **The session is ready to complete.** The planner does not run the completion judge when `coordination_open` is true. That is the case when an ask has no delivered answer and its asker waits.

## Conversations that continue between rounds

Ostra also continues a conversation when an agent does the next round of the same work. This is a pair loop. The new run gets the same subagent ID, uses the same executor and model, and reuses the prompt cache. Its first message is the header from `continuation_note`, then the new spawn block.

`SessionState::continuation` picks the previous run for these purposes:

- a spec or a plan that already has a current document,
- a fact check of the same target,
- a review of the same phase and the same test flag,
- a fix, blocker fix, rescue, or resume run of an implement or write-test phase.

The fold starts a fresh run when any of these facts is true:

- The previous run did not end `Ok`, `Stuck`, or `Handoff` with a submit.
- The head of the conversation has a different agent, or did not end with a submit.
- A forced executor for the agent differs from the executor of the head.
- The head is a harness run with no native session ID.
- A delivered amendment came after the previous run started.
- The conversation already has `MAX_CONVERSATION_RUNS` runs (6).

The planner also keeps one live run for each conversation. If a spawn continues a conversation that has a live run, `conversation_busy` holds the spawn back.

## What the agent prompt says

Ostra adds [`assets/coordination.md`](assets/coordination.md) to the prompt of each agent that has the `Coordinate` capability. The text names the three tools with the placeholders `{{tool_subagent_list}}`, `{{tool_subagent_ask}}`, and `{{tool_subagent_reply}}`, which Ostra replaces for each executor. See [Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md).

The prompt tells the agent these rules:

- Ask only when the answer saves real work, because every question starts or wakes a model run.
- Make every other call first, because the run waits after the question.
- Write a question that stands on its own, with the need, the reason, and the file paths. The receiver does not see the conversation of the asker.
- After the ask returns, end the turn. Ostra wakes the run with the answer as the next message.
- Check an answer against the code or the cited page before work depends on it.
- Do not hand your own task to another agent. A helper researches, and the asker still does and submits its work.

The prompt also says that Ostra can continue a conversation for the next round of the same work.

## Evals for coordination

[`tests/evals/coordination.toml`](tests/evals/coordination.toml) defines the cases. `crates/ostra-server/tests/coordination_evals.rs` runs each case as a real session of a real `Engine` on a snapshot of Ostra's source, with scripted judges. A router sends each run either to the native loop on the model under test (the runs in `live`) or to a scripted actor. Thus the wakes, the consult runs, the pair-loop continuations, and the freed slots all use the real engine code, and only the live runs cost tokens.

A run address has the form `agent[:kind][#n]`. The kinds are `explore`, `spec`, `fact_check`, `implement`, `review`, and `consult`. A case can end with `stop_after` or `stop_before`. It checks asks, replies, statuses, files, submits, and a rubric. The cases are in three tiers:

| Tier | Topic | Cases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Answering | `t1-consult-answers-from-its-conversation`, `t1-consult-declines-to-edit`, `t1-consult-looks-up-what-it-does-not-remember`, `t1-woken-with-a-question-replies-then-waits` |
| 2 | Deciding whether, whom, and what to ask | `t2-implementer-asks-a-helper-for-an-external-fact`, `t2-checker-finds-and-asks-the-author`, plus the controls `t2-checker-does-not-ask-when-everything-traces` and `t2-implementer-does-not-ask-for-a-local-rename` |
| 3 | Loops of live runs | `t3-fact-check-re-pass-continues-the-checker`, `t3-review-loop-continues-both-sides`, `t3-helper-and-author-talk-back-and-forth` |

The controls check that an agent does not ask when asking costs money and gives nothing. Unit tests also cover the parse rules (`ask_needs_one_target_and_a_message` in `ostra-core`), the native wait and finish (`an_ask_ends_the_run_waiting_and_a_consult_reply_ends_it_ok`), and the engine loop (`subagents_wake_each_other_and_pair_loops_continue_conversations` in `crates/ostra-engine/tests/runner.rs`). See [Testing and verification](testing.md) for the commands.

## Where the code lives

Each layer of the coordination code has one job:

- `ostra-core`: names, input parsing, caps, the `RunEnd` and `CoordReply` types, and the fixed texts. It has no state.
- `ostra-engine` `coord.rs`: `SessionState` methods for subagents, routes, deliveries, and the event fold. Everything there is a pure function of the log.
- `ostra-engine` `runner.rs`: `Engine::coordinate` runs one tool call, appends the event, and gives the tool result. It also holds `deliver_mail` and the slot code.
- `ostra-tools` `coord.rs`: the `Coordinate` trait, the `CoordConnector` trait, and `run`, which calls the handle that the tool configuration holds.
- `ostra-server` `coord.rs`: `Coordination` implements `CoordConnector`. `ExecCoord` finds the workspace of the run by its folded root path and calls `Engine::coordinate`. It holds a `Weak` reference to the app, so a coordination handle does not keep the server alive.

The server opens a handle only when the execution has the `Coordinate` capability and runs in a session. Over MCP, the harness shim lists the coordination tools only when the run has a handle.

sections.title: Native executor and model providers
sections.summary: How Ostra runs one agent on an API key: the turn loop, token continues, compaction, tool dispatch through the policy engine, the submit call, the Anthropic and OpenAI providers, retries, streaming, the mock provider, and credentials.
sections.body:
The native executor runs one agent from start to end on a model API key. Without it, Ostra can run an agent only through an installed CLI (see [Harness executors](harness-executors.md)). The native executor sends the conversation to a model, runs the tool calls that the model returns, and repeats until the agent calls its `submit_<agent>` tool. Every tool call passes the policy engine before it runs. The executor lives in the `ostra-exec-native` crate. The `ostra-providers` crate holds the model providers behind one neutral chat interface.

This page covers:

- The agent loop and its limits.
- Compaction and context windows.
- Tool-call dispatch and the submit call.
- Resume from a stored transcript.
- The Anthropic and OpenAI providers, streaming, and retries.
- Provider credentials and the provider registry.
- The scripted mock provider.

The tools themselves are on [Native tools and their limits](tools.md). The policy rules are on [Policy engine](policy-guards.md). The sandbox is on [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

## Start of a native run

The type `NativeExecutor` implements the `Executor` trait. Its constructor `NativeExecutor::new` takes the provider registry (`Providers`), a `SkillResolver`, and an optional `CodeNav`. The builder methods `with_mcp`, `with_manage`, and `with_coord` add the MCP, manage, and coordination connectors.

The method `run` takes an `ExecutionSpec`, an `ExecutionHost`, and a `CancellationToken`. It races three things with `tokio::select!`: the run itself, the cancel token, and a timer set to `spec.timeout_secs` (at least 1 second).

The run then does these steps in order:

1. Resolve `spec.route.model` (written `provider:model`) to a provider with `Providers::for_model`.
2. Open the MCP tools, when an MCP connector exists. Each note from the connector becomes a `Status` delta.
3. Build the `ExecutionPolicy` from the project profile (see [Policy inputs](#policy-inputs-from-the-project-profile)).
4. Build the `ToolEnv` and the sandbox (see [Sandbox for each run](#sandbox-for-each-run)).
5. Build the tool list (see [Tool list for the model](#tool-list-for-the-model)).
6. Build the first messages: the first user message, or the rebuilt transcript on a resume.
7. Run the turn loop.

### What happens when the run cannot start

- If the provider has no key, the run fails with this text: ``The `<provider>` provider has no API key. Set its key in the environment or the OS keychain.`` The check covers only the names `anthropic` and `openai`.
- If the model string is not `provider:model` or the provider name is unknown, the run fails with `Cannot run model `<model>`: <error>`.
- If the sandbox cannot start (scratch directory, egress proxy, or decoy files), the run fails with the cause.

Each failure sets the execution status to `Error`, emits a `Status` delta with the message, and returns the usage so far.

## Timeout and cancel

The run ends with `Cancelled` when the cancel token fires and with `Error` when the timer fires. Both cases do the same cleanup. The executor cancels an inner token that every model call and every tool call watch. Then it waits up to `CLEANUP_GRACE` (3 seconds) for the run future to stop its tools. The result carries the usage that the run counted.

A timeout returns the error text `timed out after <N> s` and emits a `Status` delta `Timed out after <N> s.` A cancel emits the `Status` delta `Cancelled.`

The timer covers the whole run, including the time that the run waits for a user to answer a permission ask. The test `cancel_is_immediate` shows that a cancel stops a `sleep 30` Bash command in under 5 seconds.

## Turn loop

A turn is one model request and the tool calls that follow it. The loop runs at most `MAX_TURNS` (400) turns. If the run reaches that count without a submit call, it fails with `The run passed 400 model turns without calling <submit tool>.` The cap stops a loop that never submits.

Each turn builds a `ChatRequest` with these fields:

- `system`: one `SystemBlock` that holds the agent prompt, marked for the prompt cache.
- `tools`: the tool list.
- `server_tools`: the provider tools that the run uses.
- `effort`: `spec.effort`.
- `max_tokens`: the output limit of the model from the models.dev catalog, or `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` (32,000) when the catalog does not list the model. The request asks for the whole limit, so no effort level is cut short. The user chose the effort and agreed to what it spends.
- `tool_choice`: `Auto`.

After the response arrives, the loop does these steps:

1. Compute `context_tokens` as `input_tokens + cache_read_tokens + cache_write_tokens + output_tokens`. This is the size that the next request starts from.
2. Emit a `Turn` delta with the usage of this response and the ids of its tool calls. Then emit a `Usage` delta with the running total. The `Turn` delta comes before the `ToolCall` deltas, so each response reports its own cost first.
3. Keep the text of the response as `final_text` when the text is not blank.
4. Record the assistant message with `host.record_message` and add it to the message list.
5. Branch on the stop reason.

### Turn flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Start turn"] --> B{"Cancelled?"}
  B -- yes --> Z1["Return Cancelled"]
  B -- no --> C{"Context at 95 percent and last message is from user?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Compact"]
  C -- no --> E["Send chat request"]
  D --> E
  E --> F{"Stop reason"}
  F -- "pause_turn" --> A
  F -- "refusal" --> X["Fail with refusal text"]
  F -- "max tokens, no tool calls" --> G["Add continue message, 3 times at most"]
  G --> A
  F -- "no tool calls" --> H{"Reminded before?"}
  H -- no --> I["Send submit reminder"]
  I --> A
  H -- yes --> J["Return Ok without submit"]
  F -- "tool calls" --> K["Run tools"]
  K --> L{"Submit accepted?"}
  L -- yes --> M["Return result"]
  L -- no --> A
```

### Stop reasons

- **`PauseTurn`:** a server-side tool loop paused. The loop starts the next turn at once. The assistant turn is already in the message list, so the provider resumes the loop.
- **`Refusal`:** the run fails with `The model refused to continue (category <c>): <text>`. The category appears only when the provider names one.
