- **`MaxTokens` with no tool call:** the loop adds the user message `You reached the output limit. Continue from exactly where you stopped.` It allows `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` (3) such continues. A fourth cut-off fails the run with `The model kept hitting its output limit without finishing.`
- **No tool call:** the loop sends one reminder. If the agent owes a reply to another agent (`ctx.owes_reply`), the reminder tells it to call the reply tool. Otherwise the reminder reads `Call <submit tool> now with your result. The engine reads only that call, so a result given in text is lost.` If the next response again has no tool call, the run ends with status `Ok`, no `submit` value, and the last text as `final_text`. The engine then decides what to do with a run that has no submit.
- **Tool calls:** the loop runs the tools and adds their results as a user message.

A failed model call (after the retries in [Retries](#retries)) ends the run with `The model call failed: <error>`. A cancel during the call ends it with `Cancelled`.

## Compaction and context windows

Compaction replaces the whole conversation with a summary when the context is nearly full. Without it, a long run reaches the context window of the model and fails. The window size comes from the models.dev catalog (`ostra_core::pricing::context_window`). If the catalog does not list the model, the loop uses `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200,000 tokens). Until the server installs a catalog, every model counts as unlisted.

### When compaction starts

The loop compacts before a request when all three conditions hold:

- The estimated size of the next request is at least `COMPACT_AT` (0.95) times the window.
- The last message is a user message. This means no tool call is open, and compaction needs that.
- No earlier compaction failed, or the size grew by at least `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` (0.02) of the window since that failure.

The size estimate is the `context_tokens` of the last response plus an estimate for the messages added after it. The estimate is the character count divided by 4 (`estimate_tokens`). The growth rule exists because each compaction try sends the whole conversation, which costs money.

### What compaction does

1. The loop emits the `Status` delta `Compacting the conversation: about <tokens> of <window> context tokens used.`
2. The loop calls `Provider::compact` with the request and `COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS`. The instructions tell the summarizer to keep the task and every requirement, the files that it read, the files that changed, the decisions, the failed commands, what is left, and the exact next step.
3. The loop adds the usage of the summary call to the run total.
4. If a summary returns, the loop appends the user text `AFTER_COMPACTION` to the summary message. The text tells the model to continue from the next step and to read a file again when it needs the content. The loop stores the new window as a message with the role `compaction` (`COMPACTION_RECORD`) and replaces the message list with it.
5. If no summary returns, the loop emits `Compaction returned no summary, so the run continues without it.` and remembers the size. The run continues with the full conversation.

### What happens when compaction fails

- A provider error other than a cancel emits `Compaction failed, so the run continues without it: <error>` and sets the retry size. The run does not fail.
- A cancel during compaction ends the run with `Cancelled`.
- A summary that stopped for any reason other than a normal end counts as no summary. The test `a_compaction_without_summary_is_not_retried_every_turn` shows one ask for two turns near the limit.

### How each provider compacts

| Provider | Method | Summary form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anthropic, model with `compaction` support | A request with `compaction: {type: "summarize", instructions}` and the beta `compact-2026-09-04` | A signed `Compaction` block in an assistant message |
| Anthropic, other models | `compact_on_client` | A `Compaction` block with text only |
| OpenAI | `POST /v1/responses/compact` (the instructions are not sent) | Kept messages as text and an encrypted `compaction` item |

The function `compact_on_client` adds the instructions as a last user turn, so the cached prefix stays the same. It sets `tool_choice` to `None` and uses the text answer as the summary. It accepts the answer only when the stop reason is `EndTurn` and the text is not blank. A cut-off summary is not used.

Anthropic and OpenAI both fall back to `compact_on_client` when the compaction request returns `InvalidRequest`. A compatible gateway or a newer model can lack the compaction feature.

A signed or encrypted compaction block goes back verbatim to the provider that made it. Any other provider gets the `summary` text. The Anthropic provider adds the compaction beta header when the request holds a signed Anthropic block.

## Tool list for the model

The loop builds the tool list once, before the first turn. The list holds these tools, in this order:

1. The tools that `ostra_tools::definitions(capabilities)` returns for the agent.
2. The document tool of the agent, when the agent has the `Document` capability.
3. The MCP tools that the MCP connector opened.
4. The submit tool (`spec.agent.submit_tool_name()`). It is the only tool with `cache: true`. If `spec.submit_schema` is not null, it replaces the default input schema.

The provider decides which server-side tools it offers (`Provider::server_tools`). Anthropic offers `web_search` and `web_fetch`. OpenAI offers `web_search` only. The run uses `web_search` when the provider offers it and the agent wants it. The run uses `web_fetch` on the server only when the provider offers it and the agent has the `WebFetch` capability. In that case the loop removes the local `WebFetch` tool from the list. For OpenAI, the local `WebFetch` tool stays.

## Tool-call dispatch

The method `run_tools` processes the tool calls of one response in order. It returns one result block for each call.

### Groups of calls

- **Run together:** `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and each code tool. A run of such calls next to each other in one response runs at the same time (`join_all`). These tools only read.
- **Run one at a time:** every other tool, such as `Write`, `Edit`, and `Bash`. The order of the model is kept, because one call can change what the next call reads.
- **Coordination tools:** the native tools `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, and `SubagentReply`. The function `ostra_core::coord::is_coord_tool` tests for these names. The lowercase names `subagent_list`, `subagent_ask`, and `subagent_reply` belong to the MCP server of Ostra, not to the native loop. The native tools run one at a time and can end the run (see [Coordination tools end the run](#coordination-tools-end-the-run)). The tools are on [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md).
- **Submit call:** the call whose name is the submit tool name. It ends the run when it passes the checks.

### Steps of one tool call

The method `tool_end` does these steps for each call:

1. Turn relative paths and the Bash working directory into absolute ones (`canonical_call`). The policy check, the user approval, and the tool then all see the same target.
2. Emit a `ToolCall` delta and add 1 to `usage.tool_calls`.
3. If the input holds the key `__invalid_json`, return an error result and do not run the tool. The provider sets this key when the streamed JSON did not parse. The message text is in [What happens when](#what-happens-when).
4. Pass the current YOLO state of the host to the policy (`policy.set_yolo`), then call `policy.check`. Emit the decision as a `Policy` delta.
5. Act on the decision (see [Policy decisions](#policy-decisions)).
6. Run the tool with `ostra_tools::execute`. Output chunks reach the host as `ToolOutput` deltas during the run of the tool.
7. For `Bash`: repair any git metadata that the command changed, and add the duration to `usage.build_ms` when the command is a build or test command.
8. Call `policy.observe` and apply each observation to the result text (see [Observations after a tool](#observations-after-a-tool)).
9. Emit a `ToolResult` delta and return the result block.

The `ToolResult` delta carries the result cut to `EMIT_LIMIT` (8 KB, 8192 bytes). The model gets the full text. The cut keeps the Activity log small. If the tool returned a diff, the delta shows the text and the diff.

### Policy decisions

- **Deny:** the result is an error with the text ``Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>``. The model sees the text and can change its plan.
- **Ask:** the executor calls `host.ask_permission` and waits for the user. `AllowOnce` runs the call. `AlwaysInWorkspace` adds a session allow rule when the policy can suggest one, then runs the call. `Deny` returns the error `The user denied this call (<reason>). Continue without it, or explain in your report why it is needed.`
- **Allow:** the tool runs.

In YOLO mode the host reports `yolo() == true`, and the policy does not return Ask. The test `yolo_skips_asks` shows no ask and a written file. The rules of the policy are on [Policy engine](policy-guards.md). The meaning of YOLO is on [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

### Observations after a tool

The policy returns observations for a finished call. The executor handles two kinds:

- `AppendNote`: add the note to the result text after a blank line.
- `RecallLessons { query }`: open the lesson memory (`MemoryStore`), recall up to 5 lessons for the query, and append them as a numbered list headed `Lessons recorded earlier that may apply to this failure:`. This happens after a streak of failed builds. The test `build_streak_recalls_lessons` covers it.

When a Bash command planted git metadata that the sandbox forbids, `repair_git_dirs` undoes it. The executor appends a note to the result and emits a `Policy` deny delta for the `GIT_METADATA` guard, so the event counts as a containment signal.

### Coordination tools end the run

A coordination tool returns a `RunEnd` value. `Continue` keeps the loop going. `Wait` ends the run with status `Waiting`, because the agent asked another agent and waits for the answer. `Finish` ends the run with status `Ok`, because a consult run gave its answer. After a coordination tool ends the run, each later call in the same response gets the result `Not run: the run stopped to wait for another subagent.` The submit value of the run is the payload that `ostra_core::coord::end_payload` builds from the message. A tool that returned an error never ends the run. See [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md).

## Submit call

The submit call is the way an agent gives its result to the engine. The engine reads only this call, so a result in plain text is lost. The tool name is `submit_<agent>` (for example `submit_explore` and `submit_implementer`). Typed contracts for each agent are on [Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md).

Before `run_tools` checks the submit call, it converts string values that hold JSON into JSON values where the schema asks for them (`coerce_json_strings`). The `submit` method then applies these checks in order:

1. The input must not hold `__invalid_json`. If it does, the result says `The <name> input was not valid JSON. Call <name> again with a valid object.`
2. The policy must not deny the call. The submit call never asks the user.
3. `validate_submit` must accept the input against the schema of the agent. A failure returns `The <name> input is invalid: <error>. Fix it and call <name> again.`
4. `doc::check_submit` must accept the structured document of the agent (research, spec, plan, or profile). A failure returns the error plus `Nothing was recorded.`
5. If the status is `ok` and the run has a report file, the file must exist. The error reads `Write your report to <path> before you call <name>, because the engine reads the report at that path.` The code reviewer is the exception: it has no report check.

A failed check returns an error result, and the loop continues. The agent can fix the input and call again. The test `invalid_submit_is_retried` covers this.

If all checks pass, the executor emits the result `Result received.` and returns it as the tool result. Every other call of the same response gets `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.` The run ends with the status from the input field `status`: `stuck` gives `Stuck`, `handoff` gives `Handoff`, and any other value gives `Ok`. The input itself becomes `ExecutionResult.submit`.

## Resume from a stored transcript

A resume starts a run from the messages that an earlier run stored. The executor reads them with `host.transcript(resume.from)`. The function `stored_messages` rebuilds them with these rules:

- It reads the roles `user` and `assistant`. It skips blocks that do not parse and messages with no content.
- It merges adjacent messages of one role, because a resume that stopped after a user turn stores its note as a message of its own.
- A record with the role `compaction` replaces all messages before it with the stored window.

The function `resume_turn` then builds the next user turn. If the last message is an assistant message, each tool call that it left open gets the error result `Interrupted: this call did not finish.` The turn ends with the note of the resume, or with `The previous run was interrupted. Continue from where it stopped.` when no note exists. If the transcript is empty, the run starts from the first message of the spec.

The executor decides which messages to record (Rule P2):

- **Resume in place** (`resume.from` equals the id of this execution, and the transcript is not empty): the executor records only the new turn. The earlier prefix is the same, so the prompt cache hits it.
- **Resume from another execution:** the executor records every message in the new execution, so its transcript is complete.

The public function `rebuild_transcript` does the same rebuild for callers outside the loop.

## Streaming to the Activity log

The provider streams events to the executor during the response. The executor handles three kinds: `TextDelta`, `ThinkingDelta`, and `ServerToolUsed`. The other kinds (`ToolUseStarted` and `ToolInputDelta`) exist for other consumers.

A `Coalescer` joins the small deltas, so the Activity log shows readable chunks and not one row for each token. It sends a `Text` or `Thinking` delta when the buffer reaches `FLUSH_AT` (160 bytes), when the buffer ends with a newline, or when the kind changes from text to thinking or the reverse. It also sends the rest of the buffer when the response ends or when a server tool runs. A server tool emits the `Status` delta `<name>: <summary>`, for example `web_search: <query>`.

## Policy inputs from the project profile

The function `policy_inputs` reads the project profile (`paths::project_profile`) and lists the commands that the policy treats as build commands and test commands. The build list holds `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck`. The test list holds `test` and `test_one`. The function drops blank values and the placeholder value that is one em dash character (U+2014). If the profile does not load, both lists are empty.

The policy also gets the read-only MCP tools of the opened MCP servers, so it can allow them without an ask.

## Sandbox for each run

The function `sandbox_for` reads the global config at the start of each run. Thus a change to the `[sandbox]` table applies to the next run and not to a run in progress. The workspace mode, when the workspace sets one, replaces the global mode. Every Bash call of the run shares one egress proxy and one set of decoy files, and both report to the host.

If the decision is `Sandboxed`, the executor creates a scratch directory (the `/tmp` of the sandbox) and a `Profile`. The `Scratch` value removes the directory when the run future ends or drops. If the decision is `Unsandboxed`, the run continues. When a warning exists, the executor emits the `Status` delta `Bash runs without a sandbox. <warning>` and logs the warning once for the process. The sandbox rules are on [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

### Credential variables that agent commands do not inherit

The executor also removes credential variables from the environment of agent commands. The function `mcp_secret_vars` returns the full set that `ostra_core::config::credential_env_names` builds from the global config and the MCP servers of the workspace. The set holds three groups:

- The provider variables: `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV` and the `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, and `base_url_env` names of each configured provider.
- The bridge variables of `BRIDGE_ENV`.
- The `oauth.client_secret_env` name of each MCP server of the workspace.

The function returns an empty list when `ctx.workspace_root` is empty, because it cannot read `workspace.toml` without a workspace. The executor passes the list to `ToolEnv::with_scrub_env`. The `ToolEnv` also starts with the global names of `credential_env_names`, so a global provider name is removed even for an empty list. The Bash tool removes each name of the list, and every inherited variable that starts with `OSTRA_`, from the child process. The list is the same set that [Provider credentials](#provider-credentials) names.

## Anthropic provider

The `Anthropic` provider calls the Messages API at `<base URL>/v1/messages` with `stream: true` and reads the answer as server-sent events. The default base URL is `https://api.anthropic.com` (`DEFAULT_BASE_URL`). The provider removes a trailing slash from a custom URL.

### Request headers

- `x-api-key` carries the key. When the key is a bearer token (see [Provider credentials](#provider-credentials)), the provider sends `Authorization: Bearer` instead.
- `anthropic-version` is `2023-06-01` (`API_VERSION`).
- `accept` is `text/event-stream`.
- `anthropic-beta` lists the beta flags that the request needs, joined with commas. It is absent when no flag applies.

The HTTP client has a connect timeout of 20 seconds and follows no redirects. Ostra follows no redirects because a redirect to another host can receive the key header.

### Beta flags

| Constant | Value | When the request adds it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `COMPACT_BETA` | `compact-2026-09-04` | A compaction request, or a message that holds a signed Anthropic compaction block |
| `FALLBACK_BETA` | `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` | The request sets `fallbacks: "default"` |
| `INTERLEAVED_BETA` | `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14` | A budget-thinking model that supports interleaving, with at least one client tool, and thinking enabled |
| `WINDOW_BETA` | `model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26` | Models before Claude 4.5. Without it, input plus `max_tokens` past the window fails validation. |

### Model capabilities

The function `caps` maps a model id to its capabilities. A dated snapshot such as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` counts as the same model: `is_model` accepts the suffix `-` plus 8 digits.

| Models | Thinking | Effort | Forced tool choice | Server-side fallbacks | Server-side compaction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-mythos-5-1`, `claude-opus-5-5` | adaptive | all levels | no | yes | yes |
| `claude-opus-5` | adaptive | all levels | yes | yes | yes |
| `claude-sonnet-5-5` | adaptive | all levels | no | no | yes |
| `claude-fable-5`, `claude-mythos-5`, `claude-opus-4-8`, `claude-opus-4-7`, `claude-sonnet-5` | adaptive | all levels | yes | no | yes |
| `claude-opus-4-6`, `claude-sonnet-4-6` | adaptive | `xhigh` becomes `high` | yes | no | yes |
| `claude-opus-4-5` | budget | `low`, `medium`, `high` | yes | no | no |
| `claude-haiku-4-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, `claude-sonnet-4`, `claude-3` (prefix match) | budget | none | yes | no | no |
| Any other model id | adaptive | all levels | no | no | yes |

An unknown model id gets the surface that every current model accepts, because the build assumes that an unknown id is a newer model. The older models match by prefix, longest first, so `claude-sonnet-4-5` is not read as `claude-sonnet-4`. Haiku 4.5 and `claude-3` cannot interleave thinking with tool calls.

### Thinking and effort

- **Adaptive models:** the body sets `thinking: {type: "adaptive", display: "summarized"}` and `output_config.effort`. When the request forces a tool call, the body has no `thinking` field.
- **Budget models:** the body sets `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens}` unless a tool call is forced. The budget is a share of the output limit of the model: `medium` is 1/8, `high` is 1/4, `xhigh` is 1/2, and `max` is the limit minus `ANSWER_RESERVE` (16,000 tokens). `low` sets no thinking. Without interleaving, the budget cannot pass `max_tokens` minus 16,000, because the budget must stay below `max_tokens` and an answer can be a whole file that a tool call writes. A budget under `MIN_BUDGET` (1,024 tokens, the smallest value that the API accepts) is dropped. With interleaving, the budget spans the whole turn and can pass `max_tokens`.

### Output limit

The body sets `max_tokens` to the smaller of the request value and the output limit that models.dev lists for the model. If the catalog does not list the model, the request value stands. The native loop asks for the whole limit, so the request value and the limit agree for listed models.

### Forced tool choice

The provider sends `tool_choice` as `auto`, `none`, `any`, or `tool` with a name. When the request forces a call (`Any` or `Tool`) and the model rejects forced calls, the provider downgrades the choice to `auto`. The judge call `structured` relies on this and sends one reminder (see [Structured decisions for judges](#structured-decisions-for-judges)).

### Prompt cache marks

Every mark uses a TTL of 1 hour (`cache_mark`). A run can pause for more than 5 minutes (a long build or a permission ask). A mix of TTLs needs the longer entries first, so the provider uses one TTL. The provider marks these places:

- The system blocks that have `cache: true`. When more than two have it, the last two get the mark. When none has it, the last system block gets the mark.
- The last tool in the list. In the native loop this is the submit tool.
- The last block of the most recent user message, when the block is text or a tool result.

### Server tools and fallbacks

The provider sends the server tools `web_search_20250305` and `web_fetch_20250910`. It uses these versions on purpose: the 20260209 versions run inside code execution, and their failures cost one turn each. All client tools carry `eager_input_streaming: true`.

When a model supports server-side fallbacks and the request allows them (`refusal_fallback`, true by default), the body sets `fallbacks: "default"`. If a fallback happens in the middle of an output, `strip_before_fallback` removes the declined part. It drops thinking, tool use, and unpaired server tool use before the last fallback marker, so the executor neither runs nor echoes the declined partial.

### Stop reasons and usage

The provider maps the API stop reasons like this: `end_turn` and `stop_sequence` give `EndTurn`, `tool_use` gives `ToolUse`, `max_tokens` and `model_context_window_exceeded` give `MaxTokens`, `pause_turn` gives `PauseTurn`, `refusal` gives `Refusal`, and any other value gives `Other`.

The provider reads `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and the 1-hour part of the cache writes. It computes `cost_usd` with `pricing::cost`, which adds a fee for each web search. A compaction request reports zero tokens at the top level and bills its summary call in `usage.iterations`, so the provider adds those entries to the usage.

## OpenAI provider

The `OpenAi` provider calls the Responses API at `<base URL>/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The default base URL is `https://api.openai.com`. The client has the same 20-second connect timeout and no redirects as the Anthropic client. The provider always sends the key as `Authorization: Bearer`.

The provider runs stateless: the body sets `store: false`, and the full conversation goes in `input` on each request. It converts each block like this:

- A user text block becomes a `message` item with `input_text`. An assistant text block becomes a `message` item with the text.
- A tool use becomes a `function_call` item with the arguments as a JSON string. A tool result becomes a `function_call_output` item. An error result gets the prefix `Error: ` unless it already starts with `Error`.
- A `reasoning` block from OpenAI goes back as a `reasoning` item with its `encrypted_content`. Blocks of other providers are dropped, and so are thinking blocks.
- A compaction block from OpenAI goes back verbatim. Any other compaction block becomes a user message with its summary.

The system blocks join with a blank line into the `instructions` field. OpenAI has no prompt-cache marks in the request.

A model counts as a reasoning model when its id starts with `gpt-5`, `gpt-6`, or `o`. For such a model the body sets `reasoning: {effort, summary: "auto"}` and `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`. The effort string is the `Effort` name (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`) with no mapping. The body sets `max_output_tokens` to `max_tokens`, `parallel_tool_calls` to true, and `tool_choice` to `auto`, `required`, `none`, or the named function. The server tool is `web_search`. OpenAI has no server-side fetch, so the agent keeps its local `WebFetch` tool.

The provider maps the final event to a stop reason:

- `response.incomplete` with `max_output_tokens` gives `MaxTokens`, with `content_filter` gives `Refusal`, and any other reason gives `Other`.
- `response.completed` gives `Refusal` when a message part is a refusal, `ToolUse` when the output has a tool call, and `EndTurn` otherwise.

The usage subtracts the cached tokens and the cache write tokens from `input_tokens`, so `input_tokens` never counts a cache token twice.

The event `response.failed` becomes a `Server` error with status 500. The stream event `error` maps by code: `rate_limit_exceeded` gives `RateLimited`, `server_error`, `server_is_overloaded`, and `slow_down` give `Server`, and any other code gives `InvalidRequest`.

## Streaming and tool input

Both providers read the response as server-sent events (SSE). The function `sse::json_events` turns the HTTP body into a stream of JSON values. It skips empty data and the `[DONE]` sentinel. A bad JSON payload becomes a `Decode` error. A transport error becomes a `Network` error.

Each provider has an `Accumulator` that builds the response from the events. It sends `StreamEvent` values to the caller during the read. The provider stops reading at `message_stop` (Anthropic) or at `response.completed` and `response.incomplete` (OpenAI). If the stream ends before that event, the provider returns a `Network` error.

A tool call arrives as JSON text in pieces. When the pieces do not parse as JSON at the end, the provider builds the input `{"__invalid_json": "<raw text>"}` (`INVALID_INPUT_KEY`). The executor answers such a call with an error result and does not run the tool. An empty input becomes `{}`.

## Retries

The function `retry::run` repeats a provider call when it fails with a retryable error. Both providers use it for `chat` and for compaction requests. It retries only when output has not started. Output has started when the stream sent its first content block or output item. After that, a retry sends the same text twice and runs a tool twice.

### Retry rules

- A retryable error is `RateLimited`, `Overloaded`, `Server`, or `Network` (`ProviderError::is_retryable`).
- If output has started and the error is retryable, the call fails at once with `Stream` (`stream failed: <error>`). The loop does not retry `Stream`.
- `Auth`, `InvalidRequest`, `Decode`, and `Cancelled` are never retried.
- The default `RetryPolicy` allows `max_retries` of 4, so a call runs at most 5 times.
- A cancel stops the call or the wait at once with `Cancelled`.

### Delay

The delay for attempt `n` (counting from 0) is `base_delay` (1,000 ms) times 2 to the power `n`, with the power capped at 16. The result is capped at `max_delay` (60 seconds). Then the delay is multiplied by a jitter between 0.5 and 1.0, taken from the sub-second part of the clock. If the error carries a `Retry-After` value, the wait is at least that many seconds. The provider reads the `Retry-After` header as seconds and rounds up.

### How HTTP statuses map to errors

| Status | Error | Retried |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 401, 403 | `Auth` | no |
| 429 | `RateLimited` | yes |
| 529 | `Overloaded` | yes |
| Any status with the error type `overloaded_error` | `Overloaded` | yes |
| 408, 409, 500 to 599 | `Server` | yes |
| Any other status | `InvalidRequest` | no |

The error message is `error.message` from the JSON body. If the body has none, the message is the first 300 characters of the body. A network error drops the URL from its text, because the URL can hold a secret.

An error event inside an Anthropic stream maps by type: `overloaded_error` gives `Overloaded`, `rate_limit_error` gives `RateLimited`, `api_error` gives `Server`, and any other type gives `InvalidRequest`. The tests `retries_then_succeeds`, `no_retry_after_output_started`, and `gives_up_on_non_retryable` cover the rules. `RetryPolicy::fast` gives delays of 1 to 5 ms for tests.

## Provider credentials

The function `lookup_key` finds the key for one provider. It tries these sources in order and stops at the first value that is not blank:

1. The environment variable that `api_key_env` names. The key is sent as an API key. The source label is `env:<NAME>`.
2. The environment variable that `auth_token_env` names. The key is a bearer token. The source label is `env:<NAME>`.
3. The API key saved from the browser. The source label is `saved`.
4. The auth token saved from the browser. It is a bearer token. The source label is `saved`.
5. The OS keychain entry with the service `keychain_service` and the user name equal to the provider name. The source label is `keychain`. This step runs only when `keychain_service` is set.

The environment wins over saved values. Thus an operator can override a key that a user saved in the browser. The test `environment_overrides_saved_credentials` covers this order.

The default config has two providers:

| Provider | `api_key_env` | `auth_token_env` | `base_url_env` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | none | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` |

`DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV` lists these five variable names. The function `credential_env_names` returns a set of every variable that holds a credential. The set holds `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`, the `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, and `base_url_env` names of each provider in the global config, the names in `BRIDGE_ENV`, and the `client_secret_env` of each MCP server. Ostra removes these variables from the environment of agent processes. The native executor builds the same set for Bash (see [Credential variables that agent commands do not inherit](#credential-variables-that-agent-commands-do-not-inherit)). The settings catalog is on [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md). The storage of saved credentials is on [Server security](server-security.md).

### Base URL

The function `resolve_base_url` picks the base URL from these sources in order: `base_url` in `config.toml` (label `config`), the variable that `base_url_env` names (label `env:<NAME>`), the URL saved from the browser (label `saved`), and then the default (label `default`). The config value wins, so a fixed URL for a test or a proxy cannot change by accident.

The function `display_url` prepares a base URL for the browser. It removes the user name, the password, the query, and the fragment, because each can carry a credential. It returns `(not a valid URL)` when the URL does not parse.

### Key values never print

The type `ApiKey` prints as `ApiKey(***)` with `Debug` and as `***` with `Display`. Only the provider code in the crate can read the value. The type `SavedCredentials` also masks its key and token in `Debug`.

## Provider registry

The type `Providers` holds the providers that have a usable key. The server builds it from the global config and the saved credentials with `Providers::from_config`. The method `reload` rebuilds it in place when the config or the saved credentials change. Executors hold the registry, so the next model call uses the new keys. A reload keeps the providers that were added with `register`.

The method `status` returns one `ProviderStatus` for each configured provider: the name, `has_key`, the key source, the shown base URL, the base URL source, and what the browser saved. It never returns a key. The method `available` lists the names of providers that have a key.

The method `for_model` splits `provider:model` at the first colon. Both parts must be present. It returns these errors:

- `BadModel` when the string is not in the form `provider:model`.
- `NoKey` when the provider is `anthropic` or `openai` and has no key.
- `UnknownProvider` for any other name that is not registered.

A provider name in the config other than `anthropic` and `openai` logs a warning and is ignored, even when it has a key. Only these two names have provider code.

### Default models for the native executor

The default tier table for the native executor maps the four tiers to Anthropic models: `fast` is `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, `balanced` is `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5`, `advanced` is `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`, and `frontier` is `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1`. The enum `Tier` (`Fast`, `Balanced`, `Advanced`, `Frontier`) and the enum `Effort` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`) live in `ostra-core/src/model.rs`. The enum `Complexity` (`low`, `medium`, `high`) is the `**Complexity:**` value of a plan phase, and work with no phase file counts as `low`. How a workspace routes an agent to a tier is on [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## Structured decisions for judges

The function `structured` makes one structured decision for a judge call. It sends a request with one tool named `decide` (`DECIDE_TOOL`) and forces the model to call it (`ToolChoice::Tool`). The request uses `max_tokens` of 16,000. Some models reject a forced call, so the function allows one reminder: if the first answer has no `decide` call, it adds the answer and the user text ``Call the `decide` tool now with your decision. Do not answer in text.`` and asks again. A refusal or a second miss returns a `Decode` error. The usage of every attempt is added. The judge calls are on [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

## Scripted mock provider

The `ScriptedProvider` replaces a real provider in tests, so no test needs a key or a network. Its default name is `mock`. The method `Providers::register` adds it to the registry with the source label `registered`, and a reload keeps it.

The provider answers each request with the next queued response. When the queue is empty, it calls the responder function that `with_responder` set. The responder suits parallel runs, where the order of requests is not fixed. If neither exists, the call fails with a `Decode` error: `the scripted provider has no response left`. If the cancel token is already cancelled, the call returns `Cancelled`.

The provider records every request. Tests read them with `requests()` and the number of unused responses with `remaining()`.

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `push(response)` | Queue a response |
| `push_error(error)` | Queue an error |
| `push_text(text)` | Queue a text response with `EndTurn` |
| `push_tool_use(name, input)` | Queue one tool call with `ToolUse` |
| `push_tool_uses(calls)` | Queue several tool calls in one response |
| `tool_id()` | Return a new id such as `toolu_mock_1` |

The helper functions `mock::response` and `mock::tool_use_response` build responses with zero usage and the model name `mock`. The provider sends stream events for text, thinking, and tool calls, so the Coalescer and the Activity log get the same events that a real provider sends.

The tests of the native executor use this provider. They check, for example, that a read outside the write scope is denied, that a missing submit gets one reminder, that a cancel is immediate, and that the loop compacts near the window and continues from the summary.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_TURNS` | 400 | Model turns in one run |
| `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` | 3 | Continue messages after an output cut-off with no tool call |
| `COMPACT_AT` | 0.95 | Share of the context window that starts compaction |
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 200,000 tokens | Window for a model that the catalog does not list |
| `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` | 32,000 tokens | Output limit for a model that the catalog does not list |
| `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` | 0.02 of the window | Growth that must pass before a retry after a failed compaction |
| `EMIT_LIMIT` | 8 KB (8 * 1024 bytes) | Size of a tool result in the Activity log. The model gets the full text. |
| `CLEANUP_GRACE` | 3 seconds | Time that a cancelled or timed-out run has to stop its tools |
| `Coalescer::FLUSH_AT` | 160 bytes | Buffer size that sends a text delta |
| `ChatRequest::new` `max_tokens` | 32,000 | Default output limit of a request |
| `ANSWER_RESERVE` | 16,000 tokens | Output room that a thinking budget leaves |
| `MIN_BUDGET` | 1,024 tokens | Smallest thinking budget |
| `RetryPolicy` `max_retries` | 4 | Retries after the first try |
| `RetryPolicy` `base_delay` | 1,000 ms | Delay before the first retry |
| `RetryPolicy` `max_delay` | 60 seconds | Largest delay before the retry-after rule |
| Connect timeout | 20 seconds | HTTP connect of both providers |
| `structured` `max_tokens` | 16,000 | Output limit of a judge call |
| `DECIDE_TOOL` | `decide` | Tool name of a judge call |
| `COMPACTION_RECORD` | `compaction` | Role name of a stored compaction window |
| `INVALID_INPUT_KEY` | `__invalid_json` | Key that marks a tool input that did not parse |
| Invalid tool input echo | 500 bytes | Part of the raw input that the error text shows (`truncate` in `Run::tool_end`) |

The run timeout is `spec.timeout_secs`. The workspace settings set it. See [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md). A page that lists the named constants of all execution crates is [Reference: executor, tool, policy, and sandbox limits](reference-execution-limits.md).

## Cases that change the result

### What happens when

- **The model returns two tool calls and the second is the submit call.** The first call runs (or both run together when both only read). Then the submit call is checked. If it passes, the run ends and later calls get `Not run: the run ended with the submit call.`
- **The submit call is invalid.** The agent gets an error result and can call again. The run does not end.
- **The agent never calls submit.** It gets one reminder. After a second turn with no tool call, the run ends with `Ok` and no `submit` value.
- **The provider fails after output started.** The call fails with `Stream`, the run fails with `The model call failed: stream failed: ...`, and the executor does not retry.
- **The provider returns 429 before any output.** The provider waits and retries up to 4 times. The wait follows the `Retry-After` header when the header asks for more than the backoff.
- **The key changes while a run is in progress.** The run keeps its provider. The next `for_model` call, in a new run, uses the reloaded key.
- **The context passes 95 percent after an assistant turn with tool calls.** The loop waits. The tool results make the last message a user message, and compaction then starts at the next turn.
- **A cancel arrives during a tool call.** The inner token stops the tool (for example a Bash process). The run waits up to 3 seconds, then returns `Cancelled`.
- **The model is not in the models.dev catalog.** The loop uses a 200,000-token window and a 32,000-token output limit. Costs are 0 until a catalog is installed.
- **The input of an ordinary tool is not valid JSON.** The tool does not run. `Run::tool_end` (`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`) returns the error `The tool input was not valid JSON, so the call did not run: <raw input>`. It calls `truncate` on the JSON text of the raw input with a limit of 500 bytes. The helper moves the cut back to a character boundary and appends a line `... (N more bytes)`, where N is the number of bytes that it cut. The unit is bytes and not characters. The run continues.
- **The input of a `submit_<agent>` call is not valid JSON.** The submit check returns the error `The <name> input was not valid JSON. Call <name> again with a valid object.` The agent can call again. The run continues.

## Where to look

The execution state shows in the console as Activity rows. The `Status`, `Turn`, `Usage`, `ToolCall`, `Policy`, `ToolResult`, and `ToolOutput` deltas come from the loop. The provider status (key source and base URL source) shows in the provider settings of the console. See [Server API](server-api.md) for the routes.

code_refs.note: Agent loop, compaction, tool dispatch, submit checks, resume, and the `truncate` helper.
Tests with the mock provider: cancel, compaction, submit retry, YOLO, and build streak.
Provider registry, credential lookup, base URL resolution, and the `structured` judge call.
Messages API provider: beta flags, model capabilities, thinking, and cache marks.
Responses API provider: stateless input, reasoning, and stop reason mapping.
`retry::run`, `RetryPolicy`, and the delay rule.
`json_events`: server-sent events to JSON values.
Scripted provider for tests.
`Tier`, `Effort`, and `Complexity` enums.

sections.title: Harness executors: Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity
sections.summary: How Ostra runs an installed CLI under a PTY, routes each tool call through a hook bridge, serves its tools through an MCP shim, and ends the execution from the submit call.
sections.body:
## What the harness executor does

An execution can run on the native loop with an API key, or inside a vendor CLI that the user has installed. This page covers the CLI case. The four CLIs are Claude Code (`claude`), Codex (`codex`), Grok Build (`grok`), and Antigravity (`agy`). Ostra calls each CLI a harness. The type `HarnessKind` in `ostra-core` names them.

A CLI has its own tools, its own permission prompts, and its own session files. Without a bridge, a tool call of the CLI runs outside the guards of Ostra, and the result of the agent never reaches the engine. The `HarnessExecutor` in `crates/ostra-exec-harness` closes both gaps:

- It starts the CLI in a pseudo-terminal (PTY), so the user can watch the CLI and type into it in the Terminal tab.
- It registers hooks in the CLI. Each hook runs `ostra hook`, which asks the server to check the tool call.
- It registers an MCP server in the CLI. The server is `ostra mcp-stdio`. It serves the `submit_<agent>` tool and the other tools of Ostra.
- It takes the result of the execution from the `submit_<agent>` call, and never from the text on the screen.

This page stops before the rules that decide a tool call. [policy-guards.md](policy-guards.md) owns them. [sandbox.md](sandbox.md) owns the kernel sandbox. [native-executor.md](native-executor.md) covers the other executor. [agent-coordination.md](agent-coordination.md) owns the helper and reply tools. [reference-execution-limits.md](reference-execution-limits.md) lists the named constants of `ostra-exec-harness` with the constants of the other executor crates. The terminal channels of the WebSocket belong to [server-api.md](server-api.md).

## Parts of the crate and where each runs

Most code is in `crates/ostra-exec-harness`. The server wires it in through `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`. The `ostra` binary also runs two subcommands that the CLI starts: `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio`. [running-ostra.md](running-ostra.md) lists the subcommands.

| File | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `executor.rs` | `HarnessExecutor`: launch, the supervise loop, and the end of an execution |
| `launch.rs` | The command line, the environment, and the config files for each CLI |
| `bridge.rs` | `HarnessBridge` (server side) and `run_hook_cli` and `run_mcp_stdio` (subprocess side) |
| `protocol.rs` | The wire shapes and the `OSTRA_*` environment names |
| `adapters/` | One adapter for each harness: payload in, decision out |
| `live.rs` | `LiveRegistry`: the state of each running execution, and its token |
| `outcome.rs` | The mapping from how the execution ended to an `ExecutionResult` |
| `pty.rs` | `PtySession` and `PtyRegistry` |
| `term_log.rs` | The terminal transcript on disk |
| `transcript.rs`, `usage_watch.rs` | Final message and token usage from the session file of the CLI |
| `sandbox.rs` | The wrap of the CLI in the execution sandbox |
| `setup.rs`, `command.rs` | Install and login status, the Antigravity integration, and Windows command resolution |
| `services.rs` | The `BridgeServices` trait that the server implements |

## Life of one execution

The engine gives the executor an `ExecutionSpec`. The spec holds the route, the system prompt, the first message, the capabilities, the timeout, and the optional `resume` data. These steps follow:

1. The server wrapper `Wrapped` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` opens the MCP tools of the workspace. It does this first because the CLI lists the tools once, at startup. Then it builds an `ExecutionPolicy` and a `ToolEnv` and stores them in the server registry under the execution ID.
2. `HarnessExecutor::run` registers the execution in the `LiveRegistry`. The registry mints a token for the execution.
3. `launch` checks that the CLI is installed, writes the config files, wraps the command in the sandbox, and starts the PTY.
4. A follower task reads the session file of the CLI and reports token usage during the execution.
5. `supervise` loops until one of the end conditions in the list below happens.
6. The executor stops the follower, closes the CLI, removes the private files, and builds the `ExecutionResult`.

### What one tool call passes

The diagram shows one PreToolUse hook event. The CLI waits for the answer of the hook before it runs the tool.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant CLI as Harness CLI
participant Hook as ostra hook
participant Srv as Server routes
participant Br as HarnessBridge
participant Pol as ExecutionPolicy
CLI->>Hook: run the hook command with the payload on stdin
Hook->>Srv: POST /internal/policy with the bearer token
Srv->>Br: handle_policy
Br->>Br: check the token and parse the payload with the adapter
Br->>Pol: policy_check
Pol-->>Br: allow, deny, or ask
Br-->>Srv: PolicyResponse
Srv-->>Hook: JSON body with stdout and exit_code
Hook-->>CLI: print the decision on stdout
```

If the decision is `ask`, the bridge calls `resolve_ask` and waits. The answer comes from a card in the browser, or from YOLO mode. [judges-and-yolo.md](judges-and-yolo.md) covers YOLO mode.

## Settings that choose the CLI

The machine config has one table for each harness: `[harness.claude]`, `[harness.codex]`, `[harness.grok]`, and `[harness.agy]`. Each table has two keys, in the `HarnessConfig` struct:

- `command`: the program to start. If the key is empty or absent, `GlobalConfig::harness_command` returns the harness name, for example `claude`.
- `args`: extra arguments that Ostra adds to every launch of that CLI.

The executor reads the settings again for every execution. The server calls `HarnessExecutor::set_global` when the settings change, so a change applies to the next execution without a restart.

`HarnessExecutorConfig` also holds `idle_nudge`, `cols`, and `rows`. The server builds it with `HarnessExecutorConfig::new`, which sets `idle_nudge` to 240 seconds, `cols` to 120, and `rows` to 40. The code that this page covers does not expose these three values as settings. The `harness_probe` example sets `idle_nudge` to 90 seconds for its own runs.

The routing of an agent to a harness and a model belongs to [workspaces-and-settings.md](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## Start the CLI: the launch steps

`HarnessExecutor::launch` runs these steps in order. Each failure returns an error text that starts with `harness-launch:` (`LAUNCH_PREFIX`).

1. Read the sandbox settings for the workspace and the command name for the harness.
2. Run `which::which` on the command. If it is not on `PATH`, fail with the text that the command is not installed.
3. For Antigravity only, call `ensure_agy_integration`. See the Antigravity section below.
4. Create the config directory of the execution with `harness_execution_dir`. Its path is the `harness/<execution id>` folder under the state folder of the session.
5. Build the `LaunchInput` and call `launch::plan`. The plan holds the program, the arguments, the environment, the files, and the links.
6. Call `launch::materialize`. It writes each file that the plan lists. The files are readable by their owner only, because the Grok config holds the token of the execution.
7. Call `sandbox::wrap`. It returns the wrapped plan, the sandbox members, and an optional warning.
8. If the warning exists, send a status line that the CLI runs without a sandbox. The log shows the warning once for each process.
9. Create the terminal transcript file, then start the PTY with `PtySession::spawn`.
10. Send a status line that the CLI runs in the terminal and that its tool calls go through the guards.

### What happens when a launch step fails

- The CLI is not installed: the execution ends with an error, and the text names the command and the harness.
- The sandbox config requires a sandbox and the machine cannot provide one: `wrap` returns an error, and the launch fails. If the config allows no sandbox, the CLI starts with a warning instead.
- A file cannot be written, or the PTY cannot start: the launch fails with the reason from the operating system.
- The transcript file cannot be created: the execution still runs, but without a transcript.

## Launch arguments for each harness

Every plan puts the extra `args` of the machine config first, except Codex when it resumes. Codex puts `resume <id>` before the extra `args`. Every plan sets the working directory to the repo root of the project. The sections below list the fixed arguments in order.

### The first message and the resume message

The first message goes on the command line as the last argument, or after `-i` for Antigravity. If the message is longer than `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` (96 KiB, 98,304 bytes), Ostra writes it to `first-message.md` in the config directory. The argument then tells the agent to read that file before its first other tool call. The reason is the size limit of a command line.

A resumed execution starts with the `note` of the resume data. If the note is empty, the text says that Ostra resumed the session after an interruption. It tells the agent to check what is done, finish the rest, and call its `submit_<agent>` tool. A resumed execution uses the session ID that the previous execution reported.

### Claude Code

- `--session-id <uuid>` for a new session, or `--resume <id>` for a resumed one. Ostra picks the UUID, so it knows the session ID before the first hook.
- `--setting-sources user`, `--settings <config dir>/claude-settings.json`, and `--strict-mcp-config`. The CLI then loads only the user settings and the MCP config of Ostra. Project and local settings are files of the repository, and their hooks run outside the guards.
- `--mcp-config <config dir>/claude-mcp.json`. The file registers the stdio server `ostra` with the arguments `mcp-stdio --execution <id>`.
- `--append-system-prompt-file <config dir>/system-prompt.md`.
- `--add-dir` for the session directory, and for the workspace artifacts folder and the books folder when they exist.
- `--disallowed-tools Agent,Task,AskUserQuestion,EnterPlanMode,ExitPlanMode`.
- `--tools <list>`. The list comes from the capabilities of the agent: `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebSearch`, and `WebFetch`. A `Skill` capability adds `Read`. The list always ends with `ToolSearch`, because interactive Claude Code exposes MCP tools only as deferred tools, and the model cannot reach `mcp__ostra__*` without it.
- `--permission-mode default`, `--model <route model>`, and `--effort <effort>`. Ostra lowers the effort to `max` if the route asks for more.

The settings file turns hooks on and registers five events: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `PostToolUseFailure` (each with the matcher `*`), and `Stop` and `SessionStart`. It sets `disableAllHooks` to `false`. Flag settings win over user settings, so a user settings file cannot turn the hooks off. If Ostra runs the CLI in its own sandbox, the file also sets `sandbox.enabled` to `false`, because macOS cannot nest Seatbelt sandboxes.

### Codex

- `resume <id>` first, when the execution resumes a session. Then the extra `args`.
- Pairs of `-c key=value` for the hooks `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` (matcher `.*`), and `Stop` and `SessionStart`.
- `-c mcp_servers.ostra.command`, `.args`, `.env_vars`, and `.tool_timeout_sec`. The `env_vars` list names `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`, so the shim inherits them.
- `-c check_for_update_on_startup=false`. Codex updates itself at startup and then exits. This ends the execution before it starts.
- `-c developer_instructions=<system prompt>` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=<effort>`. The effort has the ceiling `xhigh`.
- `-p ostra-restricted-<execution id>`, unless the extra `args` already hold `-p`, `--profile`, or `--profile=`. See the trust rule below.
- `--disable multi_agent`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`. The last flag is needed because the hooks change for every execution and cannot hold saved trust.
- `-C <repo root>` and `-m <route model>`.

Codex reads folder trust only from config files. Ostra writes a profile file named `ostra-restricted-<id>.config.toml` in the Codex home folder (`CODEX_HOME`, or `~/.codex`). The profile marks the repo root as `untrusted`, and so each parent folder up to the git root (at most 32 levels). Codex then opens the folder restricted: the `.codex/` config, the hooks, and the exec policies of the repository stay off, and the saved trust of the user does not change. The executor removes the profile when the execution ends.

### Grok Build

Grok reads hooks and MCP servers from its home folder. Ostra builds a private home for each execution at `<config dir>/grok-home` and sets `GROK_HOME` to it:

- The private home holds symlinks to every entry of the real Grok home, except the names in `GROK_PRIVATE` (`config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `leader.sock`), names that start with `leader-`, and names that end with `.lock`. The session then runs its own leader process and reads the hooks of this execution.
- `config.toml` is the user config without any `[mcp_servers.ostra]` table, plus the four hooks, the `ostra` MCP server, and an `env` table with the four `OSTRA_*` values.
- `trusted_folders.toml` is the user list plus the session directory. The repository is trusted only if the user trusted it in Grok.

The arguments are `--session-id <uuid>` or `--resume <id>`, then `--leader-socket <home>/leader-ostra.sock`, `--cwd <repo root>`, `--no-subagents`, `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, `--rules <system prompt>`, `-m <model>`, and `--reasoning-effort <effort>` with the ceiling `high`. The environment adds `GROK_HOME` and `GROK_SUBAGENTS=0`.

### Antigravity

Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. Ostra installs one global integration and passes the execution through the environment. The plan writes an agent file for the execution. The arguments are:

- `--conversation <id>` when it resumes a session.
- `--agent ostra-<agent>`, `--add-dir <session dir>`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model <model>`, and `--effort <effort>` with the ceiling `high`.
- `--add-dir` for the artifacts folder and the books folder when they exist.
- `-i <prompt>`. An inspection has no prompt.

## Environment and credentials of the CLI

`launch::plan` and `PtySession::spawn` build the environment of the CLI in this order:

1. The full environment of the `ostra` process.
2. Remove the names in `PARENT_SESSION_ENV` (16 names, for example `CLAUDECODE`, `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, `GROK_SESSION_ID`, and `ANTIGRAVITY_AGENT`). If a child inherits them, the CLI runs as a nested child of the session that started Ostra. Claude Code does not save such a session, so the session cannot resume.
3. Remove the credential variables that the plan lists in `env_remove`. The list holds the credential names of Ostra (`credential_env_names`) minus the sign-in variables of the CLI. A CLI keeps the variables that it needs to sign in: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` for Claude Code, `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` for Codex, and `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `GOOGLE_API_KEY` for Antigravity. Grok keeps none. The shell commands of the agent inside the CLI can still read the kept variables.
4. Set `TERM` to `xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM` to `truecolor`.
5. Set the plan variables: `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS` (`ENV_URL`, `ENV_EXECUTION`, `ENV_TOKEN`, `ENV_HARNESS`), plus the git variables from `ostra_core::git::agent_env`.

## The hook bridge

A hook is a command that the CLI runs at a point of its turn. The CLI sends the event as JSON on stdin and reads the answer on stdout. The bridge turns each hook into a call to the server. It has a subprocess side and a server side.

### The subprocess side: `ostra hook`

The command line is `ostra hook --execution <id> --harness <name> --event <event>`. The events are `pre_tool_use`, `post_tool_use`, `post_tool_use_failure`, `stop`, `session_start`, `pre_invocation`, and `post_invocation` (`HookEvent`). `parse_hook_args` also accepts the CamelCase spelling. If `--execution` or `--harness` is absent, it reads `OSTRA_EXECUTION` or `OSTRA_HARNESS`.

`run_hook_cli` does these steps:

1. Read all of stdin.
2. If no execution ID is set, exit 0 and print nothing. The Antigravity integration is global, so its hooks also run in sessions that Ostra did not start. In those sessions the hook does nothing.
3. Read `OSTRA_URL` and `OSTRA_TOKEN`.
4. Send `POST /internal/policy` (`POLICY_PATH`) with the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header and the body `PolicyRequest`.
5. Print the `stdout` of the `PolicyResponse` and exit with its `exit_code`.

A PreToolUse request has no HTTP timeout, because a permission ask waits for the user. For this reason `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` is 86,400 seconds (24 hours) in every hook registration. Other events have a 60-second timeout.

### What happens when the hook cannot reach the server

The hook never fails open. If `OSTRA_URL` or `OSTRA_TOKEN` is missing, if the HTTP client cannot start, if the server is unreachable, if the server answers with an error status, or if the answer is not valid JSON, `ostra hook` acts as follows:

- For `pre_tool_use`, it prints a deny decision in the format of the harness: stop and end the turn, because Ostra could not check the call.
- For every other event, it prints nothing and exits 0, because those events cannot block a tool.

### The server side: `HarnessBridge::handle_policy`

The route `/internal/policy` calls `handle_policy` with the token from the bearer header. A request without a bearer header gets status 401. Then the bridge does these checks in order:

1. `authorize`: the token must match the live execution (constant-time compare), and the server must still run that execution (`BridgeServices::authorize`). If not, a PreToolUse event gets a deny with the text that the execution is not running under Ostra. Other events get `{}`.
2. The harness in the request must equal the harness of the execution. If not, the answer is a deny.
3. The adapter reads the session ID and the transcript path from the payload, and the live state stores them.
4. The event decides the next step:
   - `PreToolUse`: the adapter parses the payload. A refusal (see the adapter section) becomes a deny. Otherwise the bridge counts the tool call and calls `decide`.
   - `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure`: the bridge marks activity, parses the result, and gives it to `policy_observe`. The notes that come back go to the model as extra context.
   - `Stop`: the bridge calls `stop_event` and `LiveExecution::on_stop`. The adapter formats the verdict.
   - `SessionStart`, `PreInvocation`, and `PostInvocation`: the bridge marks activity and answers `{}`.

`decide` has two parts. First, a tool named `submit_<other agent>` is denied with the name of the correct submit tool. Then `policy_check` returns one of three answers. `Allow` lets the call run. `Deny` returns the reason, then the rule in the form `(Ostra <layer>: <rule>)`, so the model reads the correction first. `Ask` calls `resolve_ask` and waits. If the user denies, the model reads that the user denied the call and that it must continue without it or choose another way.

### What the server does with the bridge

`ServerBridge` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` implements `BridgeServices` with the policy engine and the tool crate:

- `policy_check` sets the YOLO flag from the host, runs `ExecutionPolicy::check`, and sends the `ToolCall` and `Policy` deltas to the host. A workspace MCP tool and a management tool pass the hook unchecked, because the MCP path checks and logs them when it runs them (Rules M2 and O1). With this rule, an ask reaches the user once.
- `resolve_ask` sends the question to the host. If the answer is `AlwaysInWorkspace`, it adds a session allow rule.
- `policy_observe` reports successful writes to the live file sink, runs `ExecutionPolicy::observe`, and recalls lessons for a failure when the policy asks for it. It returns notes for the model.
- `stop_event` sends the status line that the harness ended its turn.

The server serves the bridge on two routes: `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp`, both `POST`. When a sandbox has its own network, `serve_bridge_socket` also serves only these two routes on a Unix socket. The sandbox then reaches the bridge and cannot reach `/api`. The server answers 401 to a request without a bearer token. The [server-security.md](server-security.md) page covers the sign-in of the browser.

## The MCP stdio shim

The CLI starts `ostra mcp-stdio` as an MCP server on stdio. The shim does no work of its own. It forwards each JSON-RPC message to `POST /internal/mcp` (`MCP_PATH`) and prints the answer. The server side is `HarnessBridge::handle_mcp`.

### What the shim does

`run_mcp_stdio` reads the execution from `--execution` or `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, and the URL and token from the environment. Then it reads one JSON message for each line of stdin. A line can hold one message or a batch array. Each message runs in its own task, so a slow tool call does not block `ping`. The shim writes each answer as one line on stdout.

- A line that is not valid JSON gets the error `-32700` (parse error).
- A notification (no `id`) gets no answer.
- A failed request to the server gets the error `-32603` with the text `Ostra server error` and the reason.
- If the execution, URL, or token is missing, the shim runs offline. It answers `initialize`, `server/discover`, and `ping`, returns an empty tool list, and answers `tools/call` with the text that Ostra tools work only inside an Ostra execution. A global registration is therefore inert outside Ostra.

### What the server answers

`handle_mcp` checks the token like `handle_policy`. If it fails, the error is `-32001` (the execution is not running under Ostra). Then the method decides:

| Method | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize` | The protocol version that the client asked for, if it is in `MCP_VERSIONS`. Otherwise `2025-11-25` (`MCP_INITIALIZE_DEFAULT`). The capabilities hold `tools` with `listChanged` set to `false`. |
| `server/discover` | `supportedVersions` and the capabilities |
| `ping` | `{}` |
| `tools/list` | The `submit_<agent>` tool, then the other tools of the execution |
| `tools/call` | See the next section |
| `resources/list`, `prompts/list` | Empty lists |
| Other methods | Error `-32601` (method not found) |

`MCP_VERSIONS` is `2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The version `2026-07-28` is left out on purpose. Its results need `resultType`, `ttlMs`, and `cacheScope`. Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` answer without them, so the execution gets no Ostra tools. Without that version in `server/discover`, clients use the `initialize` handshake.

The server name is `ostra` (`MCP_SERVER_NAME`). A CLI therefore shows the tools as `mcp__ostra__<tool>` (Claude Code) or in a similar form that `ostra_mcp_tool` accepts. The adapter section lists the accepted prefixes. The MCP client side of Ostra, which connects to other servers, belongs to [integrations.md](integrations.md).

### The tools in the list

The server decides the tool list in `ServerBridge::mcp_tools`. A read-only inspection gets an empty list. Otherwise the list holds:

- `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, and `docs_search`.
- One `code_<op>` tool for each code operation.
- The project tools, only if the agent holds the management handle.
- The coordination tools (`subagent_list`, `subagent_ask`, `subagent_reply`), only if the execution has a coordination handle.
- The tools of the workspace MCP servers, with the bare names from `ostra_core::mcp`.

[tools.md](tools.md) describes the input of each tool. [agent-coordination.md](agent-coordination.md) describes the coordination tools.

### How a `tools/call` runs

There are three cases:

1. **The submit tool of the agent.** If the run owes a reply to another agent (Rule H3), the call fails and the text tells the model to call the reply tool first. Otherwise Ostra converts JSON strings to the types in the schema, runs `validate_submit`, and runs `ostra_core::doc::check_submit`. If a check fails, the text says `Nothing was recorded` and the model must call again. If all checks pass, `record_submit` stores the payload. The first payload wins. A second call gets the error that a result exists already. The success text tells the model to end its turn.
2. **The submit tool of another agent.** The call fails with the name of the correct tool.
3. **Any other tool.** The bridge maps the name to the canonical tool name, counts the call, and calls `decide`. If the answer is a deny, the model gets the reason as a tool error. Otherwise `ServerBridge::mcp_call` checks the policy again, runs `ostra_tools::execute`, sends the `ToolResult` delta, and adds the notes from `policy_observe` to the text. A failed tool returns `isError: true`.

The result of a coordination tool can change the run. `RunEnd::Wait` sets the run to waiting (Rule H2). `RunEnd::Finish` records a submit payload of the form `{coordination, message}`, so the execution ends without a normal submit. `RunEnd::Continue` changes nothing.

## The four adapters

Each CLI has its own payload shape and its own accepted answer shape. An adapter (`Adapter` trait in `adapters/mod.rs`) hides this. It has seven methods: `kind`, `meta`, `parse_pre`, `parse_post`, `pre_response`, `post_response`, and `stop_response`. `for_harness` returns the adapter for a `HarnessKind`. All adapters map native tool names to the canonical tool names of Claude Code, so the policy engine has one set of names.

### Rules that all adapters share

- A spawn tool is refused without a policy check. The names are `Task`, `Agent`, `task`, `spawn_agent`, `spawn_subagent`, `invoke_subagent`, `define_subagent`, and any name that ends in `spawn_agent`. The text (`LEAF_REFUSAL`) says that every Ostra agent is a leaf: a delegated task runs outside the guards, and its result never reaches the engine.
- A user question tool is refused. The names are `AskUserQuestion`, `ask_user_question`, `request_user_input`, and `ask_question`. The text (`ASK_REFUSAL`) tells the agent to put the question in the submit call, because the pipeline asks the user from its gate and nobody watches the terminal for questions.
- A tool that the adapter does not know becomes `Other:<name>`.
- `ostra_mcp_tool` accepts these prefixes for an Ostra tool: `mcp__ostra__`, `mcp_ostra_`, `ostra__`, `ostra/`, `ostra.`, and `ostra:`. `canonical_ostra_tool` then maps `report` to `Report`, `memory_recall` to `MemoryRecall`, `code_callers` to `CodeCallers`, and so on. A workspace tool such as `github__search` becomes `mcp__github__search`. `submit_*` keeps its name.
- The result of a tool goes to the policy observer with at most 64 KiB of output (`MAX_OUTCOME_CHARS`). A longer output ends with `[output truncated]`.
- The exit code comes from the text. `exit_code_from` tries four patterns (`PATTERNS`), for example `Exit code 2` and `exited with code 1`. A Bash call with no code gets 1 if the result is flagged as an error, otherwise 0. An interrupted call has no code.

### Differences between the adapters

| | Claude Code | Codex | Grok Build | Antigravity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Payload keys | `tool_name`, `tool_input`, `session_id` | the same, snake_case | camelCase with snake_case aliases | `toolCall.name` and `toolCall.args`, with PascalCase arguments |
| Shell tool | `Bash`, and `PowerShell` as an opaque shell | `Bash`, `exec_command`, `shell`, `local_shell`. On Windows, `PowerShell` unless the command starts `bash` or `sh` | `run_terminal_command`, `Bash`, `monitor` | `run_command`, `send_command_input` |
| Other mappings | `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` become `Edit`. `LS` becomes `Glob`. | `apply_patch` becomes `ApplyPatch` | `read_file`, `write_file`, `search_replace`, `grep`, `glob`, `web_fetch`, and the `use_tool` wrapper | `view_file`, `write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`, `grep_search`, `find_by_name`, `read_url_content`, `search_web`, and `call_mcp_tool` |
| Allow answer | `permissionDecision: allow` inside `hookSpecificOutput` | `{}` | like Claude Code | `{decision: allow}` |
| Deny answer | `permissionDecision: deny` with the reason | the same | the same, with the reason clipped | `{decision: deny, reason}` |
| Stop block | `{decision: block, reason}` | the same | the same, with the reason clipped | never blocks: always `{}` |
| Post answer | extra context from notes | extra context | extra context | `{}` |
| Result in post event | full response | output text, no exit status | full response | none: only `stepIdx` and `error` |

The reasons for the differences come from the schema of each CLI:

- **Claude Code.** Rewrites and decisions go only inside `hookSpecificOutput`, because a top-level `overwrite` field fails its hook schema. Claude Code reports a failed tool as its own event, `PostToolUseFailure`.
- **Codex.** The PreToolUse schema rejects `allow` without `updatedInput`, and it rejects `ask`. An allowed call therefore answers `{}`. A shell command that comes as an array is joined with POSIX quoting, so the policy reads the words that Codex runs. Codex gives hooks the raw output without the exit status, so the code stays unknown and the policy judges the output text.
- **Grok Build.** Grok clips a reason to 256 characters (`GROK_REASON_MAX`). `fit_reason` keeps the head and the last sentence, joined with an ellipsis, because Ostra reasons start with the correction and end with the instruction. If the head is shorter than 120 characters (`MIN_HEAD`), it cuts the text at 256 characters. Grok also caps the hook payload at 128 KiB and then marks `toolInput` as truncated (`toolInputTruncated`). A truncated input cannot be judged, so the adapter refuses it with a text that tells the agent to split the call into smaller calls (`TRUNCATED_REFUSAL`).
- **Antigravity.** The output of a hook is validated against a proto schema, and an unknown field discards the whole answer. PreToolUse therefore answers only `decision` and `reason`. Because the post event carries no result, the outcome has `result_known` set to `false`. A Bash call with no error gets exit code 0.

## How the supervise loop ends an execution

`HarnessExecutor::supervise` runs one loop until an `End` value returns. The loop wakes every 500 milliseconds, or sooner when the live state changes. The budget is `timeout_secs` of the spec, with a minimum of 30 seconds.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T["Wake every 500 ms or on a live change"] --> C{"Cancel token fired?"}
  C -- yes --> E1["End Cancelled"]
  C -- no --> X{"CLI exited?"}
  X -- yes --> E2["End Submitted if a submit exists, else End Exited"]
  X -- no --> S{"Submit recorded?"}
  S -- yes --> S2{"Stop seen, Antigravity quiet 4 s, or 20 s passed?"}
  S2 -- yes --> E3["End Submitted"]
  S2 -- no --> T
  S -- no --> W{"Run waiting?"}
  W -- yes --> W2["Wait for a wake message and type it in"] --> T
  W -- no --> G{"Stop let through without a submit?"}
  G -- yes --> E4["End GaveUp"]
  G -- no --> D{"Deadline passed?"}
  D -- yes --> E5["End Timeout"]
  D -- no --> M["Answer prompts, End Auth or Fatal, nudge, or End Idle"] --> T
```

In each loop turn, before these checks, the executor does two small jobs. Every 2 seconds (`GIT_CHECK_EVERY`) it runs the git repair (see the sandbox section). When the live state has a new session ID, it sends a `NativeSessionId` delta, so the engine can resume the session later.

### The end values and their results

`outcome::result` turns an `End` into an `ExecutionResult`. It reads the transcript for the final message and the token usage. The tool call count is the larger of the transcript count and the hook count.

| End | Condition | Status and text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Submitted` | A submit exists, and a Stop followed it, or Antigravity was quiet for 4 seconds (`AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT`), or 20 seconds passed (`AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE`). The CLI exit also counts if the submit exists. | `status` of the payload: `stuck` gives `Stuck`, `handoff` gives `Handoff`, anything else gives `Ok`. The result holds the payload. |
| `Cancelled` | The cancel token fired | `Cancelled`, no error text |
| `Auth` | A sign-in marker showed in the first 120 seconds | `Error`, text starts with `harness-auth:` and says the CLI is not logged in |
| `Exited` (early) | The CLI exited within 20 seconds (`LAUNCH_WINDOW`) with no tool call | `Error`. The text starts with `harness-auth:` if the screen holds a sign-in marker, else `harness-launch:`. It has the last 12 non-empty lines of the screen. |
| `Exited` (late) | The CLI exited before a submit | `Error`: the CLI exited with its code before the agent called the submit tool |
| `GaveUp` | A Stop passed without a submit after two blocks | `Error`: the agent ended its turn three times without the submit call |
| `Idle` | The execution stayed quiet after two reminders | `Error`: the session went quiet without a submit, and two reminders did not help |
| `Fatal` | A fatal marker showed, or a trust prompt was refused | `Error`, text starts with `harness-launch:` and holds the reason and the screen tail |
| `Timeout` | The deadline passed | `Error`: the execution passed its budget in seconds and was stopped |

The three prefixes tell a reader the cause. `harness-auth:` means the user must log in. `harness-launch:` means the CLI could not start a session. Text without a prefix means the CLI started but did not finish the work. The retry rules for a failed execution belong to [engine-runtime.md](engine-runtime.md).

If the CLI is Antigravity, the end is `Auth`, and the Seatbelt sandbox is active, the text is different. It tells the user to set `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in the environment of Ostra, because on macOS the CLI keeps its login in the keychain, and the sandbox closes the keychain to agents.

### What happens after the end

1. The usage follower stops, and the executor waits for it. A late reading cannot overwrite the final result.
2. If the end is `Cancelled`, the executor sends the Esc key and waits 400 milliseconds. Esc ends the turn of the CLI, so the CLI saves its session whole and the session can resume.
3. `terminate` asks the CLI to exit. On Unix it sends SIGTERM to the process group. On Windows it closes the pseudoconsole. After a grace period of 3 seconds it kills the process tree and waits up to 2 more seconds. Then it kills what is left in the sandbox, even if the CLI exited first.
4. The executor removes the PTY from the registry and calls `sandbox::cleanup`. The cleanup deletes the Claude config copy, the Grok config with the token, and the scratch folder `tmp`. For Codex it also deletes the profile file.
5. The live execution leaves the registry, and the token stops working.

## Submit, Stop, and idle nudges

The engine reads only the submit call. A CLI that ends its turn without it leaves the execution with no result. Two nudges push the agent to submit.

### Stop block

When a CLI sends a Stop hook, `LiveExecution::on_stop` decides. This excerpt shows the decision:

```rust
let verdict = if self.inspect.load(Ordering::SeqCst) || s.waiting {
    StopVerdict::Allow
} else if s.submit.is_some() {
    s.stopped_after_submit = true;
    StopVerdict::Allow
} else if s.stops_without_submit < MAX_STOP_NUDGES {
    s.stops_without_submit += 1;
    let nudge = if self.owes_reply.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
        ... // the instruction to call the reply tool
    } else { missing_submit_instruction(self.agent) };
    StopVerdict::Block(nudge)
} else {
    s.gave_up = true;
    StopVerdict::Allow
};
```

`MAX_STOP_NUDGES` is 2. The first two Stop events without a submit return `Block`. The CLI shows the instruction to the model and continues its turn. The third Stop is allowed, and the execution ends with `GaveUp`. The nudge text tells the agent to call its submit tool before it stops, because Ostra reads only that call. If the run owes a reply to another agent, the text names the reply tool instead (Rule H3). Antigravity has no Stop hook, so this mechanism does not apply to it.

### Idle nudge

A session can go quiet with no Stop, for example when the CLI waits on a prompt. The executor measures the quiet time as the smaller of two values: the time since the last hook event, and the time since the last terminal output. If this value reaches `idle_nudge` (default `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE`, 240 seconds), the executor acts:

- If it sent fewer than `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` (2) nudges, it resets the activity clock, types the nudge text into the terminal with `type_line`, and sends the status line that Ostra reminded the session to submit.
- If it sent 2 nudges already, the execution ends with `Idle`.

`type_line` pastes the text in a bracketed paste, waits 150 milliseconds, and presses Enter. The bracketed paste stops a TUI from treating a newline inside the text as a submit.

The idle nudge does not run in three cases: after a submit, when the run waits for a message, and in an inspection session.

## Detect a login screen, a trust prompt, or a startup failure

In the first 120 seconds, and only if the agent has made no tool call, the executor reads the screen text of the PTY on every loop turn. It lowercases the text and looks for marker strings. The markers are constants in `executor.rs`.

### Sign-in markers

`AUTH_MARKERS` has 14 strings.
