sections.title: Policy engine: guards, permissions, and containment
sections.summary: How every tool call passes layer 1 guards and then layer 2 permissions, how Bash is parsed, how build failures are counted, how containment signals pause a session, and what the policy does not guarantee.
sections.body:
## Why the policy engine exists

An agent calls tools that write files, run commands, and read files. Without a check, a model can write outside its scope, forge a pipeline record, read a credential, or run the Ostra binary. The `ostra-policy` crate checks every tool call from every executor before the tool runs. The [native executor](native-executor.md) calls the policy in the same process. The [harness executors](harness-executors.md) call it through the hook bridge.

The crate has two layers:

- **Layer 1, guards.** A guard refuses a call. Nothing overrides a guard: not a permission rule, not a user answer, and not YOLO mode.
- **Layer 2, permissions.** A permission mode and the allow, ask, and deny rules decide the calls that the guards let through. This layer follows the model of Claude Code.

Many guards port a hook library of Ultracode, and the source comment above the guard function names that library. Not every guard has that source:

- `manage-tools` (Rule O2) has no Ultracode source. Its source comment says that the code is Ostra code.
- `answer-only` and `reply-first` cite Rule H3.
- `windows-path` cites the note WINDOWS_HANDOVER 1.4.

This page covers the order of the checks, each guard and its reason, the permission modes and rules, the Bash parser, the build-failure history, the containment signals, and the limits of the policy. The [sandbox](sandbox.md) page covers the kernel limits that apply when a command runs. The [YOLO page](judges-and-yolo.md) covers who answers an ask in YOLO mode.

## Order of checks for one tool call

`ExecutionPolicy::check` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` decides one call. The executor builds one `ExecutionPolicy` for each execution from an `ExecContext` and a `PolicyInputs` value. The result is a `PolicyDecision`: `Allow`, `Ask`, or `Deny`.

`Ask` and `Deny` always carry a `RuleRef` with a `layer` (`guard` or `permission`) and a `rule`. `Allow` holds `rule: Option<RuleRef>`, so an allow can carry no `RuleRef`. These allows carry none:

- An allow of the read family (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, and a `Skill` with a path).
- An allow of a known tool, such as `Report`, `Memory`, a code tool, or a `submit_*` tool.
- An allow of a workspace MCP tool.
- The pass-through of the hook bridge for an MCP tool or a project tool.

The Activity view shows the `RuleRef` with each decision that has one.

### Flow of one call

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Tool call arrives"] --> B["Parse the Bash command"]
  B --> C{"Layer 1: does a guard deny?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Deny with the guard id"]
  C -- no --> E{"Layer 2: rules and mode"}
  E -- deny --> F["Deny with the permission rule"]
  E -- allow --> H["Allow"]
  E -- ask --> I{"Is YOLO on?"}
  I -- yes --> J["Allow with rule yolo"]
  I -- no --> K["Open a permission gate"]
  K --> L["User answers allow-once, always-in-workspace, or deny"]
```

### Steps

1. For a `Bash` call, `bash::parse` splits the command into simple commands.
2. `layer1` runs the guards. The first denial ends the check.
3. `layer2` applies the permission rules and the permission mode.
4. If YOLO is on, `check` changes every `Ask` to `Allow` with the rule `yolo`. It also changes an allow from `mode:bypass` to the rule `yolo`. A denial stays a denial.

The executor emits an `ExecutionDelta::Policy` event for each decision, so the Activity view shows allowed calls and refused calls.

### What happens after each decision

This page owns the denial texts. Other pages link here.

- **Deny.** The executor returns an error to the model. Each reason starts with the correction, because Grok clips a reason to 256 characters. The text depends on the layer:
  - The native executor wraps every denial as ``Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>``. The `<layer>` is `guard` or `permission`. For a guard, `<reason>` is the guard text, which names the allowed directory or the correct tool.
  - A deny rule from `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` gives the `<reason>` ``Do not <action>: the permission rule `<rule>` refuses it. If the task needs it, say so in your report.`` For Bash, `<action>` is ``run `<command>` ``.
  - A denial in `plan` mode gives a reason that starts with `Stay read-only: this session is in plan mode`. The rest of the text depends on the call.
- **Ask.** The executor calls `ask_permission` on the host. The engine opens a gate with a `GatePayload::Permission` and waits for the answer. A run without a session, such as a side-panel run, never asks, and the answer is `Deny`.
- **Allow.** The tool runs. After the tool ends, the executor calls `observe` to update the build-failure history.

The texts above are the start of each message. Each guard and each mode adds its own wording after the correction. Read the guard function in `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs` for the full text of one guard.

### The three answers to a permission gate

`PermissionAnswer` has three values:

- `AllowOnce`: the call runs one time.
- `AlwaysInWorkspace`: the call runs. The policy adds the suggested rule to the `session_allow` list of this execution. The engine also adds the rule to the workspace allow list when the user answers through `answer_gate`.
- `Deny`: the native executor gives the model the message ``The user denied this call (<reason>). Continue without it, or explain in your report why it is needed.`` This text belongs to the native executor only. The harness bridge (`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`) and the server bridge (`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`) use their own texts. The harness bridge says `The user denied this call. Continue without it, or choose another way.` and adds the rule in parentheses. The server bridge says `The user denied this call (<reason>).`

Under YOLO, the engine opens the gate, answers it at once with source `Yolo` and `AllowOnce`, and records the reason `Under YOLO every permission ask is allowed.`

## Tool enforcement setting

The setting `tool_enforcement` decides whether layer 1 checks where tool calls read and write. The values are `enabled` and `disabled`. The default is `disabled`. A workspace value replaces the global value. The engine resolves the value when the execution starts and stores it in `ExecContext.enforce_tool_calls`. The policy keeps it as `Roots.strict` (Rule G1).

When the value is `disabled`, an agent can reach files by any route, for example with one script that edits several files. These checks still apply:

- The `secret-read`, `git-metadata`, `state-ownership`, `artifact-ownership`, and `no-tests-from-implementer` guards.
- The workflow gates: `lesson-gate` and `build-streak`.
- The permission rules.
- The [sandbox](sandbox.md).

When the value is `enabled`, layer 1 adds these checks:

- `write-scope`.
- `report-path`.
- `self-protection`, with the shell and interpreter checks behind it.

The reason for the setting: a strict write scope stops a script that edits many files, and some users need that route. The checks that protect secrets, records, and git metadata have no such use, so they never depend on the setting.

## Layer 1 check order

`layer1` tests the guards in this order. The first denial wins.

1. **`answer-only`.** If the run is a consult run (`ExecContext.answer_only`), a call that writes is refused. A call writes if it has a write path, is `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, or a project management tool, or is a shell command with a write target.
2. **`Report`.** The call is refused only when a lesson is pending and the `reason` field is empty. Otherwise it is allowed, and no other guard runs.
3. **`Document`.** `check_document` checks the target path.
4. **Project tools.** `check_manage` checks `ProjectCreate`.
5. **`submit_*` when the run owes a reply.** `reply-first` refuses the call.
6. **`submit_*` with status `ok`.** `lesson-gate` refuses the call if a lesson is pending. A submit with another status passes, so `stuck` always works.
7. **`PowerShell` and `Cmd`.** `check_opaque_shell` scans the raw text.
8. **Write paths.** `check_write` checks each target path of `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, and `ApplyPatch`. For `ApplyPatch`, `apply_patch_paths` reads each path after `*** Add File:`, `*** Update File:`, `*** Delete File:`, and `*** Move to:`.
9. **Read paths.** The Windows path check and `check_read` check the path of a file tool.
10. **Bash.** `check_shell`, `check_shell_reads`, and then each write target of the command. After these checks, the build-streak gate runs.

`check_write` has its own order for one target:

1. `manage-tools` (a run that must create its project first).
2. `windows-path`.
3. `self-protection` (strict only).
4. `workspace-artifacts`.
5. `workspace-docs`.
6. `git-metadata`.
7. `state-ownership`.
8. `artifact-ownership` and `document-tool`.
9. `no-tests-from-implementer` and `write-scope`.
10. `report-path`, and the lesson gate on the declared report file.

A relative path in a tool call resolves against the `cwd` that the tool reports. If no `cwd` is absolute, the path resolves against the repo root. A path that starts with `~` resolves against the home directory. On Windows, Git Bash paths such as `/c/Users/me` translate to Windows paths before the guards compare them.

## Write scope and test guards

The `write-scope` guard keeps each agent inside the files that its role needs. It applies only when tool enforcement is `enabled`. Each refusal names the allowed directory, so the agent can correct the call.

### Write scope by agent

- **Every agent:** can write inside its session dir.
- **`quick-answer`:** writes nothing. Its answer goes in its submit call.
- **Session-only agents:** `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture`. They can write in the session dir and in OS temp. They never write project source.
- **`initializer`:** can write in the project runtime dir and in `.agents/skills/`. It cannot write new skills in the older skills dir. Ostra reads the older dir but never writes new skills to it (Rule I2).
- **Other agents:** can write anywhere inside the repo root.
- **Outside the repo and session dir:** every agent is refused, except a session-only agent that writes in OS temp. A project that itself lives under OS temp is project source, not scratch.

The `Document` tool target must be inside the session dir when enforcement is `enabled`, because the next stage reads the session dir.

### No tests from the implementer

The `no-tests-from-implementer` guard refuses a write by the `implementer` agent to a test path inside the repo. It applies in both enforcement modes. The reason: the implementer never writes or fixes tests (implementer Constraint 6). Tests run only after the user asks for them at the closing gate, and the `write-test` agent writes them.

`is_test_path` judges the path relative to the repo root. A path is a test path in these cases:

- A directory named `__tests__`, `__mocks__`, `test`, or `tests`, at any depth and in any letter case (`TEST_DIR`).
- A file named `*.test.*` or `*.spec.*` with a JavaScript or TypeScript extension.
- A file named `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, `*_test.go`, `*_spec.rb`, or `spec_*.rb`.
- A file that ends in `Test`, `Tests`, `test`, or `tests` with the extension `java`, `kt`, `kts`, or `cs` (`TEST_FILE`).

The paths `src/testing/helpers.ts` and `src/contest.ts` are not test paths. The unit test `test_paths` in `guards.rs` checks both.

## State and artifact ownership guards

Some files record something that already happened. A hand-written value in such a file forges a pipeline decision. The ownership guards keep each of these files under its owner.

### Engine state

`state-ownership` refuses a write to engine state: the `.state` dir of this session, the `.state` dir of any session, and the memory database. The memory database is the lesson store. Its message says to use the `Memory` tool, because later sessions recall lessons as fact. For other engine state the message says that the engine records the result of the work.

### Files with one owner

The guard also refuses a write by file name. The name check works anywhere in the repo.

| File name pattern | Who can write it | Reason in the code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `knowledge.sqlite3` and its `-wal`, `-shm`, `-journal` files | The `Memory` tool only | Later sessions recall the lessons as fact |
| `workspace.db`, `registry.db` and their `-wal`, `-shm`, `-journal` files | The engine only | The record of every event, gate, and decision |
| `ostra-review-ledger*.md` | `code-reviewer`, `implementer`, `write-test` | The engine counts its iterations to cap the review loop |
| `ostra-security-block.json` | `code-reviewer` | It records unwaivable BLOCKER findings |
| `ostra-implementer-progress*.md` | `implementer` | Re-runs read it to learn which steps already succeeded |

The constants are `TOOL_OWNED` and `AGENT_OWNED` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`.

### Artifact ownership

`artifact-ownership` allows only one agent to write each document family:

| File name pattern | Owner | Reason in the code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-spec-*.md` and `.json` | `generate-spec` | The spec is the requirements contract (Rules D3 and D10) |
| `ostra-plan-*.md` and `.json` | `plan` | The plan and its phase files have one writer (Rule D10) |
| `ostra-research-*.md` and `.json` | `explore` | Research documents have one writer |

The guard skips a path that has an ancestor dir named `factcheck-snapshot-*`, because a fact-check copy is not the artifact. See [Artifacts and documents](artifacts-and-documents.md) for these files.

### Document tool

The `document-tool` guard refuses a direct write to a file in the session dir that Ostra renders from a typed document. The message tells the agent to use the `Document` tool with `update`. The reason: Ostra renders the file from the typed document, so a direct write is overwritten and the browser does not show it.

### Report path

`report-path` applies when the execution has a declared report file and enforcement is `enabled`. A write to another `ostra-*` file in the session root is refused, and the message names the declared path. The reason: the next stage reads that exact path. Any mechanism can write the declared path, including a shell heredoc. A file with an owner in `AGENT_OWNED` is exempt for its owner. Without enforcement, any `ostra-*` name is allowed.

## Secret read guard

The `secret-read` guard refuses a read of a credential or of the memory of another process. It applies to every tool and every mode, and no setting turns it off. The refusal message tells the agent to ask for a credential in its report.

### Paths that count as secret

`Roots::is_secret` marks a path as secret in these cases:

- A path inside the Ostra data dir, except the `assets` dir inside it. Agents read the assets.
- The file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names.
- A path under the home directory that `HOME_CREDENTIALS` in `ostra-core` lists. The list includes `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `.azure`, `.kube`, `.docker`, `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.vault-token`, browser profile dirs, and the macOS `Library/Keychains` dir.
- The workspace database and its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files. The database holds every tool output of every session.
- `/proc/self`, `/proc/thread-self`, and `/proc/<pid>`. The `environ` and `fd` entries expose the environment and open files of the server.
- The `harness` dir of any execution, under `.state` of any session. It holds the bridge token of that execution.

### Which calls the guard checks

- A file tool path: `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Write`, `Edit`, and the other edit tools. A `Skill` or `Document` call with a path is also checked.
- Each word of a Bash command that has a `/`, starts with `~`, or (on Windows) looks like a path. The check includes redirect targets. For an option such as `--file=/x`, it checks the value after the `=`.
- A word that matches `/proc/<x>/environ`, `/proc/<x>/mem`, or `/proc/<x>/fd` (`PROC_SECRET`). The guard matches the source text, because `$pid` is dynamic.
- The commands `echo` and `printf` are skipped, because printing a path names it but does not open it.
- For `PowerShell` and `Cmd`, the guard checks each path-like candidate in the raw text.

## Self-protection and git metadata guards

These two guards protect the files that enforce the pipeline and the files that decide which programs git runs. Both produce [containment signals](#containment-signals-and-the-session-pause).

### Self-protection

`self-protection` applies when enforcement is `enabled`. It has four parts:

- **Writes to protected paths.** Protected paths are the paths in `ExecContext.protected_paths` (the Ostra binary, its config, its databases, and every engine state dir), the `workspace.toml` file, and the workspace database. Agents can read these files but never write, move, or delete them, because they enforce the pipeline.
- **Running Ostra.** A command whose name is `ostra`, or whose path points to a protected file, is refused. Without this rule, a caller can grant itself what the guards withhold.
- **Opaque write channels.** Inline interpreter code that writes to the file system (`WRITE_API`, `PY_OPEN_WRITE`) is refused. The reason: the write guards read the paths that a call names, and inline code names none. The agent must use the `Write` or `Edit` tool or a shell redirect.
- **Spawned children.** Inline interpreter code that starts another process (`SPAWN_API`) is refused, because a child is invisible to the guards.

Outside these four parts, a command that touches a protected path with anything other than a plain reader is refused. A plain reader is a command in `PLAIN_READERS`, such as `cat`, `grep`, `head`, `ls`, `find`, `jq`, and `sed` without an in-place flag.

The interpreter checks for engine state (`STATE_NAME`) apply in both modes. The checks for `WRITE_API` and `SPAWN_API` apply only with enforcement, because the [sandbox](sandbox.md) bounds a script that runs without enforcement.

### Git metadata

`git-metadata` refuses a direct write to any path that has a `.git` component. It applies in every mode. The reason: files under `.git` decide which programs git runs later (hooks, `fsmonitor`, a gitfile that points to another git dir). The agent must change them through git commands.

The native executor also records this guard when the sandbox repairs a git dir after a `Bash` call. It emits a denial with the rule `git-metadata` and the repair note, so the repair counts as a containment signal.

## Lesson gate and build streak guard

These two guards use the [build-failure history](#build-failure-history). They are workflow gates, and they apply in both enforcement modes.

### Build streak

The `build-streak` guard refuses a build or test command after 5 consecutive failures in one execution. Only the build loop is refused. Other commands still run. The message tells the agent to call its submit tool with status `stuck` and to give the failing command, the diagnostic, the ruled-out hypotheses, and the fact that it needs. It also forbids a retry under a different spelling of the command. The reason in the message: the agent does not yet have the information that the fix needs, so a retry is not the next step.

### Lesson gate

A pending lesson exists when a build passed after a streak of 3 or more failures with a known diagnostic. When a lesson is pending, `lesson-gate` refuses three calls:

- `Report` with an empty `reason`.
- Any `submit_*` call with status `ok`.
- A write to the declared report file.

The agent has two ways out:

- Call the `Memory` tool with `area` set to the affected module and `lesson` set to the diagnostic and the correct pattern. A `Memory` call that succeeds clears all pending lessons.
- Call `Report` with a non-empty `reason` that says that the fix was situational. This also clears all pending lessons.

The reason for the gate: the diagnostic recurs across sessions, and a recorded lesson stops the next run from deriving the fix again. See [Storage](storage.md) for the lesson store.

## Other guards

These guards protect other records. Each has a rule ID in the source.

| Guard id | What it refuses | Reason in the code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace-artifacts` | A write, move, or delete in the workspace artifacts dir (Rule W1) | Artifacts belong to the user. Agents read them and propose changes in a report |
| `workspace-docs` | A write in the workspace books dir (Rule B5) | The engine writes the books from the submit calls of the docs stage |
| `manage-tools` | `ProjectCreate` from any run but the implementer of a phase in a project that does not exist yet, a wrong `key`, and any write outside the session dir and OS temp before the project exists (Rule O2) | No project root exists to hold the work, and the user must not be asked about a project that cannot run |
| `answer-only` | Any write from a consult run (Rule H3) | A consult run answers with `SubagentReply` and changes nothing |
| `reply-first` | A `submit_*` call from a run that owes a reply (Rule H3) | Another subagent waits for the answer |
| `windows-path` | On Windows: alternate data streams, device names such as `CON` and `COM1`, UNC and device paths, drive-relative paths such as `C:foo`, and a `..` after a junction or symlink | Such a spelling can name a protected file under a name that the guards do not check (WINDOWS_HANDOVER 1.4) |

See [Agent coordination](agent-coordination.md) for consult runs and replies.

## Permission modes

The permission mode sets the default answer for a call that no rule decides. `PermissionMode` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` has four values. The setting `permissions.mode` holds the value, and the default is `default`.

| Mode | Value in settings | Default answer for an unlisted call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default | `default` | Ask for edits and for commands that are not read-only. The rule shown is `mode:default` |
| Accept edits | `acceptEdits` | Allow edits inside the repo and the commands `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, and `mv` inside the repo. Ask for the rest. The rule shown is `mode:acceptEdits` |
| Plan | `plan` | Deny every write and every command that is not read-only. The rule shown is `mode:plan` |
| Bypass | `bypass` | Allow every call that no deny rule or ask rule refuses. The rule shown is `mode:bypass` |

When YOLO is on, `mode()` returns `bypass` and ignores the saved mode. Ask rules and deny rules still apply first. See [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

The rule lists merge in the order global, workspace, session. The lists concatenate (`PermissionRules::merged`). The settings keys are `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, and `permissions.deny`. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) for where these settings live.

## Permission rule syntax and matching

A rule has the form `Tool` or `Tool(spec)`. `parse_rule` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/perms.rs` reads a rule. A rule without a spec matches every use of the tool.

### Valid tool names

A rule can name one of the 29 tools in `KNOWN_TOOLS`: `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd`, `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap`, `ProjectList`, and `ProjectCreate`. A rule can also name a tool that starts with `mcp__`, `Other:`, or `submit_`.

### Invalid rules

`validate_rule` rejects a rule in settings validation. The cases are an empty rule, a missing closing parenthesis, empty parentheses, a tool name that Ostra does not know, a path pattern that does not compile, and a `WebFetch` spec that does not start with `domain:`. At run time, `ExecutionPolicy::new` ignores an invalid rule and writes a warning to the log. A bad rule never stops a run.

### Rule families

The tool in a rule puts it in a family. `family` in `perms.rs` assigns each tool:

- **Bash:** `Bash`.
- **Edit:** `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, and `ApplyPatch`. An `Edit` rule covers every file-writing tool.
- **Read:** `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob`. A `Read` rule covers all three. A `Grep` rule covers only `Grep`.
- **WebFetch:** `WebFetch`.
- **Other:** every other tool.

### Bash specs

A Bash spec is a glob over one simple command. The `*` matches any text. These forms exist:

- `Bash(npm run test *)` matches `npm run test --watch` and also the bare `npm run test`. A trailing ` *` matches the bare command.
- `Bash(npm test:*)` is the older prefix form. It matches `npm test` and `npm test -- foo`, but not `npm tests`.
- `Bash(rm -rf /*)` matches `sudo rm -rf /var`, because the match also tries the command without wrappers.
- `Bash(./mvnw *)` matches `FOO=1 ./mvnw -q compile`, because the match also tries the command without leading assignments.

`bash_forms` builds three texts for each command: all words, the words without leading assignments, and the words from the effective command. The wrappers that the parser skips are listed in [Bash command parsing](#bash-command-parsing).

### Path specs

A path spec follows the gitignore style. `anchor` turns it into an absolute pattern:

- `//x` is the absolute path `/x`.
- `~/x` is under the home directory.
- `./x` and `/x` are relative to the repo root.
- `x/y` (a name with a slash) is relative to the repo root.
- A bare name such as `*.env` matches at any depth.
- A trailing `/` adds `**`.

The `*` does not cross a `/`. The pattern `dir/**` also matches `dir`. A rule matches if the pattern matches the target path or any parent of it. On Windows, the match ignores letter case.

### WebFetch specs

`WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)` matches the host `docs.rs` and every subdomain of it. The host comes from the same URL parser that the request uses (`url_host`). Thus a rule cannot match a different host than the request reaches. For example, `https://evil.example\@docs.rs/` has the host `evil.example`. The hosts `evil-docs.rs` and `docs.rs.evil.com` do not match.

### MCP tool specs

A rule with the name `mcp__github` covers every tool of that server, as in Claude Code. A spec on a tool of the Other family matches nothing, because the policy has no text to match.

### Suggested rules

When the user answers `always-in-workspace`, the policy suggests a rule. `suggestion_for_bash` makes `Bash(<command> *)` and adds the next word if it has no `-` and no `/`. For example, `npm run test --watch` gives `Bash(npm run *)`. `suggestion_for_path` makes `Edit(/src/**)` for a file inside a subdir of the repo, and `Edit(/README.md)` for a file in the repo root. A `WebFetch` call gives `WebFetch(domain:<host>)`. `ProjectCreate` gives no rule, because no allow rule stands in for the user's answer (Rule O1).

## How layer 2 decides for each tool family

In every family, a deny rule beats an ask rule, and an ask rule beats an allow rule (`rule_decision`). The mode decides only when no rule matches.

### Bash

`bash_permission` checks the simple commands of the parsed command in this order:

1. If a deny rule matches any simple command, the call is denied.
2. If an ask rule matches any simple command, the call asks.
3. If the command has a statement that the parser does not model, the decision depends on the mode. Such a statement is a standalone assignment, `export`, `[[ ]]`, a loop header, or a function. Bypass allows it, plan denies it, and the other modes ask with the rule `unmodelled`. The reason: such a statement can change what a later command runs (`PATH`, `GIT_CONFIG_*`) or run code when the shell evaluates it.
4. If the parser found a syntax error, the same mode split applies, and the asking rule is `unparsed`.
5. For each simple command, the first match decides:
   - An allow rule from settings or from the session. A command with a dynamic name never matches an allow rule.
   - A read-only command with all write targets in the session dir or OS temp. The rule shown is `read-only`.
   - In `acceptEdits` mode, a read-only command, or `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, or `mv`, with all targets in the repo, session dir, or OS temp.
   - Otherwise the mode decides: bypass allows, plan denies, and the other modes ask.

A write target is not known when the path has a variable, a substitution, or a glob. A relative target after a `cd` with a dynamic path is not known either. Such a command is never auto-allowed, because the guards did not check its real target.

### Read-only commands

`is_read_only` allows a command without a question in every mode. The command must be fully understood. These rules apply:

- The command name is in `READ_ONLY`: `ls`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `grep`, `rg`, `find`, `git`, `pwd`, `echo`, `printf`, `sort`, `uniq`, `diff`, `stat`, `file`, `which`, `tree`, `cd`, `true`, `test`, `[`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, `readlink`.
- The command has no assignments and no wrapper. An assignment such as `LD_PRELOAD` or `GIT_CONFIG_*` can change what runs.
- The command name has no `/`, because a path can name a script that the agent wrote.
- For the commands in `EXEC_CAPABLE` (`git`, `rg`, `sort`, `find`, `tree`, `file`, `uniq`), every argument must be static and without a glob. A dynamic word can expand to an option that starts a program.
- `find` without `-exec`, `-execdir`, `-delete`, `-fprint`, `-fprint0`, `-fprintf`, `-fls`, `-ok`, or `-okdir`.
- `rg` without `--pre`, `--pre-glob`, or `--hostname-bin`.
- `sort` without `--output`, `--compress-program`, or `-o`.
- `printf` without `-v`.
- `test` and `[` without `$`, a backquote, or `[` in an argument, because the shell evaluates a subscript.
- `git` only with a subcommand in `GIT_READ` (`status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `rev-parse`, `ls-files`, `blame`) or a listing form of `branch`, `tag`, `remote`, `describe`, or `config`. The only leading options are `-C <dir>` and those in `GIT_SAFE_GLOBAL` (`--no-pager`, `-P`, `--no-optional-locks`, `--literal-pathspecs`, `--no-replace-objects`). The options `--output`, `--ext-diff`, `--textconv`, and `--open-files-in-pager` are refused.

A git command also runs without a question only when its directory is known and inside the repo. The reason: git reads the config of a repository, and that config can name programs. The `git-metadata` guard protects the `.git` of the project.

The guards use a different list, `PLAIN_READERS`, for the question whether a command only reads. Do not confuse the two lists.

### Edit family

For each target path, `layer2` applies these tests in order:

1. A deny rule or an ask rule that matches decides the call.
2. If the path runs code later, the mode default applies. See the list below.
3. If the path is in the session dir or in OS temp, the write is allowed.
4. An allow rule allows the write.
5. In `acceptEdits` mode, a path inside the repo is allowed.
6. Otherwise the mode default applies.

One denial ends the check. If no path denies, one ask is enough to ask. The rule shown for an allowed write is the allow rule, `mode:acceptEdits`, or `session-dir`. In `plan` mode, a write to the session dir or OS temp is still allowed, because agents write their reports there.

`runs_code_later` marks files that make a tool run a program the next time someone opens the project. Test 2 comes before the allow rule in test 4, so an allow rule cannot change the result for these files. The result is the mode default:

- In `default` mode and `acceptEdits` mode, the write always asks.
- In `plan` mode, `mode_default` returns a deny with the rule `mode:plan`.
- In `bypass` mode, and under YOLO, the write is allowed.

The reason: the file outlives the session and runs outside the policy. The marked files are:

- Names: `.mcp.json`, `.envrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.lefthook.yml`, `lefthook.yml`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, `.pnpmfile.cjs`.
- Path endings: `/.claude/settings.json`, `/.claude/settings.local.json`, `/.codex/config.toml`, `/.gemini/settings.json`, `/.vscode/tasks.json`, `/.vscode/settings.json`, `/.vscode/launch.json`, `/.cargo/config.toml`, `/.cargo/config`.
- Dirs: `/.github/workflows/`, `/.github/actions/`, `/.devcontainer/`, `/.husky/`, `/.claude/hooks/`, `/.grok/`.

### Read family and Skill

A call to `Read`, `Grep`, or `Glob` is allowed unless a deny rule or an ask rule matches the path. Reads are free because the `secret-read` guard in layer 1 already refused the paths that matter. A `Skill` call with a `path` argument follows the `Read` rules for that path.

### WebFetch

A matching rule decides. If no rule matches, bypass mode allows the call, and every other mode asks, including `plan` mode.

### Other tools

- **Project creation.** `ProjectCreate` always asks the user, in every mode and whatever the allow rules say (Rule O1). A deny rule still refuses it, and `plan` mode denies it. YOLO answers the ask.
- **Known tools.** These tools are allowed unless a rule says otherwise: `WebSearch`, `Skill`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, the code tools, the project tools, the coordination tools, every `submit_*` tool, and the harness bookkeeping tools (`Other:search_tool`, `Other:ToolSearch`, `Other:TodoWrite`, `Other:todo_write`, `Other:update_plan`, `Other:update_todos`, and the Ostra MCP tools).
- **Workspace MCP tools.** These tools are allowed unless a rule says otherwise (Rule M1). In `plan` mode, only the tools that their server marks read-only are allowed (`PolicyInputs.read_only_mcp_tools`).
- **Unknown tools.** The mode default applies.

## Bash command parsing

The policy needs the simple commands of a shell line, because a permission rule and a write guard apply to one command at a time. `crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs` parses the line with tree-sitter-bash. It replaces the regex rules of the Ultracode library `shell-paths.js` and keeps its rules.

### What the parser returns

`bash::parse` returns a `Parsed` value with three fields:

- `commands`: the `SimpleCommand` values in execution order.
- `complete`: false when the parser found a syntax error or a nesting depth over the limit. The split can be wrong then.
- `modelled`: false when the source has a statement that the command list does not model.

A `SimpleCommand` holds the assignments, the `words`, the redirects, a heredoc body, the source text, a flag for piped input, and the text of the whole pipeline. Each `Word` has the `raw` text, a `value` when the word is static, and a `glob` flag for an unquoted glob or a brace expansion. A word with a variable or a substitution has no static value.

### What the parser includes

- Commands in lists, pipelines, `if` and `while` bodies, subshells, and groups. The `STRUCTURAL` list names the statement kinds that only group commands.
- Commands inside command substitutions and process substitutions.
- The argument of `bash -c`, `sh -c`, and `eval`, parsed again as shell. `SHELLS` lists `sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `dash`, `ksh`, `fish`, `ash`, and `mksh`.
- A heredoc body that is fed to a shell. A body that is fed to a data sink is content, and a body that is fed to an interpreter is interpreter code.
- The nesting limit `MAX_DEPTH` is 4. Past it, the parser sets `complete` to false.

### Effective command

`effective_index` finds the word that really runs. It skips `VAR=value` words and these wrappers: `sudo`, `doas`, `env`, `nohup`, `nice`, `ionice`, `stdbuf`, `time`, `timeout`, `command`, `exec`, `xargs`, `strace`, `watch`, and `builtin`. It also skips the options of a wrapper, and it knows which options take a value. For `timeout`, it skips the duration. Thus `FOO=1 sudo -u me timeout 5 rm -rf a` has the effective name `rm`.

A test with only plain words in `[ ]` or `[[ ]]` is not a problem. A test with a `$`, a backquote, or a bracket is not modelled, because the shell evaluates it and it can run a command.

### Write targets

`write_targets` lists each path that a command creates, overwrites, moves, or deletes. The sources are:

- Redirects that write: `>`, `>>`, `>|`, `&>`, `&>>`, `<>`, and `>&` to a name that is not a file descriptor.
- The commands `tee`, `rm`, `rmdir`, `shred`, `truncate`, `touch`, `mkdir`, and `unlink`: every word that is not a flag.
- The commands `cp`, `install`, `ln`, and `mv`. The parser understands `-t`, `--target-directory`, and its unique abbreviations. A destination that is a directory gets the source name added. A `mv` also removes each source.
- `sed` and `perl` with an in-place flag.
- `dd` with `of=`.
- A `git` subcommand in `GIT_WRITE_SUBCOMMANDS`: `checkout`, `switch`, `restore`, `reset`, `apply`, `am`, `stash`, `clean`, `rm`, `mv`, `merge`, `rebase`, `pull`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`, `commit`, and `add`. The target is the working tree, and `-C` changes the directory.

The parser skips `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, `/dev/tty`, `-`, `&1`, `&2`, and a token that has only dots, because a dot-only token is prose. A `<ID>` placeholder is not a redirect. A `~user/` path is unresolved, because the resolver does not model the home of another account.

### Working directory

`command_cwds` tracks `cd` and `pushd` across the commands of one line. A `cd` with a dynamic path keeps the last known directory. `cwd_unknown` marks commands after a dynamic `cd` or `pushd` and after `popd`. The parser does not model the scope of a subshell.

### Inline interpreter code

`inline_code` finds code that a command hands to an interpreter. `INTERPRETERS` lists `node`, `nodejs`, `bun`, `deno`, `ts-node`, `tsx`, `python`, `python2`, `python3`, `perl`, `ruby`, `php`, `Rscript`, and `osascript`. A versioned name such as `python3.12` also counts. The channels are an eval flag (`-e`, `-E`, `--eval`, `-c`, `--command`, `-p`, `--print`, `-r`, `--exec`, and `deno eval`), a heredoc, and piped standard input with no script. The guards scan this code for protected names and for write and spawn calls.

### Opaque shells

PowerShell and cmd have no parser. Layer 1 scans their raw text for protected names and for secret paths and engine-state paths (`check_opaque_shell`). Layer 2 never auto-allows these tools. The shell tools are described in [Native tools](tools.md).

## Build-failure history

The policy counts the consecutive build and test failures of one execution. The code is in `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs`, a port of the Ultracode files `build-signal.js`, `build-streak.js`, and `build-streak-gate.js`. The count has two uses: it warns the agent early, and it refuses more retries after the limit. A recovered streak also forces the agent to record a lesson.

### Which commands count

`is_build_command` decides if a `Bash` command is a build or test command. The input is the list of `build_commands` and `test_commands` that `PolicyInputs` carries from `project.toml`. The test applies in this order:

1. A configured command becomes a matcher. A `{PLACEHOLDER}` token is a wildcard, and the white space is flexible. Thus `./mvnw test -pl {MODULE}` matches `./mvnw test -pl core`.
2. The first two words of a configured command (the driver head, such as `./mvnw` or `uv run pytest`) also count when the command text contains them. The reason: agents vary the flags around the same build tool. The head must be longer than 2 characters.
3. If the project has no configured commands, the regex `FALLBACK_BUILD` matches a fixed set of patterns. The pattern must start at the start of the text or after one of these characters: a space, a pipe sign, a semicolon sign, an ampersand, or an opening parenthesis. The pattern must end at a word boundary.

The `FALLBACK_BUILD` patterns are:

| Tool | What matches |
| --- | --- |
| Any argument | `mvn`, `./mvnw`, `gradle`, `./gradlew`, `tsc`, `cargo`, `dotnet`, `make`, `pytest` |
| `go` | `go build`, `go test`, `go vet` only |
| `npm` | `npm run <x>` (any script name), `npm test`, and `npm run-script` only |
| `pnpm` | `pnpm test`, `pnpm run`, and `pnpm build` only |
| `yarn` | `yarn test`, `yarn run`, and `yarn build` only |
| `uv run` | `uv run pytest`, `uv run mypy`, and `uv run ruff` only |
| `python -m` | `python -m pytest`, `python -m mypy`, and `python -m unittest` only |

The fallback does not match every command of a tool. For example, `npm install` does not count, and `uv run script.py` does not count. The reason for the narrow list: a package install or a script run is not a build, and a failure there must not start the streak.

If the project has configured commands, the fallback is off. For example, `cargo test -p x` is not a build command when the only configured command is `npm test`.

### Did the command fail

`failed_from` returns `Some(true)`, `Some(false)`, or `None`. It checks in this order:

1. The exit code from the harness or the native tool.
2. An exit code in the text: `Exit code N`, `exited with code N`, or `exit status N`.
3. An error result with the words `timed out`, `interrupted`, `canceled`, or `cancelled` gives `None`. The streak does not change.
4. Any other error result is a failure.
5. A result that is not known and has empty text gives `None`. This case happens on Antigravity, which does not report tool results.
6. A failure marker in the text is a failure. The markers include `BUILD FAILURE`, `COMPILATION ERROR`, `error TS<n>`, `npm ERR!`, a Rust `error[E<n>]:` line, a Python traceback, and `<n> failed`.
7. Otherwise the command passed.

An exit code of 0 wins over a failure marker in the text.

### Diagnostic signature

`diagnostic_signature` makes a stable one-line fingerprint of the cause. It takes the first line, 12 to 400 characters long, that matches `DIAGNOSTIC`. The pattern covers messages such as `cannot find symbol`, `is not assignable`, `error[E<n>]`, `AssertionError`, `ImportError`, and `Unresolved reference`. `normalize_diagnostic` then removes the level prefix (`ERROR`, `WARN`, `E`, `FAIL`), replaces paths with `<path>`, removes positions and line numbers, replaces versions with `<v>`, collapses white space, and cuts the line to 160 characters. A signature shorter than 8 characters is dropped. Thus the same error gives the same signature when the path or the line changes.

### Thresholds

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 | At the second failure in a row with a known signature, the executor runs a memory recall with the signature and appends the lessons found. A known fix arrives one failure before the warning |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 | From the third failure, the policy appends a note. It asks the agent to state its root-cause belief and not to retry a variation of the same edit. It adds that the same diagnostic repeats when the signature appears more than once in the history |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 | At 5 failures in a row, `blocked` is true. The `build-streak` guard refuses further build and test commands |
| `MAX_HISTORY` | 12 | The number of signatures that the history keeps, and the number of pending recoveries that the policy keeps. The oldest entry is dropped |

From the third failure to the fourth, the warning tells the agent how many failures remain before the refusal. At 5 failures, the note tells the agent to call its submit tool with status `stuck`.

### Recovery and the pending lesson

A command that passes resets the count to 0. If the count was 3 or more and the history has a signature, the pass is a verified recovery. The policy adds a `Recovery` with the signature and the streak length to the `pending` list. It appends a note that asks the agent to call `Memory` now. A pass after a streak of 1 or 2 failures records no recovery. A streak with no known signature records none either. The `lesson-gate` guard then refuses `Report`, `submit_*`, and the report file write until the agent records the lesson or states a reason.

### Where the history runs

`ExecutionPolicy::observe` runs after each tool call. `Bash` calls update the streak. A successful `Memory` call, and a `Report` call with a non-empty `reason`, clear the pending list. The result is a list of `Observation` values: `AppendNote` adds text to the tool result that the model sees, and `RecallLessons` asks the caller to search memory. The history lives in memory for one execution. A new execution starts with a streak of 0.

## Containment signals and the session pause

Some refusals show an attempt to leave the sandbox or to read what an agent must not read. `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` names these refusals containment signals (Rule P3). The runner records each signal as an event. The third signal of one execution pauses the session.

### Signal kinds

`ContainmentSignal` has three kinds. `classify` maps an `ExecutionDelta` to a signal:

| Kind | Source | Counts as a signal when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Guard { rule, reason }` | A layer 1 denial in a `Policy` delta | The layer is `guard` and the rule is `secret-read`, `self-protection`, or `git-metadata` (`GUARDS`) |
| `Egress { host, port }` | An `Egress` delta from the [sandbox](sandbox.md) proxy | The connection is refused and the destination is loopback, private, or link-local |
| `Decoy { path }` | A `Decoy` delta | A process opened a decoy credential file |

These refusals are not signals:

- A denial from another guard, such as `write-scope`. Those guards refuse ordinary mistakes.
- A denial from the permission layer, even with the rule name `secret-read`.
- A refused connection to a public host. Builds call telemetry hosts, so the refusal shows in the Activity view only.

### Flow of a signal

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Exec as Executor
  participant Host as EngineHost
  participant State as SessionState
  Exec->>Host: emit(ExecutionDelta)
  Host->>Host: containment::classify(delta)
  Host->>State: append ContainmentSignal event
  State->>State: third signal sets paused and contained
  Host->>State: interrupt(Pause)
```

### Steps

1. `EngineHost::emit` stores the delta in the activity table and calls `classify`.
2. `record_signal` reads the signals that it has already recorded for the execution. If the count is 3 or more, it records nothing. The reason: a retry loop cannot flood the log.
3. Otherwise it appends a `SessionEvent::ContainmentSignal`.
4. When `SessionState` folds the event, it adds the signal to `signals` for that execution. If the count is exactly `PAUSE_AFTER` (3), the session is not paused, and the session is not finished, then the state sets `paused` to true, sets `contained` to the execution, and interrupts the running executions with `Interrupt::Pause`. This is the same pause as a pause by the user (Rule P1).
5. Appends are serialized, so exactly one append brings the count to 3. That append calls `interrupt(Pause)` on the session.

`describe` gives one line for the notes of the session and the Activity view. An example is `the self-protection guard refused a tool call`. The session view shows `PAUSE_AFTER` as the number of signals that pause a session.

When the user resumes the session, `SessionResumed` clears `contained`. The recorded signals stay in `signals`. The execution keeps its count, so it records no more than 3 signals in total.

## Git command hardening in ostra-core

A `.git/config` is written by whoever controls the folder, and an agent can write it. A config can name programs that git starts. `crates/ostra-core/src/git.rs` holds the config overrides for the git commands that Ostra runs. This file is separate from the permission rules, but it closes the same gap.

| Constant or function | Value | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NO_EXEC` | `core.fsmonitor=false`, `protocol.ext.allow=never`, `core.askPass=` | Every git command that Ostra starts: no `fsmonitor` program, no `ext::` transport, no askpass program from the repository |
| `AUTOMATIC` | `NO_EXEC` plus `core.hooksPath` | Git commands that Ostra runs without a user request (status, listings, diffs, staging during review): no hooks. The path is `/dev/null`. On Windows it is an empty `no-hooks` dir in the Ostra data dir, because Git for Windows reads `/dev/null/<hook>` as a path on the current drive |
| `AGENT_CONFIG` | `core.fsmonitor=false`, `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, `protocol.ext.allow=never` | Git commands that an agent process runs. Hooks stay on, because agent commits run the hooks of the repository |
| `config_env`, `agent_env` | `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>`, `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n>` | Add the pairs after the entries that the parent process already has, so both apply |
| `FILTER_QUERY` | `git config --null --get-regexp ^filter\..+\.(clean\|smudge\|process)$` | Lists the filter drivers that a repository names |
| `LFS_DRIVERS` | The three standard `git-lfs` commands | Excluded from blanking, so LFS files do not all look modified |
| `MAX_FILTER_REPOS` | 256 | The most repositories that `filter_overrides` reads. It bounds the git processes. At the limit, it writes a warning and stops |

`blank_filters` makes a `-c filter.<name>.<key>=` pair for each driver except `git-lfs`. `filter_overrides` does this for the root repository and for every submodule that git enters from the index. `submodule_filter_overrides` skips the root, for commands that the user asked for, so the filters of the repository (git-crypt, for example) still apply. A status, diff, `add`, or commit runs `git status` inside each populated submodule. That reads the config of the submodule, and an agent can create and stage one.

The guard `git-metadata` is the matching rule for agent writes. The constant `GIT_METADATA` lives in `containment.rs` so that both crates use one name.

## What happens when

- **A guard denies a call.** The executor does not run the tool. The model gets the reason with the correction first. The Activity view shows the guard id.
- **An ask rule matches.** The call waits for a user answer. If the session is paused or stopped, the gate stays open until the engine handles it. The call does not run before an answer.
- **A deny rule matches.** The call is denied with the rule text. The model gets the reason ``Do not <action>: the permission rule `<rule>` refuses it. If the task needs it, say so in your report.`` The native executor puts ``Denied by permission `<rule>`: `` before it.
- **A rule is invalid.** The policy ignores it, writes a warning, and uses the other rules.
- **The command has a syntax error.** In `default` and `acceptEdits` mode, the call asks with the rule `unparsed`. In `plan` mode it is denied. In `bypass` mode it is allowed.
- **The command has a variable, glob, or substitution in a write position.** The command is not auto-allowed, because the target is unknown.
- **A build fails 5 times in a row.** Build and test commands are refused. The agent must submit with status `stuck`. A build that passes first resets the count.
- **A build is interrupted or times out.** The streak does not change.
- **The agent recovers after 3 or more failures.** The agent must record a lesson or give a reason before it can report or submit with status `ok`.
- **An execution records its third containment signal.** The session pauses. The user can resume it. A fourth signal in the same execution is not recorded.
- **YOLO is turned on or off during a run.** The executor calls `set_yolo` before each call, so the change applies to the next call.
- **The hook bridge cannot find the execution.** `policy_check` denies the call with the guard `self-protection` and the message `This execution is not running in Ostra.`
- **A workspace MCP tool or a project tool comes through a harness hook.** The hook returns `Allow` with no `RuleRef`, because the MCP server of Ostra checks and logs the call when it runs it (Rules M2 and O1). This holds unless the execution is an inspect run.

## What the policy does not guarantee

The policy reduces risk. It does not make an agent safe by itself. Read these limits before you rely on it.

- **Enforcement is off by default.** With `tool_enforcement` set to `disabled`, `write-scope`, `report-path`, `self-protection`, and the interpreter write checks do not run. A script can then write any file that the [sandbox](sandbox.md) allows.
- **The guards read only the paths that a call names.** A program that an allowed command starts can write elsewhere. The guards cannot see what that program does. The kernel sandbox is the layer that bounds it.
- **A permission rule sees only the words of a command.** It does not see what a started program does.
- **The parser does not model everything.** It does not model the scope of a subshell, shell functions, or a variable that changes a path. It stops at a nesting depth of 4. In `default` and `acceptEdits` mode, such a command asks, but in `bypass` mode and under YOLO it runs.
- **PowerShell and cmd are scanned by text.** The guards match protected names and secret paths in the raw text. They do not parse the command.
- **Reads outside the repo are allowed.** Layer 1 refuses secret paths, but the Read family allows a read of another file outside the repo unless a rule refuses it.
- **A containment signal is a detection, not a block.** The guard still denies the call, but the signal only pauses the session after the third event in one execution. It shows an attempt and does not prove an escape.
- **YOLO and bypass remove asks.** Under YOLO, every ask becomes an allow. A deny rule and a guard still refuse.
- **Some harnesses give less data.** A harness that does not report tool results (Antigravity) gives no exit code or output, so the build streak cannot count its failures.
- **The `echo` and `printf` commands are skipped by the secret-read scan.** They print a path and do not open it.

## Limits and constants

The table lists the numeric limits of this page. [Reference: executor, tool, policy, and sandbox limits](reference-execution-limits.md) lists the constants of every crate.

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PAUSE_AFTER` (`ostra-core`) | 3 | Signals of one execution that pause the session. The runner also records no more than this many for one execution |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 | Failures in a row that trigger a lesson recall |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 | Failures in a row that trigger a warning note |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 | Failures in a row after which build commands are refused |
| `MAX_HISTORY` | 12 | Signatures and pending recoveries that the build history keeps |
| `MAX_DEPTH` (`bash.rs`) | 4 | Nesting depth of `bash -c`, `eval`, and heredoc re-parsing |
| `MAX_FILTER_REPOS` | 256 | Repositories that the filter scan reads |
| Signature line length | 12 to 400 characters | A line outside this range is not used as a diagnostic |
| Signature length | 160 characters at most, 8 at least | `normalize_diagnostic` cuts at 160. A shorter result is dropped |
| Ask text for a command | 200 characters | `truncate` cuts the command in an ask reason |
| Reason clip in Grok | 256 characters | Each denial reason starts with the correction because of this clip |

The other constants of the crate are internal lists that this page names where they apply: `WRITE_SCOPE`, `NO_TESTS`, `STATE_OWNERSHIP`, `ARTIFACT_OWNERSHIP`, `REPORT_PATH`, `DOCUMENT_TOOL`, `LESSON_GATE`, `BUILD_STREAK`, `WORKSPACE_ARTIFACTS`, `WORKSPACE_DOCS`, `MANAGE_TOOLS`, `WINDOWS_PATH`, `ANSWER_ONLY`, and `REPLY_FIRST` are guard IDs. `TOOL_OWNED`, `AGENT_OWNED`, `ARTIFACTS`, `STATE_NAME`, `TEST_DIR`, `TEST_FILE`, `PROC_SECRET`, `PLAIN_READERS`, `PATH_CANDIDATE`, `WIN_PATH_CANDIDATE`, `WRITE_API`, `PY_OPEN_WRITE`, and `SPAWN_API` are the patterns and lists of the guards. `KNOWN_TOOLS` is the list of rule tool names. `READ_ONLY`, `GIT_READ`, `GIT_SAFE_GLOBAL`, and `EXEC_CAPABLE` are the lists of the read-only test. `SHELLS`, `INTERPRETERS`, `STRUCTURAL`, and `GIT_WRITE_SUBCOMMANDS` are the lists of the parser. `FALLBACK_BUILD`, `PLACEHOLDER`, `FAILURE_MARKERS`, `EXIT_CODE_PATTERNS`, `INTERRUPTED`, `DIAGNOSTIC`, and the `NORM_*` patterns are the patterns of the build history. `SECRET_READ`, `SELF_PROTECTION`, `GIT_METADATA`, and `GUARDS` are in `containment.rs`.

## Where to see and change the behavior

- **Activity view.** It shows each policy decision with its layer and rule when the decision has a `RuleRef`. The console adds advice under a denial or an ask. For a guard, the advice comes from `GUARD_ADVICE` in `web/src/lib/events.ts`.
- **Guards with advice.** `GUARD_ADVICE` has entries for 8 guards: `write-scope`, `no-tests-from-implementer`, `state-ownership`, `artifact-ownership`, `report-path`, `lesson-gate`, `build-streak`, and `self-protection`. `denialAdvice` returns null for every other guard, such as `secret-read`, `git-metadata`, and `workspace-artifacts`.
- **Advice for permission rules.** For a deny rule, `denialAdvice` tells the user to edit the rule in the workspace settings. For an ask, it offers to allow the call once or for the whole workspace.
- **Permission gate card.** It shows the call, the reason, the rule, and a suggested rule. The user answers `allow-once`, `always-in-workspace`, or `deny`.
- **Workspace settings.** The user sets `permissions.mode`, `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, `permissions.deny`, and `tool_enforcement`. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) and [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md).
- **Project commands.** `build_commands` and `test_commands` in `project.toml` set which commands count for the build streak.
- **Tests.** `crates/ostra-policy/tests/policy.rs` holds the policy cases. The unit tests in `guards.rs`, `perms.rs`, `build.rs`, `bash.rs`, and `containment.rs` check the patterns. Run `cargo test --workspace` to run them all.
