sections.title: Sandbox: kernel enforcement under agent commands
sections.summary: How the `ostra-sandbox` crate confines agent commands with the kernel: the Profile, Backend, and Os layers, mounts, seccomp, the egress proxy, decoys, caches, git protection, modes, and the limits of the sandbox.
sections.body:
The policy layer judges each tool call by the paths that the call names. A shell command can hide a path, for example in a variable or a pipe. Without a second layer, a command that the policy cannot read runs with the full rights of the user. The `ostra-sandbox` crate adds that layer. The kernel enforces it under every command, so it does not depend on what Ostra can parse.

The sandbox gives each command these properties:

- The host file system is read-only.
- Only the roots of the execution are writable.
- Ostra's data and the credentials of the user are not reachable.
- The network leads out only through the egress proxy of Ostra.

This page covers the layers of the crate, the two backends, the mounts, the seccomp filter, the egress proxy, decoys, build caches, git protection, the modes, the status report, and what the sandbox does not cover. The settings that choose a mode, a network, and hosts are on [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) and [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md). The guards that run before a command are on [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).

## Terms used on this page

- **Sandbox**: the kernel-enforced boundary around one command.
- **Profile**: the description of one boundary, written one time for every backend (`Profile` in `profile.rs`).
- **Backend**: the code that turns a profile into a running sandbox. The two backends are bubblewrap on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS.
- **Hidden path**: a path that the command cannot read. Under bubblewrap it looks empty. Under Seatbelt it returns `EPERM`.
- **Helper**: the `ostra sandbox-init` command. It starts first inside each bubblewrap sandbox.
- **Egress proxy**: the HTTP proxy that is the only way out of a sandbox with a private network.
- **Decoy**: a fake credential file. An open of the file is a containment signal.
- **Scratch dir**: the host directory that bubblewrap mounts at `/tmp`.

## The three layers of the crate

The crate has three layers, so that a difference between operating systems lives in one place ([`lib.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/lib.rs)).

- `Profile` ([`profile.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/profile.rs)) describes the boundary of one execution without the name of a backend. It holds the mounts, the environment, the egress policy, the decoys, and the forwarded ports.
- `Backend` ([`backend.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/backend.rs)) is an enum with the values `Bubblewrap` and `Seatbelt`. Each value maps to an `Enforcer` that renders a profile into a command. The rendering code in `bwrap.rs` and `seatbelt.rs` is plain code that compiles on every OS. Tests can check the rendering on any machine.
- `sys` ([`sys/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/mod.rs)) is the only code that calls the kernel. Each OS has one implementation of the `Os` trait. The module `sys/mod.rs` picks the implementation at compile time: `Linux`, `MacOs`, or `Other`.

Other code never matches on the backend to choose a behavior. It calls `Backend::enforcer`, so a quirk of one backend stays in its own file. For example, `Backend::has_mount_namespace` tells a caller whether paths can be remapped. Bubblewrap returns true. Seatbelt returns false.

### Layer flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Caller["Bash tool, harness launch, host_command"] --> Profile["Profile"]
  Profile --> Backend["Backend::enforcer"]
  Backend --> Bwrap["bwrap.rs: bwrap arguments"]
  Backend --> Seat["seatbelt.rs: SBPL policy"]
  Bwrap --> Os["sys::Platform: Os trait"]
  Seat --> Os
  Os --> Kernel["Kernel"]
```

## The Os trait

The `Os` trait holds every call that depends on the operating system. The members are:

| Member | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `UNAVAILABLE` | The text that tells the user what to do when no sandbox works on this OS. |
| `probe` | Returns the backend that works on this machine, or the reason that none works. |
| `run_helper` | Runs `ostra sandbox-init` (Linux only). |
| `scrub_startup_env` | Moves the startup environment of Ostra where other processes cannot read it (macOS only). |
| `user_id`, `user_temp_dir`, `symlink_file` | Small queries for the profile. |
| `marked`, `kill` | Find and kill the processes of a sandbox where a process can leave its process tree. |
| `socket_dir`, `bind_local`, `accept_local`, `connect_local` | Unix sockets for the egress proxy. |
| `watch_opens`, `watch_refusals`, `refusals_readable`, `start_refusal_reports` | Report the open of a decoy. |

The `Other` implementation (`sys/other.rs`) serves Windows and every OS without a sandbox. Its `probe` returns `The Windows sandbox is not built yet.` on Windows and `The sandbox needs Linux or macOS.` elsewhere. The other members of `Other` act as follows:

- **Return an error:** `probe`, `run_helper`, `symlink_file`, `bind_local`, `connect_local`, `watch_opens`, and `watch_refusals`.
- **Return `None`:** `user_id` and `user_temp_dir`.
- **Return an empty value:** `marked` returns an empty list, `kill` returns false, and `refusals_readable` returns false.
- **Create the directory:** `socket_dir` creates the directory.
- **Do nothing:** `scrub_startup_env` and `start_refusal_reports`.

The member `accept_local` cannot run on `Other`, because `bind_local` never returns a listener.

## Sandbox modes

The sandbox mode (`SandboxMode` in `ostra-core`) decides what an execution does about the sandbox. The function `decide` in `backend.rs` applies it.

| Mode | Backend works | No backend works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `required` | Run sandboxed. | Return an error. The execution does not start. |
| `auto` | Run sandboxed. | Run unsandboxed with a warning. |
| `off` | Run unsandboxed with no warning. | Run unsandboxed with no warning. |

The default mode is `required` on Linux and macOS. The default is `auto` on Windows, because Windows has no backend yet and `required` refuses every execution there. The workspace can set its own mode. A workspace mode replaces the global `[sandbox] mode` of `config.toml`.

```rust
pub fn decide(cfg: &SandboxConfig) -> Result<Decision, String> {
    match (cfg.mode, backend()) {
        (SandboxMode::Off, _) => Ok(Decision::Unsandboxed(None)),
        (_, Some(b)) => Ok(Decision::Sandboxed(b.clone())),
        (SandboxMode::Auto, None) => Ok(Decision::Unsandboxed(Some(unavailable_message()))),
        (SandboxMode::Required, None) => Err(format!("The sandbox is required ... {}", unavailable_message())),
    }
}
```

The probe runs one time for each process (`backend()` reads a `OnceLock`). The function `first_warning` returns true on its first call only, so the warning about a missing sandbox reaches the log one time.

### What happens when

- **The mode is `required` and no backend works.** `decide` returns an error with the probe reason and the `UNAVAILABLE` text. The execution does not start.
- **The mode is `auto` and no backend works.** The execution runs without a sandbox. The `Decision::Unsandboxed` value carries the warning.
- **The mode is `off`.** The execution runs without a sandbox and without a warning. The user chose this on purpose.
- **The user changes the mode.** Executions read the `[sandbox]` table fresh at each start. A change applies to the next execution. A running execution keeps its sandbox.

## Network modes

The network mode (`SandboxNetwork`) decides what a sandboxed program reaches. Every mode except `host` gives each sandbox a private network. Loopback, the local network, and the services of the host are then out of reach. Traffic leaves only through the egress proxy.

| Mode | What the command reaches |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | Nothing. A harness CLI still reaches its own model API. |
| `allowlist` (default) | The built-in package and source hosts, the model hosts of all four harness CLIs, and the hosts that the user lists. |
| `public` | Any public address, and the listed hosts. Loopback, private, and link-local addresses stay refused. |
| `host` | The host network with no filter. No private network and no proxy. |

The workspace can replace the network mode. Its `allowed_hosts` add to the global list. A workspace never removes a global host or a built-in host (`SandboxConfig::for_workspace`).

Under `none`, the listed hosts do not apply, because the policy starts with no hosts. The refusal text tells the user to set the network to `allowlist` and add the host.

On macOS, every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. The `LoopbackAccess` setting then chooses which loopback ports a command can connect to. The value `open` (default) allows every port except the blocked ports and the port of the Ostra server. The value `listed` allows only the loopback ports in `allowed_hosts`. On Linux each sandbox has its own loopback, so the setting changes nothing. The `open` value applies under `allowlist` and `public` only, because `none` reaches nothing (`Policy::shared_loopback`).

## What a profile contains

A `Profile` is a list of mounts plus an environment, an egress policy, decoys, and forwarded ports. There are two constructors.

- `Profile::for_execution(ctx, cfg, home)` builds the profile of an agent execution. It uses the `ExecContext` of the execution.
- `Profile::for_program(roots, cfg, home)` builds the profile of a program that Ostra starts for a project or workspace. The same rules apply, with `roots` writable.

### Mount kinds

The private `Mount` enum has six kinds.

| Kind | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Writable` | A host path bound read-write. |
| `ReadOnly` | A path that stays read-only. A missing path gets an empty read-only placeholder where it is safe to create one. |
| `Hidden` | A path that the command cannot read. |
| `HomeTmpfs`, `HomeEntry` | The overlay of the home folder (bubblewrap only). |
| `Link` | A symlink placed inside the overlaid home (bubblewrap only). |

### What is writable

For an agent execution, these paths are writable:

- The workspace root, the repo root, the session root, and the session dir, when each is set.
- Each path in `[sandbox] extra_writable`.
- The tool caches of the sandbox. See [Build caches](#build-caches).
- A harness CLI's own state dirs. The harness executor adds these with `Profile::writable`.

### What stays read-only inside a writable root

These paths are read-only even where their folder is writable:

- The state dir of the session (`paths::session_state_dir`). The workspace artifacts dir and the book dir are also read-only. Agents read artifacts and books and never write them (rules W1 and B5).
- The `workspace.toml` file and the database files of the workspace, with the suffixes `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal`.
- The memory database files, and each path in `ctx.protected_paths`.
- The git paths that choose programs. See [Git protection](#git-protection).
- The files in `PERSISTENCE_IN_HOME` (`profile.rs`). These files run code in a later shell, login, or build of the user: `.bashrc`, `.bash_profile`, `.bash_login`, `.bash_logout`, `.profile`, `.zshrc`, `.zshenv`, `.zprofile`, `.zlogin`, `.config/fish/`, `.gitconfig`, `.config/git/`, `.config/autostart/`, `.config/systemd/`, `.config/environment.d/`, `.pam_environment`, `.xprofile`, `.xsessionrc`, `.npmrc`, `.local/bin/`, `.cargo/bin/`, `.cargo/config`, `.cargo/config.toml`, and several `Library/` and Windows startup folders. The reason: an agent must not leave a program behind for the user.

### What is hidden

These paths are hidden:

- The data dir of Ostra, and the config dir of Ostra. When `OSTRA_CONFIG` places the config file in a shared dir, only that file is hidden.
- The runtime dir of the user: `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, or `/run/user/<uid>`. This dir holds the session bus.
- The file named by `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` and the file named by `XAUTHORITY`, when set.
- Every entry of `paths::HOME_CREDENTIALS` under the home folder, except the sign-in file of the harness that runs. A harness keeps only its own sign-in file.
- Each path in `[sandbox] extra_hidden`.
- The sockets of container engines (`DOCKER_SOCKETS`): Docker, Podman, OrbStack, Colima, and Rancher Desktop. A read-only file does not stop `connect`, and a program that reaches a container engine can start a container that mounts the host.
- The sessions dir of the workspace, and the harness dir of the session, which holds the bridge tokens of other executions. The session of the execution is bound again below the hidden dir.

One path inside a hidden dir stays visible: the `assets` dir of the data dir. It is read-only (`revealed`), because agents read skills and references from it.

### Environment

The profile sets `TMPDIR` to `/tmp` and the cache variables of the next section. The profile unsets the variables in `UNSET_VARS`, because each points a command at a desktop session, an agent, or a daemon socket: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, `DISPLAY`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `XAUTHORITY`, `DOCKER_HOST`, and `GPG_AGENT_INFO`.

### How rules are ordered

Both backends use the same order (`Profile::ordered`). The list is sorted by path depth, then by path, then by rank. A shallower path comes first, so the deepest rule for a path wins. When two rules name the same path, the more restrictive one stays. The rank from least to most restrictive is: `HomeTmpfs`, `HomeEntry`, `Writable`, `ReadOnly`, `Hidden`, `Link`.

Paths that do not exist yet need care. `real_or_missing` resolves the longest existing ancestor and appends the missing rest. Bubblewrap mounts at real paths, and Seatbelt matches real paths, so the profile resolves every symlink first.

### The scratch dir

Under bubblewrap, `/tmp` is private. A native execution gets a fresh owner-only dir from `new_scratch` (`ostra-scratch-<uuid>` under the OS temp dir). A harness gets a `tmp` dir inside its own config dir. The profile mounts the dir at `/tmp` and at its own path, so both names reach the same files. `Profile::to_host` translates a path inside `/tmp` to the host path of the same file. Without a scratch dir, `/tmp` is an empty tmpfs. Seatbelt cannot remap `/tmp`, so it denies the shared temp dirs and sets `TMPDIR` to the scratch dir or to the `tmp` dir of the cache.

## The bubblewrap backend

The bubblewrap backend (`bwrap.rs`) runs on Linux. The sandbox gets its own mount, pid, and IPC namespaces. A private network mode adds a network namespace. The command line that `Profile::args` renders has this order:

1. `--ro-bind / /`, `--dev /dev`, and `--proc /proc`. The whole host is read-only.
2. `/tmp`: `--bind <scratch> /tmp`, or `--tmpfs /tmp`.
3. The planned mounts, sorted by depth. A writable mount is `--bind`. A read-only mount is `--ro-bind`. A hidden dir is `--tmpfs`. A hidden file is `--ro-bind /dev/null <file>`. A `Mount::Link` is `--symlink`. A `Mount::HomeEntry(p, Some(target))` is `--symlink`. A `Mount::HomeEntry(p, None)` is `--ro-bind p p`, so a home entry is not always a symlink.
4. The decoy files, as `--ro-bind` mounts.
5. `--unsetenv` for each variable in `UNSET_VARS`, then `--setenv` for the profile environment.
6. `--unshare-pid` and `--unshare-ipc`.
7. For a private network: `--unshare-net`, and a `--bind` for the socket of the egress proxy and each forwarded port.
8. `--die-with-parent`, `--new-session` when `new_session` is true, and `--chdir`.
9. A `--bind` for each file in `writable_files`.

After `--`, the command is `ostra sandbox-init [--proxy <socket>] [--forward <port>=<socket>]... -- <program> <args>`.

### Planning the mounts

The function `Profile::plan` adjusts the ordered mounts before rendering:

- A read-only bind whose nearest mounted ancestor is hidden is dropped, because the bind exposes the hidden dir again. The exception is a `revealed` mount.
- A missing read-only path gets a placeholder only where its nearest ancestor is a writable host dir. The placeholder is an empty dir, an empty file, or the file `{}` when the extension is `json`. Without the placeholder, the agent can create the file, for example a settings file.
- A mount point cannot be renamed, but the dirs above it can. Without a fix, the command `mv repo r && git init repo` leaves a protected `.git` under another name. So each dir between a writable bind and a mount inside it is bound onto itself (a pin).

### The helper

The helper is the `ostra` binary with the subcommand `sandbox-init` ([`init.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/init.rs), [`sys/linux/helper.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/linux/helper.rs)). The server calls `set_helper` with its own path before the first probe. Without `set_helper`, `helper()` looks for an `ostra` next to the current program or one dir up.

The helper does these steps in order:

1. Bind the fixed ports on `127.0.0.1` of the sandbox, and on `::1` when the namespace has it. A fixed port is a forwarded port, for example the hook bridge.
2. Bind a free port on `127.0.0.1` for the proxy. Set `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, and related variables (`proxy_env`) for the command.
3. Load the seccomp filter when the helper has one thread, so the filter covers every thread that the helper starts.
4. Start one thread for each listener. Each thread accepts a TCP connection and splices it to the Unix socket that Ostra bound in. A listener serves at most 256 open connections.
5. Start the command, ignore the terminal signals, and wait. The helper exits with the status of the command. When the command dies from a signal, the helper raises the same signal and returns `128 + signal`.

The helper exits with status `125` (`FAILED`) when it cannot start the command. The `env` and `timeout` commands use the same status. The helper uses std threads and no async runtime.

### The seccomp filter

The filter ([`sys/linux/seccomp.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/linux/seccomp.rs)) is a BPF program. The helper loads it with `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` and `PR_SET_SECCOMP`. Every process that the command starts inherits it. A refusal returns an error code, so programs that probe for a feature fall back and do not die.

| Action | Calls |
| --- | --- |
| Refuse with `EPERM` | `bpf`, `userfaultfd`, `perf_event_open`, `keyctl`, `add_key`, `request_key`, `kexec_load`, `kexec_file_load`, `init_module`, `finit_module`, `delete_module`, `open_by_handle_at` |
| Return `ENOSYS` | `clone3`, `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter`, `io_uring_register` |
| Refuse with `EPERM` when the flags include `CLONE_NEWUSER` | `unshare`, `clone` |
| Refuse with `EPERM` | `ioctl` with the request `TIOCSTI` or `TIOCLINUX` (the low 32 bits count) |
| Kill the process | Any call from another architecture than the build target |
| Return `ENOSYS` | x32 call numbers (x86_64 only, `X32_SYSCALL_BIT` = `0x4000_0000`) |

The reasons, from the code comments:

- A new user namespace gives the command capabilities over fresh namespaces and mounts.
- `clone3` passes its flags in memory that a filter cannot read. The `ENOSYS` answer makes glibc fall back to `clone`, whose flags the filter can read.
- `TIOCSTI` types into a terminal. `setsid` (`--new-session`) also blocks it for the terminal where Ostra started.
- Builds and tests do not need the other refused calls, and the calls widen the kernel surface.

The filter exists for `x86_64` and `aarch64` only. On another architecture the helper loads no filter, and `known_gaps` returns this text: run Ostra on x86_64 or aarch64 where agent commands must not create user namespaces.

### The probe

The Linux probe (`probe_bwrap`) finds `bwrap` on `PATH`. It then runs a test sandbox with the helper: `--ro-bind / /`, `--unshare-pid`, `--unshare-net`, and `sandbox-init --proxy /dev/null -- true`. The test checks that the new network namespace brings up its loopback. When it fails, the error tells the user to allow user namespaces. In a container, the default seccomp or AppArmor profile blocks them. On a host, set `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`, for example.

## The Seatbelt backend

The Seatbelt backend (`seatbelt.rs`) renders a profile as an SBPL policy and runs it with `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` (`SANDBOX_EXEC`). Ostra calls the program by its absolute path and checks that root owns it and that no other user can write it, because the Homebrew prefix on `PATH` is writable by the user. The probe runs `sandbox-exec -p "(version 1)(allow default)" /usr/bin/true`. When the output has `sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted`, Ostra runs inside another sandbox. macOS cannot nest sandboxes, so the user must start Ostra outside it.

Seatbelt has no mount namespace. These differences follow:

- A hidden path returns `EPERM` and does not look empty.
- `/tmp` is denied and not private. `TMPDIR` points at the scratch dir, and `TMPPREFIX` points at `<tmp>/zsh`, because zsh writes heredocs under it.
- A harness gets no disposable home, so its writes at the top of the home folder fail. The CLIs survive this.
- Every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. The policy of each sandbox names the ports that it can use.
- A process can leave the process tree of its sandbox. See [Processes of a sandbox](#processes-of-a-sandbox).

### The base policy

The constant `SEATBELT_BASE` starts every policy. It begins with `(deny default)` and then allows what git, cargo, npm, go, pip, clang, and the four harness CLIs need. The authors measured the list with those tools. The policy allows these things:

- `process-exec` and `process-fork`, and signals inside the same sandbox.
- A measured list of `sysctl` names (`hw.`, `machdep.cpu.`, and the `kern.*` names in the policy).
- Reads of all files (`file-read*`). The profile then denies hidden paths.
- Writes to `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, and `/dev/fd/N`.
- A short list of mach services. The keychain, the pasteboard, LaunchServices, Apple Events, the window server, and TCC stay denied, because each reaches something outside the sandbox.

The policy denies every terminal device (`/dev/tty*`), so nothing reads or injects keystrokes in another terminal of the user. A PTY program gets its own terminal through the `-D TTY=<path>` parameter (`TTY_PARAM`).

The policy also denies `process-info*` before it allows the same sandbox. A process can read the arguments and startup environment of another process through `KERN_PROCARGS2`. Either `sysctl-read` or `process-info-pidinfo` opens this path, and `(deny default)` does not cover the second. So the policy closes both. The authors measured this on macOS 26.

### Rules from the profile

`Profile::seatbelt` renders the ordered mounts. Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, so a deeper path overrides a shallower one.

- A writable path gets `(allow file-read* file-write* (subpath P))` and a network-bind rule.
- A read-only path gets `(deny file-write* network-bind ...)`. A `literal` rule also covers a missing path in any letter case, so no placeholder is needed.
- A hidden path gets `(deny file-read* file-write* (subpath P))`.
- The shared temp dirs (`/private/tmp`, `/private/var/tmp`, and the per-user temp dir) are denied.
- Each allowed path needs `file-read-metadata` on the dirs above it, so the policy allows `stat` on those ancestors.
- A pin: `(deny file-write-unlink ...)` on every writable dir above a protected path. The command `mv .git .g` cannot carry `.git/config` out from under its rule.

A path that is not UTF-8 or that holds a control character is an error (`sbpl_str`). A path that ends the policy string early rewrites the policy.

### Network rules under Seatbelt

Under a private network mode, the policy allows a listener on loopback. It allows outbound connections to the ports of the proxy and the forwards of the sandbox. It allows every loopback port when the workspace uses `LoopbackAccess::Open`, and the listed loopback ports otherwise. It always denies the blocked ports and the port of the Ostra server (`set_server_port`), because that port serves the API of the console. The policy has no DNS resolver, because the proxy resolves names and a lookup carries data out in the name. `localhost` still resolves from `/etc/hosts`.

Under `host`, the policy allows outbound IP, a listener on loopback, and the DNS resolver socket. The SSH agent, Docker, password managers, and IDE sockets stay denied.

## The egress proxy

Without a filter, a command can send a file from the workspace to any server. The egress proxy ([`egress.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/egress.rs)) is the one way out of a private network. It sees the destination host and port of every connection and lets through only what the policy allows. It connects to the address that it checked and does not look the name up a second time.

One process-wide Tokio runtime with 2 worker threads (`ostra-egress`) runs all proxies and splices.

### How the proxy is reached

| Platform | Listener | How the command reaches it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | A Unix socket in `<data dir>/egress`, mode `0700`, named `<16 hex digits>.sock`. | `--bind` puts it into the sandbox. The helper forwards a port on the sandbox loopback to it. |
| macOS | A port on `127.0.0.1`, IPv4 only. | The Seatbelt policy names the port. The URL is `http://ostra:<credential>@127.0.0.1:<port>`. |

On macOS, the sandbox of a workspace with open loopback can reach the proxy ports of other executions. So each loopback proxy has its own credential. The user name is `ostra` (`PROXY_USER`) and the password is a random UUID. A request without the right `Proxy-Authorization` header gets `407 Proxy Authentication Required`. The check compares in constant time.

The path of a Unix socket is limited to 107 bytes. When `bind` fails, the error tells the user to keep the data dir path short.

The function `proxy_env` sets `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` (each in upper and lower case), `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy` (`localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`), and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`.

A profile starts one proxy with `Profile::start_egress`. All commands of the profile share it. A command that is wrapped without a profile proxy starts its own proxy, and its decisions go to the log only (`log_decision`). Dropping a `Listener` stops it, ends its open connections, and removes its socket.

### The decision for one request

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Read request head"] --> B{"Proxy credential valid?"}
  B -- "no" --> R407["407"]
  B -- "yes" --> C{"Host and port listed?"}
  C -- "no" --> R403["403 with the setting to change"]
  C -- "yes" --> D{"Address allowed?"}
  D -- "no" --> R403
  D -- "yes" --> E{"Upstream proxy set?"}
  E -- "yes" --> F["Connect through upstream"]
  E -- "no" --> G["Connect to the checked address"]
  F --> H{"TLS name equals CONNECT host?"}
  G --> H
  H -- "no" --> X["Close tunnel, report refusal"]
  H -- "yes" --> S["Splice both directions"]
```

### Host rules

A host rule (`HostRule::parse`) is one `allowed_hosts` entry. The accepted forms are:

- A host name, such as `registry.npmjs.org`.
- `*.domain`: every name below `domain`, and not `domain` itself.
- An IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets, such as `[::1]`.
- Each form with an optional `:port`.

Without a port, a rule allows ports 443 and 80. A rule cannot hold whitespace, `/`, `@`, `?`, or `#`, because the proxy matches hosts and not URLs. A port is 1 to 65535. A name has at most 253 characters and each label at most 63. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address becomes the IPv4 address.

A loopback rule (`localhost` or a loopback address) must have a port. Clients skip the proxy for loopback, so such a rule works only as a forwarded port. The sandbox forwards the loopback ports of trusted rules to the host loopback, except the blocked ports.

### Built-in hosts

Under `allowlist`, the built-in list is `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` plus the model hosts of all four harness CLIs.

- **Package and source hosts (26):** `index.crates.io`, `static.crates.io`, `static.rust-lang.org`, `registry.npmjs.org`, `registry.yarnpkg.com`, `repo.yarnpkg.com`, `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `crates.io`, `github.com`, `codeload.github.com`, `objects.githubusercontent.com`, `raw.githubusercontent.com`, `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`, `repo.maven.apache.org`, `repo1.maven.org`, `services.gradle.org`, `plugins.gradle.org`, `plugins-artifacts.gradle.org`, `dl.google.com`, `maven.google.com`, `rubygems.org`, `index.rubygems.org`, `api.nuget.org`.
- **Claude:** `api.anthropic.com`, `console.anthropic.com`, `platform.claude.com`, `claude.ai`.
- **Codex:** `api.openai.com`, `chatgpt.com`, `auth.openai.com`.
- **Grok:** `api.x.ai`, `auth.x.ai`, `accounts.x.ai`, `grok.com`, `cli-chat-proxy.grok.com`.
- **Antigravity (`Agy`):** `cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`, `generativelanguage.googleapis.com`, `oauth2.googleapis.com`, `www.googleapis.com`, `lh3.googleusercontent.com`.

The authors measured the model hosts with one run of each CLI. A harness gets its own model hosts under every network mode, also under `none` (`Profile::allow_hosts`). Under `allowlist`, every command reaches all of them, so a build or a test can call a model API.

### Three classes of access

The policy (`Policy`) puts each destination in one of three classes:

- **Trusted:** the hosts that the user chose (`allowed_hosts`) and the base-URL hosts that a harness launch passes. They can resolve to any address, a private address included.
- **Built-in, or any host under `public`:** the destination must resolve to a public address. The proxy drops private addresses. When every address is private, it refuses.
- **Unlisted:** refused.

A private address (`is_private`) is loopback, private, link-local (the cloud metadata address included), carrier-grade NAT (`100.64.0.0/10`), the benchmark range, multicast, broadcast, unspecified, reserved (`240.0.0.0` and above), unique-local IPv6, site-local IPv6, and the IPv4 addresses inside IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, and NAT64 IPv6 addresses.

The proxy does not look up a local-only name for a non-trusted destination. A local-only name is `localhost`, a name with no dot, or a name that ends in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, or `.home.arpa`. A lookup of such a name goes out on the local network. On macOS, a lookup for `.local` takes seconds before it fails.

### Upstream proxy

A machine that reaches the internet only through a corporate proxy sets `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` to `http://host:port`. The proxy then routes as follows:

- A destination that resolves to a private address goes direct, because an internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy.
- A public destination goes through the upstream proxy with `CONNECT`, or with an absolute-form request for plain HTTP.
- A name that does not resolve here goes through the upstream proxy, except a local-only name that the user did not list. Such a name reaches the network of the upstream proxy unchecked.

### Requests the proxy accepts

The proxy accepts `CONNECT host:port` and plain HTTP with an absolute `http://` URL. It speaks HTTP/1.x only. For plain HTTP it rewrites the head to origin form, removes `Proxy-*`, `Host`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers, adds `Connection: close`, and refuses folded header lines.

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400 Bad Request` | The head is not valid, is not UTF-8, is over 8 KiB, or the connection closed early. |
| `403 Forbidden` | The destination is not allowed. The body tells the user which setting to change, because the refusal text starts with the correction. |
| `407 Proxy Authentication Required` | The credential is missing or wrong (macOS loopback proxy). |
| `502 Bad Gateway` | The proxy cannot connect to the destination or the upstream proxy. |

### The TLS server name check

An allowed name must also be the TLS server name. Without this check, a content delivery network that routes by the server name (SNI) carries a tunnel to any site that it serves. After `CONNECT` to a name, the proxy reads the first bytes of the tunnel and parses the ClientHello. It closes the tunnel and reports a refusal in two cases: the server name differs from the CONNECT host, or the ClientHello cannot be read (`Invalid`). A ClientHello is capped at 32 KiB (`MAX_HELLO`). A tunnel without a server name is not refused. When the destination speaks first, such as an SSH banner, the proxy treats the tunnel as not TLS. The check applies to names and not to IP addresses.

### Decisions reach the engine

The proxy reports the first allowed connection and the first refusal for each host, port, and result. A retry loop then reports one time. The callback (`OnDecision`) must not block. The function `report::egress` sends each decision to the execution host as `ExecutionDelta::Egress` with `host`, `port`, `allowed`, `reason`, and `local`. It uses a thread of its own (`ostra-egress-report`), because the proxy runtime must not wait on the host. The flag `local` is true when the destination is loopback, private, or link-local.

## Forwarded ports

Some sockets must reach into the sandbox, such as the hook bridge of a harness. `Profile::forward` and `Profile::forward_socket` do this. They do nothing under the `host` network, because the target is reachable as it is.

- **Bubblewrap:** a socket is bound into the sandbox. The helper listens on `127.0.0.1:<port>` and splices to it.
- **Seatbelt:** a new loopback port is opened, and the policy names it. `Profile::forwarded_port` returns the port that the command must use.

The bridge socket of the server answers only `/internal/*`, so a sandbox cannot reach `/api`. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

## Decoys

A decoy is a fake credential file that an agent has no reason to read (rule P3). When a command opens the file, the kernel reports it. A `cat` in the shell is seen as well as a tool call, which the policy cannot always see. The result is a containment signal. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) for how the signal is used.

The built-in decoys (`HOME_DECOYS`) are `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.git-credentials`, and `~/.vault-token`. The file `~/.netrc` is not a decoy, because Python `requests` and Go module downloads read it on every fetch. A workspace adds decoys with `sandbox_decoys`. It cannot remove a built-in decoy (`decoy::wanted`).

The contents look real and authenticate nowhere: an OpenSSH private key block, a `https://git:<40 hex>@github.com` line, `hvs.<24 characters>`, or 40 hex digits.

| Backend | How the decoy works |
| --- | --- |
| Bubblewrap | A fake file in `<data dir>/decoys/<16 hex>/` is bound read-only into the sandbox. It goes where a hidden dir can hold a new file, or over an existing file, so the host is never written. An inotify watch on the host file reports the first open. |
| Seatbelt | Seatbelt cannot bind a file in. A decoy is an existing file that the policy refuses to read, with a message tag `dev.ostra.decoy.<16 hex>`. Ostra reads the refusal from the system log (`log stream`). |

The watch reports the first open of each decoy only. A `stat` or a directory listing is not an open. Dropping the `Decoys` value ends the watch and removes the files.

### What happens when

- **A network mode reaches port 22.** The SSH key decoys are skipped (`Policy::reaches_port`), because `ssh` reads its keys when it authenticates and raises a false signal. This applies under `public`, under `host`, and when a listed host has port 22.
- **macOS, a non-admin user.** The system log shows sandbox reports to admin accounts only (group 80). Decoys are not supported (`status.decoys` is false), and the execution runs without them. A missing file raises no report, so only existing files become decoys.
- **macOS, the log reader cannot start.** The execution runs without decoys and logs a warning.
- **The server starts.** `decoy::watch_reports` starts the log reader and waits up to 10 seconds until `log stream` is attached, so the first command is watched. `decoy::remove_stale` removes decoys of an earlier server.
- **The entry is invalid.** `decoy::invalid` rejects a path that does not start with `~/`, has an empty, `.`, or `..` part, or is the sign-in file of a harness CLI. A decoy on that file signs the CLI out in the sandbox.

A workspace can list at most 32 decoys (`MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS`), because each is a watch and a bind mount.

## Build caches

Builds download and extract code, and the next build runs that code. If one session wrote the user cache, a later session or a build on the host runs what the first session left. So the sandbox keeps the user caches (`~/.cargo`, `~/.npm`, `~/.cache`, and on macOS `~/Library/Caches`) read-only. It gives each sandbox its own writable caches ([`cache.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/cache.rs)).

The caches live under `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox/`, or under `$OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` when set. The profile sets these variables (`CACHE_ENV`), each to a sub dir:

| Variable | Sub dir |
| --- | --- |
| `CARGO_HOME` | `cargo` |
| `npm_config_cache` | `npm` |
| `npm_config_store_dir` | `pnpm-store` |
| `XDG_CACHE_HOME` | `xdg` |
| `GOMODCACHE` | `go-mod` |
| `GOCACHE` | `go-build` |
| `PIP_CACHE_DIR` | `pip` |
| `YARN_CACHE_FOLDER` | `yarn` |
| `UV_CACHE_DIR` | `uv` |
| `CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH` | `clang-modules` |

macOS tools ignore `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and write under `~/Library/Caches`, so they get their own variables. The `tmp` sub dir of the cache is private (mode `0700`).

The user cargo settings `config.toml` and `config` (`CARGO_SETTINGS`) are linked into the cache `cargo` dir. Builds then keep the linker and registry settings of the user. Credentials are not linked.

The cache dir depends on the kind of run:

- **An execution of a session:** `session-<session id>`. One session's downloads cannot feed another session's builds.
- **An execution outside a session:** a dir named by `stable_hex("agents", workspace root)`. The repo root replaces the workspace root when the workspace root is empty.
- **A program that Ostra starts** (`for_program`): a dir named by `stable_hex("", first root)`.

The function `stable_hex` returns 16 hex digits: the first 8 bytes of SHA-256 over the salt, a zero byte, and the path. It does not use `DefaultHasher`, because the algorithm of `DefaultHasher` can change between Rust releases and then moves the dirs.

When a session ends, `remove_session_cache` removes its caches on a thread of its own (`ostra-cache-remove`), because they can hold gigabytes. At server start, `sweep_session_caches` removes the caches of sessions that this data dir knows as `Completed` or `Failed`. It touches no other cache, because other data dirs share the cache root.

## Git protection

A repository runs programs that its config names: `core.fsmonitor`, `credential.helper`, and hooks. An agent that can write `.git/config` can make the user's next `git status` run a program outside the sandbox. So each `.git` stays writable (git must commit), but the paths that choose programs are read-only ([`git.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/git.rs)).

The protected paths (`GIT_PROTECTED`) in each git dir are `config`, `config.worktree`, `hooks/`, and `info/`. The file `config.worktree` is read only with `extensions.worktreeConfig`, which `config` sets. So the empty placeholder that a missing file gets is harmless.

### Finding repositories

`git_repos` walks the roots breadth first and returns every dir that holds a `.git` dir or a `.git` file, at any depth. It does not enter symlinks, `node_modules`, or dirs that have a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file (Cargo tags `target/` this way). The walk stops after 20,000 dirs (`GIT_WALK_DIRS`) or 128 repos (`GIT_WALK_REPOS`), and logs a warning. Repos below the stop point keep a writable `.git/config`.

`git_dirs` adds the git dir of each submodule under `modules/`, up to 256 git dirs in all.

A `.git` file that names a git dir makes the file itself read-only, so it cannot name a planted git dir. A linked worktree reads the config of its main repo, which the entry of the main repo covers. So for a linked worktree, only `config.worktree` is protected.

### Repairing planted files

A `commondir` file makes git load another repository's config. The placeholder trick does not work for it, because git refuses to open a repository with an empty `commondir`. So `repair_git_dirs` undoes the damage after the fact:

- It removes a `commondir` in the own git dir of a repository. Git never writes one there.
- It restores a linked worktree's `commondir` to `../..` when it names anything else.

The function returns the paths that it changed. The native executor (`ostra-exec-native`), the harness executor (`ostra-exec-harness`), the engine runner (`ostra-engine`, `runner.rs`), and the server git routes (`ostra-server`) call it. The agent receives the note from `git_repair_note`: leave the path to git, because Ostra undid it.

For a program that Ostra starts, `host_command` also sets git environment settings (`ostra_core::git::agent_env`): `core.fsmonitor=false`, `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, and `protocol.ext.allow=never`.

## Processes of a sandbox

A sandbox must not leave a process behind. A `Members` value ([`members.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/members.rs)) holds what one sandboxed command needs during its run: the egress proxy and forwarded sockets, and the decoys. Dropping it kills what the command left running.

- **Linux:** the pid namespace and `--die-with-parent` end every process of a sandbox with it. `Os::marked` returns no process.
- **macOS:** Seatbelt has no pid namespace. A child that calls `setsid` or forks twice outlives its shell. Each policy allows two mach service names that no daemon registers: one for the command and one for the whole data dir. The kernel answers for any process whether its policy allows a name (`sandbox_check`), and a process cannot drop its policy. So Ostra finds every descendant by the name. A process also must be refused a canary name (`dev.ostra.sandbox.canary`), because some system sandboxes allow every name.

`Members::kill` sends SIGKILL to the marked processes. It repeats up to 20 times with a 10 ms pause until none is left. `kill_leftovers` does the same for the name of the data dir. The server calls it at start, before recovery starts executions, when no other server runs. It also calls `egress::remove_stale_sockets` and `decoy::remove_stale` then.

## Programs that Ostra starts

Ostra also starts programs for a project: a format command, a language server, a code provider, and a stdio MCP server. `host_command` ([`host.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/host.rs)) wraps them with the same rules. It reads the global config fresh and applies the workspace sandbox settings. The result (`HostCommand`) has the program, arguments, environment, and the `Members`.

- It removes the credential variables that Ostra holds, and every variable that starts with `OSTRA_`.
- It adds the git settings of `agent_env`.
- Under mode `off`, or `auto` without a backend, it returns the command unchanged except for the environment.
- Otherwise it finds the program (a path with `/`, else the first match on `PATH`) before the sandbox starts, so a missing program reads as missing. It then wraps the command with `Profile::for_program`.
- Mode `required` without a backend returns an error.

## Status reports and settings checks

The function `status(cfg)` ([`status.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/status.rs)) builds the `SandboxStatus` that the setup check and the console show. The server calls it at start, for the setup check, and for the runtime of each workspace.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `mode` | The mode in force. |
| `default_mode` | The default mode on this OS: `required` on Linux and macOS, `auto` on Windows. |
| `available` | A backend works here. |
| `backend` | `bubblewrap` or `seatbelt`, when available. |
| `active` | Executions start sandboxed under the mode. |
| `message` | The warning or error when a sandbox is wanted and missing. |
| `gaps` | What the working sandbox cannot enforce (`known_gaps`). Set only when active. |
| `decoys` | Decoys work here. |
| `builtin_decoys` | The built-in decoys as `~/` paths. |
| `builtin_hosts` | The built-in hosts: package hosts and model hosts. |

The module `validate.rs` checks the sandbox settings at save time, so a value that the sandbox cannot enforce is a validation issue and never a silent fallback at spawn time. The workspace settings check calls `validate::workspace`. The server calls `validate::global` at start.

| Setting | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox.allowed_hosts` | Each entry parses as a `HostRule`. A loopback entry needs a port. |
| `sandbox_decoys` | Each entry passes `decoy::invalid`. At most 32 entries. |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Each port is 1 to 65535. At most 64 entries (`MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS`), because each is a rule in every sandbox policy. |
| `sandbox.extra_writable`, `sandbox.extra_hidden` | Each path is absolute or starts with `~/`, because a relative path depends on where an execution starts. |
| `sandbox.upstream_proxy` | The form is `http://host:port`, with no path and no credentials. |

Each issue message starts with the correction and then gives the reason.

## Limits and constants

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_HEAD` (`egress.rs`) | 8 KiB | Largest request head that the proxy accepts. |
| `MAX_CONNECTIONS` | 256 | Open connections for each listener. Extra connections are dropped. |
| `HEAD_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds | Time to read a request head, an upstream answer, or a ClientHello. |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 10 seconds | Time to connect to one address. |
| `MAX_HELLO` | 32 KiB | Largest ClientHello that the proxy parses. |
| `PROXY_USER` | `ostra` | User name in the URL of a loopback proxy. |
| `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | 26 hosts | Built-in package and source hosts. |
| `MAX_OPEN` (helper `forward`) | 256 | Open connections for each helper listener. |
| `FAILED` (`init.rs`) | 125 | Exit status when the helper cannot start the command. |
| `GIT_PROTECTED` | 4 paths | Read-only paths in a git dir. |
| `GIT_WALK_DIRS` | 20,000 | Dirs that `git_repos` reads before it stops. |
| `GIT_WALK_REPOS` | 128 | Repos that `git_repos` returns at most. |
| `HOME_DECOYS` | 4 files | Built-in decoys. |
| `MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS` | 32 | Decoys that a workspace adds at most. |
| `MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS` (`validate.rs`) | 64 | Blocked loopback ports that a workspace lists at most. |
| `CACHE_ENV`, `CARGO_SETTINGS` | 10 variables, 2 files | Cache variables and linked cargo settings. |
| `PERSISTENCE_IN_HOME`, `UNSET_VARS`, `DOCKER_SOCKETS` | 32, 7, and 7 entries | Read-only home files, unset variables, hidden container sockets. |
| `SANDBOX_EXEC` | `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` | Seatbelt front end. |
| `TTY_PARAM` | `TTY` | `sandbox-exec -D` parameter for the PTY path. |
| `SEATBELT_BASE`, `SEATBELT_HOST_NETWORK`, `SEATBELT_LOOPBACK_LISTEN` | text | Policy parts that come before or after the profile rules. |
| `SERVER_PORT` | set at start | Port of the Ostra server, which no Seatbelt sandbox connects to. |
| `TAG_PREFIX` | `dev.ostra.decoy.` | Start of every Seatbelt decoy message. |
| `B64`, `HEX` (`decoy.rs`) | alphabets | Characters for decoy contents. |
| `PREDICATE` (`sys/macos/log.rs`) | log filter | Matches only the kernel Sandbox extension and the decoy tag. |
| `ADMIN_GID` | 80 | The `admin` group, which `log stream` requires. |
| `READY` | 10 seconds to attach | State of the log reader. |
| `CANARY` (`sys/macos/mod.rs`) | `dev.ostra.sandbox.canary` | Mach name that every Ostra policy refuses. |
| `FILTER_NONE`, `FILTER_GLOBAL_NAME`, `NO_REPORT` | 0, 2, `0x4000_0000` | Arguments to `sandbox_check`. |
| `ARCH`, `ARCH_OFFSET`, `X32_SYSCALL_BIT`, `REFUSED`, `MISSING`, `TTY_REFUSED` | see the seccomp table | Constants of the seccomp filter. |
| `PROBE`, `WARNED`, `HELPER` | statics | The probe result, the one-time warning flag, and the helper path. |
| `HEAD` (`inotify.rs`) | size of an inotify event header | Read size for decoy events. |
| `UNAVAILABLE` | text for each OS | Advice when no sandbox works. |

The other limits of the sandbox crate are also on [Reference: executor, tool, policy, and sandbox limits](reference-execution-limits.md).

## What the sandbox does not cover

The sandbox lowers risk. It does not guarantee that an agent cannot harm the machine. These limits apply.

- **It is off in some cases.** In mode `off`, or in mode `auto` without a backend, nothing is enforced. A command can then read the data dir and the sign-in files of the user, write anywhere the user can write, and reach any host. The `[sandbox]` network setting does not apply.
- **Windows has no sandbox.** Ostra has no Windows backend. Use WSL 2 or Docker.
- **Writable roots stay writable.** The agent can change any file inside the workspace and repo roots. Only the listed git paths, the listed home files, and the state files of Ostra are read-only. A file in a root that the user runs later, such as a build script, stays writable.
- **The proxy checks the destination and not the content.** A listed host receives any data that the command sends to it. The TLS name check does not apply to IP addresses. A tunnel that has no server name passes.
- **The `host` network is unfiltered.** The command shares the loopback of the host and the abstract Unix sockets.
- **Bubblewrap limits.** The seccomp filter exists for `x86_64` and `aarch64` only. Inside a container with a default seccomp or AppArmor profile, bubblewrap cannot start.
- **Seatbelt limits.** A hidden path returns `EPERM` and does not look empty. No `/tmp` is private. A harness gets no disposable home. All sandboxes share the loopback. Ostra cannot start a sandbox inside another sandbox. Decoys need an existing file and an admin account.
- **Decoys detect and do not block.** On Linux, a read of a decoy succeeds and returns fake data. The report is a signal for the policy layer.
- **The native file tools are not in the sandbox.** Only commands run in it. The Bash tool of the native executor and the harness CLIs use it. The other native tools run in the Ostra process, and the guards of the [policy engine](policy-guards.md) judge them.
- **Kernel flaws are out of scope.** The sandbox relies on namespaces, seccomp, and Seatbelt. A flaw in them is outside the sandbox.

## Where the sandbox is used

- The Bash tool of the native executor: see [Native tools and their limits](tools.md) and [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md). Every Bash call of one execution shares one egress proxy and one set of decoys.
- The harness CLIs: see [Harness executors](harness-executors.md). A harness runs with `new_session(false)`, a home overlay (bubblewrap), and its own state dirs writable.
- Programs for a project through `host_command`: language servers, code providers, format commands, and stdio MCP servers. See [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) and [Integrations](integrations.md).
- The settings check and the console: see [Server security](server-security.md) and [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).
