sections.title: Workspaces, projects, and settings
sections.summary: How Ostra stores, routes, validates, and protects workspace settings, how it adds and removes projects, how it approves commands from folder files, and how pricing feeds the session budget.
sections.body:
## Purpose and scope

A workspace is a folder that Ostra manages. A project is a folder that the workspace lists under a key in its settings. Without strict rules, a file that arrives with a `git pull` or an agent edit can start a program, raise a spend limit, or turn off the sandbox. This page explains how Ostra reads, checks, saves, and protects workspace settings. It also explains how Ostra adds and removes projects, and what an open workspace holds in memory.

The page covers:

- the files that hold workspace data, and the settings that never leave the registry
- routing of executor, model, effort, and tier per agent and per phase complexity
- validation of settings, and the fixes that Ostra applies
- instructions, permissions, limits, and the YOLO default
- creation of a workspace, and import, clone, creation, and removal of a project
- approval of commands that come from folder files
- the runtime of an open workspace, and the saved layout of the console
- the pricing catalog, the cost report, and the session budget

The page stops before the full list of settings keys. [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md) owns that list. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) and [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) own what the sandbox and the permission rules do at run time. [Overview](overview.md) defines the terms session, gate, and executor.

## Where the data of a workspace lives

Ostra keeps workspace data in two places. The registry lives in the data folder of the machine and never arrives with a repository. The workspace folder can arrive with a repository, so Ostra does not trust its files for security choices. Every path derivation lives in `crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`, so every reader and writer resolves state the same way.

| Location | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `<data dir>/registry.db` | The list of workspaces, command approvals, permission mode, YOLO, limits, sandbox choices, and encrypted secrets |
| `<root>/.ostra/workspace.toml` | The settings that a user can share: projects, routing, instructions, permission rules, notifications, MCP servers |
| `<root>/.ostra/workspace.db` | Sessions, events, and the saved console layout. See [Storage](storage.md) |
| `<root>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>/` | The files of one session |
| `<root>/.ostra/uploads` | Uploads that no session claimed yet |
| `<project>/.ostra/INVENTORY.md` | The file that marks a project as initialized |
| `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | The project profile: stack, commands, module map, skills |
| `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | The lesson memory of the project |
| `<project>/.agents/skills` | The project skills. Ostra still reads the legacy `<project>/.ostra/skills` and never writes it |
| `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `AGENT.md` in the project root | The instruction files, matched in any letter case, in that order |

The data folder is the value of `OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, or the `ostra` folder in the local data folder of the operating system. The machine config file is the value of `OSTRA_CONFIG`, or `ostra/config.toml` in the config folder of the operating system. [Running Ostra](running-ostra.md) describes both files.

The server lists `workspace.toml` and `workspace.db` as protected paths of the workspace (`ServerServices::protected_paths`). [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) explains how protected paths work.

## Settings in workspace.toml

`WorkspaceSettings` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` is the typed form of `<root>/.ostra/workspace.toml`. Ostra reads the file on every call that needs settings, so an edit applies without a restart. If Ostra cannot read or parse the file, `WorkspaceRt::settings` logs a warning and returns `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`. Ostra writes the file with `save_toml`. That function writes a temporary file and renames it, so a reader never sees half a file.

### Top-level keys

| Key | Seeded default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | The name in the create request | The workspace name. A save with a new name also renames the registry entry |
| `projects` | Empty list | One `[[projects]]` entry per project: `key`, `path`, optional `stack`, `code_provider`, `language_servers` |
| `routing` | Seeded routes | Executor, model, and effort per agent. See the routing part below |
| `instructions` | None | Text that Ostra adds to the first message of agents |
| `yolo.default` | `false` | Starts every new session in YOLO mode |
| `permissions` | Mode `default`, empty rule lists | Permission mode and allow, ask, and deny rules |
| `notifications.push` | `true` | Sends a push notification for gates and finished sessions |
| `limits` | 3 executions, 25.0 dollars | Parallel executions and session budget |
| `mcp_servers` | Empty list | External MCP servers. See [Integrations](integrations.md) |

The constant `SETTING_KEYS` lists every dotted key with a one-line description for the workspace search. A test checks that each key names a field. The full list is in [Reference: workspace settings and paths](reference-settings.md).

### Sample file

```toml
name = "shop"

[[projects]]
key = "backend"
path = "/home/me/code/shop-backend"

[routing.executor.byAgent]
implementer = "harness:codex"

[routing.model.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "fast"
medium = "fast"
high = "balanced"

[permissions]
allow = ["Bash(./mvnw *)"]
```

### Settings that live only in the registry

Ostra keeps 10 settings in the registry under the key `workspace_access:<root>`, never in the file. `write_file` removes them from the TOML before it saves. `overlay` puts them back every time Ostra reads the settings. A file that carries these keys has no effect on them.

The reason (Rule A2): a repository can otherwise lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session.

| Setting | Values | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.mode` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `bypass` | `default` |
| `yolo.default` | `true`, `false` | `false` |
| `limits` | `max_parallel_executions`, `session_budget_usd` | 3 and 25.0 |
| `sandbox_mode` | `auto`, `required`, `off`, or none | None: follows the global `[sandbox] mode`. That mode is `required` on Linux and macOS and `auto` on Windows |
| `tool_enforcement` | `enabled`, `disabled`, or none | None: follows the global value, which is `disabled` |
| `sandbox_network` | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, `host`, or none | None: follows the global value, which is `allowlist` |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | List of hosts | Empty. Ostra adds them to the global list |
| `sandbox_decoys` | List of `~/...` paths | Empty. Ostra adds them to the built-in decoys |
| `sandbox_loopback` | `open`, `listed` | `open`. Applies on macOS only |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | List of ports | Empty. Applies on macOS only |

A registry record that Ostra saved before limits moved there has no `limits` field. Ostra then uses the default limits. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) explains the sandbox values.

### Seeded defaults for a new workspace

`WorkspaceSettings::seeded` gives every route key a route, so a new workspace validates:

- Tier `advanced`: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `judge`, `advisor`.
- Tier `balanced`: `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`.
- `implementer` and `write-test`: tier `fast` for `low` and `medium` phases, and `balanced` for `high` phases.
- Executor routes: none, so every agent runs on the native executor.

## Route an agent to an executor, a model, and an effort

Each agent run needs three choices: which executor runs it, which model it uses, and how much reasoning effort it gets. The `[routing]` tables hold these choices. Ostra resolves them with `resolve_route` when it spawns a run. Ostra also resolves them when it validates settings. Thus a route that cannot resolve is an error at save time, not at spawn time.

### Route keys and tables

A route key is the name that a routing table uses. The 14 `AgentName` values are route keys. The key `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`) is a 15th key for judge calls, which are engine calls and not agent runs. `route_keys()` returns all 15.

Each of `executor`, `model`, and `effort` has two tables:

- `byAgent`: one value per route key.
- `byPhaseComplexity`: one value per route key and per complexity (`low`, `medium`, or `high`).

The `byPhaseComplexity` value wins over the `byAgent` value. The complexity of a run comes from the `**Complexity:**` line of its plan phase. A run outside a phase has no complexity. A phase without a phase file counts as `low`. Every lookup treats a missing complexity as `low`.

Only `implementer` and `write-test` run per plan phase (`AgentName::routes_by_complexity`). Ostra refuses a `byPhaseComplexity` effort entry for any other key. The executor and model tables do not check this.

### Resolve the executor

`resolve_executor` picks the first match in this order:

1. The key is `judge`: the executor is `native`, always.
2. `executor.byPhaseComplexity.<key>.<complexity>`.
3. `executor.byAgent.<key>`.
4. No entry: `native`.

An executor value is `native` or `harness:<name>`, where `<name>` is `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`.

### Resolve the model and the tier

`resolve_route` takes the model choice from `model.byPhaseComplexity.<key>.<complexity>`, and then from `model.byAgent.<key>`. The value has one of four forms:

| Value | Result |
| --- | --- |
| A tier name: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, `frontier` | The model that the tier table of the executor names |
| `default` | The tier from the `default_tier` of the agent in `agent.toml` (tier `advanced` for `judge`) |
| Any other text | That model. A native model must be `anthropic:<model>`, `openai:<model>`, or `mock:<model>`. A harness model is the name that the CLI uses |
| A table such as `{ native = "anthropic:x", codex = "gpt-y" }` | The entry for the tier table of the executor. The entry can be a tier name or a model |

The tier tables live in the machine config file, in `[tiers.native]`, `[tiers.claude]`, `[tiers.codex]`, `[tiers.grok]`, and `[tiers.agy]`. Ostra picks the table with `ExecutorKind::tier_table`. The defaults are:

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

### Resolve the effort

`resolve_effort` returns `effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>.<complexity>`, or else `effort.byAgent.<key>`. An effort value is `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. If neither entry exists, Ostra uses `ostra_agents::effort_for`. That function reads the `effort` table of `agent.toml` for the tier table of the executor, falls back to the `native` entry, and then to `high`. The older flat form of `routing.effort`, a table of agent to effort, reads as `byAgent`.

### Flow of a model route

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["resolve_route(key, complexity)"] --> B{"executor_override set?"}
  B -- yes --> D["Use the forced executor"]
  B -- no --> C["resolve_executor"]
  C --> D
  D --> E{"tier_override set?"}
  E -- yes --> H["Tier table of the executor"]
  E -- no --> F["model_choice: byPhaseComplexity, then byAgent"]
  F --> G{"Form of the value"}
  G -- "tier name or default" --> H
  G -- "concrete model" --> I["check_model"]
  G -- "per-executor table" --> J["Entry for the tier table"]
  J --> H
  J --> I
  H --> K["ResolvedRoute"]
  I --> K
```

### Overrides at spawn time

The engine can override a route when it spawns a run:

- A generate-skill run of the `initializer` uses `tier_override` with tier `advanced`, whatever the model route says.
- `SessionState::forced_executor` (`crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`) forces the executor `native` through `executor_override`. It does so in three cases:
  - The agent already failed on a harness in this session (the `native_fallback` set).
  - The session category is `QuickChange`. A native run skips the startup cost of a harness.
  - The agent is `quick-answer`. It runs the side panel, and quick answers run on the native executor only.
- A run that continues a paused or earlier conversation keeps the executor and the model that the conversation started on. This also keeps the prompt cache.

### Presets for new workspaces

The setup wizard offers a `RoutingPreset`. `native` puts every agent on the native executor. `codex` and `claude` move only `implementer` and `write-test` to `harness:codex` or `harness:claude`. A preset replaces the executor routes and keeps the model routes, because tiers resolve per executor.

### What happens when

- **A route key has no model route.** Validation reports `` `<key>` has no model route. Add `<key>` under `[routing.model.byAgent]` ``. The fix part below sets the value to `default`.
- **The tier table has no entry for the tier.** Validation reports that `[tiers.<table>]` in the global config has no entry for the tier.
- **A native model has no `anthropic:` or `openai:` prefix.** Validation reports that native models use that form.
- **A route names a harness that is not installed.** Validation reports `` `<key>` routes to <name>, which is not installed on this machine `` on `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>`.
- **A native route names a provider without a usable API key.** Validation reports it on `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`. The provider `mock` is exempt.
- **A route key is `judge` in the executor table.** Validation refuses it, because judge calls always run natively.
- **`quick-answer` has a non-native executor.** Validation refuses it, because quick answers run on the native executor only.
- **A key names no agent.** Validation reports `` `<key>` is not an agent ``. The retired name `module-documentation` (`RETIRED_AGENTS`) is exempt, so an old file still loads.
- **A route fails at spawn time.** Another edit can break a saved route. The engine then starts no execution and records it as denied with the text `route: <error>`.
- **The executor is not available.** The engine records the run as denied with `The <executor> executor is not available.`
- **Settings change during a run.** The next spawn reads the new settings. A run that already started keeps its route.

## Validate settings and apply fixes

Save-time validation finds every problem in the settings and reports each one with a dotted path, so the console can show the problem next to the field. `validate_settings` in `crates/ostra-workspace/src/settings.rs` builds the list from three sources:

1. `ostra_sandbox::validate::workspace` checks the sandbox entries.
2. `validate_workspace` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` checks the rest.
3. `ostra_policy::validate_rule` checks each rule in `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, and `permissions.deny`. The path of an issue is `permissions.<list>[<index>]`.

The workspace adds one more check. An absolute project path that is not a folder gives `projects[<i>].path`. A relative path already has its own issue.

### Checks in validate_workspace

| Path | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The name is not blank |
| `projects[i].key` | The key matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`, and no other project uses it |
| `projects[i].path` | The path is absolute. A rooted path without a Windows drive counts as absolute, to keep configs portable |
| `projects[i].stack` | See the project part below |
| `projects[i].code_provider` | The first item of `command` names a program. `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 120 |
| `projects[i].language_servers[j]` | The command names a program. `languages` is not empty, each language is in `NAV_LANGUAGES`, and no two servers claim one language. `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 120 |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>` and `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` | The key is an agent or `judge`. The `judge` and `quick-answer` rules above apply |
| `routing.effort.byAgent.<key>` | The key is an agent |
| `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>` | The key runs per plan phase |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | The value is 1 or more |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | The value is finite and 0 or more. The value 0 means no limit |
| `mcp_servers` | `ostra_core::mcp::validate` checks the servers. See [Integrations](integrations.md) |
| Every route key on every complexity | The route resolves, the harness is installed, and the provider of a native model has a key |

Ostra sorts the issues by path and message and removes duplicates. The `Environment` value supplies two machine facts: the installed harnesses and the providers with a usable key. The server builds it from its last environment scan, and `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}` and the create routes refresh a stale scan first.

`WorkspaceRt::validate` adds one check to `validate_settings` (Rule W3). It checks each tag in `instructions.all` and `instructions.agents.<agent>` with `ostra_core::artifacts::tag_issues`. `WorkspaceRt::detail` calls `validate_settings` and not `validate`. Thus the issue list in the detail does not show tag problems, but a save does.

### Routes of validation in the API

| Route | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}` | Returns `WorkspaceDetail`: settings, projects, `validation`, `fixes`, `agents`, `pendingCommands`, and sandbox status |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` | Returns the issues for a settings body. Nothing is saved |
| `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}` | Saves the settings. It refuses a body that has issues, and returns the issues |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` | Applies the fixes that the detail lists |
| `POST /api/workspaces/validate` | Validates a create request. See the create part below |

[Server API](server-api.md) owns the route table.

### Fixes that Ostra applies

A fix is a change that Ostra can make without a decision from the user. Only one kind exists. `keys_without_route` finds each route key that has no model route on some complexity. This happens when a new agent ships and a workspace that was saved before has no entry for it. `settings_fixes` turns each such key into a `SettingsFix`:

- `path`: `routing.model.byAgent.<key>`
- `value`: `default`, which resolves to the default tier of the agent
- `label`: for example ``Route `plan` to its default tier (advanced)``

`WorkspaceRt::apply_fixes` sets each value and writes the file. It does not validate the rest of the settings, because an unrelated problem must not block a fix. It returns the number of fixes. If the number is 0, it writes nothing.

### What happens when

- **A new Ostra version adds an agent.** The old workspace file has no route for it. Validation reports the key, and the console offers the fix.
- **A save has an issue.** `save_settings` writes nothing and returns every issue.
- **A settings file is saved with a valid body.** `save_settings` writes the file, then calls `sync_projects`.
- **The default tier of a key is unknown.** `default_tier` returns `advanced` for `judge`, the `default_tier` of the agent for an agent name, and `balanced` for any other key.

## Instructions for agents

Instructions are text that a user adds to every spawn of an agent. `instructions.all` is one string for every agent. `instructions.agents.<agent>` is one string for one agent. `WorkspaceSettings::instructions_for` returns the `all` text first and the agent text second. It skips a blank text, so an agent gets 0, 1, or 2 texts.

The spawn factory adds these texts to the repo brief in the first message of the agent. [Agents and prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) describes the brief. A tag in an instruction names a file or an artifact. Ostra then adds the absolute path of the file, so every executor can read it (Rule W3). A tag that names a hidden or missing artifact resolves to nothing, and `WorkspaceRt::validate` reports it.

Ostra does not check that a key in `instructions.agents` names an agent. A key that matches no agent is never used.

## Permissions, limits, and the YOLO default

### Permissions

The `[permissions]` table has a mode and three rule lists: `allow`, `ask`, and `deny`.

| Mode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | Ask for edits and for commands that no rule lists |
| `acceptEdits` | Allow edits inside the project |
| `plan` | Read-only |
| `bypass` | Ask nothing |

The rules of the global config, the workspace, and the session merge in that order, and `PermissionRules::merged` joins the lists. The global config denies `Bash(rm -rf /*)` by default. The mode lives in the registry. The three rule lists live in the file. [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) explains how rules decide a tool call.

When a user answers a permission gate with "always in this workspace", the engine calls `Services::add_allow_rule`. The server then adds the rule to `permissions.allow` with `save_workspace`. An approved file stays approved with the new rule. A file that waits for approval keeps waiting.

### Limits

`limits.max_parallel_executions` (default 3) is the number of executions that run at the same time in one workspace. A further spawn waits for a free slot. The engine reads the limit from the settings each time it checks, so a change applies without a restart. [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) explains the slot. The value 0 is invalid, and the engine treats a value below 1 as 1.

`limits.session_budget_usd` (default 25.0) is the number of dollars that one session can spend before it pauses for a decision. The value 0 means no limit. The part about the session budget below explains the check.

The reason for both limits: a fan-out stage, such as init scouts, skill generation, or explores, can otherwise start dozens of top-tier executions at once.

### The YOLO default

`yolo.default` is `false` for a new workspace. If a workspace sets it to `true`, every new session starts in YOLO mode, and an init session does too. A session cannot turn YOLO off when the workspace default is on. [Judges and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md) explains what YOLO answers for the user. The create request can set the value (`yolo.default`), and the console can change it later. A folder file cannot set it.

## Create a workspace

A create request becomes complete settings that Ostra validates as a whole. If any issue remains, Ostra writes nothing. Only `name` and `root` are required. The setup wizard sends the rest: `projects`, `permissions.mode`, `yolo.default`, `notifications.push`, and `routing_preset`. Enum values arrive as strings, so an unknown value becomes an issue on its own field and not a parse error.

### Flow of a create request

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant Server
  participant Create as create.rs
  participant Trust as trust.rs
  participant Registry
  participant Disk
  Browser->>Server: POST /api/workspaces/validate
  Server->>Create: validate(host, body)
  Create-->>Browser: issues, nothing written
  Browser->>Server: POST /api/workspaces
  Server->>Create: register(host, body)
  Create->>Disk: create_dir_all(root)
  Create->>Trust: create_workspace(settings, adopted)
  Trust->>Disk: write workspace.toml without registry-only keys
  Trust->>Registry: set_access and record approval hash
  Create->>Registry: add_workspace(id, name, root)
  Server->>Server: attach(id, root) opens WorkspaceRt
  Server-->>Browser: WorkspaceDetail
```

### Steps of draft

`create::draft` builds the settings and the issue list. It reads the file system and writes nothing:

1. Trim the name. Check the root: it must be non-empty, absolute, not a file, and not a registered workspace.
2. If the root already holds a readable `workspace.toml`, build on it (an adopted file). Otherwise start from `WorkspaceSettings::seeded`.
3. Add each project of the request. Report a path that another entry already uses, or a path inside `<root>/.ostra`.
4. Apply `permissions.mode` (`default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, or `bypass`), `yolo.default`, `notifications.push`, and the routing preset (`native`, `codex`, or `claude`).
5. Run `validate_settings`. Map each path back to the request, so `projects[3].key` becomes `projects[1].key` when the old file already held 2 projects. An issue in an older entry belongs to `root`.
6. Sort the issues and remove duplicates.

`create::register` runs `draft`, creates the folder, resolves the canonical root, and checks again that no workspace uses the root. It then calls `trust::create_workspace`, creates a new `WorkspaceId`, and adds the registry entry. The server then attaches the workspace and marks the first-run onboarding as done.

### Adopt an existing workspace file

If the folder already holds a `workspace.toml`, the request builds on it. This lets a user register a folder again after the registry lost it. Ostra treats such a file as untrusted (Rule A2). It resets the permission mode, YOLO, limits, tool enforcement, and every sandbox setting from the file, and only the request sets them. The file's commands wait for approval, because `create_workspace` stores no approval for an adopted file. If the file cannot be read, the request gets an issue on `root`.

### What happens when

- **The root is empty or relative.** The issue is on `root`: `Choose a folder for the workspace.` or `Choose an absolute folder for the workspace.`
- **The root is a file.** The issue is on `root`: it names the file and asks for a folder.
- **The root is a registered workspace.** The issue is `That folder is already a registered workspace.` A second check inside `register` catches a race.
- **The mode or preset is unknown.** The issues are on `permissions.mode` and `routing_preset`.
- **The preset needs a harness that is not installed.** The issues are on `routing.executor.byAgent.implementer` and `routing.executor.byAgent.write-test`.
- **Any issue exists.** `register` returns `CreateError::Invalid` and writes nothing.
- **The file write fails.** `register` returns `CreateError::Failed` with the cause.

## Add a project: import, clone, and create

A project joins a workspace through one of three paths. All three end in `WorkspaceRt::import_project`, which appends a `ProjectEntry` to `workspace.toml` and then calls `sync_projects`.

### Keys and stacks

`key_and_stack` checks the two text fields that every path shares. It trims both values and reports each problem on its field.

| Field | Rule | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | Matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`, and no project in the workspace has it | The key names the project in routes, folders, and tool calls |
| `stack` | Optional. A blank value counts as none. Otherwise it is trimmed, at most 64 characters (`MAX_STACK_LEN`), and has no control character | A stack is free text such as `rust`, `elixir-phoenix`, or `Kotlin Ktor`, because the set of real stacks has no end |

If the stack is empty, the initializer detects it from the code.

### Import a folder

`import_entry` handles `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects`. It returns the new entry or every issue at once:

- `path` must be absolute, must exist, and must be a folder. Ostra stores the canonical path.
- `path` must not already be a project, and must not lie inside `<root>/.ostra`.
- The new entry has no `code_provider` and no `language_servers`.

### Pick a folder for a new project

Clone and create use `new_folder_issues` for the destination folder. The folder must not exist, or must exist and be empty. It must not lie inside `<root>/.ostra`. It must not lie inside another project and must not contain one. The function returns whether the folder already existed.

### Clone a repository

`POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/clone` takes `url` and `key`. It also takes optional `stack`, `path`, `branch`, and `credential`.

1. `clone_plan` checks the request. The issues are on `url`, `key`, `stack`, `path`, `branch`, or `credential`. The default folder is `<root>/<key>`. A given `path` must be absolute. A branch name must not be empty, start with `-`, contain `..`, or contain whitespace, a control character, or one of `~ ^ : ? * [` and a backslash. A saved git credential must exist and must match the URL: SSH for an SSH URL, HTTPS otherwise. Without a `credential`, Ostra picks one for the URL.
2. `claim` reserves the key and the folder. If another clone, pull, or project creation holds the key, or a folder that contains or lies inside the new folder, the request fails with a busy error.
3. Ostra runs `git clone --progress` in a task of its own, so a closed browser tab does not stop git halfway and leave a partial checkout. The timeout is 30 minutes (`CLONE_TIMEOUT`). Ostra sends the output lines as `GitProgress` messages to the channel `workspace:<id>`, at most one every 250 ms (`PROGRESS_EVERY`), with secrets removed.
4. If git fails, `clear_failed` removes the new folder, or empties a folder that existed. The request returns the git error.
5. If git succeeds, Ostra imports the checkout and sends `WorkspaceUpdated` to `workspace:<id>` and `home`.

[Project files, git, and workspace search](project-files-and-git.md) describes the git backend and the credentials.

### Create a project from a plan

An agent creates a project with the `ProjectCreate` tool. Only an approved plan phase of the `implementer` can do it (Rule O2). `create_target` (Rule O3) picks the folder: `folder` under the workspace root, which is `<root>/<key>` by default. It checks the key and the folder like the Add project dialog does. It also refuses a folder that equals the workspace root, and a folder that a symbolic link in its path moves outside the root. The server then creates the folder, runs `git init --quiet` if the request asks for it (the default), and imports the project. If any step fails, `clear_failed` undoes the folder. The new project joins the scope of the session. [Native tools and their limits](tools.md) describes the tool input.

### What the project list shows

`WorkspaceRt::project_views` builds a `ProjectView` for each project:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `init_status` | `missing` if the folder is gone. `initializing` if an init session for the project is `running`, `waiting`, or `paused`. `initialized` if `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` exists. Otherwise `not_initialized` |
| `is_git` | `.git` exists in the project folder |
| `git_branch` | The branch that `.git/HEAD` names, or the first 7 characters of a detached commit id. Ostra reads the file directly, because a git process for each project on each read is too slow. A `.git` file, like the one in a worktree or a submodule, points to the real git directory |
| `stack` | The stack of the entry, or else the stack in `project.toml` |
| `ultracode_bootstrap` | `.ultracode/INVENTORY.md` and `.ultracode/repo-profile.json` both exist |
| `profile` | The parsed `project.toml`, if it exists |

`sync_projects` runs after every open and save. It deletes each project row in `workspace.db` that the settings no longer list, and updates a row for each listed project with its init status.

A pipeline session needs at least one initialized project, because every agent routes its work by the inventory of the project. The engine refuses to start otherwise.

## Old workspaces and deletion

Removing a project deletes nothing on disk. Deleting a workspace deletes the workspace file, the workspace database with its two side files, and the registry entry. Both actions first check that nothing runs, because a removal under a live session loses the state of that session.

### Remove a project

`WorkspaceRt::remove_project` runs these steps:

1. Remove the entry from a copy of the settings. If the key does not exist, return `NotFound` (HTTP 404).
2. Try to take the `work` lock exclusively. If a request holds it, return `Busy` with the `STARTING` text.
3. Run `project_busy`. It refuses if a live session can use the project, if an execution runs in the project, or if a clone or pull runs on it. A session is live when it is `running`, `waiting`, or `paused`. A session can use the project if it has no scope and the project was one of its starting projects, or if the project is in its scope. A session that has no log yet counts as a session that can use any project.
4. Write the settings and call `sync_projects`.

The route is `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}`. A `Busy` result gives HTTP 409 and names the session or execution to stop.

### Delete a workspace

`DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}` runs `App::delete_workspace`:

1. Read the registry record. If it is missing, return 404.
2. Hold the open-workspace map exclusively. Call `WorkspaceRt::retire`. It takes the `work` lock exclusively and runs `busy`. Any live session, any running execution, or any clone refuses the delete with HTTP 409. If nothing runs, `retire` marks the workspace as deleted, so later requests get 404.
3. Call `unregister`: remove the registry entry, call `trust::forget`, and delete `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, `workspace.db-wal`, and `workspace.db-shm`. A missing file is not an error. Another failure is logged and does not stop the delete.
4. Forget the navigation and MCP state of the workspace, and send `WorkspaceUpdated` on `workspace:<id>` and `home`.

Project folders, session artifact folders, and the `.ostra` files of each project stay on disk. A later create request for the same folder starts without a workspace-file approval, because `trust::forget` deleted it. The `trust:format:<project>` approvals stay in the registry, so an approved format command stays approved after Ostra creates the workspace again.

### What trust::forget deletes

`trust::forget` (`crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs`) deletes these registry keys of the workspace root:

- `trust:workspace:`, the approval of the workspace file.
- `trust:migrated:` and `trust:migrated-paths:`, the two migration markers.
- `workspace_access:`, the registry-only settings.
- Every key with the prefix `mcp_secret:`, the saved MCP values.
- Every key with the prefix `mcp_oauth:`, the MCP sign-in records.

It does not delete `trust:format:<project>`.

## Approve commands that come from folder files

`<root>/.ostra/workspace.toml` and `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` can arrive with a repository, a `git pull`, or an agent edit. Thus the programs that they name start only after the user approved exactly that content (Rule A1). An approval is a stored hash of the command-bearing content. If the content changes, the hash no longer matches and the commands wait again.

### What the hash covers

`workspace_hash` is the SHA-256 of a JSON form of these parts of the workspace file:

| Part | Fields in the hash |
| --- | --- |
| MCP servers | `name`, `enabled`, `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, `oauth` for every server |
| Code providers and language servers | `key`, `path`, `code_provider`, `language_servers` of each project that has one |
| Allow rules | `permissions.allow` |
| Projects outside the workspace folder | `key` and `path` of each such project |

If all four parts are empty, the hash is `None` and the file needs no approval. A project outside the workspace folder counts because agents can write in their project. A folder file that points a project at `$HOME` widens what the agents can change. The hash leaves out the "outside" part when it is empty, so a file without such projects keeps the hash that it had before.

The format command of a project has its own hash: `commands.format` of `project.toml`, trimmed. It is the one project command that Ostra runs itself.

The registry stores the approved hashes in its key-value table under `trust:workspace:<root>` and `trust:format:<project>`.

### Flow of an approval

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["workspace.toml changes"] --> B{"Saved by Ostra?"}
  B -- "yes, file was approved" --> C["Record the new hash"]
  B -- "yes, file was waiting" --> D["Keep waiting"]
  B -- "no: pull, hand edit, agent" --> E{"Hash equals stored hash?"}
  E -- yes --> F["Approved"]
  E -- no --> D
  C --> F
  D --> G["effective: no MCP, no code provider, no language server, no allow rule, no outside project"]
  D --> H["pending list in WorkspaceDetail"]
  H --> I["POST /api/workspaces/ws/approve with hash"]
  I --> J{"Hash still current?"}
  J -- yes --> F
  J -- no --> K["409: review again"]
```

### What waits when a file is not approved

`trust::effective` builds the settings that programs start from. It applies the registry values first. If the file is not approved, it also:

- disables every MCP server,
- removes each `code_provider` and each language server,
- clears `permissions.allow`,
- drops each project outside the workspace folder.

The engine, the code navigation, and the MCP client use these settings. `WorkspaceRt::settings` returns the settings as the user edits them, with no such removal. A program that Ostra does not start for this reason shows `PENDING_MESSAGE`: `Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra.`

### Pending commands in the detail

`trust::pending` lists each file that waits as a `PendingCommands` value: the project (none for the workspace file), the file path, the hash, and the items. An item has one of six kinds (`PendingKind`):

| Kind | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| `mcpServer` | Name, enabled flag, shell-quoted command, URL, the names of `env` and `headers`, and the names of the `${VAR}` variables that the values read |
| `codeProvider` | The command of the code provider of a project |
| `languageServer` | The command of a language server of a project |
| `allowRule` | The text of an allow rule |
| `projectOutside` | The folder of a project outside the workspace folder |
| `formatCommand` | The format command of a project |

Ostra never sends the values of `env` and `headers`, because they can hold secrets.

### Approve

`POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve` takes `hash` and an optional `project`. `trust::approve` compares the hash with the current hash of the file on disk. If they differ, it returns `Changed` and the server answers HTTP 409 with `Review the commands again, because the file changed after they were shown.` An unknown project gives HTTP 404. On success the server resets the MCP state of the workspace and sends `WorkspaceUpdated`. The hash in the request is the reason that a file that changed again is never approved unseen.

### Saves from Ostra keep approval current

`save_workspace` records the new hash only if the file was approved before the save, or did not exist. A save from the console therefore never asks again. A save of a file that waits keeps waiting, so a save cannot approve commands that the user did not see. `saved_format` applies the same rule to the format command when a user saves the commands of a project. `start` code that must run a program uses `approved_workspace_file`, which returns the copy that Ostra checked, because a second read could see a file that changed after the check.

### Old workspaces and approval markers

- `migrate` runs when `WorkspaceRt::open` opens a workspace that was registered before approvals existed. It approves the current files once, moves the mode and YOLO from the file to the registry, and sets a marker, so it runs once.
- `migrate_paths` runs once for approvals that Ostra recorded before project paths counted. It keeps the old approval valid for the current file. A later change needs approval.
- `forget` deletes the workspace-file approval, the two migration markers, the access record, the saved MCP values, and the MCP sign-in records of a deleted workspace. It keeps the `trust:format:<project>` approvals.

### Literal MCP values

A header or env value of an MCP server that is plain text, and not a `${VAR}` reference, is a literal value. `seal_mcp_values` moves each literal value into the encrypted registry and writes the marker `${ostra_secret}` (`SAVED_SECRET`) in its place. The registry key holds the server name and the first 16 characters of the hash of its `url` and `command`. Thus pointing a server at another URL or command never sends it the old value. `seal_file_secrets` seals literal values that a folder file still holds when the workspace opens. `browser_view` shows the marker in place of any literal value that reached the file since the last save, because only the connection can read it. [Server security](server-security.md) describes the encrypted store.

## Runtime of an open workspace

`WorkspaceRt` in `crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs` is one open workspace in the server process. It owns the settings access, the database, the engine, and the project operations.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `root` | The workspace id and its canonical folder |
| `db` | The `WorkspaceDb` of `<root>/.ostra/workspace.db` |
| `engine` | The `Engine` that runs sessions for this workspace |
| `host` | The `WorkspaceHost` of the process |
| `cloning` | The project keys and folders with a clone or pull in progress |
| `work` | A read-write lock around a flag that is true after deletion. Requests that start work hold it shared. A project removal or a workspace deletion holds it exclusively |

`WorkspaceRt::open` runs these steps: `trust::migrate`, `trust::seal_file_secrets`, open the database, store the workspace id, build the engine services from the host, create the `Engine`, and call `sync_projects`.

The `work` lock exists so that no work starts between the busy check and the removal. A request that starts work (`start_work` in the API) takes the lock shared and gets 404 if the flag is true. A removal that cannot get the lock returns the `STARTING` text: `Wait a moment and try again, because Ostra is starting work in this workspace.`

### What the process provides

The `WorkspaceHost` trait is what a workspace needs from the process that opens it. The server implements it on its shared state.

| Method | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `registry()` | The registry. It holds approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, and sealed secrets, which never come from a folder file |
| `global()` | The machine config. Ostra reads it on every call, so an edit applies without a restart. If the file does not parse, the server logs a warning and uses the last good config |
| `environment()` | The installed harnesses and the providers with a key, for validation |
| `providers()`, `harnesses()` | The status lists for the detail |
| `services(id, root)` | The services of the engine for the workspace |

### Settings views

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `settings()` | The file with the registry values. The console edits this |
| `effective_settings()` | The settings that programs start from. Unapproved commands are removed |
| `detail()` | `WorkspaceDetail` with the settings in `browser_view` form, `validation`, `fixes`, `agents` (each with its resolved route and its default route), `pendingCommands`, and sandbox status |

## Saved console layout

The console layout is stored per workspace, so another browser restores it. The route is `GET` and `PATCH` on `/api/workspaces/{ws}/ui`. The state is JSON in the `meta` table of `workspace.db` under the key `ui_state` (`META_KEY`). If no value is stored, or the stored text no longer parses, `ui_state()` returns the default.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tabs` | List | The open editor tabs in order. Each tab has `id`, `pinned`, and `preview` |
| `active` | Optional text | The id of the focused tab |
| `left_tab` | Optional text | The left dock tab: `sessions` or `files` |
| `files_project` | Optional text | The project key that the Files tab shows |
| `sidebar_open` | Optional flag | Null means the default of the UI |
| `dock_open` | Flag | Whether the quick-question dock is open |
| `theme` | Optional text | `light` or `dark`. Null follows the system |

`PATCH` merges the top-level fields of the body onto the stored state. A field that the body omits keeps its value. Unknown fields are dropped. After the merge, a pinned tab is never the preview tab, and pinned tabs come first in their order.

A `null` clears only the optional fields: `active`, `left_tab`, `files_project`, `sidebar_open`, and `theme`. A `null` for `tabs` or `dock_open` fails in `ui_state::merge`, because those fields are not optional. The server then answers HTTP 400 (`UiStateError::Invalid`).

The size limit is `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES`, 64 KiB (65,536 bytes) of JSON. Ostra checks the body and the merged result.

### What happens when

- **The body is larger than the limit, or the merged state is.** The server answers HTTP 413 with `Keep the UI state under 64 KiB of JSON.`
- **The body is not a JSON object, or a field has the wrong type.** The server answers HTTP 400.
- **A `null` arrives for `tabs` or `dock_open`.** The server answers HTTP 400.
- **The database write fails.** The server answers HTTP 500.

[Web console](web-console.md) describes the tabs and the layout in the browser.

## Pricing catalog, cost, and session budget

Without prices, a cost limit cannot work. Ostra computes `Usage::cost_usd` for each response from a price catalog, and the session budget adds these costs.

### Source and refresh of the catalog

The catalog is the `api.json` document of models.dev (`MODELS_DEV_URL`, `https://models.dev/api.json`). `prices::start` in `crates/ostra-server/src/prices.rs` runs at startup:

1. Read the cache file `<data dir>/models-dev.json`, parse it, and install it with `pricing::install`. A missing or invalid cache leaves the catalog empty.
2. If `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` is set to an empty value, stop. This turns fetching off, for tests and for machines without network access. A non-empty value replaces the URL.
3. Start a background task. If the cache is younger than 24 hours (`REFRESH_EVERY`), wait for the rest of the 24 hours. Otherwise fetch the catalog with a 60-second timeout.
4. A fetch that succeeds and parses must list at least one priced model. Ostra then writes the text to a temporary file, renames it over the cache, and installs the catalog. Then it waits 24 hours.
5. A fetch that fails is logged as a warning. Ostra keeps the cached prices and retries after 1 hour (`RETRY_AFTER`).

### How a price is found and a cost is computed

`Catalog::from_models_dev` skips every model that lacks an input price or an output price. All prices are dollars per million tokens. Missing values get defaults: a cache read costs the input rate, and a 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour cache write costs 2 times the input rate on Anthropic and the same as a 5-minute write on other providers, because models.dev lists only the 5-minute write. A model can have context tiers. Each tier replaces the base rates when the prompt has more tokens than the tier size.

`Catalog::price` looks up a model id with or without a `provider:` prefix:

1. Find an exact match in the first-party providers (`FIRST_PARTY`): the hinted provider first, then `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `mistral`, `deepseek`. A first-party listing wins over a reseller that lists the same id at another price.
2. Else find the longest first-party id that is a prefix of the model id and is followed by `-`. This prices a dated snapshot such as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` as its base id. The model `claude-opus-50` does not match `claude-opus-5`.
3. Else find an exact match in any provider, in sorted order of provider name.

`pricing::cost(model, usage, web_searches)` computes the cost of one response:

```rust
let r = p.rates(input + cache_read + cache_write);   // context tier by prompt size
let write_1h = cache_write_1h.min(cache_write);
cost = input * r.input / 1e6
     + output * r.output / 1e6
     + cache_read * r.cache_read / 1e6
     + (cache_write - write_1h) * r.cache_write / 1e6
     + write_1h * r.cache_write_1h / 1e6
     + web_searches * 0.01;        // WEB_SEARCH_USD
```

`input_tokens` excludes cache reads and writes, because every provider and harness transcript is normalized to that form before this call. The native providers and the harness transcript reader both call `pricing::cost`. The same catalog also gives the context window and the maximum output of a model (`context_window`, `max_output`). The native executor uses them. See [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md).

### The session budget

The planner checks the budget each time it returns a `Spawn` step (`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Planner returns a Spawn step"] --> B{"session_budget_usd above 0?"}
  B -- no --> G["Spawn proceeds"]
  B -- yes --> C{"spent_usd at or above budget plus budget_raised?"}
  C -- no --> G
  C -- yes --> D{"BudgetReached gate open?"}
  D -- no --> E["Open the BudgetReached gate"]
  D -- yes --> F["Drop the spawn"]
  E --> F
  F --> H["User answers: raise or stop"]
```

- `spent_usd` is the sum of `cost_usd` over the executions of the session that have a result. A running execution does not count until it ends. Judge calls do not count either. The session summary shows the cost with judge calls added.
- The limit is `limits.session_budget_usd` plus the dollars that the user raised.
- Executions that already run finish. Only new spawns wait.
- The gate is titled `The session reached its budget`. It shows the spent amount and the limit.
- If the user answers `raise`, Ostra adds the amount in the answer text (a leading `$` is allowed, and the number must be positive and finite). With no valid amount, it adds the limit that the gate showed, but at least 1 dollar. It also adds the amount by which the spend passed the limit.
- Any other answer stops the session with `Stopped at the session budget after spending $<amount>.`

### Cost report and the Cost screen

`GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/cost` returns a `CostReport`. The optional query `since` is an RFC 3339 time that counts executions that started at or after it. An invalid time gives HTTP 400 with the text `` `since` must be an RFC 3339 time such as 2026-09-24T00:00:00Z, not `<value>`. `` Here `<value>` is the text that the client sent. The report has `by_session`, `by_stage`, `by_agent`, `by_executor`, and `total`. Each row has the number of executions and the usage: input, output, cache reads, cache writes (5-minute and 1-hour), tool calls, build time, and cost.

The console shows the report on the screen `ws:cost` (`web/src/screens/CostScreen.tsx`):

- Two ranges: `This week` (the default) and `All time`. The week starts at `WorkspaceActivity.week_since` of the server, so the totals match the status bar.
- Four tables (`COST_GROUPS`): by session, by stage, by agent, and by executor. Rows sort by cost, highest first, and show their share of the total.
- The key `side-panel` shows as `Side-panel questions`. The stage key `none` shows as `No stage`.
- The screen reloads at most once every 2,000 ms when an `activity` or `session_updated` message arrives on the channel `workspace:<ws>`.
- The column `Cache / tool call` divides cache reads by tool calls. A rising value means that each tool call re-reads more context. The column `Build time` shows the time in build and test commands.

### What happens when

- **No catalog is installed**, for example on a first run without network access. Every cost is 0, so the budget never pauses a session and the report shows 0.
- **A model is not in the catalog.** Its cost is 0. The budget does not count it.
- **A fetch fails.** Ostra keeps the cached prices and retries after 1 hour.
- **The fetched catalog lists no priced model.** Ostra refuses it and keeps the old cache.
- **The budget is 0.** The planner sets no limit.
- **The budget is reached.** No new execution starts. Executions that run finish, and the gate waits for the user.

## Limits and constants of this page

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Limits::default().max_parallel_executions` | 3 | Executions that run at once in a workspace |
| `Limits::default().session_budget_usd` | 25.0 | Dollars that a session can spend before a gate. 0 means no limit |
| `MAX_STACK_LEN` | 64 characters | Longest project stack |
| `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` | 120 seconds | Highest `timeout_secs` for a code provider or a language server. The lowest is 1 |
| `default_provider_timeout` | 10 seconds | Default `timeout_secs` of a code provider or a language server |
| `default_mcp_timeout` | 120 seconds | Default `timeout_secs` of an MCP server |
| `JUDGE_ROUTE` | `judge` | The route key of judge calls |
| `RETIRED_AGENTS` | `module-documentation` | An agent name that old settings can still carry. Validation ignores it |
| `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES` | 64 KiB | Largest saved console layout |
| `META_KEY` | `ui_state` | The `meta` key of the console layout |
| `STARTING` | `Wait a moment and try again, because Ostra is starting work in this workspace.` | The busy text when the `work` lock is not free |
| `PENDING_MESSAGE` | `Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra.` | The text where a program waits for approval |
| `MODELS_DEV_URL` | `https://models.dev/api.json` | The price catalog source |
| `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` (`URL_ENV`) | none | Replaces the catalog URL. An empty value turns fetching off |
| `REFRESH_EVERY` | 24 hours | Time between catalog fetches |
| `RETRY_AFTER` | 1 hour | Wait after a failed fetch |
| Fetch timeout | 60 seconds | Timeout of one catalog fetch |
| `WEB_SEARCH_USD` | 0.01 dollars | Cost of one server-side web search |
| `FIRST_PARTY` | `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `mistral`, `deepseek` | Providers whose listing wins over resellers |
| `RUNTIME_DIR` | `.ostra` | The runtime folder of a workspace and of a project |
| `SKILLS_DIR` | `.agents/skills` | The folder where Ostra writes project skills |
| `LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR` | `.ostra/skills` | A skills folder that Ostra reads and never writes |
| `INSTRUCTION_FILES` | `claude.md`, `agents.md`, `agent.md` | Instruction files of a project, matched in any letter case |
| `ARTIFACT_PREFIX` | `ostra-` | The prefix of artifact file names |
| `HOME_CREDENTIALS` | List of `HomeCredential` values | Credential stores and personal data under `$HOME`. Each entry has a `path` and a `harness` field. The `harness` names the one CLI that signs in with that store and can see it. The policy refuses tool calls that name the paths, the sandbox hides them, and Grep and Glob skip them |
| `RESERVED_NAMES` | Windows device names such as `con`, `prn`, `aux`, `com1`, `lpt1` | Names that open a device on Windows. `is_reserved_device` refuses them, except `NUL` |
| `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | Variables that Ostra keeps from agent processes and MCP servers |
| `BRIDGE_ENV` | `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_HARNESS` | Variables that give a harness or MCP child its own identity. Ostra drops them and sets them again |

## What these rules do not guarantee

- **Approval covers only the command-bearing parts.** The hash covers MCP servers, code providers, language servers, allow rules, projects outside the workspace folder, and the format command. A pulled file can still change routing, instructions, `ask` and `deny` rules, notifications, and projects inside the workspace folder without an approval.
- **Approval is not a review of the program.** The user sees the command line. Ostra does not check what the program does.
- **A project inside the workspace folder needs no approval.** Agents can write in it, like in any project.
- **Validation reflects the machine at save time.** A harness that is installed or a provider key that exists when the user saves can be gone at spawn time. The engine then denies the spawn.
- **Instructions are text.** Ostra does not check that an agent follows them. It checks only the tags.
- **Cost is an estimate.** It depends on the catalog and on usage numbers that providers and harness transcripts report. A model that is not in the catalog costs 0.
- **The budget is a pause and not a hard cap.** Running executions finish after the limit, and judge calls do not count. The spend can pass the limit.
- **Registry-only settings protect against a file, not against a user.** A person who can use the console can change them.
