sections.title: Storage: workspace database, registry, and lesson memory
sections.summary: The three SQLite files that Ostra keeps, each table and migration, the event log and its materialized columns, tool output limits, lesson memory and recall, and workspace search.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra stores state in SQLite

Ostra must keep a session across a server restart, and it must keep credentials and lessons apart from that session data. One store does not fit all three needs, so the `ostra-store` crate keeps three kinds of SQLite file. Each file has one owner type and one lifetime.

This page covers:

- The three files and where each one lives.
- How a connection opens: journal mode, locking, file permissions, and `.gitignore`.
- The migrations and the `user_version` rule.
- Each table of the workspace database, the machine registry, and the lesson memory.
- The event log and the columns that the engine materializes beside it.
- The tool output limit.
- Encrypted secrets in the registry.
- Lesson recall.
- Workspace search: the text index and the ranking of the search route.

[Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) explains how the engine folds events into `SessionState`. [Server security](server-security.md) explains the master key. [Tools](tools.md) explains the `Memory` and `MemoryRecall` tool inputs.

## The three SQLite files

| File | Path | Rust type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace database | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` | `WorkspaceDb` | The event log, the tables that the engine materializes beside it, and the text search index |
| Machine registry | `registry.db` in the data directory | `RegistryDb` | The workspace list, push subscriptions, and a key and value table with encrypted credentials |
| Lesson memory | `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | `MemoryStore` | The lessons of one project |

The data directory is the value of the `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` environment variable when it is set. Otherwise it is the `ostra` folder in the platform local data directory (`data_dir` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](../crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs)). The doc comment in `registry.rs` names `~/.local/share/ostra/registry.db`, which is the Linux default.

The paths come from `workspace_db`, `registry_db_path`, and `project_memory_db` in the same `paths.rs` file. The workspace database and the lesson memory live inside a folder that the user owns. The registry lives once for each machine and is shared by all workspaces.

### Why the files are separate

- The workspace database holds every tool output. It stays with its workspace, and the `.gitignore` rule below keeps it out of commits.
- The registry holds credentials. It is the only file that has an encryption key.
- The lesson memory belongs to a project, not to a workspace. Several workspaces can use the same project, and the lessons stay with the project folder. The lesson store is also never capped and never expires, so its lifetime differs from a session.

## How a connection opens

`WorkspaceDb` and `RegistryDb` both call `open_connection` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs`](../crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs). The function runs these steps in order:

1. Create the parent folder, and set its mode to `0700` on Unix.
2. Open the SQLite file.
3. Set the busy timeout to 5000 milliseconds.
4. Set `journal_mode` to `WAL`.
5. Set `foreign_keys` to `ON`.
6. Run the pending migrations.
7. Set the mode of the database file, the `-wal` file, and the `-shm` file to `0600` on Unix.

The code sets the modes after the migrations because SQLite creates the side files with the process umask. The event log holds tool output and the registry holds credentials, so no other user on the machine must read them. A file that does not exist yet is skipped without an error. On other platforms than Unix the step does nothing.

The migrations declare no `FOREIGN KEY` clause. The `foreign_keys` pragma therefore has no effect on the current tables.

`RegistryDb::open` also sets `secure_delete` to `ON`. SQLite then zeroes freed pages, so a replaced plaintext credential does not stay in the file.

### One connection, one lock

A `WorkspaceDb` clone shares one connection inside `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`. Each method locks the mutex for its whole statement or transaction. If a thread panics when it holds the lock, the next caller takes the connection anyway (`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`). Writers that compute the next sequence number use an `IMMEDIATE` transaction, so two writers cannot read the same maximum.

`MemoryStore` works the other way. It stores only the file path and opens a fresh connection for each call. Parallel executions then wait on the SQLite file lock, with a 5000-millisecond busy timeout, and do not share one handle.

### The workspace .gitignore

`WorkspaceDb::open` writes `<workspace>/.ostra/.gitignore` when the file does not exist. It holds three patterns: `workspace.db*`, `sessions/`, and `uploads/`. The reason is that the event log keeps every tool output, so a `git add -A` in the workspace root must not publish it. If the file exists, the code does not change it.

## Migrations

Each database has a `MIGRATIONS` list of SQL scripts. The `migrate` function reads `PRAGMA user_version`. For each script at an index at or after that number, it runs the script and sets `user_version` to the index plus one. Script and version update run in one transaction, so a failed script leaves the version unchanged.

| Database | Version | What the script does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workspace | 1 | Creates `meta`, `projects`, `sessions`, `events`, `executions`, `messages`, `activity`, `gates`, `decisions`, `tool_calls`, and their indexes |
| Workspace | 2 | Adds `sessions.title` and `executions.summary` |
| Workspace | 3 | Creates `search_docs`, the `search_fts` virtual table, its triggers, and the session triggers. Then it copies every existing session into `search_docs` |
| Registry | 1 | Creates `workspaces`, `push_subscriptions`, and `kv` |

Three rules follow from the code and its tests:

- A database from an older version gains the new columns when it opens. The test `a_version_one_database_gains_the_new_columns` opens a version 1 file and reads `title` as empty.
- Version 3 fills the search index from the sessions that exist. The test `search_index_backfills_sessions_from_before_the_migration` drops the index, sets version 2, and finds the session again after the open.
- To change a table, append a script to `MIGRATIONS`. Do not edit an earlier script, because a database that ran it does not run it again.

The in-memory variants `WorkspaceDb::open_in_memory` and `RegistryDb::open_in_memory` run the same scripts. They skip the file permissions and the `.gitignore` file.

The lesson memory has no `user_version`. It runs its `SCHEMA` text with `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` on every connection.

## Workspace database tables

The doc comment of `workspace.rs` states the split: the session event log is the source of truth, and the engine materializes the other tables beside it for the UI.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    sessions ||--o{ events : "session_id, seq"
    sessions ||--o{ executions : "session_id"
    sessions ||--o{ gates : "session_id"
    sessions ||--o{ decisions : "session_id"
    executions ||--o{ messages : "execution_id, seq"
    executions ||--o{ activity : "execution_id, seq"
    executions ||--o{ tool_calls : "execution_id"
    sessions ||--o| search_docs : "kind session"
    search_docs ||--|| search_fts : "content rowid"
```

The links in the diagram are logical. No table declares a foreign key.

| Table | Key | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `meta` | `key` | Text values: the `workspace_id` and the saved UI state under `ui_state` |
| `projects` | `key` | The project `path`, `init_status`, and `stack` |
| `sessions` | `id` | One row for each session: request, category, status, lane, stage label, projects, YOLO flag, cost, title, and times |
| `events` | `(session_id, seq)` | The event log. Each row has `type`, JSON `payload`, and `at` |
| `executions` | `id` | One row for each agent run, and for each side-panel run that has a `NULL` `session_id` |
| `messages` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The conversation of a native execution, each row a `role` and JSON `content` |
| `activity` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The `ExecutionDelta` values that the UI streams, as JSON |
| `gates` | `id` | The approval and permission gates of a session, and their answers |
| `decisions` | `id` | The judge decisions, with the override flags |
| `tool_calls` | `id` (autoincrement) | One row for each tool call: input, policy decision, rule, duration, and output |
| `search_docs` | `id`, unique `(kind, ref)` | The text that the workspace search indexes |
| `search_fts` | rowid of `search_docs` | An FTS5 index over `label` and `body` |

### Storage formats

- Times are RFC 3339 text in UTC with millisecond precision, for example `2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`. The `now` function in [`crates/ostra-store/src/util.rs`](../crates/ostra-store/src/util.rs) writes them. A value that does not parse returns `StoreError::Invalid` with the text `bad timestamp`.
- A unit-variant enum is stored as its serde name in a `TEXT` column (`enum_str` and `enum_from`). This applies to `status`, `lane`, `category`, `stage`, `init_status`, `judge`, and `source`.
- The session `kind`, the `projects` list, `purpose`, `usage`, gate `payload` and `answer`, and decision `output` are JSON text.
- The executor is stored as its `Display` text and the agent as its name.

## The event log

The `events` table is the append-only history of a session. `WorkspaceDb::append_event` runs one `IMMEDIATE` transaction that does these steps:

1. Read `MAX(seq) + 1` for the session. The first event has `seq` 1.
2. Serialize the `SessionEvent`, and take its `type` field as the `type` column. If the field is missing, the column holds `unknown`.
3. Insert the row with the current time.
4. Set `sessions.updated_at` to the same time.
5. Return a `StoredEvent` with `seq`, `at`, and the event.

The sequence number belongs to one session, so two sessions both have an event with `seq` 1. The primary key `(session_id, seq)` rejects a duplicate. The test `concurrent_appends_get_distinct_seqs` runs 8 threads with 10 appends each and checks that all sequence numbers differ.

`events` returns every event of a session in `seq` order. `events_after` returns the events with a `seq` greater than a given number, so a reader can resume from its last event.

The store never edits or deletes an event. After a restart, the engine reads the events of each session and folds them into `SessionState` (see [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md)). The other tables help the UI read the state quickly. They are not the truth.

## Materialized tables and columns

The engine writes the tables below while it handles events. A reader can rebuild their meaning from the log, but the UI reads them directly.

### Column lists

Four constants in [`crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs`](../crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs) fix the column order of the read queries. The `raw_*` and `*_from_raw` functions map each row by position, so a change to a list must change the mapping too.

| Constant | Columns, in order |
| --- | --- |
| `SESSION_COLS` | `id, kind, request, category, status, lane, stage_label, projects, yolo, cost_usd, created_at, updated_at, title` |
| `EXECUTION_COLS` | `id, session_id, agent, purpose, stage, project, executor, model, status, started_at, ended_at, usage, report_path, native_session_id, spawn_block, error, summary` |
| `GATE_COLS` | `id, session_id, title, explanation, payload, answer, source, reason, opened_at, answered_at` |
| `DECISION_COLS` | `id, judge, subject, input_summary, output, reason, overridden, can_override, at` |

### Sessions

`create_session` inserts a row with status `running`, lane `research`, stage label `Intake`, cost `0`, and equal `created_at` and `updated_at`. `update_session` changes only the fields that a `SessionUpdate` sets. A `None` leaves a field as it is. The `category` and `title` fields use a nested option, so a caller can set them to `NULL` with `Some(None)`. The method always sets `updated_at`, and it returns `StoreError::NotFound` when the session does not exist.

`list_sessions` returns the newest session first, by `created_at` then `id`. The `open_gates` count of a `SessionSummary` is not a column. Each read counts the gates of the session that have a `NULL` `answer`.

### Executions

An `executions` row holds both the spawn data and the result. The `usage` column holds the `Usage` JSON, and `cost_usd` holds a copy of its cost. The `spend_since` method sums `cost_usd`. The `cost_report` method reads the `usage` JSON instead. Both count the executions that started at or after a given time.

`execution_from_raw` builds an `ExecutionView`. Four fields have no column: `has_transcript` and `has_terminal` start as `false`, `pending_gate` as `None`, and `repo_root` as `None`. The engine fills them. `can_resume` is `true` when the executor is a harness and `native_session_id` is set.

### Gates and decisions

- `upsert_gate` inserts a gate. If the `id` exists, it refreshes `title`, `explanation`, and `payload` and keeps the answer.
- `answer_gate` stores the answer JSON, the `source`, the `reason`, and `answered_at`. It returns `NotFound` for an unknown id.
- `open_gates` returns the gates with a `NULL` answer, for one session or for the whole workspace, oldest first.
- `insert_decision` stores a judge decision. `overridden` starts at `0` and `can_override` at `1`.
- `mark_overridden` sets `overridden` to `1` and replaces the `output` and the `reason`. `set_can_override` changes the flag.

[Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md) explains when the engine writes each one.

### Messages and activity

`append_message` and `append_activity` use the same method as the event log. Each runs an `IMMEDIATE` transaction, reads `MAX(seq) + 1` for the execution, and inserts the row. `messages` keeps the native conversation. `activity` keeps the deltas. `activity_after` returns the items after a `seq`, so a client that reconnects asks only for what it missed.

### Projects and meta

`upsert_project` inserts or replaces the `path`, `init_status`, and `stack` of a project key. `list_projects` sorts by key. `meta_set` and `meta_get` store free text. The workspace runtime keeps its saved UI state under the `ui_state` key, and the `workspace_id` key holds the ID of the workspace that owns the file.

## Execution lifecycle and restart

The store has one method for each step of an execution row:

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `insert_execution` | Adds the row with status `running`, an empty `Usage`, and cost `0` |
| `update_execution_usage` | Writes live usage and cost when the execution runs |
| `set_execution_summary` | Writes the one-line summary: the last tool call or status message |
| `set_native_session_id` | Stores the ID that a harness needs to resume |
| `set_execution_status` | Changes the status. Only a terminal status sets `ended_at`, and other statuses keep the old value |
| `finish_execution` | Writes status, usage, cost, error, submit payload, final text, and `ended_at`. It keeps the old `native_session_id` when the result has none |
| `reopen_execution` | Sets the status to `running`, clears `error` and `ended_at`, and keeps usage, transcript, and activity |

The comment on `reopen_execution` cites Rule P2: a paused execution runs again under its own ID, so the resumed run adds to its usage and transcript.

### What happens when the server restarts

- `Engine::recover` (in `ostra-engine`, file `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`) reads every session at start. For each execution that is still `running`, it writes a result.
- If the execution has an open ask, the status is `Waiting` (Rule H2). The code decides this only from `st.open_ask_of(&r.id).is_some()`. It does not test that a process is alive. The Rule H2 comment says that a harness run that waited with its process alive still waits, and its answer resumes the harness session.
- If the execution has no open ask, the status is `Interrupted` and the error is `The server restarted while this execution ran.`
- The recovery keeps the usage and the native session ID that the store already holds, because the usage deltas were stored when the execution ran.
- `recover` denies every open permission gate of the session (`GatePayload::Permission`). Each gate gets a `Deny` answer from the engine with the reason `The execution that asked ended when the server restarted.` The code does not check that the asking execution is dead, so a gate of an execution that was set to `Waiting` (Rule H2) is also denied.
- `recover` then calls `mark_running_interrupted`. The method sets every execution that is still `running` to `Interrupted` and returns the views.

## Tool call records and the output limit

`record_tool_call` writes one `tool_calls` row for each tool call: execution, `call_id`, tool name, input JSON, the policy decision JSON, the rule, the duration in milliseconds, and the output.

The store cuts the stored output to `TOOL_OUTPUT_LIMIT`, which is `8 * 1024` bytes (8192 bytes). The `truncate_utf8` function moves the cut back to a character boundary, so a multi-byte character is never split. It then appends a line `[truncated: N bytes]`, where `N` is the full length of the original output.

```rust
fn truncate_utf8(s: &str, limit: usize) -> String {
    if s.len() <= limit {
        return s.to_string();
    }
    let mut end = limit;
    while !s.is_char_boundary(end) {
        end -= 1;
    }
    format!("{}\n[truncated: {} bytes]", &s[..end], s.len())
}
```

The limit applies only to the `output` column. The code does not cut the tool `input`, the event payloads, the messages, or the activity deltas. The model still sees the full output from the tool. The limit protects the database, not the agent. Because the output can still reach 8 KB for each call, the database file stays private (see [How a connection opens](#how-a-connection-opens)). The tool crate has its own output caps, which [Tools](tools.md) lists.

`tool_calls` returns the rows of an execution in insertion order, by the autoincrement `id`.

## The workspace text index

The `search_docs` table feeds workspace search. Each row has a `kind`, a `ref`, a `session_id`, a `label`, a `body`, and an `mtime`. The pair `(kind, ref)` is unique. Two kinds exist:

- `session`: `ref` is the session ID, `label` is the title (or an empty string), and `body` is the request.
- `artifact`: `ref` is the absolute file path, `label` is the artifact label, and `body` is the file name followed by one heading on each line.

`search_fts` is an FTS5 table with external content (`content='search_docs'`). Its tokenizer is `unicode61 remove_diacritics 2`, and it builds prefix indexes for 2 and 3 characters (`prefix='2 3'`). Three triggers (`search_docs_ai`, `search_docs_ad`, `search_docs_au`) keep it equal to `search_docs`.

### How rows get into the index

- A trigger on `sessions` inserts a `session` row when a session is created.
- A second trigger updates the row when `title` or `request` changes.
- The server calls `index_artifacts` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs) each time it rebuilds the node of a session. Agents write artifacts through their tools, so the index catches up at that point.

For each artifact, `index_artifacts` does these steps:

1. Skip the artifact when its path is not absolute or its file is missing.
2. Read `indexed_artifacts`. Skip the artifact when the stored label and `mtime` equal the current ones. The `mtime` is the file modification time in milliseconds.
3. Build the body from the file name.
4. If the file is at most `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` (4 MiB, `4 * 1024 * 1024` bytes) and can be read as text, add each heading of the file.
5. Call `index_artifact`. It inserts the row, or updates it on a `(kind, ref)` conflict. A later index of the same file replaces the old text.

A larger artifact is indexed by label and file name only. A failure to index writes a warning to the log and does not stop the session.

### The text query

`fts_prefix_query` turns user text into an FTS5 query. It splits the text at every character that is not alphanumeric, quotes each word, adds `*`, and joins the words with spaces. The text `canc ord` becomes `"canc"* "ord"*`. Every word must match, each as a word prefix. Because only alphanumeric characters stay in a word, FTS syntax in the user text cannot change the query. The test `text_search_over_sessions_and_artifacts` sends `"zz*) OR (` and gets no hits and no error.

`search_text(text, limit)` returns `TextHit` values (`kind`, `reference`, `session`, `label`, `body`, `rank`). It sorts by `bm25(search_fts, 4.0, 1.0)`, so a match in the `label` counts four times as much as a match in the `body`. A lower rank is better. If the query has no words, the method returns an empty list.

## Workspace search route

`GET /api/workspaces/:ws/search?q=&limit=` returns one ranked list across seven kinds of result. The code is in [`crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/nav/search.rs). The route table is in [Server API](server-api.md). The Files view and its file name index are in [Project files, git, and workspace search](project-files-and-git.md).

| `SearchKind` | Id format | Source | How it matches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Session` | `session:<id>` | Text index | Every word as a word prefix, then scored in memory |
| `Execution` | `exec:<id>` | Sessions tree | Agent name and run label, in memory |
| `Artifact` | `artifact:<path>` | Text index and the Sessions tree | Label, file name, and headings |
| `File` | `file:<project>:<path>` | File name index of each project | Path match |
| `Project` | `project:<key>` | Workspace settings | Key and folder name |
| `Lesson` | `lesson:<project>:<id>` | Lesson memory of each project | Any word, full words |
| `Setting` | `setting:<key>` | `SETTING_KEYS` | Key and description |

### How a query runs

1. Clamp `limit` to the range 1 to `MAX_LIMIT` (200). The default is `DEFAULT_LIMIT` (50).
2. If the query is empty after trimming, return the most recently updated sessions. Their scores start at `1.0` and fall by `0.001` for each place.
3. Otherwise, score projects and settings in memory.
4. In a blocking task, build the sessions tree, score executions and artifact names, read the text index with `TEXT_ROWS` (200) rows, and read the lessons.
5. For each project, ask the file name index for its paths and score the best `limit` of them. A project whose index fails adds no files.
6. Merge all hits: sort by score, then by shorter label, then by id. Keep the best hit for each id. Cut the list to `limit`.

### Scores

Every source gives a score from 0 to 1 so that one sort can merge them. `Needle::text_score` gives the base score of a text. The query is trimmed and lowercased first.

| Match | Base score |
| --- | --- |
| The text equals the query | 1.0 |
| The text starts with the query | 0.9 |
| The query starts at a word start | 0.8 |
| The query is a substring | 0.65 |
| The query has several words and each is a substring | 0.55 |
| The query is a subsequence of the text | 0.3 |

The function subtracts a length penalty of 0.0005 for each extra character in the text, up to 0.05. Among equal matches, the shorter text ranks first.

`Needle::file_score` uses the file name first and the path second:

| Match | Base score |
| --- | --- |
| File name equals the query | 1.0 |
| File name starts with the query | 0.88 |
| File name contains the query | 0.74 |
| Path contains the query | 0.6 |
| Query is a subsequence of the file name | 0.4 |
| Query is a subsequence of the path | 0.3 |

Each source then adjusts the score:

- Executions: the best of the agent name, the run label, and both together, plus 0.02.
- Artifacts from the tree: the label, or the file name times 0.95, plus 0.03.
- Projects: the key, or the folder name times 0.9, plus 0.03.
- Settings: the key, the last part of the key times 0.95, or the description times 0.85. No bonus.
- Sessions from the text index: the title, or the request times 0.95, plus 0.04, minus 0.0001 for each place in the index order. If the in-memory score finds no match, the score is `INDEX_ONLY` (0.45) because the index matched a word prefix.
- Artifacts from the text index: the label, or the best heading times 0.95, plus 0.03, minus the same place penalty. The fallback is also `INDEX_ONLY`.
- Lessons: the lesson text, or the area times 0.9, minus 0.0001 for each place. The fallback is `INDEX_ONLY`.

### What happens when

- A project has no lesson file: the search skips it. Opening a `MemoryStore` creates its file, and a search must not write into a project.
- A lesson matches only by word prefix, for example `canc` for `cancel`: the lesson query does not match it, because lesson search uses full words. A session does match.
- The same artifact appears from the tree and from the text index: `merge` keeps the higher score.
- A session has an empty title, or a title that has only whitespace: `session_label` uses the request. It calls `clip(request)`, and `clip` calls `ostra_core::api::summary_line`. That function joins all words of the whole request with single spaces, so newlines collapse and the code takes no first line. It cuts the text to `SUMMARY_CHARS` (120 characters, with an ellipsis), and then `.take(HINT_CHARS)` keeps 80 characters. A multi-line request therefore shows words from later lines in the label.
- The blocking task fails: the route returns status 500.

The search reads each project's lessons with `LESSONS_PER_PROJECT` (20) as the limit.

## Machine registry tables

The registry migration creates three tables.

| Table | Columns | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspaces` | `id` (primary key), `name`, `root` (unique), `created_at` | `add_workspace` returns `Invalid` when the root is already registered, with the ID of the other workspace in the message |
| `push_subscriptions` | `endpoint` (primary key), `p256dh`, `auth`, `workspace_id`, `created_at` | `add_push_subscription` updates the keys and the workspace when the endpoint exists, and keeps `created_at` |
| `kv` | `key` (primary key), `value` (blob) | A general key and value table |

`remove_workspace` runs in one transaction. It deletes the push subscriptions that belong to the workspace, then the workspace row. It deletes nothing on disk. Subscriptions with a `NULL` `workspace_id` stay. `list_workspaces` sorts by `created_at`, then `id`.

### The kv table

Other crates store small values in `kv` under a key prefix. The store has these operations:

- `kv_get`, `kv_set`, and `kv_delete` read, upsert, and remove one key.
- `kv_scan(prefix)` returns every entry whose key starts with the prefix, in key order.
- `kv_replace(key, expected, new)` sets the value only if it still holds `expected`. It returns `true` when it changed the row. Two callers cannot both win. The test `kv_replace_lets_only_one_caller_claim_a_value` shows this with a sign-in token.

Two keys belong to the store: `onboarded_at` (`ONBOARDED_AT`) and `secrets_vacuumed` (`SECRETS_VACUUMED`). `mark_onboarded` uses `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so a second call keeps the first time. `onboarded_at` returns that time. The server calls `mark_onboarded` when first-run setup completes.

## Encrypted secrets in the registry

The registry encrypts credentials before it writes them to `kv`. [Server security](server-security.md) explains where the master key comes from. This section states what the store does with it.

The `Sealer` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs`](../crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs) seals a value with AES-256-GCM. For each value it:

1. Makes a random nonce of `NONCE_LEN` (12) bytes.
2. Encrypts the value, and uses the row key as associated data.
3. Stores `enc:v1:` followed by the base64 text of the nonce and the ciphertext.

The row key as associated data binds a value to its row. A sealed value that someone copies to another row does not open. A new nonce for each seal means that two seals of one value differ.

`SECRET_KEYS` lists the rows that hold credentials. A key that ends with `:` is a prefix. Any other key is an exact name.

| Entry | Match |
| --- | --- |
| `vapid_private` | Exact |
| `provider_credentials:` | Prefix |
| `git_credential:` | Prefix |
| `mcp_oauth:` | Prefix |
| `mcp_secret:` | Prefix |

`secret_get`, `secret_set`, and `secret_scan` use the sealer. In a debug build, only `secret_get` and `secret_set` call `debug_assert!(is_secret_key(key), ...)`, so they panic when the key is not in `SECRET_KEYS`. `secret_scan` has no assertion. It takes a prefix, calls `kv_scan`, and opens each value with the sealer.

### What happens when

- The registry has no sealer: `RegistryDb::open` makes a registry without one, and `with_sealer` adds it. Until then, each secret call returns `StoreError::Locked`: "the registry has no encryption key, so credentials cannot be read or saved".
- A value does not open because the key changed or someone altered the value: `secret_get` returns `None`, and the log shows a warning that asks the user to enter the credential again. `secret_scan` skips the value.
- A stored value has no `enc:v1:` prefix: `Sealer::open` returns it as it is, because registries from before encryption hold plaintext until the migration seals them.
- The server starts: `seal_plaintext_secrets` seals each secret row that is still plaintext. It writes each row with `kv_replace`, so a concurrent writer is not overwritten. If it sealed a row, or the `secrets_vacuumed` marker is absent, it then runs `VACUUM`, empties the write-ahead log with `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`, and sets the marker. The marker makes sure that plaintext from an interrupted run is removed at the next start. The method returns the number of sealed rows.
- An in-memory registry opens: it gets an ephemeral key that lives for the life of the process.

The registry encryption does not protect a credential from a process that has the master key, and it does not protect the `workspace.db` file. The workspace database has no encryption. It relies on the `0600` mode and the `.gitignore` rule.

## Lesson memory

A lesson is a short fact about a project that an agent recorded and that later runs can find. The store keeps lessons in `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. The schema comes from Ultracode's `mcp/lib/memory.js`. The store never caps the number of lessons and never expires one.

The `lessons` table has these columns: `id` (autoincrement), `area`, `lesson`, `source`, and `created_at`. The pair `(area, lesson)` is unique. `lessons_fts` is an FTS5 index over `area` and `lesson` with external content. Three triggers (`lessons_ai`, `lessons_ad`, `lessons_au`) keep it current. It uses the default tokenizer, without prefix indexes.

An `area` names a module, for example `orders::Service`. The text `area::sub` is a sub-scope of `area`.

### Operations

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `open` | Creates the folder, the file, and the schema |
| `record(area, lesson, source)` | Inserts a lesson. If the pair exists, it updates `source` and `created_at`, so the newest occurrence wins. It returns the total number of lessons |
| `recall(area, query, limit)` | Returns the best lessons. The next section explains the order |
| `forget(area, lesson)` | Deletes one exact pair. It returns `false` when the pair is absent |
| `list(query, limit, offset)` | For the memory browser: all lessons newest first, or the lessons that match the query by `bm25` |
| `update(id, area, lesson)` | A user edit. It sets `source` to `user` and `created_at` to now. It returns `NotFound` for an unknown id |
| `delete(id)` | Deletes one lesson by id |

`recall`, `forget`, `list`, and `delete` return an empty result when the file does not exist. They do not create it. The test `missing_store_recalls_nothing` checks this. Only `open`, `record`, and `update` create the file.

### Which agents write and read lessons

- The `Memory` tool calls `record`. The `area` and `lesson` inputs must not be empty. If the `source` input is empty, the tool uses the `memory_source` value of its configuration.
- The `MemoryRecall` tool calls `recall`. The default limit is `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` (8 lessons). The tool clamps a given limit to the range 1 to `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` (50, in `ostra-tools`).
- The native executor recalls up to 5 lessons for a failed build, when the policy engine returns the observation `RecallLessons`. It adds them to the tool result.
- The memory browser in the console uses `list`, `update`, and `delete`.

[Tools](tools.md) gives the tool inputs. [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) explains the lesson gate and the build streak that trigger the recall.

## How lesson recall orders results

`recall` builds up to two buckets of lessons and then fills the result from the first bucket to the last. The query text is split at non-alphanumeric characters. Each word is quoted, and the words are joined with `OR`, so one matching word is enough. The area is trimmed, and an empty area counts as no area.

| Area | Query | Bucket 1 | Bucket 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Yes | Yes | Lessons in the area or in `area::*` that match the query, by `bm25` | All lessons that match the query, by `bm25` |
| Yes | No | Lessons in the area or in `area::*`, newest first | None |
| No | Yes | All lessons that match the query, by `bm25` | None |
| No | No | All lessons, newest first | None |

When the loop fills the result, it skips a lesson whose `(area, lesson)` pair it already has. It stops at `limit` lessons. The effect is that the area lessons come first and a global match fills the remaining places. The test `area_scope_then_global_fill` shows it: a query for `ownership` in the area `orders` returns `orders::Service` first and `billing` second, and leaves out the unrelated `web` lesson.

Note that a query with an area and no query text never adds lessons from other areas.

## Errors from the store

All methods return `StoreError` ([`crates/ostra-store/src/lib.rs`](../crates/ostra-store/src/lib.rs)).

| Variant | Message text | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Sqlite` | `sqlite: ...` | A SQLite error, for example a constraint failure |
| `Io` | `io: ...` | A file or folder error |
| `Json` | `json: ...` | A value did not serialize or parse |
| `NotFound` | `not found: ...` | The row does not exist. Methods that update a row by ID return it |
| `Invalid` | The message itself | A rule failed: a bad timestamp, a duplicate workspace root, or a value that is not a string enum |
| `Locked` | `the registry has no encryption key, so credentials cannot be read or saved` | A secret call ran before the registry had a sealer |

The [server limits reference](reference-server-limits.md) lists the same constants next to the other server limits.
