sections.title: Code navigation: index, graph, LSP, and code tools
sections.summary: How the `ostra-code` crate tokenizes 22 languages, keeps an incremental per-project index, builds the dependency graph, resolves usages, runs language servers, and serves the Files view, the editor, and the agent code tools.
sections.body:
Ostra must find definitions, usages, imports, and dependencies in a project. It must do this for the Files view, for the editor, and for agents. A build or a language server is not a good base for this work. A build is slow and fails on broken code. A language server needs a separate install for each language and is slow to start. The `ostra-code` crate solves this with a tokenizer and an index that need no build and no install. A project can add its own program or language servers on top.

This page covers these parts:

- The tokenizer and the language table.
- The outline pass and import resolution.
- The incremental index.
- The dependency graph and its caps.
- Usage resolution.
- The provider chain and the `code_provider` program.
- Language servers, with their idle and retry rules.
- The code tools that agents call.
- Editor hints over the WebSocket.
- The file watcher that triggers a reindex.

The route table is on [Server API](server-api.md). The file list that the index reads is on [Project files, git, and workspace search](project-files-and-git.md). The generic tool rules are on [Native tools and their limits](tools.md).

## How a request reaches an answer

Three kinds of caller use the same index. The Files view calls REST routes. The editor sends hint messages over the WebSocket. Agents call code tools. The built-in index is the base layer for all three. A `code_provider` program and language servers sit above it for some requests.

### Flow of the callers and the providers

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  FV["Files view REST routes"] -->|"Code::ask"| CH["Provider chain"]
  ED["Editor WebSocket hints"] -->|"Code::complete, signature, navigate"| HR["Hint rig"]
  AG["Agent code tools"] -->|"CodeTools::call"| IX["Built-in index"]
  CH --> CP["code_provider program"]
  CH --> LS["Language servers"]
  CH --> IX
  HR --> LS
  HR --> IX
  FV -->|"Code::graph"| IX
  WT["File watcher"] -->|"Code::touch"| IX
  WT -->|"Code::touch"| LS
  WR["Write tools and saves"] -->|"Code::touch"| IX
```

### Which route uses which layer

| Request | Layers, in order | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET .../code/file` | `code_provider`, language servers, built-in index | Display tokens, outline, and imports of one file. |
| `GET .../code/usages` | `code_provider`, language servers, built-in index | With `uri`, only the language server that named the outside file answers. |
| `GET .../code/deps` | `code_provider`, built-in index | Language servers answer `None` for dependencies. |
| `GET .../code/symbols` | `code_provider`, language servers, built-in index | Definitions that match a name. |
| `GET .../code/graph` | Built-in index only | Four views of the dependency graph. |
| `POST .../code/reindex` | Built-in index only | Drops the index and builds it again. |
| `GET .../code/external` | One language server | Reads a file outside the project that the server named. |
| `code_complete` message | Language servers, then built-in index | Completions at the cursor. |
| `code_signature` message | Language servers only | The built-in index has no signature help. |
| `code_navigate` message | Built-in index, then language servers | Supertypes or implementations. |
| Agent code tools | Built-in index only | Eight tools, each answers as text. |

All REST paths start with `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/`. The server reads the project settings for each request. A saved change to `code_provider` or `language_servers` therefore applies to the next request. The approval hash of folder commands covers these settings. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) for the approval flow.

## Tokenizer and language table

The tokenizer in `crates/ostra-code/src/lex.rs` turns source text into tokens for every language of the table in `crates/ostra-code/src/lang.rs`. It never fails. Text that it does not understand is skipped. The table is data, not code, so one entry covers display, outline, usages, and imports for a language.

Each `Lang` entry holds these fields:

- `id`, such as `rust`.
- `family`, which selects the definition and import rules.
- Line comment markers, one optional block comment pair, and a flag for nested block comments.
- String quote bytes, and flags for multiline strings and triple-quoted strings.
- Keywords, builtin type names, and builtin constants.
- Extra identifier bytes, a flag for `@name` attributes, and the definition keywords with the kind of the name after them.

### Languages and families

The table has 22 languages. The constant `ALL` lists them. Sixteen languages have a family with definition and import rules. These 16 ids are the constant `NAV_LANGUAGES` in `crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs`. A language server entry can name only these ids. Six languages are display-only.

| Family | Languages | Indexed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Rust` | `rust` | Yes |
| `Js` | `typescript`, `javascript` | Yes |
| `Python` | `python` | Yes |
| `Go` | `go` | Yes |
| `Jvm` | `java`, `kotlin`, `scala`, `csharp`, `swift`, `php` | Yes |
| `C` | `c`, `cpp` | Yes |
| `Ruby` | `ruby` | Yes |
| `Lua` | `lua` | Yes |
| `Shell` | `shell` | Yes |
| `Data` | `sql`, `toml`, `yaml`, `json`, `css`, `html` | No |

A `Data` file gets colors only. It has no definitions and no imports. `Lang::indexed` returns false for it, so the index skips it.

Some entries copy the fields of another entry with Rust struct update syntax (`..BASE`) and then set their own fields. These entries do so:

- `JAVASCRIPT` uses `..TYPESCRIPT` and sets an empty `types` list.
- `KOTLIN`, `SCALA`, `CSHARP`, `SWIFT`, and `PHP` use `..JAVA`.
- `CPP` uses `..C`.
- `YAML` and `JSON` use `..TOML`.
- `HTML` uses `..CSS`.

The other entries are full definitions: `RUST`, `TYPESCRIPT`, `PYTHON`, `GO`, `JAVA`, `C`, `RUBY`, `LUA`, `SHELL`, `SQL`, `TOML`, and `CSS`. The `TOML` entry is a full definition, and `YAML` and `JSON` build on it.

`lang::for_path` picks the language of a project-relative path:

- `Makefile` and `Dockerfile` have no language.
- `Gemfile` and `Rakefile` are `ruby`.
- `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, and `.profile` are `shell`.
- Other names use the lowercase extension. For example, `tsx`, `mts`, and `cts` are `typescript`. `h` is `c`. `m` and `mm` are `cpp`. `vue`, `svelte`, `svg`, and `xml` are `html`.
- An unknown extension has no language, and the file shows as plain text.

### Token shape

A token has a kind, a byte range, a 1-based line, a 0-based UTF-16 column, and a UTF-16 length. The kinds are `Ident`, `Keyword`, `Type`, `Constant`, `Str`, `Num`, `Comment`, `Attr`, `Macro`, `Lifetime`, and `Punct`. The browser counts columns in UTF-16 units, so the lexer converts byte offsets to UTF-16. A 4-byte UTF-8 character counts as 2 units.

A comment or string that spans lines comes out as one token for each line. The `cont` flag marks the later lines. Because of this rule, a token never spans lines, and the browser can color each line alone.

Family rules handle special forms:

- Rust: attributes `#[...]` and `#![...]`, lifetimes, raw strings `r#"..."#`, byte strings, and macro names with their `!`.
- C and C++: preprocessor lines, and `<...>` after `#include` or `#import`.
- Python: string prefixes of up to 2 letters from `r`, `b`, `f`, and `u`.
- Ruby: symbols such as `:name`, and `@` and `$` variables.
- Shell: `$name` and `${name}`. A `#` starts a comment only at the start of a word.
- Lua: `[[...]]` strings.
- PHP: `#[` starts an attribute, not a comment.
- C#: `@"..."` verbatim strings.

### Display classes

`render` in `crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs` makes the `CodeFile` answer. It maps tokens to 11 display classes. The constant `CLASSES` fixes their order: `Keyword`, `Type`, `Function`, `Name`, `Constant`, `Macro`, `Attribute`, `String`, `Number`, `Comment`, and `Operator`. The `tokens` field is a flat list of 4 numbers for each token: line, column, length, and the index into `classes`. Punctuation and plain words of data files get no class and no entry.

### What happens when

- A file is larger than `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1,048,576 bytes), so the native provider returns it without tokens and with a warning. The warning says that the file shows without color.
- A file has an unknown language, so `render` returns an empty answer with `language` set to null.
- A string is not closed, so it ends at the end of the line. A backtick string and a block comment end at the end of the file.

## Outline pass and import extraction

The outline pass in `crates/ostra-code/src/outline.rs` reads the tokens of one file once. It produces display classes, definitions, raw import specs, and supertype links. It matches names by text. It has no type information, and this limit is the reason why usages are a best guess for some names.

Definitions come from three sources:

1. Keyword rules, such as `fn`, `class`, and `def`, from the `defs` field of the language entry.
2. Member rules inside class bodies. Modifiers in `JVM_MODIFIERS` can stand between the start of a member and its name.
3. Family forms: C function bodies, Go receivers and `const (`, `var (`, `type (` blocks, and Python indentation.

A member name cannot follow some keywords. The constant `NOT_BEFORE_MEMBER` lists 16: `new`, `return`, `await`, `throw`, `typeof`, `case`, `yield`, `else`, `in`, `of`, `is`, `as`, `extends`, `implements`, `delete`, and `void`. The word `void` is a return type in every language except JavaScript, where it is an operator. This rule keeps expressions such as `return foo(` from becoming a method named `foo`.

A `Symbol` has a name, a kind, a line, a column, a length, an optional end line, an optional `container`, and an optional `via`. The `container` is the enclosing type, module, or impl. The `via` is the trait or interface of the enclosing impl. For example, `fmt` in `impl Display for Point` has `via` set to `Display`. The 11 symbol kinds are `Function`, `Method`, `Class`, `Enum`, `Interface`, `Type`, `Module`, `Constant`, `Variable`, `Field`, and `Macro`.

A `Super` link records that a subtype names a supertype: `class A extends B`, `impl B for A`, or `trait A: B`. The usage and implementation features read these links.

A `RawImport` has a spec, a line, and a style. The styles are `Use` (a path of names), `Mod` (Rust `mod name;`), `Module` (a string spec, as in JS, Go, and Lua), `Include` (C, with a flag for quotes), and `Require` (with a flag for relative). It can also hold alternative specs to try first (`from a import b` tries `a.b`), a `star` flag for `export * from`, and the names that a JS import brings in.

## Import resolution

A `Resolver` in `crates/ostra-code/src/resolve.rs` turns each raw import into a project file or folder. It reads only the project file list and the manifests. It does not read source files, so building it costs little next to a full index.

The resolver reads these manifests for names. A `Cargo.toml` gives the crate name, and `-` becomes `_`. A `package.json` gives the package name and its entry points from `exports`, `types`, `module`, or `main`. A `package.json` under `node_modules` is skipped. A `go.mod` gives the module path.

The constant `MANIFESTS` lists 13 names that mark a package folder: `Cargo.toml`, `package.json`, `go.mod`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle`, `build.gradle.kts`, `composer.json`, `Gemfile`, `Package.swift`, and `mix.exs`. A name that ends with `.csproj`, `.gemspec`, or `.rockspec` also marks one. The nearest folder with a manifest is the package unit of a file. The top folder is the unit when no manifest exists.

Each family resolves in its own way:

- **Rust:** `crate::`, `self::`, `super::`, other workspace crates by name, and child modules. A `mod name;` finds `name.rs` or `name/mod.rs`.
- **JS and TS:** relative specs, `@/` and `~/` aliases, workspace packages, and absolute specs. The resolver tries the extensions in `JS_EXTS` (11 values: `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.mts`, `.cts`, `.vue`, `.svelte`) and `index` files. A `.js` spec also tries `.ts` and `.tsx`.
- **Python:** relative dots, then each ancestor folder and `src`. It tries `.py`, `.pyi`, and `__init__.py`, then a folder.
- **Go:** the `go.mod` module path as a prefix. The target is a folder, because a Go import names a package.
- **JVM family:** dotted names matched by file suffix, with the extension of the language. A `.*` import resolves to a folder.
- **C and C++:** quoted includes try the file folder, the root, `include`, and `src`. Then the resolver matches by file suffix.
- **Ruby, Lua, and Shell:** `lib` or root paths, `init.lua`, and files next to the importer.

A spec that matches no project file has no target. The outline tool prints `external` for it.

### What happens when

- Two files match a suffix, so the resolver picks the one that shares the most path segments with the importing file. A shorter path wins a tie.
- A spec leaves the project with `..`, so `join` returns nothing and the import has no target.
- A manifest is not valid, so the resolver skips it. The package then falls back to the next folder above.

## Incremental code index

The index in `crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs` keeps three things for each file: the names that the file mentions, its definitions, and its imports. It never keeps the text. A usages query reads again only the files that mention the name. This design keeps the index small and always current with the disk.

One `Indexes` value holds one slot for each project. A slot is created on first use. The key is the pair of workspace ID and project key. `Indexes::with` brings the index up to date and then runs a closure on it. It blocks, and the first call on a project reads every source file. The server runs it in `spawn_blocking`.

### How sync decides what to read

On each `with` call, the slot does these steps:

1. Reset the index when the project root changed.
2. Take the set of dirty paths that `touch` collected. A write never waits on an index build, because the dirty set has its own lock.
3. Build a new resolver when the file list is a new `Arc`.
4. Run a full sync when the file list changed or the last full sync is older than `FULL_SYNC` (30 seconds). A full sync checks every listed path and drops the paths that left the list.
5. Otherwise, sync only the dirty paths, when the set is not empty.

A sync compares a stamp of file size and modification time. It analyzes only the files with a changed stamp. It uses up to 8 worker threads, and fewer when the machine reports fewer cores or when the job list is shorter. The full sync every 30 seconds catches edits that no one reported, such as a branch checkout.

### What the index skips

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| The language is not indexed (`Data` family) or unknown | The file is not in the index. |
| The file is larger than `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1 MiB) | The file is removed from the index. |
| The first 8,000 bytes hold a NUL byte | The file is treated as binary and skipped. |
| The file is larger than 50,000 bytes and has more than 1,000 bytes for each line on average | The file is treated as minified and skipped. |
| The sum of file sizes exceeds `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` (256 MiB) | The file is skipped and `truncated` is set. |

The native provider adds the warning from `TRUNCATED` to usage and symbol answers when `truncated` is set. The warning text says that the project is larger than the size Ostra indexes, so some files are not searched. The file list also leaves out ignored files. The error text of the graph route says so.

### Name interning and links

The index interns each name as a number. A posting list maps a name to the sorted files that mention it. A second map gives the definitions of a name. The `link` step resolves each import to a target and builds the importer lists, including folder importers for Go. Any insert, any removal, or a new resolver clears the `linked` flag. The next query then links again and drops the cached graph.

### Queries

- **Usages by name** (`usages`): finds definitions from the definition map and references from the posting list. It reads at most `MAX_SCAN_FILES` (4,000) files. It orders files so that the asked file comes first, then its folder, then the rest by path. It stops at the limit and sets `truncated`.
- **Dependencies** (`deps`): returns the imports of a file with targets, and the importers of the file. It returns at most `MAX_IMPORTERS` (2,000) importers. A Go folder import counts as an importer of every file in the folder.
- **Symbols** (`symbols`): scores each definition name against the query, ignoring case. The score is 110 for an exact match, 100 for a match that differs only in case, 80 for a prefix, 60 for a substring, and 40 for initials. For initials, the query must have 2 or more letters. For example, `pn` matches `parse_name` and `ParseName`. Ties sort by shorter name, then by name.

### Reindex

`POST .../code/reindex` clears the cached file list, drops the index, and builds it again. It returns `indexed_files`, `millis`, and `truncated`. Use it when the index looks wrong. It is not needed for normal edits, because the watcher and the 30-second check keep the index current.

### What happens when

- A write tool saves a file, so `Code::touch` marks the path dirty. The next query re-reads only that file.
- A file is deleted, so the sync finds it missing from the list or the disk and removes it.
- Two queries arrive for one project, so they wait for each other on the slot lock. They never see a half-built index.
- The server forgets a project (`Indexes::forget`), so the next query builds a fresh index.

## Dependency graph and its caps

The graph in `crates/ostra-code/src/graph.rs` derives from the index without reading files. It builds on the first graph query after a link. The next link drops it. Callers and callees read again only the files that they report on.

### Edges and tiers

A file-to-file edge comes from two sources. Import edges come from the resolver. Reference edges come from the names that a file mentions. The resolver picks the definition that a mention most likely means. It searches in tiers, nearest first:

| Tier | Where the definition is |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | In a file that the mentioning file imports, or in an imported folder. |
| 1 | In the same folder. |
| 2 | In the same package unit. |
| 3 | In a package that the package of the mentioning file imports. |

The highest tier that a file can see depends on the family. `Js` and `Python` see only tier 0. `Go` sees tiers 0 and 1. Other families see all 4 tiers. A file can see a farther definition when a nearby file re-exports it up to 2 files deep, or when an import spells the name. The reason: JS, Python, and Go need an explicit import or a shared package for a bare name.

These rules limit false links:

- A name with only one character is not linked.
- A mention links only to definitions of the same family. Module-kind definitions are skipped, because the import that spells the module already links the file.
- A non-test file does not link to a definition in a test file. A test file can link to both. The function `is_test` detects test folders such as `test`, `tests`, `__tests__`, `spec`, `specs`, `testdata`, and `fixtures`, and names such as `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, `test_*`, `*_test.go`, `*_test.py`, `*_test.rs`, `*_spec.rb`, `*Test.java`, and `*Tests.cs`.
- A name that is defined in more than `MAX_DEF_FILES` (3) files links none of them, unless the mentioning file imports a defining file directly. This rule stops names such as `new` or `main` from linking everything to everything.
- A mention after `.` links only to a member whose type the file names, or to a top-level definition of an imported module.

An edge weighs `2 * min(names, 8) + 1` when the file also has an import. Neighbor lists sort by weight, strongest first.

### Hub files and walks

An index module gathers and re-exports a folder. The stems `lib`, `main`, `mod`, `index`, and `__init__` mark a hub file. A file with `export * from` is also a hub. A transitive walk follows an edge when the edge has names, or when it is a real import that does not point into a hub. A Rust `mod` declaration is containment, not use, so a walk does not follow it. Without this rule, every walk passes through `lib.rs` and reaches the whole crate.

### Caps

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_DEF_FILES` | 3 | A name defined in more files links none of them, unless the importer names the file. |
| `MAX_LINK_NAMES` | 8 | Names listed for each step of a walk or chain. |
| `MAX_REACH` | 5,000 | Files that a transitive walk visits before it stops and sets `truncated`. |
| `MAX_CALLER_REFS` | 5,000 | References that a callers query reads. |
| `MAX_BRIDGE_DEGREE` | 200 | A file with more links is not a stepping stone for the related-files list. |
| `MAX_VIEW_FILES` | 150 | Files in a package view. |
| `MAX_VIEW_NEIGHBORS` | 80 | Files in a file view. A symbol view uses 80 for users and 40 for what the symbol uses. |
| `MAX_VIEW_CALLEES` | 200 | Callees that a symbol view reads for each definition. |
| `MAX_MEMBERS` | 40 | Members that a type node lists. |
| `MAX_FILE_DEFS` | 30 | Top-level definitions that a node lists from its file. |
| `MAX_VIEW_EDGES` | 300 | Links that a symbol view draws. Implementation links stay first, then the heaviest references. |

The constants `NONE` (`u32::MAX`) and `TOP` (`u32::MAX`) are internal sentinels. `NONE` marks an unvisited node in the cycle search. `TOP` stands for the top level of a file in a symbol view.

### Graph queries

- **Neighbors:** what a file uses and what uses it, strongest link first. A related-files list adds files that share neighbors. A second-step file scores a quarter of the smaller link weight.
- **Reach:** files within a number of hops, nearest first, in the direction `Dependents` or `Dependencies`.
- **Units:** the package list with file counts, test counts, and the links between packages. A cycle search over packages uses a strongly connected components algorithm (iterative Tarjan).
- **Cycles:** files that import each other in a loop. Only real imports count. Name references, `mod` declarations, and imports of hub files do not count.
- **Hubs:** the files that the most other files depend on.
- **Callers:** the definitions that mention a symbol, with their lines. With a defining file, only mentions that can mean that definition count.
- **Callees:** the definitions that the body of one symbol names.
- **Symbol impact:** the definitions that use a symbol, then the definitions that use those, for up to `depth` hops. It follows names, so a file that uses something else from the same file is left out.
- **Implementations:** what a type or method implements and what implements it, from the `Super` links. Go has no declared link, so Ostra matches method sets.

### Graph views for the Files view

`GET .../code/graph` takes `package`, `path`, `symbol`, `line`, and `depth`. It returns a `CodeGraph` with one of four views:

| View | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `Packages` | Every package and the links between them. |
| `Package` | One package's files, and the packages they use. |
| `File` | One file and the files within `depth` hops. |
| `Symbol` | One definition, what references it to the left, and what it calls or names to the right. |

The server clamps `depth` to 1 through `MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH` (3). Each node has a column. A node sits left of what it uses. Nodes that use each other in a loop share a column. Sinks are in column 0 and users take negative columns. The answer has `truncated` set when nodes were left out. The route returns 404 when the package, file, or symbol is not in the index. The web layout constants are on [Reference: web console and design constants](reference-web-limits.md).

## Usage resolution

A name search finds every mention of a name, including mentions of other definitions with the same name. `usages_at` in `crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs` narrows the result to one definition. A request that carries a path and a line uses it. A request without a line uses the name-only search.

### Steps of `usages_at`

1. Find the token on the asked line whose text equals the symbol. When the request has a column, pick the nearest token.
2. If the token is a definition, that definition is the target. Otherwise, work out what the mention means (`meaning`).
3. If the meaning is empty and not certain, fall back to the name-only list.
4. Add the methods that the target implements in supertypes, up to `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH` (8) hops. A call through an interface method can reach the target.
5. Read the files that mention the name. Keep a mention when it is certain to mean a target. For an uncertain mention, keep it when the name means nothing else in the language, or when the file can name the type that holds the target.

The rule in step 5 trades recall for precision. The guess counts only when it is safe.

### How the receiver type is found

A member after `.`, `->`, or `::` resolves through the type of its receiver. The scan reads declarations from the tokens of the file: `Repo repo`, `repo: Repo`, `repo = new Repo()`, `Repo::new()`, and Go `repo *Repo`. These constants tune the scan:

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH` | 8 | Supertype hops that a member lookup follows. |
| `WRAPPERS` | 8 names | `Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `Option`, `Result`, `Optional`, `Readonly`, `Promise`. Their members are the members of their first type argument. |
| `PASSTHROUGH` | 14 names | Calls that return the wrapped value, such as `unwrap`, `expect`, `get`, `orElseThrow`, `clone`, and `borrow_mut`. |
| `FIRST_ARG` | 3 names | `verify`, `spy`, and `requireNonNull`. They return their first argument, as in `verify(repo).save(x)`. |
| `MAX_CHAIN` | 6 | Calls that a receiver chain follows back, as in `a.b().c().d()`. |

A bare name inside a class body can mean a member of that class in the `Jvm` and `C` families. The scan treats those names as implicit `this` members.

### What happens when

- The tokens do not tell the receiver type, so the lookup falls back to the graph guess.
- Two unrelated classes both have a field `name`, so `a.name` and `b.name` stay apart when the receivers have declared types.
- The asked file is not in the index, or the text at the position does not match, so the answer is the name-only list.

## Provider chain and the code_provider program

The Files view asks a chain of providers and takes the first answer. `Code::ask` in `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs` builds the chain for each request in this order:

1. The project's `code_provider` program, when the project sets one.
2. One `LspProvider` for each entry of `language_servers`, in the order of the settings.
3. The built-in `NativeProvider`.

A provider returns `Ok(Some(answer))`, `Ok(None)`, or `Err`. `None` hands the request to the next provider. An error also goes to the next provider, and the final answer carries a warning such as: the code provider failed, so the built-in index answered. The answer names the provider that gave it. The name is `native` for the built-in index and the program name for the others. If no provider answers, the route returns status 400 with a message.

The server checks each request before it builds the chain:

- A path must be inside the project root and must name a file.
- A symbol must be 1 to `MAX_SYMBOL_LEN` (256) bytes, with no whitespace and no control characters. A query for symbols is cut to 256 characters.
- The usages limit defaults to `DEFAULT_USAGES` (500) and clamps to 1 through `MAX_USAGES` (2,000).
- The symbols limit defaults to `DEFAULT_SYMBOLS` (50) and clamps to 1 through `MAX_SYMBOLS` (200).

### The `code_provider` program

A project can replace the answers of the index with its own program. The setting is `[projects.code_provider]` in `workspace.toml`. It has `command` (program and arguments) and `timeout_secs`. The default for `timeout_secs` is 10. The valid range is 1 through `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` (120). Settings validation reports an empty command or a timeout outside the range.

Ostra runs the program once for each request, in the project folder, under the workspace sandbox. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md). It sets `OSTRA_CODE_PROTOCOL` to `PROTOCOL_VERSION` (1). It writes one JSON object and a newline on stdin. The object has an `op` field of `file`, `usages`, `deps`, or `symbols`, plus `version`, `root`, and the fields of the operation. The program writes one JSON value on stdout. An empty answer or `null` hands the request to the next provider.

Ostra checks the answer before it uses it:

- Stdout is at most `MAX_OUTPUT` (64 MiB). Ostra keeps at most `MAX_STDERR` (1 MiB) of stderr for the error message.
- The text must be UTF-8 and must match the shape of the operation.
- A file answer sends tokens in groups of 4 numbers. Each token needs a 1-based line and a class index inside `classes`. The token list has at most `MAX_TOKENS` (16,777,216) numbers.
- A list of symbols, imports, importers, or locations has at most `MAX_ITEMS` (20,000) items.
- Every path is project-relative, with no leading `/`, no `\\`, no NUL, and no `.` or `..` segment. Every line is 1-based.
- Ostra clears the `uri` of each location, because only a language server can name an outside file.

### What happens when

- The program cannot start, exits with an error, or runs past `timeout_secs`, so the next provider answers and the warning names the cause. The child process is killed when the request ends.
- The answer breaks a check, so the next provider answers and the warning quotes the check.
- The program does not read its input, so Ostra ignores the closed pipe.

## Language servers and their idle and retry rules

A project can add language servers. The setting is `[[projects.language_servers]]`. Each entry has `command`, `languages`, `timeout_secs`, and optional `initialization_options`. The `languages` ids come from `NAV_LANGUAGES`. Settings validation requires a program in `command`, at least one language, and a timeout from 1 to 120 seconds. The default timeout is 10 seconds. It also rejects a language that two entries both claim, because each file asks one server.

The `LspPool` in `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/mod.rs` starts a server on the first request for one of its languages. It keeps the server running after each request until `IDLE` passes with no request. Then it stops the server. The pool runs each server under the workspace sandbox, because a server runs the project's build scripts and macros.

### Lifecycle of one server

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Starting: first LspPool.get
  Starting --> Running: initialize succeeds
  Starting --> Failed: start error or INIT_TIMEOUT
  Running --> Dead: process exits or message too large
  Running --> Stopped: idle, evicted, sandbox changed, or forget
  Failed --> Starting: request when RETRY has passed since begun
  Dead --> Starting: request when RETRY has passed since begun
  Stopped --> [*]
```

### Pool rules

| Constant | Value | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `IDLE` | 10 minutes | A server with no request for this long is stopped. |
| `SWEEP` | 60 seconds | A background task checks for idle and dead servers at this interval. The first `get` starts it. |
| `MAX_SERVERS` | 8 | Running servers across all projects. A new server stops the least recently used one. |
| `RETRY` | 30 seconds | The minimum age of a failed or dead entry before the pool replaces it. The age counts from `begun`, the time that the pool created the entry. |
| `INIT_TIMEOUT` | 60 seconds | The `initialize` request can take longer than other requests, because some servers read the project first. |
| `MAX_OPEN` | 32 | Documents that one server keeps open. A new document closes the least recently used one. |
| `MAX_DEFINITIONS` | 50 | Definitions that a name search through `workspace/symbol` keeps. |
| `MAX_EXTERNALS` | 20,000 | Outside URIs that the pool remembers across projects. The oldest is forgotten first. |

The pool keys a server by project and command. `Entry::stale` decides when a request starts a server again. It measures `RETRY` from `begun`, not from the time of the failure or the death. This gives two cases:

- A server that ran longer than 30 seconds before it died is stale at once. The next request replaces it.
- A server that failed to start, or that died within 30 seconds of `begun`, is not started again before 30 seconds have passed since `begun`.

A request waits at most the entry timeout for a starting server. Hints wait `HINT_WAIT` (3 seconds). The start continues in its own task when the caller stops waiting. The caller gets: the server is still starting, ask again in a moment. The next request then finds the server ready.

### What happens when

- A server dies after more than 30 seconds of running, so the next request starts a new server. In the meantime, a request that reaches the dead entry returns the reason with the last stderr line.
- A server dies or fails to start within 30 seconds of `begun`, so requests return the reason until 30 seconds have passed. Then the next request starts a new server. The built-in index answers in the meantime.
- The workspace sandbox settings change, so the next request replaces the running server. A saved change applies without a restart of Ostra.
- Eight servers run and a ninth starts, so the pool stops the least recently used server.
- A file changes on disk, so `LspPool::touch` sends `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles` to each running server of the project. The type is 2 (changed) when the file exists and 3 (deleted) when it does not.
- The server reports columns in an encoding other than UTF-16, so Ostra closes it and reports an error. Ostra needs UTF-16.
- The server is still loading the project, so the answer carries a warning. The warning says that the answer can be incomplete. The server reports this through progress tokens or the `experimental/serverStatus` message.
- A request returns the LSP error `ContentModified` (`CONTENT_MODIFIED`, -32801) or `ServerCancelled` (`SERVER_CANCELLED`, -32802), so Ostra reports that the server is still loading and dropped the request.

### Connection details

The client in `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/rpc.rs` speaks JSON-RPC with `Content-Length` framing. A message larger than `MAX_MESSAGE` (256 MiB) ends the connection. The client keeps the last `STDERR_LINES` (20) lines of stderr, each cut to 300 characters, and adds the last line to a death message. A request whose caller stops waiting sends `$/cancelRequest`. On close, the client sends `shutdown` (3-second limit) and `exit`, waits 2 seconds, and then kills the process.

The client answers a few requests from the server. `workspace/configuration` gets a list of nulls. `workspace/workspaceFolders` gets the project folder. Registration, progress creation, and refresh requests get null. `workspace/applyEdit` gets `applied: false`, because Ostra never edits files for a server. Any other request gets error -32601.

For `java` servers, Ostra adds `extendedClientCapabilities.classFileContentsSupport: true` to the initialization options unless the settings already set it. The server then answers definitions in jars with `jdt://` URIs.

## What a language server answers

Each provider operation maps to LSP requests. Each answer falls back to the next provider when the server lacks the capability.

- **File:** the built-in answer comes first. If it already has a warning, such as a file over 1 MiB, Ostra returns it unchanged. Otherwise Ostra asks for `semanticTokens/full` and `documentSymbol`. Server tokens replace built-in tokens that overlap them. The rest of the built-in tokens stay, so imports and punctuation still have color. A non-empty server outline replaces the built-in outline. The imports always come from the built-in answer.
- **Usages:** with a path and a line, Ostra opens the file, finds the name nearest the column, and asks `textDocument/definition` and `textDocument/references`. Without a line, Ostra asks `workspace/symbol` for exact name matches and uses the first one as the origin. Ostra drops references outside the project, because the uses inside a library crowd out the uses in the project. The file named in the request sorts first. The answer holds at most `limit` items in total.
- **Symbols:** `workspace/symbol`, with the kind and container of each item.
- **Dependencies:** a language server never answers. The built-in index does.

Ostra sends a document to the server with `didOpen`. It hashes the text. When the hash changes, it sends `didChange` with the full text and a new version. Ostra reads project files only as UTF-8 text of at most `MAX_FILE_BYTES`.

### Files outside the project

A server can point at a place outside the project, such as a library source or a class in a jar. Ostra shows such a file read-only. `GET .../code/external?uri=` reads it. The route accepts only a URI that a server of this project answered with after Ostra started. Thus the browser cannot name an arbitrary file. A URI is at most `MAX_URI_LEN` (4,096) bytes.

Only two schemes work. A `file://` URI is read from disk, at most 1 MiB, as UTF-8. A `jdt://` URI is read with the request `java/classFileContents`. Paths under the home folder show as `~/...`. Jar classes show as `<jar> › <class path>`. The route returns 404 when the URI is unknown or when the server is no longer in the project settings. A usages request with `uri`, `line`, and `symbol` asks the same server for the definitions and the project references of a name in the outside file.

## Agent code tools

Agents call eight code tools. They answer from the built-in index in compact text. The list is the constant `CODE_TOOLS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`. Each entry pairs an operation with a native tool name. Over MCP the tool name is `code_` plus the operation.

| Native tool | MCP name | Input | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CodeOutline` | `code_outline` | `path`, `limit` | Language, line count, imports with targets, and definitions with line ranges. |
| `CodeFind` | `code_find` | `query`, `limit` | Definitions that match a name, best match first, with the first line of each. |
| `CodeCallers` | `code_callers` | `symbol`, `path`, `limit` | Definitions that use the symbol, grouped by the enclosing definition, with lines. |
| `CodeCallees` | `code_callees` | `path`, `symbol`, `line`, `limit` | Project definitions that the body of the symbol names. |
| `CodeImplementations` | `code_implementations` | `symbol`, `path`, `line`, `limit` | What the symbol implements and what implements it. |
| `CodeNeighbors` | `code_neighbors` | `path`, `limit` | Files that the file uses and files that use it, plus related files. |
| `CodeImpact` | `code_impact` | `symbol` with `path`, or `paths`, plus `direction`, `depth`, `limit` | Hop-by-hop list of what a change can break, and the files to recheck. |
| `CodeMap` | `code_map` | `prefix` | Packages with links, package cycles, the most depended-on files, and import cycles. |

Every input rejects unknown fields. A path can be project-relative, absolute inside the project, or start with `./`. When an agent works across a workspace, it can start a path with the project folder name. Ostra strips that name when the file exists only without it.

### Limits and defaults

| Constant or default | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_LIMIT` | 40 | Entries that a tool returns when the call has no `limit`. |
| `MAX_LIMIT` | 300 | The largest accepted `limit`. `CodeOutline` uses 300 when the call has no `limit`. |
| `MAX_NAMES` | 12 | Names listed for one link. More show as `+N more`. |
| `MAX_IMPL_GROUPS` | 8 | Definitions that `CodeImplementations` lists when the name has several. |
| `CodeImpact` `depth` | 3 by default, 1 through 10 | Hops to walk. |
| `CodeImpact` `limit` | 100 by default, at most 300 | Entries to return. |
| `CodeMap` hubs and cycles | 15 and 10 | The answer lists at most 15 most depended-on files and 10 import cycles. |
| `CodeNeighbors` related files | 5 | The answer lists at most 5 files that share a neighbor. |

### How the tools choose a definition

- `CodeCallers` without `path` uses the one defining file when the name has exactly one. If several files define the name, it counts mentions by name and adds a note to pass `path`.
- `CodeCallees` needs `path` and `symbol`. `line` picks the nearest definition when the file defines the name more than once. It warns when the end of the body is unknown, and then it reads only the first line.
- `CodeImpact` takes `symbol` or `paths`, never both. With `symbol` the direction must be `dependents`, because the symbol walk follows users. With several defining files and no `path`, it returns an error that lists the files.
- `CodeImplementations` ranks the definitions that have links first and lists the others only when none has a link.

### How a tool call runs

1. The tool runner checks the capability. If the run has no `CodeNav`, it returns the error: code navigation is not available in this run, use Grep, Glob, and Read instead.
2. `CodeTools::call` finds the project whose folder holds the repo root. When projects nest, it picks the innermost one. If no project holds the folder, it returns an error that names the folder.
3. The server reads the file list, starts the file watch with `ensure_watch`, and runs `ostra_code::tools::run` in `spawn_blocking` on the index.
4. The answer is text. An error text is a tool error that the agent can read.

The server binds the app to `CodeTools` after it builds the executors, because executors exist before the app. Before the bind, or after shutdown, a call returns: the Ostra server is shutting down.

### Who gets the tools, and the guide

An agent gets the tools when its `agent.toml` lists the `code` capability. For example, `implementer`, `plan`, and `documentation` have it. The native executor offers the eight native tools. Harness executors call them over the MCP names `code_outline` and the others. The policy engine treats these tools as known tools and allows them unless a permission rule says otherwise. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).

The prompt renderer puts `assets/code-tools.md` at the start of the prompt of each such agent. The placeholders, such as `{{tool_code_map}}`, become the tool name of the executor. See [Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md). The guide ends with this warning: the index matches names, not types. An answer can include a definition that only shares the name, or miss a use through a value whose type the index cannot see. The guide tells the agent to use text search to confirm an answer before it changes code. The reason is the name-based design described above.

## Editor hints over the WebSocket

The file editor asks for completions, signature help, and supertype or implementation jumps at the cursor of unsaved text. The three requests use the WebSocket at `/ws`, because they happen on each key press and a newer request replaces an older one.

| Client message | Server message | Answer type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code_complete` | `code_completion` | `CodeCompletion` |
| `code_signature` | `code_signature_help` | `CodeSignatureHelp`, or null outside a call |
| `code_navigate` | `code_navigation` | `CodeNavigation`, or null when no one knows the name |

Each message carries `id`, `workspace`, `key`, `path`, `text`, `line`, and `col`. `code_complete` and `code_signature` also carry `trigger` (the typed character) and `retrigger`. `code_navigate` carries `target`, which is `supertypes` or `implementations`. The answer repeats `id`, and holds `result` and `error`. A failure sets `error` and leaves `result` null.

### Flow of one completion

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant Socket
  participant Code
  participant Lsp
  participant Index
  Browser->>Socket: code_complete
  Socket->>Code: Code::complete(HintAsk)
  Code->>Code: hint_rig checks the request
  Code->>Lsp: LspProvider::complete(At, HINT_WAIT)
  Lsp-->>Code: Ok(Some) or Ok(None) or Err
  Code->>Index: hint::from_index (no server answered)
  Index-->>Code: CodeCompletion
  Code-->>Socket: result or error
  Socket-->>Browser: code_completion
```

### Checks before an answer

`hint_rig` rejects a request with status 400 in these cases:

- The path leaves the project or names a folder.
- The text is larger than `MAX_FILE_BYTES` (1 MiB).
- The line is 0 or past the last line of the text.
- The `trigger` is not exactly one character.

The server also starts the file watch for the project at this point.

### Rules for each hint

- **Completion:** the first language server that answers for the file wins. A server answers `Ok(None)` for a language it does not own. When a trigger character is not in the `triggerCharacters` of the server, the answer is an empty list. If no server answers, `hint::from_index` returns names that the index defines and that start with the word at the cursor. The index list has at most `MAX_INDEX_COMPLETIONS` (50) items, is marked `incomplete`, so the editor asks again as the word grows, and is empty after a trigger character, because the index does not know members. Server problems show as a warning. A server list over `MAX_COMPLETIONS` (1,000) items is cut and marked incomplete.
- **Signature help:** language servers only. If every server answers `None` and none fails, the result is null. If a server fails and none answers, `error` holds the reasons.
- **Navigation:** the index answers first, because it is fast and holds every parsed language. It reads the supertype and implementation links of the name at the cursor. A name that the file defines means that definition. Another name asks up to `NAVIGATION_GROUPS` (8) definitions across the project. The answer holds at most `MAX_NAVIGATION` (50) locations. Language servers answer only when the index does not hold the file or does not know the name. They use `typeHierarchy/supertypes` or `textDocument/implementation`.

### What happens when

- A newer request of the same kind arrives on the socket, so the task of the older one stops and the older request never gets an answer. The keys are `hint:complete`, `hint:signature`, and `hint:navigate`. The reason: the editor only needs the answer for the latest cursor.
- A language server is still starting, so a hint waits `HINT_WAIT` (3 seconds), then the index answers. The server keeps starting.
- Answers wait in a queue of `HINT_QUEUE` (8) messages for each socket.
- The workspace ID is unknown, so the answer has an `error` and no `result`.

The browser side is on [Web console](web-console.md). The other socket messages are on [Server API](server-api.md).

## File watcher and reindex trigger

Edits made outside Ostra's write tools, such as a shell command, the editor of the user, or a checkout, must reach the index. The periodic check finds them within 30 seconds. The watcher in `crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs` finds them sooner.

### How the watcher works

1. `Code::ensure_watch` starts a watch for a project. It runs at the first graph query, hint, or agent code tool for the project. A watch on an old root is replaced when the root changes.
2. The watcher watches the project root and each folder that holds a listed file. Each watch is non-recursive. Ignored build output therefore adds no watches.
3. A thread named `ostra-code-watch` collects events into a batch. It waits for `QUIET` (250 milliseconds) with no new event, or for `MAX_WAIT` (2 seconds) from the first event, whichever comes first.
4. It drops events for paths that `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` of the root ignores, and for any path with a `.git` segment.
5. A create, a remove, or a rename marks the batch as `structural`. A data change does not. Other event kinds are ignored.
6. When a folder is created or renamed, the watcher adds a watch on it.
7. The batch handler `on_outside_change` runs.

### What the batch handler does

- A structural batch clears the cached file list, so the next query lists the project again.
- Each changed path goes to `Code::touch`. The code index marks the path dirty, and the running language servers get `didChangeWatchedFiles`.
- The server sends `ProjectFsChanged` with `workspace`, `key`, and `paths` on the channel `workspace:<id>`. When a batch holds more than `MAX_PUSHED_PATHS` (200) paths, the `paths` list is empty and the browser reloads the whole listing.

Other events also call `Code::touch`: a write tool of an execution (after it changes a file) and a save by the user (`announce_save`).

### What happens when

- The platform refuses the watch on the root, so `start` returns nothing. The server logs a warning. Outside edits then reach the index within 30 seconds (`FULL_SYNC`).
- The operating system refuses watches for some folders, for example because of a watch limit, so the server logs how many. The periodic check covers those folders.
- The server drops the `ProjectWatch`, so the notify watcher drops, its channel closes, and the thread ends.
- The index is wrong for another reason, so call `POST .../code/reindex`.

The watcher does not read file content. It only reports paths. The index reads a changed file at the next query.

## Summary of named constants

This table lists the constants of this page. The sections above explain each one. See also [Reference: server, code, store, and notify limits](reference-server-limits.md).

| File | Constant | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs` | `MAX_FILE_BYTES` | 1,048,576 bytes |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs` | `CLASSES` | 11 display classes |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs` | `MAX` in `signature` | 300 bytes (`String::len`) |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lib.rs` | `MAX` in `preview` | 240 bytes (`String::len`) |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs` | `MAX_INDEX_BYTES` | 256 MiB |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs` | `MAX_SCAN_FILES` | 4,000 files |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs` | `MAX_IMPORTERS` | 2,000 importers |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/index.rs` | `FULL_SYNC` | 30 seconds |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/hint.rs` | `MAX_INDEX_COMPLETIONS`, `MAX_NAVIGATION`, `NAVIGATION_GROUPS` | 50, 50, 8 |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/mod.rs` | `IDLE`, `SWEEP`, `RETRY`, `INIT_TIMEOUT` | 600, 60, 30, 60 seconds |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/mod.rs` | `MAX_SERVERS`, `MAX_OPEN`, `MAX_DEFINITIONS`, `MAX_EXTERNALS` | 8, 32, 50, 20,000 |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/convert.rs` | `MAX_COMPLETIONS`, `KINDS` | 1,000 items, 25 completion kinds |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/rpc.rs` | `MAX_MESSAGE`, `STDERR_LINES` | 256 MiB, 20 lines |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/lsp/rpc.rs` | `CONTENT_MODIFIED`, `SERVER_CANCELLED` | -32801, -32802 |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/provider.rs` | `MAX_OUTPUT`, `MAX_STDERR`, `MAX_TOKENS`, `MAX_ITEMS` | 64 MiB, 1 MiB, 16,777,216, 20,000 |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/tools.rs` | `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, `MAX_LIMIT`, `MAX_NAMES`, `MAX_IMPL_GROUPS` | 40, 300, 12, 8 |
| `crates/ostra-code/src/usage.rs` | `MAX_SUPER_DEPTH`, `MAX_CHAIN` | 8, 6 |
| `crates/ostra-core/src/code.rs` | `PROTOCOL_VERSION`, `NAV_LANGUAGES`, `NATIVE_PROVIDER` | 1, 16 ids, `native` |
| `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` | `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` | 120 seconds (default timeout 10) |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs` | `DEFAULT_USAGES`, `MAX_USAGES` | 500, 2,000 |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs` | `DEFAULT_SYMBOLS`, `MAX_SYMBOLS`, `MAX_SYMBOL_LEN` | 50, 200, 256 |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/code.rs` | `HINT_WAIT`, `MAX_URI_LEN`, `MAX_GRAPH_DEPTH`, `MAX_PUSHED_PATHS` | 3 seconds, 4,096, 3, 200 |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/code_watch.rs` | `QUIET`, `MAX_WAIT` | 250 milliseconds, 2 seconds |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs` | `HINT_COMPLETE`, `HINT_SIGNATURE`, `HINT_NAVIGATE`, `HINT_QUEUE` | three stream keys, 8 queued answers |
