sections.title: Integrations: MCP servers and web push
sections.summary: How Ostra connects to external MCP servers (stdio and streamable HTTP, OAuth sign-in, tool names, result cap), how agents get those tools, and how Ostra sends encrypted Web Push notifications with VAPID.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra has one MCP client and one push sender

Agents need tools that Ostra does not ship, such as an issue tracker or a database. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets a program list and call such tools. Without a shared client, each executor holds its own connections, its own sign-ins, and its own permission checks. Ostra instead runs one MCP client inside the Ostra server. The client keeps one connection for each MCP server, signs in, discovers tools, and serves the tools to every executor. One policy and one allowlist then cover every executor.

A second problem is that the user is not always at the console when a gate opens. Web Push sends a browser notification to a user who has the console closed. Ostra encrypts each message and signs each request with pure Rust code, without OpenSSL.

This page covers these parts:

- The MCP client crate `ostra-mcp` and its two transports.
- The gateway `McpGateway` in `ostra-server`, which owns connections, sign-in, and the tool lists.
- The naming rules for external tools in `ostra-core`.
- The way native runs and harness runs get the tools, and the policy rules that apply.
- The crate `ostra-notify`: RFC 8291 encryption and VAPID authentication.

The page does not describe the policy engine, the sandbox, or the harness shim in full. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md), [Sandbox](sandbox.md), and [Harness executors](harness-executors.md). The route table is in [Server API](server-api.md). The settings file is in [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

## How the pieces fit together

The `McpGateway` is the only owner of MCP connections. It reads the `mcp_servers` list of the workspace settings, connects to each enabled server, and keeps the connection and the tool list in memory. The type `Connector` wraps the gateway for the executors. When an execution starts, the executor calls `Connector::open` and receives the tools of that execution.

### Flow of an external tool call

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CFG["workspace.toml mcp_servers"] --> GW["McpGateway"]
    GW --> CL["Client in ostra-mcp"]
    CL --> STD["Local server process (stdio)"]
    CL --> HTTP["Remote server (streamable HTTP)"]
    GW --> OPEN["Connector::open"]
    OPEN --> NAT["Native run: ToolEnv mcp"]
    OPEN --> HAR["Harness run: Wrapped::run"]
    HAR --> SHIM["Ostra MCP server /internal/mcp"]
    NAT --> POL["Policy check"]
    SHIM --> POL
    POL --> CALL["ExecMcp::call"]
    CALL --> CL
```

The native executor and the harness runtime both receive the same `Connector`. The server sets it in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` with `with_mcp` for the native executor and `set_mcp` for the harness runtime.

## Configure an MCP server

A workspace lists its MCP servers as `[[mcp_servers]]` tables in `workspace.toml`. Each table is an `McpServerConfig`. A server is local or remote. A local server has a `command`. A remote server has a `url`. A table must have one of the two and not both.

| Field | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | none | The server name. It forms the tool names. |
| `enabled` | `true` | A disabled server is not connected. Its status is `disabled`. |
| `command` | empty | Program and arguments of a local server. Ostra runs it in the workspace root. |
| `env` | empty | Environment variables for a local server. |
| `url` | none | The `http` or `https` URL of a remote server. |
| `headers` | empty | HTTP headers for a remote server. |
| `oauth` | none | OAuth client settings: `client_id`, `client_secret_env`, `scopes`. |
| `disabled_tools` | empty | Tool names (as the server spells them) that Ostra does not offer to agents. |
| `agents` | empty | Agent names that get the tools. An empty list means every agent. |
| `timeout_secs` | `120` | Seconds that one tool call can take. |

The settings validator `mcp::validate` checks the list when the user saves settings. Each problem has a path such as `mcp_servers[2].url`. These rules apply:

- The name has lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, starts with a letter, and has at most 24 characters (`MAX_SERVER_NAME`).
- The name `ostra` is reserved because it is the name of Ostra's own MCP server.
- Two servers cannot have the same name.
- The first item of `command` is not empty.
- The `url` starts with `https://` or `http://`.
- `headers` and `oauth` apply to remote servers only. A local server gets secrets in `env`.
- Each name in `agents` is an agent name.
- `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 600 (`MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS`).

A server name has no `__` because the first `__` of a tool name must split the server from the tool. See the next part.

## Names of external tools

One external tool has three names. The names depend on who reads them. The first `__` in a name separates the server from the tool.

| Name | Example | Who uses it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare name | `github__create_issue` | The Ostra MCP server and the `bare_name` function. |
| Canonical name | `mcp__github__create_issue` | The native loop, the policy, permission rules, and the Activity view. It is the spelling of Claude Code. |
| Harness name | `mcp__ostra__github__create_issue` | A harness. Its CLI adds the prefix `mcp__ostra__` to each tool of the Ostra MCP server. |

`bare_name(server, tool)` makes the bare name with these rules:

1. If the tool name has only ASCII letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, and `server__tool` has at most 52 characters, the bare name is `server__tool`.
2. Otherwise, Ostra replaces each other character with `_`. It cuts the result to the room that is left. Then it appends `_` and an 8-digit hexadecimal FNV-1a hash of the original tool name.

The limit `MAX_BARE_NAME` is 52 because a harness adds the 12 characters of `mcp__ostra__` and providers cap tool names at 64 characters. The hash makes sure that two tools never share a name. For example, `search.pages/v2` and `search_pages_v2` give two different names.

These helper functions in `crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs` decide what a name is:

- `is_gateway_tool(tool)` is true when the name starts with `mcp__` and the rest contains `__`. The name `mcp__github` is not a tool. A permission rule can use it to cover every tool of the server `github`.
- `is_gateway_bare(bare)` is true when the bare name contains `__`. Ostra's own tools never contain `__`.
- `server_of(name)` returns the server of a canonical or bare name.
- A harness-native MCP call arrives as `Other:mcp__...`. It does not count as a gateway tool.

## Connect to a server and discover its tools

The `Client` in `crates/ostra-mcp/src/lib.rs` is one live connection to one MCP server. `Client::connect` takes an `Endpoint` and a timeout. An `Endpoint` is `Stdio` (program, arguments, environment, variables to remove, working directory, and a guard) or `Http` (URL, headers, and an optional token source).

### Sequence of connect, list, and call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Run as Execution
    participant GW as McpGateway
    participant CL as Client
    participant SRV as MCP server
    Run->>GW: Connector::open(spec)
    GW->>CL: Client::connect(endpoint, 30 s)
    CL->>SRV: initialize (protocolVersion 2025-11-25)
    SRV-->>CL: result with protocolVersion and serverInfo
    CL->>SRV: notifications/initialized
    GW->>CL: list_tools(30 s)
    CL->>SRV: tools/list (cursor)
    SRV-->>CL: tools and nextCursor
    GW-->>Run: McpOpened with tools and notes
    Run->>GW: ExecMcp::call(tool, input)
    GW->>CL: call_tool(name, arguments, timeout_secs)
    CL->>SRV: tools/call
    SRV-->>CL: content and isError
    CL-->>Run: text, capped at MAX_RESULT
```

### Protocol versions

The client sends `protocolVersion` `2025-11-25` (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`) in `initialize`. It sends `capabilities` as an empty object and `clientInfo` with the name `ostra`. The server answers with the version that it wants. The client accepts a version in `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`: `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. If the answer has no version, the client uses `2025-11-25`. If the version is not in the list, `connect` fails with the message "the server speaks MCP {version}, which Ostra does not support".

After the version is accepted, the client sends `notifications/initialized`. The HTTP transport also stores the version and sends it in the header `mcp-protocol-version` on each later request. The client keeps the server name and version from `serverInfo` as `server_info`, for example `fake 2`.

Ostra declares no client capabilities. Thus, it answers only `ping` when a server sends a request. For each other method, it answers with error `-32601` and the text "Ostra does not support {method}". Ostra uses only the tools part of MCP. It does not use resources or prompts.

### Tool discovery

`Client::list_tools` calls `tools/list` and follows `nextCursor`. It stops after 50 pages because each page is one round trip. It reads each tool with these rules:

- A tool without a `name` is skipped.
- The description is `description`. If it is missing, the description is `title`. If both are missing, it is empty.
- The input schema must be a JSON object. Otherwise, the client uses `{"type": "object", "properties": {}}`.
- `read_only` is the value of `annotations.readOnlyHint`. It is `false` when the server does not send it.

When a server sends `notifications/tools/list_changed`, the client sets a flag. `take_tools_changed` reads and clears the flag. The gateway then lists the tools again.

### Connection reuse in the gateway

The gateway keeps one `Conn` for each pair of workspace root and server name. These rules decide when `McpGateway::ready` reuses, lists again, or reconnects:

1. Each `Conn` has a fingerprint. The fingerprint holds `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, `oauth`, and the workspace sandbox settings `mode`, `network`, `allowed_hosts`, `loopback`, and `blocked_ports`. If any of them changes, the gateway makes a new connection. A sandbox change matters because a local server runs inside the sandbox.
2. A lock on the `Conn` makes parallel executions share one connect. Without the lock, each execution starts the server again.
3. If the client is alive and the tool list is not older than 30 seconds (`RELIST_AFTER`), the gateway returns the saved list. A `tools/list_changed` notice also forces a new list.
4. If the list call fails, the gateway reconnects.
5. If the last connect failed less than 20 seconds ago (`RETRY_AFTER`), the gateway returns the saved error. This stops parallel executions from starting a failing server again and again.
6. Otherwise, the gateway connects with a timeout of 30 seconds (`CONNECT_TIMEOUT`) and lists the tools.

The status route can force a reconnect. See [Status and sign-in routes](#status-and-sign-in-routes).

### Approval of the workspace file

Rule A1: no server starts from a workspace file that waits for approval, and it starts from the approved copy. The gateway calls `trust::approved_workspace_file`. If the file waits for approval, or the approved copy has no equal server entry, the connect fails with the text "Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra." The reason is that a local server runs a command from a file that another person or tool can change. The same rule applies to sign-in, because sign-in sends `oauth.client_secret_env` to the endpoints of the server. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

### What happens when a connect fails

- **The server needs a sign-in (HTTP 401, or 403 with `insufficient_scope`).** The client returns `McpError::NeedsAuth`. The status is `needs_auth`. The message is "Sign in to MCP server `{server}` in Settings, MCP servers, or give it a token in a header, because it refuses requests without one."
- **Any other error.** The status is `error`. The message is "MCP server `{server}` is not available: {error}".
- **A server is unreachable when an execution starts.** The execution does not fail. `Connector::open` adds one note for the server. The executor shows each note as a status line in the Activity view, and the run goes on without that server's tools.
- **The server process exits after the execution started.** On the next call, `ExecMcp::call` sees that the client is not alive and calls `ready` once to start the server again.

## The stdio transport

A local server is a child process that speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC on its standard input and output. The code is in `crates/ostra-mcp/src/stdio.rs`.

The gateway builds the command with `ostra_sandbox::host_command`. A local server is the program of the workspace, so it runs under the agent sandbox. The working directory is the workspace root. The sandbox adds its own variables. The gateway removes every credential variable from the environment of the child (see [Secrets in headers and env values](#secrets-in-headers-and-env-values)). The `guard` field of `Endpoint::Stdio` holds what the sandbox leaves running. Ostra drops the guard when the server ends.

The transport works in this way:

1. It starts the child with piped standard streams and `kill_on_drop`. It also puts the child in a process tree (`ostra_core::proctree`), because servers that start with `npx` or `uvx` run in grandchildren.
2. A reader task reads each line of standard output and parses it as JSON. A line that is not JSON is skipped and logged at debug level (the first 200 characters). Servers that log to standard output break the protocol, and the skip keeps the connection alive.
3. A line can hold one message or an array of messages. A response goes to the waiting request by its `id`. Other messages go to `on_server_message`, which answers requests and notes `tools/list_changed`.
4. A request stores a one-shot channel under its `id` and writes the message. The write lock on standard input makes writes one at a time.
5. A second task reads standard error and keeps the last 4096 bytes (`STDERR_TAIL`).

### What happens when a stdio server exits

When standard output closes, the reader sets `alive` to false and drops every waiting request. Each waiting request then fails with `McpError::Closed`. The transport waits up to 500 ms for standard error to end. Then it reports the last 5 lines of standard error joined with ` / `, as in "the server exited: {lines}". If standard error is empty, the text is "the server exited".

When the `Stdio` value drops, it terminates the whole process tree. On Windows, dropping the tree closes its job object, and that kills the processes.

## The streamable HTTP transport

A remote server is a URL. Each JSON-RPC message is one HTTP `POST`. The code is in `crates/ostra-mcp/src/http.rs`.

### Request

Each request has these headers:

- The headers from the settings, after Ostra expands them.
- `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` and `Content-Type: application/json`.
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` when a token source holds a token.
- `mcp-session-id` (`SESSION_HEADER`) after the server has sent one. Ostra stores the value from any successful response.
- `mcp-protocol-version` (`VERSION_HEADER`) after `initialize` succeeded.

The client sends the user agent `ostra/<version>` and has a connect timeout of 15 seconds.

### Response

The server answers with JSON or with a Server-Sent Events stream. The client checks the `Content-Type` header. For JSON, the body is one message or an array. The client picks the response with the same `id`. It sends every other message to `on_server_message`, and it sends the reply for a server request with another `POST`. For a stream, the client reads each event, ignores empty and invalid data, and returns when it finds the response with the right `id`. If the stream ends first, the request fails with `McpError::Closed` and the text "the event stream ended before the response".

### What happens when the HTTP status is not 2xx

- **401, or 403 with `insufficient_scope` in `WWW-Authenticate`.** If a token source exists, the client asks it for a fresh token with `refused` and sends the request again, one time. If that fails, the client returns `McpError::NeedsAuth` with the `WWW-Authenticate` header. The gateway later reads the header for sign-in.
- **403 without `insufficient_scope`.** This is a plain refusal and not a sign-in request. The client returns a transport error: "the server refused the request (403): {first 300 characters of the body}".
- **404 after the server gave a session id.** The server ended the session. The client sets `alive` to false and returns `McpError::Closed`.
- **Other statuses.** The client returns "the server answered {status}: {body snippet}". The snippet has at most 300 characters, or "no body".
- **A redirect.** The client follows a redirect only inside the origin of the first request (`same_origin_redirects`). More than 5 redirects is an error. The reason is that a header with a secret (an API key, a bearer token, or a client secret in a form) must never reach another host and must never drop from https to http.

## Call a tool and read the result

`Client::call_tool` sends `tools/call` with the tool name and the arguments. If the arguments are not a JSON object, it sends `{}`. The call has the timeout `timeout_secs` of the server and a cancellation token of the execution.

The method `rpc` runs each request with the timeout and the token:

- On a timeout, the call fails with `McpError::Timeout` and the text "no answer after {n} s".
- On a cancel, the call fails with `McpError::Cancelled`.
- In both cases, the client forgets the request id (`abandon`). It also sends `notifications/cancelled` with the `requestId` and the reason, so the server can stop the work. It does not send the notice for `initialize`.
- An error object in the response becomes `McpError::Rpc` with the code (`-32603` if missing) and the message. The text is "{message} (code {code})".

### Convert the result to text

A tool result is text. `content::result_text` joins the parts of `content` with a newline. These rules apply to each part:

| Part type | Text that Ostra uses |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | The text. |
| `image` or `audio` | A note such as `[image image/png, 3 bytes, not shown because tool results are text]`. |
| `resource` with text | The text. |
| `resource` without text | `[binary resource <uri>]`. |
| `resource_link` | `[resource <uri> <name>]`, or `[resource <uri>]` without a name. |
| Other types | The JSON of the part. |

If every part is empty and the result has `structuredContent`, Ostra uses the pretty-printed JSON of `structuredContent`. If `isError` is true, the call returns an error with the text. If the text is empty, the error is "The tool reported an error without a message."

The text has a cap of 102400 bytes (`MAX_RESULT`, which is 100 KB). Ostra cuts at a character boundary and appends `... ({n} more bytes cut)`. The cap keeps one large result from filling the context of the model.

### Errors in the execution

`ExecMcp::call` finds the tool by its canonical name. If the name is unknown, it returns "Unknown tool `{tool}`." It maps errors to these texts:

- `NeedsAuth`: the sign-in text of the part "What happens when a connect fails".
- Other errors: "MCP server `{server}` failed: {error}".
- A result that the server marks as `isError`: the text of the result, as a tool error.

## OAuth sign-in for remote servers

A remote server can refuse a request and ask for a sign-in. Ostra then runs the OAuth 2.1 flow of the MCP authorization specification. The code is in `crates/ostra-mcp/src/oauth.rs` (the protocol steps) and `crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs` (state, storage, and routes). The flow uses these standards: protected resource metadata (RFC 9728), authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) with OpenID discovery, dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), PKCE with S256, and the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707).

### Sequence of a sign-in

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Console
    participant API as Ostra API
    participant GW as McpGateway
    participant SRV as MCP server
    participant AS as Authorization server
    UI->>API: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/login
    API->>GW: login(root, name, origin)
    GW->>SRV: GET .well-known/oauth-protected-resource
    GW->>AS: GET .well-known/oauth-authorization-server
    GW->>AS: POST registration endpoint (no saved client)
    GW-->>UI: authorization_url
    UI->>AS: open authorization_url in the browser
    AS-->>UI: redirect with code and state
    UI->>API: GET /mcp/oauth/callback
    API->>GW: callback(state, code)
    GW->>AS: POST token endpoint (code_verifier)
    GW-->>API: server name, tokens saved
    API-->>UI: Signed in page
```

### Discovery

`oauth::discover` finds the authorization server of the MCP server:

1. It reads `resource_metadata` and `scope` from the `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` challenge, if the gateway kept one from the 401 answer.
2. It tries these URLs for the protected resource metadata, in order: the `resource_metadata` URL of the challenge, `{origin}/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource{path}` (when the server URL has a path), and `{origin}/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`. The first document with `authorization_servers` wins.
3. The resource is the `resource` field of that document, or the server URL without a fragment.
4. The issuer is the first entry of `authorization_servers`. If no document exists, the issuer is the origin of the MCP server. This case covers servers from before RFC 9728, which host their own authorization server.
5. It reads the metadata of the issuer from `.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and `.well-known/openid-configuration` (with the issuer path in the places that RFC 8414 and OpenID define).
6. The scopes are, in order: the scope of the challenge, `scopes_supported` of the resource document, and `scopes_supported` of the authorization server.

If the metadata names another issuer, Ostra refuses it. RFC 8414 section 3.3 requires this, because another server could otherwise hand out endpoints for this one. If neither document exists, Ostra guesses the endpoints of the 2025-03-26 specification: `/authorize`, `/token`, and `/register` on the origin. The field `guessed` records the guess. If the resource document exists but the authorization server metadata cannot be read, discovery fails with "could not read the metadata of the authorization server {issuer}".

### Endpoint checks

An OAuth URL that Ostra fetches or opens in the browser must use `https`. Plain `http` is allowed only on a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) or on the origin of the MCP server, which the user chose. Ostra checks the resource metadata URL, the issuer, the authorization endpoint, the token endpoint, and the registration endpoint. It checks the authorization endpoint again when it builds the link. The reason is that a hostile server can put a `javascript:` URL in its metadata, and the browser runs it on the origin of Ostra. The text of the refusal says that the sign-in link carries codes and secrets.

### The OAuth client

Ostra needs a client id. It takes one in this order:

1. `oauth.client_id` from the settings. A client secret comes from the environment variable that `oauth.client_secret_env` names. Ostra refuses a variable that holds a provider key or a bridge token, and it refuses an unset variable.
2. The client that Ostra saved from an earlier sign-in. It uses the saved client only if the URL, the redirect URI, and the issuer all match.
3. Dynamic registration (`oauth::register`). Ostra registers a public client with `client_name` `Ostra`, the grant types `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`, the response type `code`, and `token_endpoint_auth_method` `none`.

If the authorization server has no registration endpoint, the error tells the user to set `oauth.client_id`. If the metadata was guessed and registration fails, the message says that the server asks for a sign-in but publishes no OAuth metadata. It tells the user to use a token in a header, such as `Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN_VAR}`.

### Authorization link, PKCE, and state

The redirect URI is the browser origin plus `/mcp/oauth/callback` (`CALLBACK_PATH`). The route takes the origin from the `Origin` header, or from the `Host` header with `http://`. The server guard has already checked both headers.

Ostra makes a PKCE verifier of 32 random bytes in URL-safe base64 (256 bits). The challenge is the base64 of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier, with method `S256`. The `state` value uses the same random generator. The link has these query parameters: `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `resource`, and `scope` (when scopes exist).

The gateway keeps each pending login in memory under its `state`. At each new login, it drops entries older than 600 seconds (`LOGIN_TTL`). A callback removes the entry, so a link works one time.

### Callback and token exchange

The route `GET /mcp/oauth/callback` is outside `/api`. The redirect of the authorization server is a cross-site navigation, so the browser does not send the `SameSite=Strict` cookie. The single-use `state` authenticates the request instead. The route needs no session cookie.

`McpGateway::callback` runs these steps:

1. It removes the pending login for the `state`. If none exists or it is older than 600 seconds, it returns "This sign-in link has expired or was already used. Start the sign-in again from Ostra."
2. It posts the form `grant_type=authorization_code`, `code`, `code_verifier`, `redirect_uri`, and `resource` to the token endpoint.
3. It saves an `OAuthRecord` (URL, discovery, client, redirect URI, tokens) in the registry secret store under the key `mcp_oauth:{root}:{name}`.
4. It resets the connection, so the next use connects with the new token.

The client authentication depends on the metadata. A client with a secret uses HTTP Basic authentication when the server lists only `client_secret_basic`. Otherwise, it sends `client_id` and `client_secret` in the form. A public client sends only `client_id`. The page that the route returns is HTML with the title "Signed in" (status 200) or "Sign-in failed" (status 400). The route escapes the text.

### Tokens and refresh

The type `Stored` is the `TokenSource` of an HTTP server. It reads the record from the registry.

- `token()` returns the access token. If the token expires in 60 seconds or less (`Tokens::expired`), it refreshes the token first.
- `refused(token)` runs when the server rejects a token. If another call already saved a different token, it returns that token. Otherwise, it refreshes.
- A refresh posts `grant_type=refresh_token`, the refresh token, and `resource`. If the server sends no new refresh token, the old one stays valid.
- If a refresh fails, Ostra clears the tokens and saves the record. The server then shows `needs_auth`.
- A lock allows one refresh at a time, because a refresh token can be single-use.

`logout` deletes the saved record and resets the connection.

## Secrets in headers and env values

A header value or an `env` value can be one of three kinds:

- **A `${VAR}` reference.** Ostra reads the variable from the environment of the Ostra server each time it connects. If the variable is not set, the error says to set it and restart the server. An unclosed `${` and a bare `$VAR` stay as written.
- **A literal value.** `is_literal_value` is true for a non-empty value without `${`. When the user saves settings, Ostra stores the literal in its registry, encrypted. The file `workspace.toml` holds `${ostra_secret}` (`SAVED_SECRET`) in its place. The value then never reaches the browser or a file in the folder.
- **The placeholder `${ostra_secret}`.** Ostra reads the saved value with `trust::mcp_secret`. If it cannot, the error says to enter the field again in settings.

Ostra refuses to give some variables to an MCP server. The set from `credential_env_names` has these members:

- The provider variables of `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`.
- The variables of each provider in the machine config (`api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, `base_url_env`).
- The bridge variables of `BRIDGE_ENV`: `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`.
- The `oauth.client_secret_env` name of each MCP server.

A `${VAR}` in `env` or `headers` that names one of these variables fails with an error that asks for a variable of the server's own. The gateway also removes all of these variables from the environment of a local server. The native executor removes the same names from the environment of agent commands (`with_scrub_env`), so an agent command cannot read an OAuth client secret. The reason is that a provider key or an OAuth secret must go only to the party that it belongs to.

## How agents get external tools

`Connector::open(spec)` makes the tool list of one execution. The list is fixed when the execution starts. These steps run:

1. If the execution is a read-only inspection of an ended session (`resume.inspect`), the connector returns no tools.
2. It selects the servers where `mcp::serves(server, agent)` is true: the server is enabled, and `agents` is empty or names the agent.
3. It connects to all selected servers in parallel with `ready`.
4. For each reachable server, it skips each tool in `disabled_tools`. It builds the canonical name and skips a name that it already has.
5. It builds a `ToolDefinition` with the canonical name, the description, and the input schema. If the description is empty, it uses "The `{tool}` tool of MCP server `{server}`."
6. It returns `McpOpened` with the tools and with one note for each unreachable server.

The executor also records `read_only()`, the names of the tools that the server marks with `readOnlyHint`. The policy uses the list.

### Native runs

The native executor calls `open` at the start of the run. It puts the result in `ToolEnvConfig.mcp`. The tool dispatcher in `crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs` sends each name that `is_gateway_tool` accepts to `mcp::run`, which calls `ExecMcp::call`. If the environment has no MCP tools, the result is "Unknown tool `{tool}`." See [Native tools and their limits](tools.md) and [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md).

### Harness runs

A harness is a CLI that Ostra runs under a PTY. The harness cannot call `ExecMcp` directly. It reaches the tools through the Ostra MCP server at `/internal/mcp`, which the `ostra mcp-stdio` shim relays. The wrapper `Wrapped::run` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` calls `open` before it starts the harness, because the harness lists the Ostra tools one time at startup. Thus, a tool that a server adds later is not visible in a harness run. The Ostra MCP server reports `listChanged: false`.

These rules apply to the Ostra MCP server:

- `mcp_tools` returns the Ostra tools (`report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, the code tools, and the management and coordination tools when the agent has them) and then the bare names of the external tools.
- `mcp_call` accepts a bare name that contains `__` as an external tool. It converts the name to the canonical name and runs the policy check.
- A `Deny` decision returns the error "Denied by {layer} `{rule}`: {reason}". An `Ask` decision goes to the user. If the user refuses, the error is "The user denied this call ({reason})."
- After the call, the bridge sends the result to the policy observer and appends its notes to the text.
- The Ostra MCP server speaks the versions `2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The version `2026-07-28` is left out on purpose, because Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` without the fields that it needs and the run gets no Ostra tools. See [Harness executors](harness-executors.md).

### Policy rules for external tools

- **Rule M1:** a tool of a workspace MCP server is allowed unless a permission rule says otherwise. In plan mode, only a tool that the server marks `readOnlyHint` is allowed. Ostra trusts the hint that the server sends.
- **Rule M2:** a workspace tool reaches a harness only through the Ostra MCP server, which checks and logs the call when it runs it. Thus, the hook path passes the call without a second check. Without this rule, the bridge and the hook path both log the call, and an `Ask` can reach the user twice.
- A permission rule `mcp__github` covers every tool of the server `github`, as in Claude Code. A rule `mcp__github__create_issue` covers one tool.

See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) for the other guards and the permission modes.

## Status and sign-in routes

The console shows each server in the settings page with its state and tools. These routes serve the page. The route table is in [Server API](server-api.md).

| Route | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp` | Connects to every server of the workspace in parallel and returns a list of `McpServerStatus`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/refresh` | Forces a new connection and a new tool list for one server. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/login` | Starts a sign-in and returns `authorization_url`. A failure returns status 502 with the text of the error. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/logout` | Deletes the saved tokens and returns the new status. |
| `GET /mcp/oauth/callback` | Ends a sign-in. It needs no cookie. |

An `McpServerStatus` has these fields: `name`, `transport` (`stdio` or `http`), `state`, `message`, `server_info`, `signed_in`, and `tools`. The `state` is `disabled`, `connected`, `needs_auth`, or `error`. The enum `McpConnState` also has `idle`, but the gateway code does not set it. `signed_in` is `Some(true)` when Ostra holds tokens for the URL, `Some(false)` when the server needs a sign-in, and `None` when Ostra never asked for tokens. Each tool in `tools` has `name`, `canonical`, `description`, `enabled` (false when the name is in `disabled_tools`), and `read_only`.

A login for a local server fails with "Sign-in applies to remote servers only: this one runs as a local command." A login for an unknown name fails with "This workspace has no MCP server `{name}`." When the workspace is deleted, `forget` drops all its connections.

## Web Push notifications

Web Push sends a notification to the browser of the user when a session needs a decision or ends. The user can then return to the console. The crate `ostra-notify` implements the protocol with the Rust crates `aes-gcm`, `hkdf`, `p256`, and `sha2`. It does not use OpenSSL. Browsers need HTTPS or `localhost` to use push.

### Flow from event to notification

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant ENG as Engine
    participant SVC as Services::notify
    participant REG as Registry
    participant NTF as Notifier
    participant PS as Push service
    ENG->>SVC: notify(Notice)
    SVC->>REG: list_push_subscriptions()
    SVC->>NTF: send(subscription, Notification)
    NTF->>NTF: encrypt (RFC 8291) and sign (VAPID)
    NTF->>PS: POST endpoint
    PS-->>NTF: status 2xx, 404, or 410
    NTF-->>SVC: Delivered, Gone, or Failed
    SVC->>REG: remove_push_subscription(endpoint) on Gone
```

### Which events send a notification

The engine calls `push_for` for each session event. These events send a `Notice`:

- `GateOpened`. In YOLO mode, the engine sends no notice, except for a `HarnessFailure` gate (the harness needs a login).
- `SessionCompleted` (title "Session complete") and `SessionFailed` (title "Session stopped").
- `PhaseBlocked`.
- `ContainmentSignal`, only when the signal is the one that pauses the session (`PAUSE_AFTER`).

The tag of a notice makes a new notice replace an older one with the same tag. For example, the tag `gate-{session}` is the same for each gate of a session. The notice has the URL `/w/{workspace}/s/{session}`, and a click in the service worker opens it. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) and [Judges, decisions, and YOLO mode](judges-and-yolo.md).

### Subscribe and unsubscribe

1. The console reads the VAPID public key from `GET /api/info` (field `vapid_public_key`).
2. The browser calls `pushManager.subscribe` with that key as `applicationServerKey`.
3. The console sends the subscription to `POST /api/push/subscribe`. The body has `endpoint` and `keys` (`p256dh` and `auth`). The route accepts only endpoints that start with `https://`, and it stores the subscription in the registry table `push_subscriptions`, with no workspace.
4. The service worker `web/public/sw.js` shows each push with `showNotification`. Its title is the `title` field or `Ostra`.

The workspace setting `notifications.push` (default `true`) turns the sending off for a workspace. When it is `false`, `Services::notify` returns at once. A subscription without a workspace receives the notices of every workspace. A subscription with a workspace receives only the notices of that workspace. See [Storage](storage.md) for the table.

### The VAPID key pair

VAPID (RFC 8292) lets the push service know which application server sends a message. The server key is a P-256 key pair. At start, `vapid_keys` reads the private key from the registry secret `vapid_private`. If it is missing or invalid, Ostra generates a new pair and saves the private bytes. Thus, the key stays the same across restarts, and existing browser subscriptions stay valid. A new key makes them fail.

For each message, Ostra makes an ES256 JSON Web Token:

- The header is `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256"}`.
- The claims are `aud` (the origin of the push endpoint), `exp` (now plus 12 hours, `JWT_TTL`), and `sub` (`mailto:ostra@localhost`).
- The signature is the 64-byte raw ECDSA signature in URL-safe base64.

The `Authorization` header is `vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>`. The public key is the 65-byte uncompressed point in URL-safe base64. The `aud` value comes from `origin_of`, which accepts only `http` and `https` endpoints. Another scheme gives `NotifyError::Endpoint`.

### Message encryption (RFC 8291)

The push service must not read the message, so Ostra encrypts it for the browser. `encrypt` runs these steps for each message:

1. Decode `p256dh` (the 65-byte public key of the browser) and `auth` (the 16-byte secret of the browser). The decoder accepts URL-safe base64 with or without padding, because browsers produce both.
2. Make a new sender P-256 key pair and a random 16-byte salt for this message.
3. Compute the ECDH shared secret from the sender private key and the browser public key.
4. Run HKDF-SHA-256 with the salt `auth`, the shared secret, and the info that has three parts: the bytes `WebPush: info` and one NUL byte (`b"WebPush: info\0"` in the source), the browser key, and the sender key. The output is 32 bytes.
5. Run HKDF-SHA-256 again with the message salt. The info `b"Content-Encoding: aes128gcm\0"` gives the 16-byte content key. The info `b"Content-Encoding: nonce\0"` gives the 12-byte nonce. In each info string, `\0` is one NUL byte at the end.
6. Append the byte `0x02` (the padding delimiter of the last record) to the plaintext. Encrypt with AES-128-GCM.
7. Build the body: salt (16 bytes), record size (4 bytes, big-endian, 4096), key id length (1 byte), sender public key (65 bytes), and the ciphertext.

The request also has `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `TTL: 86400` (`PUSH_TTL_SECS`, 24 hours), and `Urgency: high`. The HTTP client has a timeout of 20 seconds.

The plaintext is the JSON of a `Notification` with the fields `title`, `body`, `url`, and `tag`. One record holds the whole message, so the plaintext has a limit. Push services accept at most 4096 bytes of body. The header uses 86 bytes, the GCM tag 16 bytes, and the delimiter 1 byte. The limit `MAX_PLAINTEXT` is thus 4096 - 86 - 16 - 1 = 3993 bytes.

### What happens when a push fails

- **Status 200 to 299.** The result is `SendOutcome::Delivered`.
- **Status 404 or 410.** The subscription is dead. The result is `SendOutcome::Gone`, and the server deletes the subscription from the registry.
- **Any other status.** The result is `SendOutcome::Failed` with the status and the first 500 characters of the body. The server logs a warning. Ostra does not retry and does not delete the subscription.
- **A network error.** The result is `SendOutcome::Failed` with no status.
- **The payload is larger than 3993 bytes.** `send` returns `NotifyError::TooLarge`, and the server logs "push error". Ostra does not shorten the text, so a long completion summary can send no notification.
- **A subscription key is invalid.** `send` returns `NotifyError::Key`, and the server logs the error. The other subscriptions still receive the notice.

Ostra sends each notice once, in a background task that does not block the engine.

### How the tests check the code

The test `rfc8291_test_vector` in `crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs` uses the example of RFC 8291 Appendix A. The constants `PLAINTEXT` (`When I grow up, I want to be a watermelon`), `AS_PRIVATE`, `AS_PUBLIC`, `UA_PRIVATE`, `UA_PUBLIC`, `SALT`, `AUTH`, and `EXPECTED` hold the values of the RFC. The function `encrypt_with` takes the sender key and the salt as arguments, so the test can fix them and compare the body with `EXPECTED`. Other tests check a round trip with fresh keys, the size limit, the VAPID token and its signature, the audience, and padded base64.

## Limits and constants

### The MCP client (`ostra-mcp`)

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PROTOCOL_VERSION` | `2025-11-25` | Version that the client offers in `initialize`. |
| `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS` | `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, `2024-11-05` | Versions that the client accepts from a server. |
| `MAX_RESULT` | 102400 bytes (100 KB) | Longest tool result. Ostra cuts the rest and adds a note. |
| `SESSION_HEADER` | `mcp-session-id` | HTTP header for the session id of the server. |
| `VERSION_HEADER` | `mcp-protocol-version` | HTTP header for the negotiated version. |
| `STDERR_TAIL` | 4096 bytes | Standard error of a local server that Ostra keeps to explain a crash. |
| Pages of `tools/list` | 50 | Most pages that the client reads. |
| HTTP connect timeout | 15 seconds | Time to open a connection to a remote server. |
| Redirects | 5 | More than 5 redirects is an error. A redirect to another origin stops. |
| Error body snippet | 300 characters | Part of an error body in a message. |
| Wait for standard error | 500 ms | Time that the stdio transport waits to read the last lines after an exit. |

### The gateway (`ostra-server`)

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds | Time for a start, a handshake, and a tool list. |
| `RELIST_AFTER` | 30 seconds | Age after which an execution lists the tools again. |
| `RETRY_AFTER` | 20 seconds | Time during which the gateway returns the saved connect error. |
| `LOGIN_TTL` | 600 seconds | Life of a pending sign-in. |
| `CALLBACK_PATH` | `/mcp/oauth/callback` | Path of the OAuth redirect. |
| Gateway HTTP client timeout | 30 seconds | Timeout of discovery, registration, and token requests. |

### Names and settings (`ostra-core`)

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PREFIX` | `mcp__` | Start of a canonical tool name. |
| `SEPARATOR` | `__` | Separates the server from the tool. |
| `MAX_BARE_NAME` | 52 characters | Longest bare name. |
| `MAX_SERVER_NAME` | 24 characters | Longest server name. |
| `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS` | 600 | Largest `timeout_secs`. The default is 120. |
| `SAVED_SECRET` | `${ostra_secret}` | Placeholder in `workspace.toml` for a saved secret. |

### Web Push (`ostra-notify`)

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RECORD_SIZE` | 4096 | Record size in the `aes128gcm` header. |
| `MAX_PLAINTEXT` | 3993 bytes | Largest message before encryption. |
| `JWT_TTL` | 12 hours | Life of one VAPID token. |
| `PUSH_TTL_SECS` | 86400 (24 hours) | How long the push service keeps an undelivered message. |
| Request timeout | 20 seconds | Timeout of one push request. |
| Failure body | 500 characters | Part of a failure body in `SendOutcome::Failed`. |

## What these parts do not guarantee

- Ostra does not check what an MCP server says. A tool description and a tool result are text from the server, and the model reads them. A remote server can return any text.
- Ostra trusts the `readOnlyHint` of a tool. Plan mode relies on it.
- The sandbox covers local servers only. A remote server runs outside Ostra and outside the sandbox.
- A URL with `http://` is allowed for a server. Ostra does not encrypt that traffic.
- A harness run does not see tools that a server adds after the run starts.
- A push message is not certain to arrive. The push service decides when to deliver it, and Ostra sends it once.
- The push service cannot read the message, but it knows the endpoint and the time of each message.
- The VAPID subject is fixed at `mailto:ostra@localhost`.
