sections.title: Artifacts and structured documents
sections.summary: How Ostra stores workspace artifacts, uploads, and the typed research, spec, and plan documents. The page covers tags, caps, hide rules, the Document tool, checks, merge, render, and routes.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra keeps these files

Agents need files that a request text cannot carry. The user keeps some files for every task of a workspace, such as style guides and sample data. The user attaches other files to one request. Agents also write long documents that the next stage reads and that the console shows as typed parts. Each kind of file has its own folder, its own writer, and its own size cap.

This page covers:

- Workspace artifacts: folders, hidden units, path rules, tags, caps, and the rules for change.
- Uploads: staging, claiming, and caps.
- Typed documents: the research document, the spec, the plan, and its phase files, with the check, merge, store, and render steps.
- The project profile check that runs at the initializer submit.
- The Markdown outline parser.
- The routes that serve these files.

The page stops before documentation books. See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md). The route table is in [Server API](server-api.md). The guards that protect these files are in [Policy engine](policy-guards.md). The constants of `artifacts.rs` also appear in [Reference: engine, agent, and core limits](reference-engine-limits.md).

## The kinds of file and who touches them

The code uses the word artifact for two different things. A workspace artifact is a file that the user keeps. A session file is a file in a session directory, such as a report or a typed document. The route `/api/artifacts` reads a session file, not a workspace artifact.

| Kind | Where it lives | Writer | Reader |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Visible workspace artifact | `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/` | The user, through the console | Every agent |
| Hidden workspace artifact | `<data dir>/hidden-artifacts/<workspace id>/` | The user, through the console | No agent, harness, or sandboxed command |
| Staged upload | `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/<id>/<name>` | The user, through the console | The route that claims it |
| Claimed upload | `<session root>/uploads/` | Ostra, when it claims the file | Every agent |
| Typed document | The session directory: `<name>.json` and `<name>.md` | The `Document` tool only | The next agent and the console |

## Visible and hidden artifacts

A workspace artifact is a file that the user keeps for every session of one workspace. Examples are custom skills, documentation, guidelines, and sample data. Rule W1 says that agents read artifacts and that only the user changes them. Rule W2 says that a hidden artifact lives in Ostra's data directory, which no agent, harness, or sandboxed command can read.

### Folders

The functions in [`crates/ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs) name the folders:

- `artifacts::dir` returns `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/`. This is the visible folder.
- `artifacts::hidden_dir` returns `<data dir>/hidden-artifacts/<workspace id>/`. This is the hidden folder.
- `artifacts::hidden_units_file` returns `<data dir>/hidden-artifacts/<workspace id>.units.json`. The file sits next to the hidden folder, in the data directory, so no agent can change it.

### Hidden units

The user hides a folder or a file as one unit. A path is hidden when it is a unit or lies inside a unit. A hidden folder hides everything in it, including files that the user adds later.

`artifacts::is_within(path, unit)` is true when `path == unit` or `path` starts with `unit/`. Because of the slash, the unit `notes` hides `notes/later/b.md` but does not hide `notesheet.md`.

`artifacts::tidy_units` sorts the units, removes repeats, and removes each unit that lies inside another unit. For the units `notes`, `notes/a.md`, and `data/x.csv`, the result is `data/x.csv` and `notes`.

The server keeps one invariant after every change: a file is stored in the hidden folder exactly when it is inside a hidden unit.

### What happens when

- The units file does not exist or cannot be read: `hidden_units` treats each file in the hidden folder as a unit. This case covers a workspace that hid files before Ostra recorded units.
- The units file exists but holds invalid JSON: `hidden_units` returns an empty list.
- A new file arrives at a path inside a hidden unit: the server writes it in the hidden folder, so the file is hidden too.
- The Files view saves a file under the key `_artifacts`: the view lists the visible folder first and the hidden folder second. It writes a new file in the hidden folder when a hidden unit holds the path.

## Artifact paths and listing

`artifacts::normalize` turns a raw name into a canonical artifact path, or it returns a message for the user. The server uses it on every route.

The function refuses a path when any of these is true:

- The path is empty after the function trims it and removes a leading `./` and a trailing `/`.
- The path starts with `/` or is absolute.
- The path is a bare `.`, or a segment is `..`.
- A segment starts with a dot, for example `.env` or `a/.git/config`.
- A segment holds a control character.

The function changes `\` to `/`, removes a leading `./`, and removes a trailing `/`. The input `./guides\style.md` becomes `guides/style.md`.

The function does not refuse an interior `.` or an empty segment. It reads the path with `Path::components()`, which drops both. Thus `a/./b` and `a//b` both become `a/b`.

The message for a bad path has this text, where `{raw}` is the input:

```text
Name the artifact with a relative path such as `guides/style.md`. `{raw}` is not one.
```

`artifacts::list(root)` returns every file under a folder, sorted by path. It does not follow links, because an artifact is a file that the user put there and a link can name any file on the machine. It stops reading a folder when the list reaches `MAX_ARTIFACTS` entries.

`artifacts::visible_file` returns the full path of a visible artifact only when all of these are true:

- The path normalizes.
- The entry is a regular file and not a link.
- The canonical path of the entry is inside the canonical visible folder.

`artifacts::skill_path` uses `visible_file` to find a custom skill that the user keeps as `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.

## Artifact tags

A tag names a file in request text and in instructions. The form is `@<key>/<path>`. The key is a project key, or `_artifacts` for a workspace artifact. The constant `TAG_ROOT` holds `_artifacts`. No project key can take that name, because project keys start with a letter or a digit.

### Syntax

The function `artifacts::tags(text)` finds tags with the pattern `(?:^|\s)@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)/(\S+)`. These rules follow from the pattern and the code:

- A tag must start at the beginning of the text or after white space. The text `mail me@host/x` has no tag.
- The key holds letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-`.
- The path is everything up to the next white space.
- The function removes sentence punctuation from the end of the path. The constant `TRAILING` lists these characters: `.` `,` `;` `:` `!` `?` `)` `]` `}` `"` `'` and the backtick.
- Each tag appears once in the result, in the order of first use. The function drops a tag with an empty path.

For example, the text `Follow @_artifacts/style.md, and @web/src/. Again @_artifacts/style.md` gives two tags: `_artifacts` with `style.md`, and `web` with `src/`.

### How a tag resolves

Rule W3 says that an instruction carries the absolute path of each file that it tags. The function `artifacts::tagged_files` resolves each tag:

- For the key `_artifacts`, the tag resolves only when `visible_file` finds a regular file. A hidden artifact, a missing artifact, and a folder resolve to nothing.
- For a project key, the tag resolves when the project exists in the workspace, the path normalizes, and the canonical full path stays inside the canonical project root. A folder can resolve.
- Any other tag stays plain text.

At spawn time, `with_tagged_files` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs) runs on each instruction text for the agent. When at least one tag resolves, it appends this sentence: Files these instructions name. Read each before you start, because the user chose them. Then it lists each file as a line with the absolute path and the tag. Because the line holds an absolute path, every executor can read the file.

### Check at save time

`artifacts::tag_issues` runs when the settings are validated. `WorkspaceRt::validate` in `ostra-workspace` calls it for `instructions.all` and for each `instructions.agents.<agent>` text. It looks only at `_artifacts` tags. For each tag that does not resolve, it returns one message for that field:

- The tag names a hidden artifact: Unhide the artifact or remove its tag, because agents never see a hidden artifact.
- The tag names no artifact: Add the artifact on the Artifacts page or remove its tag, because the workspace has no such artifact.

The function does not check project tags.

## Artifacts in the agent brief

Every agent learns where the artifacts are. `ArtifactsBrief::read` in [`crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs`](crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs) lists the visible folder when the spawn is built. It returns nothing when the folder holds no file. It never lists hidden artifacts, because it reads only the visible folder.

The brief section has the heading `## Workspace artifacts`. It lists at most `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` files, in path order. Each line holds the full path and the size in bytes. When the folder holds more files, the last line says `and N more` and tells the agent to find them with Glob. The section tells the agent to read the files that bear on its task with Read and not to write in the folder. It also says that an artifact named `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is a skill that the agent loads with the Skill tool by its path.

The guard `workspace-artifacts` enforces the write ban. It denies a write, move, or delete inside the visible folder and tells the agent to propose the change in its report. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md). The brief itself is described in [Agents, prompts, skills, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md).

## Rules for deleting, moving, and hiding artifacts

Rule W4 says that Ostra deletes or moves an artifact only when no session is running, waiting, stalled, or paused and no execution runs. The reason is that an agent can be reading the file.

`artifacts::blocked(workspace, verb)` returns the reason for a refusal, or nothing. It checks in this order:

1. If a session has the status `Running`, `Waiting`, `Stalled`, or `Paused`, the message is: `Stop session {id} or wait for it to end, then {verb}, because its agents may be reading the artifact.`
2. If an execution runs, the message is: `Wait for execution {id} to finish, then {verb}, because it may be reading the artifact.`

The list response carries the result for the verb `delete` in the field `delete_blocked`, so the console can show the reason before the user clicks.

The delete route and the move route also try to take the write side of the workspace lock `w.work`. Code that starts work holds the read side. If the write side is not free, the route returns status 409 with the text: Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace. Because of this lock, no session starts between the busy check and the change.

The hide and show route does not run the busy check and does not take the lock.

### Delete

`artifacts::delete` removes one regular file from the visible folder or the hidden folder. It then removes each empty parent folder up to the root. If the deleted path was itself a hidden unit, it removes the unit from the units file. A folder disappears when its last file goes. The route does not delete a folder directly.

### Move

`artifacts::move_to(from, to)` moves a file or a folder. It refuses in these cases:

- A path does not normalize: status 400.
- `to` lies inside `from`: status 400 with the text Move `from` somewhere outside itself.
- The busy check fails: status 409.
- `from` does not exist: status 404.
- `to` exists: status 409 on the field `to`.

A move keeps the hidden state. A unit inside `from` follows the move. If a folder above `from` hid it, `to` becomes a unit, so the file stays hidden. A file that lands inside a hidden folder becomes hidden.

`relocate` does the move in these steps. It checks every target before it moves anything, and it refuses with status 409 on the field `path` when a target file exists. Then it creates the folders, moves each file, removes the emptied folders from the deepest up, and saves the units. A move uses a rename. If the rename fails, it copies the file and removes the source, because the data directory can be on another file system than the workspace.

### Hide and show

`artifacts::set_hidden(path, hidden)` needs an existing path, or it returns status 404. To hide, it adds the path as a unit, unless a unit above already hides it. To show, it removes the unit. If the path is hidden only because a folder above is a unit, it refuses with status 409 and the text Show the folder `<folder>` instead, because a hidden folder hides everything in it. After it changes the units, it calls `relocate` so each file moves to the folder that matches its new state.

## Artifact caps

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` | 25 MB (`25 * 1024 * 1024`) | Largest artifact that the user can upload. The server refuses a larger file with status 400. |
| `MAX_ARTIFACTS` | 2000 | Most artifacts in one workspace, visible and hidden together. `check_room` refuses a new file at this count with status 409. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` | 40 | Most artifacts that the repo brief names. |
| `TAG_ROOT` | `_artifacts` | Tag key for a workspace artifact. |
| `TRAILING` | 12 characters | Punctuation that `tags` removes from the end of a tag path. |

The reason for the count cap is in the error text: every agent's brief lists the artifacts. The reason for the size cap is also in the error text: agents read artifacts whole.

## Artifact routes

The artifact routes sit in [`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs), and the logic sits in [`crates/ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs). The full route table is in [Server API](server-api.md).

| Method and route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts` | Lists visible and hidden artifacts, sorted by path, with `dir` and `delete_blocked`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts?path=` | Adds an artifact. The body is the raw file bytes. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts?path=` | Deletes one artifact file. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/download?path=` | Sends the file as `application/octet-stream` with a `Content-Disposition` header that holds the name in RFC 5987 form. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/hidden` | Hides or shows a path. The body is `{path, hidden}`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/artifacts/move` | Moves a path. The body is `{from, to}`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads?name=` | Stages an upload for a request. |
| `GET /api/artifacts?path=` | Reads a session file. |
| `GET /api/artifacts/download?path=` | Downloads a session file. |

The routes for uploads and artifacts set a body limit of the cap plus 1024 bytes: `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES + 1024` and `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES + 1024`. After a save, the add route announces the saved file to open consoles. After a hide, move, or delete, the routes announce a change to the `_artifacts` file tree. Every route that changes the list returns the new list.

### Add an artifact

`artifacts::upload` places a new file in the visible folder or the hidden folder. The next diagram shows its decisions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["upload(raw, bytes)"] --> B["normalize(raw)"]
    B -->|bad path| E1["400 Name the artifact with a relative path"]
    B --> C{"bytes over 25 MB?"}
    C -->|yes| E2["400 Upload artifacts of at most 25 MB"]
    C -->|no| D{"path exists in either folder?"}
    D -->|yes| E3["409 already exists"]
    D -->|no| F{"2000 artifacts already?"}
    F -->|yes| E4["409 Delete an artifact first"]
    F -->|no| G{"inside a hidden unit?"}
    G -->|yes| H["write in hidden folder"]
    G -->|no| I["write in visible folder"]
```

### Read a session file

`GET /api/artifacts?path=` serves files from session directories. `session_file` canonicalizes the path. The path must lie inside the sessions folder of an open workspace, or the route returns status 403 with the text Only files inside a session directory can be opened here. A missing file gives status 404. A path that is not a file gives status 400.

The response is an `Artifact` value. If the file is valid UTF-8 text and at most `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` (4 MB) in size, the response holds the text in `content`, the outline in `headings`, and the typed document in `document` when the file has one. Otherwise, `binary` is `true`, `content` is empty, and only a download is offered.

## Uploads

An upload is a file that the user attaches to one request. A new task uploads its files before its session exists. For this reason, [`crates/ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs) works in two steps: it stages the file in the workspace first, then it claims the file into the session's `uploads/` folder (Rule C3).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Console
    participant Route as uploads route
    participant Uploads as uploads.rs
    participant Engine
    Console->>Route: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/uploads?name=
    Route->>Uploads: stage(workspace, name, bytes)
    Uploads-->>Console: UploadRef(id, name, size)
    Console->>Engine: start session or amend, with upload ids
    Engine->>Uploads: check(ids)
    Engine->>Uploads: claim(workspace, session root, ids)
    Uploads-->>Engine: UploadedFile list
```

### Stage

`uploads::stage` writes the bytes and returns an `UploadRef` with an `id`, a `name`, and a `size`. It runs these steps:

1. Refuse an empty file with the text The file is empty.
2. Refuse a file over `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` with the text Upload files of at most 25 MB, because every agent reads them.
3. Make an id with a random UUID in the simple form: 32 hexadecimal digits.
4. Make the name safe with `safe_name`.
5. Write the file in `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/<id>/<name>`.
6. If the staging folder has no `.gitignore`, write one with the line `*`.

`safe_name` keeps the last segment after `/` or `\`. It removes control characters, changes each of `: * ? " < > |` to `_`, trims white space, removes leading dots, and cuts the name to 120 characters. An empty result becomes `upload`. For example, `../../etc/passwd` becomes `passwd`, `C:\Users\me\notes.txt` becomes `notes.txt`, `.env` becomes `env`, and `a:b?.pdf` becomes `a_b_.pdf`.

### Check and claim

`uploads::check` runs before anything is created, so a bad id leaves no session behind. It refuses more than `MAX_UPLOADS` ids with the text Upload at most 20 files at a time. It also refuses an id that is not 32 hexadecimal digits or that has no staged file. The text is: An upload is missing. Upload the file again, then send. An id such as `../x` fails this test, so an id cannot point outside the staging folder.

`uploads::claim` checks the ids again, then moves each file into `<session root>/uploads/`. If the name is taken, it adds a number: `spec.pdf` then `spec (2).pdf`. No upload overwrites another. It renames the file, or copies it when the rename fails, and then removes the staging folder of that id. A staged id works once: a second claim fails with the missing-upload text.

The engine calls these functions in two places in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs). A new session calls `check`, creates the session folder, and then calls `claim`. An amendment of a running session calls `claim` and records the `RequestAmended` event with the claimed files. Ostra refuses an amendment with no text, no tagged file, and no upload. Ostra also refuses an amendment of an ended session. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for the events.

The code in `uploads.rs` does not delete a staged upload that no request claims.

### Upload caps

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 25 MB | Largest single upload. |
| `MAX_UPLOADS` | 20 | Most uploads that one request or one amendment claims. |

## Typed documents

Three agents write long documents that later stages read: `explore` writes the research document, `generate-spec` writes the spec, and `plan` writes the plan. A free-form Markdown file has no checks, so a broken reference reaches the next stage. Ostra makes each agent write the document as JSON through the `Document` tool. Ostra checks the JSON, stores it, and renders the Markdown that the next agent reads. The console shows each part natively, and the pipeline keeps reading Markdown. The code is in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs).

### Kinds and file names

`DocKind::for_agent` maps an agent to a kind. Any other agent has no kind and cannot call the `Document` tool.

| Agent | `DocKind` | File name prefix | Submit field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `Research` | `ostra-research-` | `research_path` |
| `generate-spec` | `Spec` | `ostra-spec-` | `spec_path` |
| `plan` | `Plan` | `ostra-plan-` | `master_plan_path` |

The agent names the file `<prefix>{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md` directly in its session directory. For each document, Ostra stores `<name>.json` as the source and renders `<name>.md` beside it. A plan also gets one pair of files for each phase: `<plan stem>-phase-<N>.md` and its `.json`. The function `phase_path` builds that name. A plan file name cannot contain `-phase-`, because Ostra reserves that part for phase files.

`doc_kind_for(path)` finds the kind of a session file from its name. A name must end in `.md` or `.json` and start with one of the three prefixes. Phase files report `Plan`. A name such as `ostra-implementer-phase-1.md` has no kind.

### What each document holds

The field comments in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs) are the schema descriptions that the model sees, so they read as instructions. The `Document` tool gets its JSON Schema from `DocKind::schema`, which uses `schemars`.

Each struct in `doc/mod.rs` that `ResearchDoc`, `SpecDoc`, and `PlanDoc` reach uses `deny_unknown_fields`, so an unknown field is an error. These are the structs that the `Document` tool accepts. Three types fall outside this rule:

- `PhaseDoc` has no `deny_unknown_fields` and no `JsonSchema` derive, because Ostra writes it from a plan and the agent never sends it.
- `DocumentView` has no `deny_unknown_fields`, because the server builds it for the console.
- `Question` and `QuestionOption` are in `crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs`, and they have no `deny_unknown_fields`.

#### Research document (`ResearchDoc`)

The required fields are `title`, `date` (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `repo`, `scope`, and `problem`. The other fields are lists that default to empty: `areas`, `asks`, `files`, `patterns`, `data_flow`, `dependencies`, `external`, `approaches`, `open_questions`, `sources`, `lessons`, `not_covered`, and `next_steps`. The field `recommendation` is optional. Each external fact must cite a page in `sources`.

#### Spec (`SpecDoc`)

The required fields are `title`, `date`, `objective`, and `current_behavior`. The lists use these ID forms:

| List | ID form | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `criteria` | `C1`, `C2` | One atomic demand each, with `kind`, `repo`, `grounding`, `depends_on`, and `provisional`. The kind is `Functional`, `Data`, `Integration`, `Constraint`, or `Quality`. |
| `deliverables` | `D1`, `D2` | In delivery order, with one repo each. |
| `requirements` | `R1`, `R2` | One flat sequence, D1's requirements first. Each has an EARS `pattern`, one `statement`, `covers`, `rests_on`, and `acceptance`. |
| `requirements[].acceptance` | `AC{n}.{m}` | `n` is the number of the requirement. Each has `given`, `when`, and `then`. |
| `evidence` | `E1`, `E2` | An external fact with its binding rule, source, and version. |
| `open_questions` | `Q1`, `Q2` | Question cards. |

The EARS patterns (`EarsPattern`) are `ubiquitous`, `event-driven`, `state-driven`, `unwanted`, `optional`, and `complex`. The other lists are `research`, `repos`, `in_scope`, `out_of_scope`, `contracts_provided`, `contracts_consumed`, `data_impact`, `assumptions`, and `notes`. Ostra derives the Delivery Order table, the Traceability table, and every count from these lists, so the agent does not write them.

#### Plan (`PlanDoc`)

The required fields are `title`, `date`, `spec`, `stakes` (`Low`, `Medium`, or `High`), `stakes_rationale`, and `summary`. The lists are `repos`, `success_criteria`, `clarifying_questions`, `deliverables`, `phases`, `risks`, `verification`, and `pre_checks`.

Each `Phase` has a numeric `id`, a `name`, a `deliverable`, a `repo` and `repo_root`, a `complexity` (`Level`), a `test_policy` (`Required` or `Skip`), a `test_rationale`, `depends_on` phase numbers, `areas`, `description`, `context`, `skills`, `requirements` quoted from the spec, `constraints` copied from the spec evidence, `steps`, and a `verification` command. Each `PlanStep` has an `id` in the form `{phase}.{n}`, a `title`, a `file`, a `change` (`Create`, `Modify`, or `Delete`), `read_first`, `delivers`, `action`, `binding_rules`, `skills`, a `verify` command, and a `size` (`Small`, `Medium`, or `Large`).

Ostra writes the master plan file and one phase file from each phase. A phase file holds a `PhaseDoc`: the plan title, the date, the spec path, the deliverable title, and the phase. The implementer reads only the phase file. For this reason, the checks demand that each phase quotes its requirements and its binding rules.

#### The console view

The console receives a `Document` value with the tag `kind` (`research`, `spec`, `plan`, or `phase`) and a `DocumentView`. The view holds the document and its `issues`, errors first.

## The Document tool

The `Document` tool in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs) is the only way to write a typed document. The guard `document-tool` denies a direct write to a file that has a document kind, because Ostra renders the file from its typed document and overwrites a direct write. The guard `artifact-ownership` also reserves each prefix for one agent: `ostra-spec-*` for `generate-spec`, `ostra-plan-*` for `plan`, and `ostra-research-*` for `explore`.

The tool takes `path` (required), and one of these forms:

- `document`: the whole document. It replaces what is stored.
- `update`: top-level fields to change, with optional `remove`.
- `remove`: a list of ids to delete, for example `R4` or a phase number.

The next diagram shows one write.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Tool as Document tool
    participant Merge as apply_update
    participant Store as doc::write
    participant Check as check
    participant Render as render
    participant Disk
    Agent->>Tool: Document(path, document or update, remove)
    Tool->>Tool: check kind, file name, and directory
    Tool->>Merge: apply_update(stored JSON, update, remove)
    Merge-->>Tool: merged JSON
    Tool->>Store: write(kind, md path, JSON)
    Store->>Store: DocKind::parse(JSON)
    Store->>Check: check(document)
    Check-->>Store: issues
    Store->>Disk: write name.json
    Store->>Render: render(document, md path)
    Render-->>Store: markdown
    Store->>Disk: write name.md and phase files
    Store-->>Tool: Written(files, issues)
    Tool-->>Agent: summary and issue lines
```

### What happens when

- The agent is not `explore`, `generate-spec`, or `plan`: the tool returns an error that names those three agents.
- `path` is missing or blank: the tool asks for the absolute path of the Markdown file.
- The file name does not start with the prefix, does not end in `.md`, or is a plan name with `-phase-`: the tool shows the required shape `<prefix>{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`, because later stages find the file by that name.
- The file is not directly inside the session directory: the tool refuses. It compares the paths with `ostra_core::paths::fold`, so a Windows path with a different prefix, case, or separator still matches.
- The call sends `document` together with `update` or `remove`: the tool refuses and asks for one form.
- `remove` is not a list: the tool refuses. Numbers in the list work as ids.
- `remove` is set and no document exists yet: the tool says there is nothing to remove.
- The JSON does not match the schema: nothing is written. The error names the field, for example `requirements[0].acceptance[0]: missing field `then``, or `unknown field`.
- The document parses but has issues: Ostra writes the files and returns the issues. The agent must fix each error with an `update`, because Ostra refuses the submit call while an error remains.

After a write, the tool marks each written file as read, so the agent can edit or reference it without a separate read.

## Merge: revise in place

`apply_update(base, update, remove)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs) lets an agent send only what changed. These rules apply:

- `update` must be a JSON object of top-level fields. Any other value is an error.
- A field replaces the stored field, with one exception.
- The exception: when the stored list and the sent list both hold items that each carry an `id` (a string or a number), the function merges by id. An item with a known id replaces the stored item. An item with a new id is added. A stored list that is empty also merges.
- After a merge by id, the list is sorted in natural order. `R2` comes before `R10`, and `AC1.2` comes before `AC1.10`. A new `R12` lands after `R11` wherever the agent sent it.
- `remove` drops every item with a listed id from every list in which each item has an id.
- A base that is not an object is an error. With no base, the update builds the document.

If an id in `remove` matches no item, the function returns this error and writes nothing. The text `{ids}` stands for the missing ids, joined by `, `:

```text
Nothing to remove for {ids}: no list item has that id. Check the ids and call again; nothing was written.
```

When the plan loses a phase through `remove`, `write` also deletes the phase files that the plan no longer has (see the store section).

## Check: errors and warnings

`check(&Document)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/check.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/check.rs) returns a list of `DocIssue` values. Each has a `level` (`Error` or `Warning`), an optional `element` such as `R3` or `step 2.1`, and a `message`. The list is sorted with errors first. An error is a broken reference or a rule that code can decide. An error blocks the submit call. A warning is shown to the agent and to the reader.

The issue line has the form `- error (R3): message`.

### Rules for all documents

For each list of question cards, the check reports:

- An error when two questions share an id.
- An error when a question has fewer than 2 or more than 4 options.
- An error when `recommended` is not an index of an option.
- A warning when a `tag` is longer than 12 characters, because the question card clips it.

### Research rules

- Error: an external fact cites a source URL that is not in `sources`. Every external fact cites a page that the run retrieved.
- Error: more than one approach is marked `recommended`.
- Warning: a source URL does not start with `http://` or `https://`.
- Warning: approaches exist but `recommendation` is empty.

### Spec rules

Errors:

- A criterion, deliverable, requirement, acceptance criterion, or evidence row has a repeated id.
- A `depends_on` of a criterion names an id that is not a criterion.
- A `depends_on` of a deliverable names an id that is not a deliverable.
- The deliverables form a cycle. The message names the cycle, such as `D1 -> D2 -> D1`, and asks to merge them, because delivery order must be acyclic.
- A criterion is covered by no requirement (Rule S1), because no plan builds it.
- A requirement names a deliverable that does not exist.
- A requirement id is not in the form `R{n}`.
- A requirement has an empty `covers`, or `covers` names an unknown criterion (Rule S8).
- `rests_on` names an unknown evidence row.
- A requirement has no acceptance criterion.
- An acceptance id does not have the form `AC{n}.{m}` for its requirement, or its `given`, `when`, or `then` is blank.
- A deliverable has no requirement.
- `provided_by` of a contract names an unknown deliverable, or a `consumed_by` entry of the form `D<digits>` names an unknown deliverable.

Warnings:

- A `provisional` field names an id that is not an open question.
- A requirement is out of deliverable order, or its number is not the next number in the one flat sequence.
- A statement does not hold exactly one `SHALL`.
- A deliverable covers more than 6 criteria and no note names it (Rule S4).
- An evidence row has no requirement that rests on it.

### Plan and phase rules

Errors:

- Phase ids repeat, or the ids are not the sequence `1` to `N` in order (Rule P10).
- A phase `depends_on` names a phase that does not exist, or the phases form a cycle. Ostra schedules phases as a graph.
- A phase has an empty `test_rationale` (Rule P12) or no step.
- Step ids repeat, or a step id is not `{phase}.{n}`.
- A binding rule of a step has no matching row in the phase `constraints`, or its sentence differs from the row, or it is empty (Rule P13). The implementer never reads the spec, so the rule text must travel with the step.
- A step has an empty `verify` command (Rule P5).
- Skill rules P6 and P7, below.

Warnings:

- A phase depends on a phase that comes after it.
- A phase names a deliverable that is not in `deliverables`, so the Deliverable Index cannot show its title.
- A step delivers no requirement (Rule P11), or it delivers a requirement that the phase does not quote in `requirements`.

#### Skill rules P6 and P7

The implementer loads only the skills that its phase file lists. A plan without skills therefore builds without the patterns of the project. For this reason, `plan_skills` checks each phase against the skills that are installed in the root of its repo. An installed skill is a folder in a project skills directory that holds `SKILL.md`.

- If the repo has installed skills and the phase has a step that is not a `Delete`, at least one step must name a skill. Otherwise the check reports an error that lists the installed skills.
- Each skill that a step names must be installed in that repo. Otherwise the check reports an error that names the skill.
- A repo with no installed skill is not checked.

When `DocKind::parse` reads a plan, it also makes the `skills` of each phase the union of the skills of its steps (Rule P7), so the agent does not repeat them.

## Submit check

`check_submit(agent, input)` runs when an agent calls its `submit_<agent>` tool. The native executor and the harness bridge both call it after the input schema check. A refusal returns the message and the words Nothing was recorded. The function reads files, so it runs at the tool boundary and never in the event fold.

For `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan`, the function does these steps:

1. Read the path from the submit field (`research_path`, `spec_path`, or `master_plan_path`). A missing field is an error.
2. Load the stored JSON beside the path. If none exists, the message says to write the document with the `Document` tool first.
3. Parse the document and run `check`. Any error makes the submit fail, and the message lists each error line.
4. For a spec, compare the counts in the submit with the document: `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, and `requirements`.
5. For a plan, compare `step_count` with the number of steps, compare the length of `phases`, and compare each submitted phase with the stored phase: `id`, `deliverable`, `project`, `complexity`, `test_policy`, `depends_on` (sorted), and `file`. The `file` must equal the path that `phase_path` gives. The message tells the agent which values to send.

The `initializer` agent has its own check, in the profile section below. Any other agent passes with no document check.

## Render: Markdown for the next agent

`render(&Document, md path)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/render.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/render.rs) builds the Markdown. The section names match the templates that the later prompts and the fact-check refer to. Ostra computes the derived tables, so the model does not write them. A table cell is one line, and `|` is escaped. A run of requirement ids such as `R1` to `R4` shows as `R1–R4`.

| Document | Level-1 title | Sections (second-level) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research | `# Research: <title>` | Scope of this document, Problem Statement, What the request asks, Findings (Relevant Files, Existing Patterns, Data Flow, Dependencies, External Technology, Lessons Used), Approaches, Open Questions, Not Covered, Sources, Next Steps |
| Spec | `# Specification: <title>` | Objective, Current Behavior, Scope, Criteria, Delivery Order, Requirements, Contracts Provided, Contracts Consumed, External Evidence, Data Impact, Assumptions, Open Questions, Traceability, Notes |
| Plan | `# Plan: <title>` | Summary, Success Criteria, Clarifying Questions, Deliverable Index, Phase Index, Test Policy Rationale, Requirement Traceability, Risks and Mitigations, Verification Strategy, Step Count Summary, Mechanical Pre-Checks (only when present) |
| Phase | `# Phase <N>: <name>` | Required Skills, Context, Requirements Delivered, External Constraints, Steps, Phase Verification |

The derived parts are:

- The spec header counts deliverables, requirements, and `Criteria covered: N of M`.
- The spec Delivery Order table lists, for each deliverable, its repo, areas, dependencies, requirement span, and criteria.
- The spec Traceability table maps each criterion to deliverables, requirements, and acceptance criteria. A criterion with no requirement shows `none`.
- The plan Deliverable Index and Phase Index tables, with the file path of each phase file and its step count.
- The plan Requirement Traceability table, built from the `delivers` lists of the steps.
- The plan Step Count Summary: total phases and total steps.

A spec requirement whose deliverable is missing still renders, with the note `(deliverable ... is missing)`. Every empty section prints a fixed text such as `None.`, so the headings that the prompts name always exist.

## Store: paths, load, and write

[`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/store.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/doc/store.rs) holds the file rules:

- `json_path(md)` returns the `.json` file beside a Markdown file.
- `load(md)` returns the stored JSON, or nothing when the file is missing or invalid.
- `load_view(md)` returns a `DocumentView` for a session file. It parses a phase file as a `PhaseDoc` and any other file with `DocKind::parse`. It runs `check` on the result. It returns nothing when the name has no kind or the JSON does not parse.
- `DocKind::parse(value)` parses with `serde_path_to_error`, so an error names the field path.
- `write(kind, md, value)` parses, checks, writes the JSON, renders and writes the Markdown, and returns a `Written` value with the document, the files (main file first), and the issues. `Written::errors()` counts the errors.

For a plan, `write` also writes the pair of files for each phase. It then removes each file that starts with `<plan stem>-phase-` and ends in `.md` or `.json` when the plan no longer has that phase. A revision that removes phase 2 therefore removes the files of phase 2 and keeps phase 1.

A write does not stop for issues. It stops only when the JSON does not parse or a file cannot be written. The error text then reads Could not write `<path>`.

## Project profile check

The project profile is the file `<project>/.ostra/project.toml`. It is not a `Document` kind, but it has a similar check at submit time. `ProjectProfile` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs) holds `schema_version`, `generated_at`, `stack`, `build_tool`, `commands` (`build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `run`), `test_framework`, `test_types`, `module_map` (rows of `glob` and `area`), `skills`, `conventions`, and `review_rules`. The older form of `stack` as a table with `language`, `frameworks`, and `build_tool` still loads and becomes a text value.

### Which initializer modes are checked

`InitializerMode` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs) has six variants: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`. `check_submit` sends each `initializer` submit to `check_inventory_submit` in `doc/check.rs`. That function does not read the mode. It reads the `result` object of the submit:

- If `result` has both `inventory_path` and `profile_path` as text, the function runs the two checks below.
- If `result` lacks `inventory_path` or `profile_path`, the function returns Ok and checks nothing. This case includes a `result` with neither field.

The code comment says that `generate-inventory` is the only initializer mode whose `result` names both files. Thus the checks run for `generate-inventory`, and the modes `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, and `adopt` pass with no check.

The two checks run while the agent can still fix the files, because the init fails at its last step otherwise:

- `INVENTORY.md` must exist. Otherwise the message is Write `<path>` before you submit: the file does not exist.
- `check_profile` must parse `project.toml`. If the file is missing, the message asks to write it. If it does not parse, the message names the shapes that models get wrong when they copy JSON into TOML. It puts these fixes before the parser text, because some harnesses clip a tool error.

| Mistake | Fix that the message gives |
| --- | --- |
| `key = null` | TOML has no null. Omit the key. The message gives the line number. |
| `[[conventions]]` | `conventions` is one table. Write `[conventions]`. |
| `[stack]` or `[[stack]]` | `stack` is a string, for example `stack = "rust"`. Put `build_tool` at the top level. |
| `schema_version = "0.1"` | `schema_version` is the number 1. Write `schema_version = 1`. |

`ProjectProfile::auto_fixable_ids` returns the review rule ids that the engine can apply directly. It leaves out ids that start with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ`. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for the init flow.

## Markdown outline

`outline::headings(markdown)` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/outline.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/outline.rs) returns the headings of a Markdown text as `Heading` values with an `id`, a `level` from 1 to 6, and a `title`. The session file route uses it for `headings`. The workspace search index uses it to index the heading titles of each session file.

The parser follows these rules:

- It reads ATX headings (`#` to `######`) and setext headings. A line of `=` under a paragraph makes level 1. A line of `-` under a paragraph makes level 2.
- It skips headings inside fenced code (backtick or tilde fences), inside indented code, and inside a front matter block at the start of the text.
- A fence closes only with a fence of the same character and at least the same length. An unclosed fence hides the rest of the text.
- `#######` (seven marks) and `#no-space` are not headings. The parser drops a heading with no text.
- The title is the text a reader sees: code spans, emphasis, links, and images reduce to their text.
- The `id` is a GitHub-style slug: lowercase, spaces to `-`, punctuation and symbols removed, `-` and `_` kept. A repeated slug gets `-1`, `-2`, and so on. The titles `Reqs`, `Reqs`, `Reqs-1`, `Reqs` give `reqs`, `reqs-1`, `reqs-1-1`, and `reqs-2`.

The search index adds the file name and, for a file of at most `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` (4 MB), the heading titles. The index lists a larger file by its label and file name only.

## Limits and defaults on this page

| Name | Value | Where | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` | 25 MB | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Largest workspace artifact. |
| `MAX_ARTIFACTS` | 2000 | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Most artifacts in a workspace, visible and hidden. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` | 40 | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Artifacts that the repo brief names. |
| `TAG_ROOT` | `_artifacts` | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Tag key for workspace artifacts. |
| `TRAILING` | `. , ; : ! ? ) ] } " ' backtick` | `ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` | Characters removed from the end of a tag path. |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 25 MB | `ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs` | Largest single upload. |
| `MAX_UPLOADS` | 20 | `ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs` | Uploads per request or amendment. |
| Upload name length | 120 characters | `safe_name` | Longest staged file name. |
| `ARTIFACT_LIMIT` | 4 MB | `ostra-server/src/api.rs` | Largest session file that the route returns as text. |
| `ARTIFACT_INDEX_CAP` | 4 MB | `ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs` | Largest session file whose headings the search indexes. |
| Question options | 2 to 4 | `doc/check.rs` | Options on one question card. |
| Question tag length | 12 characters | `doc/check.rs` | Longest tag before a warning. |
| Criteria per deliverable | 6 | `doc/check.rs` | Most criteria before the S4 warning. |

## Where the tests are

The tests sit beside the code. `artifacts.rs` tests path normalization, hidden units, tags, tag resolution, and listing. `uploads.rs` tests safe names and claiming. `doc/tests.rs` loads fixture JSON for each kind from `doc/fixtures/` and tests parse, check, render, plan phase files, schema errors, submit checks, and the profile check. Run them with `cargo test --workspace`.
