sections.title: Documentation books: stage, validation, and search
sections.summary: How the docs stage writes a book, which checks refuse a bad submit, how the engine stores and locks books, how DocsSearch ranks passages, and how the console reads and exports a book.
sections.body:
## The problem and what this page covers

Without a book, each agent that starts work in a workspace must read the code again to learn an area. A documentation book keeps that knowledge in files that agents search and people read. The docs stage writes the book. The engine writes every book file, and no agent writes one.

This page covers:

- The docs stage: which agents run, when they run, and what happens when one fails.
- The submit contracts `DocumentationSubmit` and `ArchitectureSubmit`, and the checks that refuse a bad submit.
- The diagram limits.
- Book identity, merge, files on disk, and the write lock.
- The `DocsSearch` tool and the ranking of its results.
- The console book reader and the HTML export.

These terms have one meaning on this page:

- **Book:** the documentation for a set of projects. A folder under `.ostra/docs/` holds it.
- **Part:** the overview and the sections of one project in a book.
- **Section:** one unit of work in a project. A section can hold sub-sections. A sub-section holds none.
- **Architecture:** the system architecture of a book. Only a book of two or more projects has one.

The rules in the code carry IDs. Search the source for the ID to find the code.

| Rule | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| B1 | A section has a fixed order of fields, with code references last. |
| B2 | Every section and sub-section lists its assumptions. |
| B3 | A diagram matches its kind and stays within its size limit. |
| B4 | A book of two or more projects has a system architecture. |
| B5 | The engine writes the books. Agents read them and never write them. |
| B6 | A set of projects names a book. A new part replaces the old part. A lock serializes writes. |
| B7 | Documentation writers run in parallel, at most 4 at a time. |
| B8 | Agents search the books by passage, and a hit shows only the passages that matched. |

## The docs stage in this version of the code

This version of the code runs one `documentation` agent for each project. Then it runs one `system-architecture` agent for a book of two or more projects. Then it does one book write. The code has no survey step, no page step, and no synthesis step. One `documentation` agent returns the whole part of its project in one `submit_documentation` call.

The planner decides when a project gets a documentation run. The function `closing_stages` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs) calls `docs_stage` only when both conditions hold:

- The closing stages of the project include docs (`closing.1`).
- The tests are done (`tests_done`).

If the closing stages include tests, `tests_done` becomes true when the test stage finishes. Docs therefore starts after the test stage. If the closing stages include no tests, `tests_done` is true at once.

The session records the closing stages for each project. If the session recorded none, `closing_stages` reads the request options. When the user asked for both tests and docs, the closing stages are tests on and docs on. Otherwise the planner opens the gate `Tests and documentation` and waits for the answer. A DOCS request sets the closing stages of each project to tests off and docs on. A TEST request sets them to tests on and docs off.

The `documentation` agent and the `system-architecture` agent have these settings in `agent.toml`:

| Agent | `default_tier` | `timeout_seconds` | `capabilities` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `documentation` | `advanced` | 2400 | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code`, `docs_search` |
| `system-architecture` | `advanced` | 1800 | `read`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, `code`, `docs_search` |

Neither agent has the `write` or `edit` capability. The reason is rule B5: the submit call is the whole output of the agent, and the engine writes the book from it. Both agents use effort `high` on every executor.

## Docs stage flow from spawn to book write

The diagram shows the calls for one book of two or more projects. A book of one project skips the architecture calls.

### Sequence of the docs stage

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Planner
    participant Runner
    participant Executor
    participant DocsWriter
    participant ArchWriter
    participant BookStore
    Planner->>Runner: Step Spawn for each project
    Runner->>DocsWriter: spawn documentation agent
    DocsWriter->>Executor: submit_documentation
    Executor-->>DocsWriter: issues from check_documentation
    Executor->>Runner: accepted submit in the execution result
    Planner->>Runner: Step Spawn SystemArchitecture
    Runner->>ArchWriter: spawn with ostra-docs-parts.json
    ArchWriter->>Executor: submit_system_architecture
    Executor->>Runner: accepted architecture
    Planner->>Runner: Step WriteBook
    Runner->>BookStore: book apply
    BookStore-->>Runner: book or io error
    Runner->>Runner: append BookWritten event
```

The steps in order:

1. **Spawn the writers.** `docs_stage` spawns one `Documentation` execution for each project with a passed phase. The inputs are the implementer reports of the passed phases and the user notes for the docs stage. `docs_in_flight` counts running and queued docs spawns. It stops new spawns at `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` (4).
2. **Give the writer its context.** The factory passes `existing_book`: the path of `book.json` when the book exists. It also passes the request text as a task note. The writer decides which sections to keep and which to rewrite.
3. **Validate the submit.** The submit tool of the executor calls `validate_submit`. For the `documentation` agent, this calls `check_documentation`. If the check finds problems, the tool returns them as text and the agent calls submit again. The native executor and the harness bridge both call `validate_submit`.
4. **Collect the parts.** `book_progress` returns the projects whose docs are done. It returns nothing when any project can still get documentation. It skips a project whose docs the user abandoned and a project with an open BLOCKER finding.
5. **Run the architecture writer.** When two or more parts exist, `book_stage` spawns `SystemArchitecture` once. Before the spawn, the runner writes `ostra-docs-parts.json` into the session folder. That file maps each project key to its `DocumentationSubmit`. The agent reads it through the `Book parts:` line.
6. **Write the book.** `book_stage` pushes `Step::WriteBook`. The runner calls `book::apply` with the update from `SessionState::book_update`. Then it records a `BookWritten` event with the book ID, the projects, and any error.

The planner writes the book once for each session. If `book_written` is already set, `book_stage` does nothing. The write is safe to repeat after a restart because `merge` replaces a part and adds a session ID only once.

### What happens when

- **An open BLOCKER finding exists in the passed phases of a project.** `docs_stage` does not start the docs run. Hard rule 21 states this.
- **A docs run fails and no gate exists.** `docs_stage` calls `exec_failed_gate`, which opens a gate for the user. See [Engine runtime](engine-runtime.md) for gates and retries.
- **The user abandons the docs run of one project.** `book_progress` leaves that project out. The planner names the book after the parts that exist, so an abandoned part does not name the book.
- **Every docs run is abandoned.** The list of parts is empty and the planner writes no book.
- **The architecture run fails.** `book_stage` opens a failure gate and waits. It writes no book until the run is done or abandoned.
- **The book write fails.** The runner records `BookWritten` with the error `The book could not be written to <folder>: <io error>`. The stage card shows `Failed` with that text, and the completion report does not link the book.
- **The write succeeds.** The stage card shows `Done` and the projects. The session files list gets the book `index.md` as a `Documentation book` entry.
- **The user asks for documentation only.** The engine writes `ostra-docs-request.md` in the project session folder when the file does not exist. The file holds the request and says that no implementer ran. The `documentation` agent reads it as its only implementer report. See [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md) for the DOCS category.

## DocumentationSubmit contract

`DocumentationSubmit` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs) is the input of `submit_documentation`. It is the part of one project. The part replaces the earlier part of the same project in the book as a whole. The book removes a section that the writer leaves out, so the writer copies each unchanged section into its submit.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | `SubmitStatus` | One of three values: `ok`, `stuck` (with `stuck` set), or `handoff` (the agent needs a specialist before it can continue). The enum is in `crates/ostra-core/src/submit.rs`. The checks run only for `ok`. |
| `summary` | string | Two or three sentences for the user. |
| `overview` | string | The introduction of the project. The default is empty. |
| `sections` | list of `DocSection` | At least one section for status `ok`. |
| `glossary` | list of `GlossaryEntry` | Terms with a definition and an optional `code_ref`. |
| `stuck` | optional `StuckInfo` | The diagnostic and the need, for status `stuck`. |

A `DocSection` and a `DocSubsection` have the same fields. Only a section holds `subsections`. The book renders the fields in this fixed order (rule B1), because readers look for each field in the same place.

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | A lowercase slug, unique in the submit. |
| `title` | Sentence-case title. |
| `purpose` | Two to four sentences: what the unit does, for whom, and when it runs. |
| `boundaries` | `owns` and `does_not_own`. Each `does_not_own` item names the owner. |
| `assumptions` | Facts that the code takes as given. Required. |
| `business_flow` | Steps with `actor`, `action`, and `outcome`. |
| `diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams with `title`, `kind` (`sequence` or `flowchart`), and `source`. |
| `tables` | Tables with `title`, `columns`, and `rows`. |
| `concerns` | Pairs of `component` and `responsibility`. |
| `code_refs` | Entries with `path`, optional `symbol`, optional `lines`, and `note`. They come last. |

## Validation rules for a documentation submit

`check_documentation` returns a list of problems. Each problem starts with the correction, so the agent knows what to change. The checks apply to `status: ok` only.

| Check | Rule and reason |
| --- | --- |
| `sections` is not empty. | The book shows only what the writer submits. |
| Each section and sub-section has a title and a purpose. | A unit without them has nothing to show in the index. |
| Each section and sub-section has at least one non-empty assumption. | Rule B2. Readers and agents rely on the list. The writer can write `None found in the code` after a check. |
| Each ID is a slug: the first character is a lowercase letter or digit, then lowercase letters, digits, or `-`, at most 64 characters. | The ID becomes a file name and a link. |
| Each ID is unique across all sections and sub-sections of the submit. | Two units with one ID overwrite one file. |
| Each table row has one cell per column, and a table has at least one column. | The renderer writes a Markdown table. |
| Each `code_refs` path is relative: not empty, no leading `/`, `\\`, or `~`, no drive letter, no `..` component. | The function `is_relative` makes sure that the book does not point outside the repository. The code gives no rule ID for this check. |
| Each diagram matches its kind and its size limit. | Rule B3. See the next part. |
| Each glossary entry has a term and a definition, and no term repeats. | The comparison ignores case and surrounding spaces. |

The validator checks structure only. It does not check the prose. The prompt in [`assets/agents/documentation/prompt.md`](assets/agents/documentation/prompt.md) sets the writing rules. Code does not check these rules:

- Write no metaphors, similes, or figures of speech, because an agent follows a figure of speech literally.
- Write one fact in each sentence, and name the real type, function, route, table, or config key.
- Define a term before its first use, and add it to the glossary.
- Use no em dashes. Give a count or a full list in place of the phrases "and more" and "various".
- Write titles in sentence case.
- Order the fields of a section in the order of the table above (rule B1).

## Diagram limits and how the validator counts

A sequence diagram has at most 8 participants (`MAX_SEQUENCE_PARTICIPANTS`) and 20 messages (`MAX_SEQUENCE_MESSAGES`). A flowchart has at most 15 nodes (`MAX_FLOWCHART_NODES`). The error text gives this reason: a reader follows a small diagram and loses a large one. The fix is to split a long flow into one diagram per step.

`check_diagram` runs these steps:

1. It reads the first line of the source that is not empty and does not start with `%%`.
2. For kind `sequence`, the first line must be exactly `sequenceDiagram`.
3. For kind `flowchart`, the first line must start with `flowchart` or `graph`.
4. It counts the size and compares it with the limit.

The counts follow these rules:

- **Sequence participants:** each name in a `participant` or `actor` line (the text before ` as `), plus each name at the two ends of a message. A name counts once.
- **Sequence messages:** each line that has a colon and one of the 10 arrows in `SEQ_ARROWS`: `-->>`, `->>`, `<<->>`, `<<-->>`, `-->`, `->`, `--x`, `-x`, `--)`, `-)`. The arrow with the lowest position wins, and a longer arrow wins a tie.
- **Flowchart nodes:** the validator skips lines that start with one of the 8 words in `SKIP`: `subgraph`, `end`, `style`, `classDef`, `class`, `linkStyle`, `click`, `direction`. On other lines it removes shapes (`[...]`, `(...)`, `{...}`, quoted text, and `|label|`). Then it removes inline edge text (`INLINE_EDGE_TEXT`), splits at edges (`EDGE`), and counts each distinct ID of letters, digits, and underscores.

Two cases follow from the counting. A node ID with a different spelling counts as a different node. A label in `[...]` does not add a node, because the validator strips shapes first. An architecture diagram must also be a flowchart.

When a diagram is too large, the error text starts with `Split` and gives the counts. When the kind and the first line disagree, the error text starts with `Start the Mermaid source`.

## ArchitectureSubmit and its validation

`ArchitectureSubmit` is the input of `submit_system_architecture`. The `system-architecture` agent writes it for a book of two or more projects (rule B4). The book shows it before every part. The agent verifies each link in source, including deployment files, and writes only what the files state.

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `architecture.overview` | Four to eight sentences about the whole system. |
| `architecture.diagram` | One flowchart with one node for each component and one labeled edge for each link. |
| `architecture.components` | `name` (unique), `project` (empty for an external system), `role`, and `owns`. |
| `architecture.links` | `from`, `to`, `protocol`, `mode` (`sync` or `async`), and `payload`. |
| `architecture.failure_recovery` | `failure`, `detection`, and `recovery`. |
| `architecture.scalability` | `component`, `scales_by`, and `limit`. |
| `glossary` | Terms that no part defines. |

`check_architecture` returns no problems when the status is not `ok`. For status `ok`, it refuses the submit in these cases:

- The field `architecture` is missing. The text is: `Return the architecture in `architecture`, because the book shows only what you submit.` The check stops there.
- The overview is empty.
- The diagram kind is not `flowchart`, or the diagram is over the limit of 15 nodes.
- The list of components has fewer than 2 unique names. Links name components, so each name must be unique.
- A link names a `from` or `to` that is not in `components`.
- `links`, `failure_recovery`, or `scalability` is empty.
- The glossary has an empty entry or a repeated term.

## Book identity, merge, and files on disk

A set of projects names a book (rule B6). A later session on the same projects therefore updates the same book. `book_id` sorts the project keys, removes duplicates, and joins them with `_`. Project keys hold no `_`, so the join keeps different sets apart. For example, `api` and `web` give the ID `api_web`.

If the ID is longer than `MAX_BOOK_ID` (80 characters), `book_id` shortens it. It computes a 64-bit FNV-1a hash of the full ID and cuts the text at a character boundary of at most 63 bytes. Then it appends `_` and the hash as 16 hex digits. The limit keeps a folder name short on every file system.

The user can pick an existing book when the user starts a session. The field is `docs_book`. `create_session` refuses an ID that `is_book_id` rejects, with the message `Pick a documentation book from the list instead of ...`. A valid ID starts with a lowercase ASCII letter or digit, has at most 80 characters, and holds only lowercase letters, digits, `-`, and `_`. `SessionState::book_id` returns the picked book, or the book named after `docs_projects`.

The merge in `book::merge` follows these rules:

- A new part replaces the old part of the same project. Parts of other projects stay.
- A new architecture replaces the old one. A session without an architecture keeps the old one.
- Glossary entries merge by term. The comparison ignores case and spaces. The newer definition wins.
- Parts sort by project key. The glossary sorts by lowercase term.
- The title is `Documentation for <projects>`, and `projects` is the sorted list of project keys in the parts.
- `sessions` lists the sessions that wrote the book, oldest first, and each session appears once.

The book lives in `<workspace>/.ostra/docs/<book id>/`. `book::write` creates these files:

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `book.json` | The whole `Book`. The console and the search read it. |
| `index.md` | The title, the update time, and links to the glossary and the architecture. For each project, it holds the overview and one line for each section with the first sentence of the purpose. |
| `glossary.md` | A table of terms, definitions, and code references. |
| `architecture.md` | Written only when the book has an architecture. |
| `<project>/<section id>.md` | One file for each section, with its sub-sections as `##` headings. |

A section file starts with the title as the level-1 heading and the line `Project: `<key>``. Then it follows rule B1: purpose, `Boundaries`, `Assumptions`, `Business flow`, diagrams, tables, `Separation of concerns`, and `Code references`. After the write, `remove_stale` deletes each file that the new book does not list and each folder that is empty. A section that the writer removed therefore leaves no file.

## Write lock and concurrent updates

`BOOK_LOCK` is one `std::sync::Mutex` for the whole process. `book::apply` holds it across the read, the merge, and the write. `book::remove` holds it across the removal. Two sessions that update one book therefore keep each other's parts (rule B6). A test starts 8 threads that update the book `shared`, and the result holds 8 parts and 8 sessions.

The lock has these limits:

- One lock covers every workspace in the process. Updates to different books also wait for each other.
- If a thread panics with the lock held, the next caller takes the lock and continues. The code uses `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`.
- `book::read` takes no lock, and `book::write` overwrites `book.json` in place. A read during a write can fail to parse. The caller then sees no book for that call.
- `book::write` called alone takes no lock. Call `book::apply` to update a book.
- Another Ostra process on the same folder does not share the lock.

The delete route needs a second guard. `book_delete` takes `work.try_write()` on the workspace first (rule W4). If a session is starting, it returns status 409 with the text `Try again in a moment, because work is starting in this workspace.` This guard makes sure that no session starts between the check and the removal.

## Read-only access for agents and the brief

Every agent can read the books, and none can write them (rule B5). Two layers enforce this:

- **Guard `WORKSPACE_DOCS`.** The policy guard denies a write to the books folder. The message tells the agent to put the documentation in its submit call. See [Policy engine](policy-guards.md).
- **Sandbox.** The profile mounts the books folder read-only with `read_only_dir`. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

The repo brief lists the books. The heading is `## Workspace documentation` (`BOOKS_HEADING`). The brief shows at most `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` (20) rows. Each row has the path of the `index.md`, the projects, the section count, and a note when the book has an architecture. If more books exist, the last row says `and N more` and tells the agent to use Glob in the books folder.

If the agent has the `docs_search` capability, the brief names the search tool and tells the agent to search before it reads code. The name depends on the executor, for example `mcp__ostra__docs_search` on a harness executor. Without the capability, the brief tells the agent to read the sections that bear on its task. In both cases the brief tells the agent to check what it finds against the code, because a book describes the code when it was written. See [Agents and prompts](agents-and-prompts.md) for the brief.

## How book search ranks results

The search in [`crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/book_search.rs) returns the best sections of the books and only the passages that matched (rule B8). A full section is long, and an agent that reads it whole spends its context on text that does not answer the question.

### Units and passages

The index has two kinds of item:

- A **unit** is a part of a book that a hit points at. The kinds are `Overview`, `Section`, `Subsection`, `Glossary`, and `Architecture`.
- A **passage** is a small piece of text of one unit. Each passage has a label, a text, and three weighted fields.

The builder cuts each unit into passages with these rules. Lists and tables go in windows of `WINDOW` (5) items.

| Unit | Passages |
| --- | --- |
| Project overview | One passage for each paragraph, label `Overview`. |
| Section or sub-section | One passage for each purpose paragraph. Windows of `Boundaries`, `Assumptions`, `Business flow`, and `Separation of concerns`. One passage for each diagram, label `Diagram: <title>`. Windows of table rows, label `Table: <title> (<columns>)`. Windows of `Code references`. |
| Glossary term | One passage, label `Definition`. |
| Architecture | Five units: overview (with the diagram), components (one passage for each component), communication (windows of links), failure (one passage for each case), and scalability (windows of scaling rows). |

A sub-section unit has the title `Section > Sub-section`. A glossary unit has the title `Glossary: <term>`. An architecture unit has the title `System architecture > <aspect>`.

### Fields and weights

Each passage has three fields. The score of a term counts the occurrences in each field with a weight.

| Field | Content | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Title | The passage label, for example `Assumptions`. | `W_TITLE` = 2.0 |
| Code | Paths and symbols of code references, the code reference of a glossary term, and the project key of an architecture component. | `W_CODE` = 1.5 |
| Body | The text. For a code reference, the notes. For a diagram, only its labels and messages. | `W_BODY` = 1.0 |

The diagram text drops the 29 words in `MERMAID_WORDS`, such as `participant`, `flowchart`, `alt`, and `end`. It also drops words of 2 characters or fewer. A query for `participant` therefore matches no diagram.

### Tokens

`tokens` turns text into lowercase, stemmed words:

- It splits at each character that is not a letter, a digit, or `_`.
- It splits an identifier at camelCase and snake_case boundaries. `SessionState` gives `sessionstate`, `session`, and `state`. The whole identifier stays as a token when the identifier has more than one part.
- It drops words of 1 character and the 82 words in `STOP`, such as `the`, `how`, `does`, and `use`.
- `stem` changes `ies` to `y` for words longer than 4 characters and `sses` to `ss`. It removes a final `s` from words longer than 3 characters. It keeps words that end in `ss`, `us`, or `is`.

### Score formula

The ranking uses BM25 with `K1` = 1.2 and `B` = 0.75. The query terms are sorted and deduplicated. The search drops a term that no passage holds. The inverse document frequency (`idf`) is `ln(1 + (n - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5))`. Here `n` is the number of passages plus units, and `df` counts the passages and unit titles that hold the term.

The score of one passage is the sum over the query terms. In the lines below from `book_search.rs`, `p` is the passage, `t` is the term, and `w` is the `idf` of the term:

```rust
let norm = K1 * (1.0 - B + B * p.len / self.avg_len);
let mut score = 0.0;
for (t, w) in &idf {
    let tf = W_TITLE * *p.title_tf.get(t).unwrap_or(&0) as f32
        + W_CODE * *p.code_tf.get(t).unwrap_or(&0) as f32
        + W_BODY * *p.body_tf.get(t).unwrap_or(&0) as f32;
    if tf > 0.0 {
        score += w * tf * (K1 + 1.0) / (tf + norm);
    }
}
```

The passage length `len` is `2.0 * title tokens + 1.5 * code tokens + 1.0 * body tokens`. The average length `avg_len` is the mean over all passages, with a minimum of 1.0.

The score of a unit uses the sorted passage scores `ps` of the unit. The variable `title` holds the unit title score:

```rust
let score = title + best + SECOND_SHARE * ps.get(1).map_or(0.0, |p| p.1);
ps.retain(|p| p.1 >= best * SHOW_SHARE);
ps.truncate(PASSAGES_PER_HIT);
```

### Flow of one query

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[Query text] --> T[Tokens with stemming and stop words]
    T --> I[IDF for each term]
    I --> P[Score each passage]
    P --> U[Group passages by unit]
    U --> S["Unit score = title + best + 0.35 x second"]
    S --> R[Sort and cut at the limit]
    R --> O[Render the matching passages]
```

### Unit score and visible passages

A unit scores `title + best + SECOND_SHARE * second`. The values are:

- `title` is the BM25 of the query terms against the unit title, with weight `W_TITLE`. It has no length normalization. The title counts once for the unit. It never picks which passages a hit shows.
- `best` is the score of the best passage of the unit.
- `second` is the score of the second best passage, or 0.0 when the unit has one passage. `SECOND_SHARE` is 0.35.

A hit shows at most `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` (2) passages. It hides a passage that scores below `SHOW_SHARE` (0.5) of the best passage. A unit that matches only by its title has no matching passage. The hit then shows the first passage of the unit with score 0. Hits sort by score, highest first, and then by unit order. The search cuts the list at the limit.

### What happens when

- **The query has only stop words or unknown words.** No term remains, and the search returns no hits.
- **The project filter is set.** The search keeps a unit only when its project equals the filter. The glossary and architecture units have an empty project, so a project filter removes them.
- **A book cannot be read.** `load_books` skips it. It reads each folder with a valid book ID, in sorted order.
- **A book changes between two calls.** The next call sees the change, because each call builds the index again.

## DocsSearch tool

`DocsSearch` lets an agent query the books of its workspace. It is a read-only tool, so calls in one response can run at the same time. The tool code is `docs_search` in [`crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs`](crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs). See [Native tools](tools.md) for the tool catalog.

| Input | Type | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | string, required | The question, with any names that the agent knows. |
| `project` | string, optional | A project key. It limits the search to the part of that project. |
| `limit` | integer, optional | The default is 5 (`DEFAULT_LIMIT`). The tool clamps it to 1 through 15 (`MAX_LIMIT`). The schema states the same range. |

The tool builds the index on every call inside `spawn_blocking`. The call searches all books of the workspace, with no book filter. Then it renders the hits.

The output starts with `N section(s) matched, most relevant first:`. Then each hit has this form:

```text
1. Execution slots (app, project `app`)
   File: `<books folder>/app/slots.md`
   Purpose:
   Caps concurrent executions.
```

The first line has the rank, the unit title, the book ID, and the project. A glossary or architecture hit shows only the book ID. The `File:` line gives the absolute path, so the agent can read the whole file when it needs it. Each passage follows with its label.

### What happens when

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `query` is missing | Error: `Pass query: the question you want the documentation books to answer.` |
| The run has no workspace root | Text: `This run has no workspace, so there are no documentation books. Read the code instead.` |
| The workspace has no books | Text: `This workspace has no documentation books yet. Read the code instead.` |
| No unit matches | Text: `No section of the documentation books matches this query. Try other names or terms, or read the code.` |
| The search task fails | Error: `The documentation search failed: <error>` |

The policy engine allows `DocsSearch` unless a user rule denies it. The capability name is `docs_search`. Twelve agents list `docs_search` in `agent.toml`: `advisor`, `code-reviewer`, `documentation`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `explore`, `fact-check`, `generate-spec`, `implementer`, `plan`, `quick-answer`, `system-architecture`, and `write-test`.

## Console book list and reader

The console shows books in two screens in [`web/src/screens/DocsScreen.tsx`](web/src/screens/DocsScreen.tsx). The data comes from three routes. See [Server API](server-api.md) for the route table.

| Route | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs` | The list of `BookSummary`, newest first, then by ID. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs/{book}` | The `Book`. Status 400 for an invalid ID, 404 when the book does not exist. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/docs/{book}` | Removes the book and returns the new list. Status 409 when work is starting. |

`DocsScreen` (resource `ws:docs`) shows a table with the columns Book, Projects, Sections, Architecture, and Updated. A click on a row opens the resource `book:<id>`. If no books exist, the screen says `No books yet.` and tells the user to start a task that asks for documentation.

`BookScreen` loads the book and shows `BookReader`. The reader has a top bar with a search box, an `Export HTML` button, and a `Delete` button. It has a contents sidebar, the page, and an `On this page` list. The page ends with Previous and Next buttons.

`bookPages` in [`web/src/features/docs/bookModel.ts`](web/src/features/docs/bookModel.ts) builds the pages from `book.json`, not from the `.md` files. The order is:

1. `overview`: the title, the project list, the update time, a table of section counts, and each project overview.
2. `glossary`: only when the book has glossary entries.
3. `architecture`: only when the book has an architecture.
4. One group for each project with at least one section. The page ID of a section is `<project>.<section id>`.

### Differences between the console page and the file on disk

The disk file and the console page of a section have the same fields in the same order. Both give each sub-section its own `### Code references` table, because `render_body` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/book.rs) also runs at level 3. The console page differs from the disk file in three ways:

- **Path prefix.** The console code reference paths start with the project key, for example `<project>/<path>`. The disk paths do not.
- **Place of the section code references.** The disk file puts the code references of a section before its sub-sections. `sectionMarkdown` puts them after all sub-sections.
- **Column header.** The console table header for the last column is `What is there`. The disk header is `What it holds`.

### Escape of agent text

The model escapes agent text, so that a book cannot change the structure of a page:

- `inlineText` escapes Markdown punctuation in titles and terms, so they render as the characters that they hold.
- `prose` keeps inline Markdown but escapes a line that starts a heading, a fence, or a thematic break. Each of these can change the page structure and its table of contents.
- `cell` and `codeCell` keep a table cell on one line and escape `|`.
- `code` writes a code span with a fence longer than the longest run of backticks in the text.

The tests in `bookModel.test.ts` check that a script tag in a title and an image tag in a term render as text.

### Search box and delete dialog

The search box in the reader works in the browser, with no server call. It starts at `MIN_QUERY` (2) characters. The search is a case-insensitive substring match over page titles, headings, and text. A title match ranks before a heading match, and a heading match ranks before a text match. It returns one hit for each page section and at most `MAX_HITS` (80) hits. The sidebar shows `80+ matches` at the cap. Each hit shows 48 characters before the match and 90 characters after. This search is different from the `DocsSearch` ranking.

The `Delete` button opens a dialog. After the user confirms, the console sends the delete request. The dialog states that the delete removes `.ostra/docs/<id>/` with every file in it. The next documentation task on the same projects writes a new book. The console shows an error from the server in the dialog.

## HTML export

The `Export HTML` button saves the whole book as one HTML file named `<book id>.html`. The code is in [`web/src/features/docs/exportHtml.ts`](web/src/features/docs/exportHtml.ts). The file loads nothing and runs nothing, so a reader can open it from any place.

The export runs these steps:

1. The reader sets `exporting`. It renders every page in a hidden `.bk-print` element with `aria-hidden`.
2. `diagramsDrawn` waits until each `.md-diagram` holds an SVG. It checks every 100 ms and stops after 15000 ms. A diagram that is not drawn falls back to its source.
3. `buildExportHtml` creates a new document with DOM calls. It imports each rendered page, cleans it, and adds a table of contents.
4. `download` creates a Blob URL, clicks a link, and revokes the URL after 1000 ms.
5. If a step throws, the reader shows the banner `The book could not be exported: <message>`.

The file has these properties:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Content security policy | `EXPORT_CSP` = `default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data:`, in a meta tag. |
| Styles | The standalone design CSS plus `EXPORT_CSS`, inline. |
| Layout | A sticky table of contents of 260 px on the left. Under 800 px width the table of contents sits above the pages. In print, the table of contents is hidden. |
| Theme | The theme of the console at the time of the export: `light` or `dark`. |
| Language | `en` |

`clean` removes what the renderer never makes and a file must not carry:

- Elements in `DROP`: `script`, `iframe`, `object`, `embed`, `frame`, `frameset`, `link`, `meta`, `base`, `form`, `input`, `button`, `foreignObject`, `audio`, `video`, `source`.
- Attributes that start with `on`.
- A `src` that is not a `data:image/` URL.
- An `href` or `xlink:href` that does not start with `#`, `http:`, `https:`, or `mailto:`.

`clean` also prefixes each element ID with `<page id>--`, because every page has its own heading IDs. It rewrites in-page links to match. It sets `rel="noreferrer"` on each external link. It replaces an image without a source with its alt text. The builder never parses book text as markup.

## Limits at a glance

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_SEQUENCE_PARTICIPANTS` | 8 | Most participants in a sequence diagram. |
| `MAX_SEQUENCE_MESSAGES` | 20 | Most messages in a sequence diagram. |
| `MAX_FLOWCHART_NODES` | 15 | Most nodes in a flowchart. |
| `MAX_BOOK_ID` | 80 | Longest book ID in characters. |
| `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` | 4 | Most documentation runs in flight. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Most book rows in the repo brief. |
| `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, `MAX_LIMIT` | 5, 15 | Default and highest `limit` of `DocsSearch`. |
| `WINDOW` | 5 | Items in one list or table passage. |
| `PASSAGES_PER_HIT` | 2 | Most passages that a hit shows. |
| `K1`, `B` | 1.2, 0.75 | BM25 constants. |
| `W_TITLE`, `W_CODE`, `W_BODY` | 2.0, 1.5, 1.0 | Field weights. |
| `SECOND_SHARE` | 0.35 | Share of the second best passage in a unit score. |
| `SHOW_SHARE` | 0.5 | A passage below this share of the best passage is hidden. |
| `MERMAID_WORDS` | 29 words | Diagram keywords that the index ignores. |
| `STOP` | 82 words | Words that the tokenizer drops. |
| `BOOK_LOCK` | 1 mutex | Serializes `apply` and `remove`. |
| `SEQ_ARROWS`, `SKIP`, `INLINE_EDGE_TEXT`, `EDGE` | 10 arrows, 8 words, 2 patterns | Diagram counting tables. |
| `MIN_QUERY` | 2 | Shortest query of the console search. |
| `MAX_HITS` | 80 | Most hits of the console search. |
| `EXPORT_CSP` | `default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; img-src data:` | Policy of the exported file. |
| `EXPORT_CSS`, `DROP` | inline styles, 16 selectors | Export styles and the removed elements. |
| `ARCHITECTURE` | `architecture` | Page ID of the architecture page in the reader. |
| `OVERVIEW`, `GLOSSARY` | `overview`, `glossary` | Page IDs of the first pages in the reader. |

sections.title: Server API: REST routes and the WebSocket
sections.summary: The axum router, every REST route by area, the /ws socket with its channels, terminal frames and editor hints, the embedded web build, and the app state that gives each workspace its engine.
sections.body:
## Why the server has one API

The browser console, the `ostra` CLI, and the harness hooks must all see the same live state of many workspaces. If each client reads the SQLite files itself, each client misses events and repeats the same checks. The `ostra-server` crate solves this with one axum router. The router has REST routes under `/api`, one WebSocket at `/ws`, two internal routes under `/internal`, and a fallback handler that serves the embedded web build. One guard middleware runs before every route.

This page covers these parts:

- The router and the guard order.
- The error format and the status codes.
- The route table, grouped by area.
- The rules that stop a session from starting when a workspace removal runs.
- The `/ws` socket: channels, message kinds, terminal frames, and editor hints.
- The embedded web build.
- The app state (`App`, `Shared`, `ServerServices`) that gives each workspace its engine.

The page links to the pages that own the logic behind a route. For the sign-in rules, read [Server security](server-security.md). For the logic of the file and git routes, read [Project files, git, and workspace search](project-files-and-git.md).

## Router and guard order

`router` in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs` builds one `axum::Router`. It registers the REST routes, adds `/ws`, merges `internal_routes()` from `bridge.rs`, and sets `static_handler` as the fallback. Then it wraps all of it in the `guard` middleware. The guard sees every request, including static files and `/internal/*`.

The guard treats a path as an API path when it starts with `/api/` or equals `/ws`. The checks run in this order:

1. The `Host` header must pass `Auth::allowed_host`. If it does not, the guard returns 421.
2. If Ostra has a private host name and the path is not under `/internal/`, the guard moves the client there. A page load gets a 307 redirect that keeps the path and the query. An API call gets 421 with the new address.
3. For `/internal/*`, the peer address must be local, and the request must carry neither an `Origin` nor a `Sec-Fetch-Site` header.
4. For an API path, the `Origin` must pass `Auth::allowed_origin`. The `Sec-Fetch-Site` header must not be `cross-site` or `same-site`. The `Sec-Fetch-Dest` header must be absent or be `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`.
5. For an API path other than `/api/auth/exchange`, the `ostra_session` cookie must pass `Auth::check_cookie`. If not, the guard returns 401 and logs the request facts. The log never holds a token or a cookie value.
6. The guard adds the security headers to the response, also when it refused the request.

The reasons are in the code comments. The private host name exists because a cookie that Ostra sets on `127.0.0.1` reaches every other local port. The `Sec-Fetch-Dest` rule exists because an image, script, or frame request is page content. An agent can write a Markdown image that points at the API, and the guard must refuse it. The `/internal/*` rules exist because only Ostra's own hook and MCP clients call those routes, and a browser tab on the same machine is a local peer too.

### Guard flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Request"] --> B{"Host allowed?"}
  B -->|no| C["421 host not allowed"]
  B -->|yes| D{"Private name due and path not /internal/?"}
  D -->|page load| E["307 to private host"]
  D -->|API call| F["421 open Ostra at private host"]
  D -->|no| G{"Refusal checks pass?"}
  G -->|no| H["403 or 401"]
  G -->|yes| I["Route handler or static fallback"]
  C --> J["Add security headers"]
  E --> J
  F --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J
```

The `secure_headers` function sets `content-security-policy`, `x-content-type-options`, `referrer-policy`, and `x-frame-options` on every response. It also sets `cache-control: no-store` on API paths. The values and the reasons are on [Server security](server-security.md).

## Error responses and status codes

Every REST error is a JSON `ApiError` with an `error` string and an `issues` list. Each issue is a `ValidationIssue` with a `path` and a `message`. The `ApiErr` type in `api.rs` holds the status and the body.

| Status | When it happens |
| --- | --- |
| 400 | The request is malformed: a bad query value, an empty question, a path that is not a file, or `GitError::Invalid`. |
| 401 | The guard found no valid cookie, or `/api/auth/exchange` refused the token. |
| 403 | The origin, the fetch headers, or an `/internal/*` check failed. A session file path outside every sessions folder also returns 403. |
| 404 | The workspace, session, gate, decision, execution, project, or book does not exist. `EngineError::NotFound` maps here. |
| 409 | The state does not allow the action. `EngineError::Invalid`, `EngineError::Ended`, `DeleteError::Busy`, `GitError::Busy`, and a work-lock conflict map here. |
| 413 | `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` received a document over `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES`. |
| 421 | The host is not allowed, or the client must use the private host name. |
| 422 | The settings or a request body have problems. The `issues` list names each field. |
| 429 | `/api/auth/exchange` rate limit. The message tells the client how many seconds to wait. |
| 500 | `EngineError::Store`, `StoreError`, or a failed blocking task. |
| 502 | `GitError::Git`: a git command failed. Also an MCP sign-in that could not start. |

The `From<EngineError>` and `From<StoreError>` impls map engine and store errors to these statuses. The function `git_err` maps `GitError`. The function `credential_err` maps the errors of the git credential routes.

Two helpers add detail. `ApiErr::conflict_on` returns 409 with one issue that names the request field that no longer matches the server state. `ApiErr::invalid_request` returns 422 and puts the issue text into `error` too. A client that shows only `error` then still shows every problem.

## Route table

In the tables, `{ws}` is a workspace ID, `{key}` is a project key, and `{id}` is the ID of the named object. Every route needs a valid session cookie except `/api/auth/exchange` and `/mcp/oauth/callback`. A route that has a request type in `ostra-core/src/api.rs` names it in the notes.

### Sign-in and server information

| Method and path | Handler | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/info` | `info` | Returns `ServerInfo`: the crate version and the VAPID public key for push. |
| `POST /api/auth/exchange` | `exchange` | Body `{"token": "..."}`, at most 64 KiB. Returns 204 with a `Set-Cookie` header. The cookie has the `Secure` flag when the `Origin` starts with `https://`. The guard already accepted this `Origin`, so `https` means that a TLS proxy runs in front of Ostra. |
| `GET /api/auth/sessions` | `list_sign_ins` | Lists `SignInSession` rows. The row of the caller has `current: true`. |
| `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}` | `revoke_sign_in` | Returns 204, or 404 when the sign-in expired or was revoked. |
| `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others` | `revoke_other_sign_ins` | Returns `{"revoked": n}`. |
| `POST /api/auth/signout` | `sign_out` | Returns 204 and a header that clears the cookie. The header carries `Secure` under the same `https://` test as `exchange`. |
| `GET /api/environment` | `environment` | Returns `EnvironmentStatus`: installed harnesses and provider keys. |
| `GET /api/onboarding` | `onboarding` | Returns `OnboardingState`. A count of zero workspaces and no `onboarded_at` means the first run. |
| `POST /api/onboarding/complete` | `complete_onboarding` | Calls `registry.mark_onboarded()`. |
| `PATCH /api/providers/{name}` | `patch_provider` | Only `anthropic` and `openai`. Body `ProviderCredentialsEdit`. Saves the credential, then reloads the providers. |
| `POST /api/harnesses/{harness}/setup` | `harness_setup` | Body `HarnessSetupRequest` with `action` `install` or `login`. Returns `HarnessSetupTerminal`. |
| `POST /api/push/subscribe` | `push_subscribe` | Body `PushSubscription`. The endpoint must start with `https://`. Returns 204. |

### Workspaces

| Method and path | Handler | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces` | `list_workspaces` | Returns `WorkspaceSummary` rows. `active_sessions` counts sessions in `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`. `available` is false when the workspace did not open. |
| `POST /api/workspaces` | `create_workspace` | Body `CreateWorkspace`. Returns `WorkspaceDetail`. 422 lists the issues. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/validate` | `validate_new_workspace` | Same body. Returns the issue list and creates nothing. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}` | `get_workspace` | Returns `WorkspaceDetail`. |
| `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}` | `patch_workspace` | Body `WorkspaceSettings`. 422 when the settings have problems. A changed `name` also renames the registry record. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}` | `delete_workspace` | Returns 204. 409 when the workspace is busy. Projects stay on disk. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` | `validate_workspace` | Body `WorkspaceSettings`. Returns the issue list and saves nothing. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` | `fix_settings` | Applies the fixes that the detail lists, such as a route for an agent added after the settings were saved. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve` | `approve_commands` | Body `ApproveCommands` with an optional `project` and a `hash`. 409 when the file changed after Ostra showed the commands. |
| `GET` and `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` | `get_ui_state`, `patch_ui_state` | The saved console layout. PATCH takes raw bytes, merges top-level fields, and drops unknown fields. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/cost` | `cost` | Query `since` as an RFC 3339 time. Returns `CostReport`. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/ask` | `ask` | Body `AskQuestion`. Returns `AskStarted` with an execution ID. Stream the answer on `execution:<id>`. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/tree` | `workspace_tree` | The Sessions tree. Runs on a blocking thread. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/search` | `search` | Query `q` and `limit`. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/activity` | `workspace_activity` | Returns `WorkspaceActivity`. Runs on a blocking thread. |

The workspace and settings pages own the meaning of these bodies. Read [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).

### Projects, git, and credentials

| Method and path | Handler | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects` | `import_project` | Body `ImportProject`. 422 or 500 on failure. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/clone` | `clone_project` | Body `CloneProject`. Runs in its own task. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}` | `remove_project` | 404, 409 (busy), or 500. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/init` | `init_project` | Starts an init session. Returns `SessionSummary`. Holds the work lock for read. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/pull` | `pull_project` | 400 when the folder has no `.git`. 409 when a session works in the project. |
| `PUT /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/commands` | `project_commands` | Body `Commands`. See the section on the project commands route below. |
| `GET .../projects/{key}/git` | `git_status` | Returns `GitRepoStatus`. |
| `GET .../projects/{key}/git/branches` | `git_branches` | Returns `GitBranch` rows. |
| `POST .../projects/{key}/git/stage` and `.../unstage` | `git_stage`, `git_unstage` | Body `GitPaths`. Returns `GitOpResult`. |
| `POST .../projects/{key}/git/commit` | `git_commit` | Body `GitCommitRequest`. |
| `POST .../projects/{key}/git/fetch` and `.../push` | `git_fetch`, `git_push` | No body. |
| `POST .../projects/{key}/git/checkout` | `git_checkout` | Body `GitCheckoutRequest`. |
| `GET` and `POST /api/git/credentials` | `git_credentials`, `create_git_credential` | Body `GitCredentialEdit`. Both return the full `GitCredentialView` list. |
| `PATCH` and `DELETE /api/git/credentials/{id}` | `patch_git_credential`, `delete_git_credential` | Both return the full list. DELETE returns 404 when the credential does not exist. |

In this table, `...` stands for `/api/workspaces/{ws}`.

### Project files and code navigation

| Method and path | Handler | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET .../projects/{key}/tree` | `project_tree` | Query `path`, `depth`, `hidden`. |
| `GET` and `PUT .../projects/{key}/file` | `project_file`, `save_project_file` | GET query `path`. PUT body `SaveProjectFile`. The PUT route accepts a body up to `8 * TEXT_CAP`. |
| `POST .../projects/{key}/mkdir` | `project_mkdir` | Body `CreateProjectFolder`. Returns the new listing. |
| `GET .../projects/{key}/files` | `project_files` | Returns the file name index (`FileIndex`). |
