## Run the eval files

The eval files in `tests/evals/` test agent behavior on real models. Model output varies from run to run. For that reason each eval counts passes and does not fail on one wrong answer. Each of the four runners has a live test and an offline test.

| File | Runner | Cases | What a case checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/evals/judges.toml` | `crates/ostra-server/tests/judge_evals.rs` | 83 | A judge picks the route that the case expects, for example the category of a request. |
| `tests/evals/advisor.toml` | `crates/ostra-server/tests/advisor_evals.rs` | 13 | The advisor decides what to do after a failed step of a created project init (rule O5). |
| `tests/evals/coordination.toml` | `crates/ostra-server/tests/coordination_evals.rs` | 11 | Helper agents ask and answer through a real `Engine` on a snapshot of the Ostra source. |
| `tests/evals/test_stage.toml` | `crates/ostra-server/tests/test_stage_evals.rs` | 13 | The execution path analyzer and `write-test` on small projects. |

Start a live eval with this form. Replace `judge_evals` with the runner that you need.

```text
OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS=anthropic:claude-opus-5-5 OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS=3 \
  cargo test -p ostra-server --test judge_evals -- --ignored --nocapture
```

Caution: do not start a live eval without a budget check. Each run calls paid models, and the cost grows with the cases, the models, and `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS`.

Each report lists pass counts and cost, and the runner writes it to `target/evals/`.

### Environment variables of the evals

| Variable | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS` | `judge_evals`: `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`. `advisor_evals`: Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. `coordination_evals` and `test_stage_evals`: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`. | Comma-separated list of models to test. |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` | `3`. `advisor_evals`: `5`. | Runs per case and model. |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_CASES` | all cases | Keeps only the cases whose id contains one of the given substrings. The judge runner accepts several, separated by commas. |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_TIERS` | all tiers | Keeps only the listed tiers, for example `1,2`. Used by `coordination_evals` and `test_stage_evals`. |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_JOBS` | `3`. `advisor_evals`: `4`. | How many sessions or runs go at the same time. `judge_evals` has no such variable. |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_GRADER` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | The grader model that checks a rubric. Used by every runner except `judge_evals`. |

The live tests fail only when no live run finished. The reason is that model results vary.

### Offline tests

Four runners have an offline test that `cargo test --workspace` runs. It costs nothing, and it finds a broken case before a paid run does:

- `eval_cases_build_their_sessions` in `judge_evals.rs` builds the session that each judge sees.
- `advisor_cases_build_their_spawns` in `advisor_evals.rs` builds the advisor spawn of each case.
- `coordination_cases_run_dry` in `coordination_evals.rs` replays each case with stand-ins for the live runs and checks that the session stops where the case says.
- `test_stage_cases_run_dry` in `test_stage_evals.rs` is the offline replay of the test stage. Read the next part.

## Read the test stage evals and the test stage project

The test stage evals check the two agents of the test stage: the execution path analyzer (`epa`) and `write-test`. Each case is a real session of a real `Engine` on a small project. The router executor sends the runs that the case lists in `live` to the native loop on the model under test. It plays every other run from the case.

### The fixture folders

The folder `tests/evals/test_stage/` holds the fixtures:

| Folder | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `projects/shop` | A Python 3.12 order service with a JSON HTTP API over SQLite, a CLI, and invoice text. It has `tests/unit`, `tests/integration`, and `tests/e2e`. |
| `projects/storefront` | A project that renders the orders that `shop` serves. A case lists it in `others`. |
| `projects/notes` | A Node project with `test/unit`, `test/integration`, and a Playwright spec in `e2e/notes.spec.js`. |
| `changes/<project>/<name>` | Overlays that the runner copies over the repository. A scripted implementer applies one overlay as the change under test. |
| `goldens/<name>` | `epa.md` stands in for the analyzer when it is not live. `files/` holds reference tests. |

The projects `projects/shop` and `projects/notes` each have a `.agents/skills` folder. The project `projects/storefront` has no `.agents` folder and no `.ostra` folder.

The root `.gitignore` ignores `.ostra/`, so the repository tracks no `.ostra/project.toml` for these projects. The function `profile_of` in `crates/ostra-server/tests/test_stage_evals.rs` (about line 362) loads the profile of a project with `load_toml(&paths::project_profile(repo))`. The READMEs of `shop` and `notes` say that `.ostra/project.toml` holds the test command for each level.

### Case fields

The loader in `test_stage_evals.rs` uses `deny_unknown_fields`, so a misspelled key fails the parse. The main fields are:

- `id`, `tier` (1 to 3), `note`, `project`, and `others`.
- `mode`: `phase` starts after a scripted implementation phase that the engine stages. `request` starts a new TEST session in which no implementer runs.
- `track`: `light` (the default) or `full`. A `phase_file` is allowed only on the full track in `phase` mode.
- `change`: the overlay that the scripted implementer applies.
- `history` and `staged`: overlays that the runner commits after the first commit, or leaves staged, to lay out what an earlier session left behind.
- `live`: the roles on a live model, `epa`, `write-test`, or both.
- `golden`: the folder under `goldens/`.
- `[case.epa]`: `has` groups, `lacks`, `cause`, and `rubric`.
- `[case.write_test]`: `status` (`ok` or `stuck`), `baseline` (`passes` or `fails`), `levels`, `run`, `files`, `has`, `stuck_has`, `cause`, and `rubric`.
- `[[case.mutant]]`: `id`, `file`, `find`, `replace`, and `note`.

The runner fills the placeholders `{repo}`, `{session}`, `{ws}`, and `{report}` in each run.

### Grading

An analyzer run passes when all of these are true:

- Its report is at the declared path.
- It changed no project file.
- The report holds each expected fact. Each `has` group is a set of alternatives, and the report must contain one of them.
- The grader model finds the rubric met.

A `write-test` run passes when all of these are true:

- Its status is the expected one.
- It changed only test files and listed all of them.
- Each `levels` group has a changed test.
- The `run` test types pass.
- Every planted mutant fails those test types.
- The files in `files` still hold the given text.
- The grader model finds the rubric met.

A `write-test` run on a golden analysis is reported as `write-test`. After a live analyzer it is reported as `stage`. The runner enforces that `status = "ok"` goes with at least one mutant, and that a `stuck` case has none.

### What the offline replay proves

The test `test_stage_cases_run_dry` replays every case with the golden analysis and the golden tests. It checks that each live run is reached and graded clean. It checks that the project tests let every mutant survive, and that the golden tests kill every mutant. A case that is wrong therefore fails here at no cost. The file has the attribute `#![cfg(unix)]` because the fixture commands run through `sh`. The helper test `glob_matches_folders_and_files` checks the glob rules that decide which files count as tests.

The 13 cases are grouped by tier:

- Tier 1: `bulk-discount-analysis`, `bulk-discount-tests`, `new-session-named-function`.
- Tier 2: `cancel-analysis`, `cancel-tests`, `new-session-after-yolo`, `separators-tests`.
- Tier 3: `regression-escalates`, `contract-change-analysis`, `browser-flow-stage`, `no-browser-level-analysis`, `new-session-staged-change`, `new-session-flow-request`.

For the stage itself, read [The session pipeline](session-pipeline.md).

## Run the browser security suite

The browser suite proves that the browser-facing defenses hold in a real Chromium. It checks the render paths of agent and repo text, the terminal, the cross-origin boundary, the sign-in token, uploads, and browser storage. It covers the console and the site. For the defenses, read [Server security](server-security.md).

Run it from the folder `tests/browser`:

```bash
cd tests/browser && npm test
```

The suite is Unix only. It writes to `/tmp` and reads `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. The setup refuses a scratch root outside `/tmp/`.

### What `npm test` does

1. It runs `npm run build` in `web` and `cargo build -p ostra-server` with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` set to `target-browser`.
2. It stops an old scratch server that `/tmp/pw-browser/server.pid` names. It kills the pid only when the command line holds `ostra` and `serve`.
3. It removes and makes `/tmp/pw-browser`, with its own config, data folder, master key, and `HOME`.
4. It starts a fake model API, an attacker page server, and a static server for the site. The site builds with an extra docs page of test strings (`VITE_TEST_DOC`).
5. It starts `ostra serve --no-open --port <free port> --bind 127.0.0.1`.
6. It signs in, makes a workspace, adds a project, and completes onboarding.
7. It adds a lesson, a skill, an MCP stub, and four uploads.
8. It runs one YOLO session against the fake model, and it writes a documentation book with test strings into `.ostra/docs/pw_book/`.
9. It stops the server at the end, unless `PW_KEEP_SERVER=1` is set.

Nothing leaves the machine. The model API is the local fake `lib/fake-model.ts`, the harness is a stub script, and the MCP server is a stub. The environment sets `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` to an empty value, so no price catalog downloads.

### Options

| Setting | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run test:fast` | Sets `PW_SKIP_BUILD=1`. It skips the web and cargo builds. The site pages still rebuild, because the test page names the port of the fake. |
| `PW_KEEP_SERVER=1` | Leaves the scratch server running. Its pid is in `/tmp/pw-browser/server.pid`. |
| `PW_CHROME=/path/to/chrome` | Overrides the Chromium binary. The default is the cached `chromium-1217` under `~/.cache/ms-playwright`. |
| `OSTRA_BIN` | Overrides the binary. The default is `target-browser/debug/ostra`. |

The Playwright config runs one worker with `fullyParallel: false`, because there is one scratch server and one PTY. A test times out after 90 seconds, and an `expect` times out after 15 seconds. The browser maps `evil-ostra.test` to `127.0.0.1` with `--host-resolver-rules`.

### The guard fixture

Every test string sets `window.__pwned` or requests `<fake>/canary/<id>` if it runs or loads. The `guard` fixture in `tests/browser/lib/guard.ts` fails a test on any of these findings:

- `window.__pwned` is set.
- A request reaches a canary URL.
- A CSP violation occurs on the app origin. The message prints the blocked URL, and its id names the render path.
- An unexpected dialog, popup, or navigation away from the app occurs.

The fixture reports through the console, because CSP cannot block the console.

### Specs

| Spec | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `00-smoke` | The app loads signed in. |
| `render` | Agent messages, tool output, artifacts, the completion report, session titles, repo file names and contents, branches and commits, MCP metadata, memory, skills, decisions, search, and the quick answer. |
| `mobile` | The same render paths in the phone layout in `web/src/mobile/`. |
| `terminal` | OSC 52, OSC 8, title sequences, and device queries through xterm.js. The PTY input must match a run with no browser attached. |
| `cross-origin` | Attacker pages on another localhost port and another site: forms, fetch, WebSocket, tags, frames, a navigation to every GET route in `api.rs`, DNS rebinding, and page content that reaches `/api`. |
| `signin` | The token leaves the URL, no request carries it, and what the profile keeps is spent. |
| `uploads` | SVG and HTML uploads never render inline, through chips, the artifact view, or raw links. |
| `storage` | `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB, and Cache Storage hold no transcripts, tokens, or keys. |
| `shortcuts` | The web app manifest and icons load under the CSP. A recorded shortcut stays in the `localStorage` entry of the workspace and runs. |
| `site` | Docs Markdown with test strings, Mermaid diagrams with hostile labels, every docs page, the homepage, and its console shot. |
| `books` | The documentation book with test strings in every field: the Docs list, each reader page, Mermaid diagrams, search, and the exported HTML file. The export must hold no script, carry its meta CSP, and render under it with nothing blocked. |

## Run the Windows probes

The Windows probes check the assumptions of the planned Windows sandbox on a real Windows machine. They are a standalone program, `winprobe`, in `tests/windows-probes`. The crate has no Ostra code. It is outside the workspace on purpose, and it has its own `Cargo.lock`. Run it only on a throwaway VM, because it creates local users, ACLs, and firewall rules.

The build uses `crt-static` through `tests/windows-probes/.cargo/config.toml`. The single exe then runs on a bare Windows VM without the Visual C++ runtime. The release profile uses `opt-level = "z"`, `lto`, `strip`, and `panic = "abort"`. Copy the exe to the VM with `scp`, and run it there by hand.

The exe has these roles:

| Command | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `winprobe setup` | Creates the probe users `OstraProbeA` and `OstraProbeB`, the ACL test tree, and per-user firewall filters under `C:\ostra-probe`. |
| `winprobe run` | Runs elevated. It starts confined probes, runs host-side checks, and writes `C:\ostra-probe\results.md`. It needs the password file from `setup`. |
| `winprobe cleanup` | Removes everything that `setup` created. |
| `winprobe asuser <group> <out>` | The confined role. It runs one check group as a probe user. |

The helper roles `markself`, `medspawn`, `sleeper`, `openone`, `spinjob`, and `netfilter` are small programs that the other roles start.

Each check writes a finding with one of four statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `PASS` | The assumption of the design held. |
| `FAIL` | A gap that the Windows sandbox must handle. |
| `INCONCLUSIVE` | The VM cannot decide the check. |
| `NEEDS_CLIENT` | The check needs a Windows 11 client or the antivirus machine. |

The file `tests/windows-probes/results-full.md` keeps a recorded run on Windows Server 2025 build 26100. The checks have numbers from 1 to 17. They cover spawn as another user, restricted tokens, Job Object kill of a process tree, ACL reads and writes in the repo and under `.git`, hard links, network filters, process isolation, desktop access, registry writes, scheduled and WMI escapes, credential stores, ACL cost on a large tree, and antivirus reaction.

The recorded run has these FAIL results:

- Windows Firewall cannot limit loopback to the proxy port, because it does not filter loopback traffic. The design needs a raw WFP filter.
- Sibling processes that share one sandbox user can open each other. Restricting SIDs do not fix it. Isolation comes from one user for each execution slot.

The probes are research evidence. No part of `cargo test --workspace` runs them.

## Add a test

Pick the kind of test that matches the risk. Then follow its steps.

### Add a Rust unit test

1. Open the `#[cfg(test)]` module in the file you change. For `ostra-agents`, `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-exec-native`, and the documents of `ostra-core`, open `src/tests.rs` or `src/doc/tests.rs`.
2. Add a function with `#[test]`. For async code, use `#[tokio::test]`.
3. Name the function after the rule that it checks, for example `a_stored_compaction_replaces_the_messages_before_it`.
4. In `ostra-exec-native`, script the model with `ScriptedProvider` and its `push_tool_use` method. Do not call a real model.
5. In `ostra-sandbox`, start with `run_in` or check `backend()`, so that the test skips on a machine without a sandbox.
6. In `ostra-core` documents, start from `RESEARCH`, `SPEC`, `PLAN`, or `PROFILE`, and change one field to cause one error.
7. Run `cargo test -p <crate>`.

### Add a conformance fixture

1. Open `tests/conformance/main.rs` and find the section for your rule ID.
2. Start the test name with the rule ID, for example `d1_` or `p3_`.
3. Build the history with `H::new` or a helper such as `H::explored`.
4. Add events with `h.classify`, `h.start`, `h.finish`, `h.run`, `h.open_gate`, and `h.answer`.
5. Assert on `h.summaries()` or on `h.state()`.
6. Run `cargo test -p ostra-engine --test conformance`.

A fixture must not call a model or read a clock. The planner is pure, and the fixture must stay pure, so that it gives the same result on each run.

### Add a test stage eval case

1. Add a `[[case]]` to `tests/evals/test_stage.toml` with a unique `id`.
2. Put the change overlay in `tests/evals/test_stage/changes/<project>/<name>`.
3. Put the golden analysis in `tests/evals/test_stage/goldens/<name>/epa.md`. Put reference tests in `files/`.
4. Add one `[[case.mutant]]` for each behavior that a good test must catch.
5. Run `cargo test -p ostra-server --test test_stage_evals`. The offline replay must pass.
6. Run the live test with `-- --ignored` and `OSTRA_EVAL_CASES=<id>` to check the case on a model.

To add a case to another eval file, follow the placeholders and the field list in the header comment of that file.

### Add a browser spec

1. Add `tests/browser/specs/<name>.spec.ts`.
2. Import `test` and `expect` from `../lib/guard`, not from `@playwright/test`. The guard fixture then watches each page.
3. Make test strings with the helpers in `lib/payloads.ts`, for example `inline` and `markdown`. Each string must set `window.__pwned` or request a canary URL if it runs.
4. If the spec needs data, add it to `tests/browser/global-setup.ts`.
5. Run `npm run test:fast` in `tests/browser`.

### Add a web test

1. Add `<name>.test.ts` or `<name>.test.tsx` next to the code, under `web/src`.
2. Use the mock fixtures in the files `fixtures.ts`, `fixtures.agents.ts`, `fixtures.books.ts`, `fixtures.documents.ts`, `fixtures.execution.ts`, `fixtures.projects.ts`, `fixtures.session.ts`, and `fixtures.workspace.ts` in `web/src/api/mock/`.
3. For a screen, render it in a memory router and call `settle`, as `web/src/App.test.tsx` does.
4. Run `npm test` in `web`.

## Limits of the tests

The tests do not prove that the system is safe. These limits apply:

- The sandbox tests skip on a machine that has no backend, so a green run on that machine says nothing about enforcement.
- The evals run on live models and give pass rates, not guarantees.
- The browser suite runs on Chromium on Unix only.
- The Windows probes ran on one Server 2025 VM. The results list checks that stay `INCONCLUSIVE` or `NEEDS_CLIENT`.
- `cargo test --workspace` does not run the web tests, the browser suite, the live evals, or the Windows probes.

sections.title: Reference: workspace settings and paths
sections.summary: Lists every workspace setting key with its type, default, store, and effect. It also covers the global config keys, a sample workspace.toml, save-time limits, and the path, pricing, MCP name, and git constants of ostra-core.
sections.body:
Ostra keeps settings in four stores, and a setting has an effect only in the store that owns it. A reader who edits the wrong store sees no change. This page maps each setting to its store, gives its type, default, and effect, and lists the named constants of `ostra-core` that a reader can look up: config limits, paths, prices, MCP names, git overrides, and a few small helpers.

The page covers these parts:

- The four stores and the environment variables that move them.
- The 29 keys of `SETTING_KEYS`, and the seeded defaults of a new workspace.
- A sample `workspace.toml`.
- Project entries, code providers, and language servers.
- MCP server settings and name limits.
- The global `config.toml`, including the default tier tables.
- Save-time validation limits.
- Path constants, derived paths, and protected credential paths.
- Pricing constants, git constants, and other core constants.

The page stops before the behavior of each setting at run time. [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) explains how Ostra routes, validates, approves, and saves settings. [Sandbox](sandbox.md), [Policy engine](policy-guards.md), and [Integrations](integrations.md) explain what the sandbox, permission, and MCP settings do.

## Where each setting lives

Ostra reads settings from four stores. The registry holds the settings that a folder file must not control. This rule is Rule A2 in `crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs`. Without it, a repository could lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session.

| Store | Location | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global config | The path in `OSTRA_CONFIG`, else `ostra/config.toml` in the config folder of the operating system | `tool_enforcement`, `providers`, `tiers`, `harness`, `permissions`, `server`, `sandbox` |
| Workspace file | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml` | Settings that a team can share: name, projects, routing, instructions, permission rules, notifications, MCP servers |
| Registry | `<data dir>/registry.db`, under the key `workspace_access:<root>` | The 10 settings that a folder file cannot set. The catalog below marks them with 11 `registry` rows, because the setting `limits` covers two keys |
| Project profile | `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | Stack, commands, module map, skills, and review rules. The initializer agent generates it |

The `registry` settings are `permissions.mode`, `yolo.default`, `limits`, `sandbox_mode`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, and `sandbox_blocked_ports`. The setting `limits` covers two keys: `limits.max_parallel_executions` and `limits.session_budget_usd`. Each key has its own row in the catalog, so the catalog has 11 `registry` rows for 10 settings. The function `write_file` removes the 10 settings from the TOML before it saves the file. The function `overlay` puts the registry values back each time Ostra reads the settings. A value for one of them in `workspace.toml` has no effect.

### Environment variables that move the stores

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG` | Full path of the global `config.toml`. `global_config_path` returns it unchanged |
| `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` | The data folder. It holds `registry.db`, the master key file, and the server log. The default is the `ostra` folder in the local data folder of the operating system |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | The path of a master key file. `secret_paths` adds it to the paths that no agent reads |

### What happens when

- **A TOML file does not exist.** `load_toml` returns the default value. Every key that the file omits also takes its default, because the structs use `#[serde(default)]`.
- **A TOML file does not parse.** `load_toml` returns `ConfigError::Parse` with the path and the parser message. A read failure other than a missing file returns `ConfigError::Io`.
- **Ostra saves a TOML file.** `save_toml` writes `<name>.toml.tmp` and renames it over the target, so a reader never sees half a file.

## Workspace settings catalog

The constant `SETTING_KEYS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` lists 29 dotted keys of `WorkspaceSettings`, each with a one-line description. The workspace search uses the list. The test `setting_keys_name_fields` checks that each key names a field of the serialized seeded settings. The key names `byAgent` and `byPhaseComplexity` use camel case. All other key names use snake case.

| Key | Type | Default | Store | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | `workspace` for `WorkspaceSettings::default()`, else the name that `seeded` receives | file | The workspace name. Validation refuses an empty name |
| `projects` | array of tables | `[]` | file | One entry per project. See the projects part below |
| `routing.executor` | table | empty | file | Parent of the two executor tables. An agent with no executor route runs on `native` |
| `routing.executor.byAgent` | table: agent to executor | empty | file | Executor per agent |
| `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` | table: agent to complexity to executor | empty | file | Executor per agent and phase complexity. It wins over `byAgent` |
| `routing.model` | table | seeded | file | Parent of the two model tables |
| `routing.model.byAgent` | table: agent to model choice | 13 seeded entries | file | Model or tier per agent |
| `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity` | table: agent to complexity to model choice | `implementer` and `write-test` | file | Model or tier per agent and phase complexity. It wins over `byAgent` |
| `routing.effort` | table | empty | file | Parent of the two effort tables |
| `routing.effort.byAgent` | table: agent to effort | empty | file | Reasoning effort per agent. It replaces the default of the agent definition. A flat table of agent to effort, the older form, reads as `byAgent` |
| `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity` | table: agent to complexity to effort | empty | file | Reasoning effort per agent and phase complexity. It wins over `byAgent` |
| `instructions.all` | string | none | file | Text that every agent receives. Ostra skips an empty or blank value |
| `instructions.agents` | table: agent to string | empty | file | Text for one agent. Ostra adds it after `instructions.all` |
| `yolo.default` | boolean | `false` | registry | Starts each new session in YOLO mode |
| `permissions.mode` | enum | `default` | registry | Permission mode for tool calls |
| `permissions.allow` | array of rule strings | `[]` | file | Tool calls that run without asking |
| `permissions.ask` | array of rule strings | `[]` | file | Tool calls that always ask |
| `permissions.deny` | array of rule strings | `[]` | file | Tool calls that Ostra always refuses |
| `notifications.push` | boolean | `true` | file | Sends a push notification for gates and finished sessions |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | integer, 1 or more | `3` | registry | Executions that can run at the same time in the workspace. Other spawns wait |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | number, 0 or more | `25.0` | registry | Dollars that one session can spend before it pauses for a decision. `0` means no limit |
| `sandbox_mode` | enum or none | none | registry | Sandbox mode of this workspace in place of the global mode. None follows the global mode |
| `tool_enforcement` | enum or none | none | registry | Whether guards check where tool calls read and write, in place of the global choice |
| `sandbox_network` | enum or none | none | registry | What sandboxed commands can reach, in place of the global choice |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | array of strings | `[]` | registry | More hosts for the egress proxy. Ostra adds them to the global list and never removes a global or built-in host |
| `sandbox_decoys` | array of `~/...` paths | `[]` | registry | More decoy credential files in agent sandboxes. The built-in decoys stay |
| `sandbox_loopback` | enum | `open` | registry | Which loopback ports sandboxed commands on macOS can connect to |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | array of port numbers | `[]` | registry | Loopback ports that sandboxed commands on macOS never connect to |
| `mcp_servers` | array of tables | `[]` | file | External MCP servers whose tools agents can use. See the MCP part below |

### Allowed values

| Value set | Members |
| --- | --- |
| Agent keys | The 14 `AgentName` values: `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`, `advisor` |
| Route keys | The 14 agent keys and `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`). Model and executor routes use route keys |
| Retired agent key | `module-documentation` (`RETIRED_AGENTS`). Validation accepts it in a route table and ignores it |
| Executor | `native`, or `harness:claude`, `harness:codex`, `harness:grok`, `harness:agy` |
| Tier | `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, `frontier` |
| Model choice | A tier, the word `default`, a concrete model, or a per-executor table such as `{ native = "anthropic:x", codex = "gpt-y" }` |
| Effort | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` |
| Complexity | `low`, `medium`, `high`. Work with no phase file counts as `low` |
| `permissions.mode` | `default` asks for edits and unlisted commands. `acceptEdits` allows edits inside the project. `plan` is read-only. `bypass` asks nothing |
| `sandbox_mode` | `auto` sandboxes when the machine can, else runs unsandboxed with a warning. `required` refuses an execution that cannot run in the sandbox. `off` turns the sandbox off |
| `sandbox_network` | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, `host`. See the global `[sandbox]` part below |
| `sandbox_loopback` | `open`, `listed`. See the global `[sandbox]` part below |
| `tool_enforcement` | `disabled`, `enabled` |

The agents `implementer` and `write-test` are the only agents that route by phase complexity (`routes_by_complexity`). A native model is written `<provider>:<model>`. The providers that validation accepts are `anthropic`, `openai`, and `mock`.

### What happens when

- **A changed `workspace.toml` waits for approval.** The function `effective` disables every MCP server, drops each code provider and language server, clears `permissions.allow`, and removes projects outside the workspace folder. The other settings stay in force. See [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md).
- **`workspace.toml` does not parse.** The runtime logs a warning and uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`.
- **A route key has no model route.** Validation reports it. The value `default` fixes it, because every agent has a default tier. This case happens when a new agent ships and a workspace saved before it has no entry.

## Seeded defaults of a new workspace

A new workspace starts from `WorkspaceSettings::seeded(name)`, and `WorkspaceSettings::default()` calls it with the name `workspace`. Seeded settings route every one of the 15 route keys, so a new workspace passes route validation without edits. Every key that the tables below do not name takes the default of the catalog above.

The seeded `routing.model.byAgent` table has 13 entries:

| Tier | Agents |
| --- | --- |
| `advanced` | `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `judge`, `advisor` |
| `balanced` | `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer` |

The seeded `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity` table has two entries, `implementer` and `write-test`. Both use `fast` for `low`, `fast` for `medium`, and `balanced` for `high`.

The setup wizard can replace the executor routes with a preset (`RoutingPreset` in `crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs`). The preset `native` routes every agent to the native executor. The presets `codex` and `claude` route the agents in `RoutingPreset::HARNESS_AGENTS` (`implementer` and `write-test`) to `harness:codex` or `harness:claude`. A preset clears the executor routes first and keeps the model routes, because tiers resolve per executor.

## Sample workspace.toml

The sample below comes from the constant `SAMPLE` in the unit tests of `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`. The test `parses_sample_and_routes` parses it and resolves routes from it.

```toml
name = "shop"

[[projects]]
key = "backend"
path = "/home/me/code/shop-backend"

[routing.executor.byAgent]
implementer = "harness:codex"
write-test = "harness:codex"

[routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "harness:codex"
medium = "harness:codex"
high = "native"

[routing.model.byAgent]
explore = "advanced"
plan = "advanced"
code-reviewer = "balanced"
judge = "advanced"
quick-answer = { native = "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5" }
# ... the other agents of the seeded table

[routing.model.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "fast"
medium = "fast"
high = "balanced"

[instructions]
all = "Write British English in comments and docs."

[instructions.agents]
implementer = "Keep functions under 40 lines."

[permissions]
allow = ["Bash(./mvnw *)"]
deny = ["Bash(git push *)"]
```

The real fixture lists every seeded agent in `[routing.model.byAgent]` except `advisor`. It also sets `[yolo] default = false`, `[permissions] mode = "default"`, and a `write-test` table by phase complexity. The excerpt above leaves those lines out.

These facts follow from the fixture and the route rules:

- `implementer` with no complexity counts as `low`. It resolves to the executor `harness:codex` and the model `gpt-5.6-luna`, the `fast` model of the `codex` tier table.
- `implementer` with `high` complexity resolves to the executor `native` and the model `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5`, the `balanced` model of the `native` tier table.
- `quick-answer` uses a per-executor table. On the native executor it resolves to `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5`.
- The `[yolo]` table and the `mode` line have no effect in the file. The registry owns them, and Ostra removes them when it saves the file.
- The fixture has no `advisor` route. Save-time validation reports it, and the value `default` fixes it.

## Project entries, code providers, and language servers

Each `[[projects]]` entry names one project folder. Ostra checks the entry when the user saves settings, so a bad entry is a settings error at save time and not a failure at spawn time.

| Field | Type | Default | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | string | required | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. It starts with a letter or digit (`is_project_key`). Each key is unique in the workspace |
| `path` | path | required | Absolute. On Windows a rooted path with no drive also counts, so configs stay portable between operating systems |
| `stack` | string | none | Free text, trimmed, 1 to `MAX_STACK_LEN` (64) characters, with no control character. An empty value is valid, and the initializer then detects the stack from the code |
| `code_provider` | table | none | An external program that answers code navigation for the Files view in place of the built-in index |
| `language_servers` | array of tables | `[]` | Language Server Protocol servers. They answer after `code_provider` and before the built-in index |

`[projects.code_provider]` has two fields. `command` is the program and its arguments, and Ostra runs it in the project folder for each request. The program reads one JSON request on stdin and writes the answer on stdout. `timeout_secs` defaults to `10`.

`[[projects.language_servers]]` has four fields. `command` is the program and its arguments, for example `["rust-analyzer"]`. `languages` lists the language ids that the server answers for. `timeout_secs` defaults to `10`. `initialization_options` is an optional value that Ostra sends as `initializationOptions` in the `initialize` request.

| Limit | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` | 120 seconds | Highest `timeout_secs` for a code provider or a language server. The lowest value is 1 |
| `default_provider_timeout` | 10 seconds | Default `timeout_secs` for both |
| `MAX_STACK_LEN` | 64 characters | Longest project stack |
| `NAV_LANGUAGES` | 16 ids | The valid values of `languages`: `rust`, `typescript`, `javascript`, `python`, `go`, `java`, `kotlin`, `scala`, `csharp`, `swift`, `php`, `c`, `cpp`, `ruby`, `lua`, `shell` |

A language id can appear in one server only, because each file asks one server. When a request takes longer than `timeout_secs`, Ostra answers with the built-in provider. Validation also requires that the first item of `command` is not empty. [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) explains the provider layers.

## MCP server settings and name limits

An external MCP server adds tools that every executor can call. The module `crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs` owns the tool names and the save-time checks. Each `[[mcp_servers]]` entry sets `command` for a local server that Ostra starts over stdio, or `url` for a remote server over streamable HTTP. [Integrations](integrations.md) explains the client and the sign-in flow.

| Field | Type | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | required | The server name. See the limits below |
| `enabled` | boolean | `true` | A disabled server serves no agent |
| `command` | array of strings | `[]` | Program and arguments of a local server. Ostra runs it in the workspace root |
| `env` | table of strings | empty | Environment of a local server |
| `url` | string | none | An `http://` or `https://` address of a remote server |
| `headers` | table of strings | empty | Headers for a remote server |
| `oauth.client_id` | string | none | A client that the user registered with the authorization server |
| `oauth.client_secret_env` | string | none | The environment variable that holds the client secret |
| `oauth.scopes` | array of strings | `[]` | Scopes to request. Empty means the scopes that the server advertises |
| `disabled_tools` | array of strings | `[]` | Tools that Ostra does not offer. It offers every other tool that the server lists |
| `agents` | array of agent names | `[]` | Agents that get the tools. Empty means every agent |
| `timeout_secs` | integer | `120` | Seconds that one tool call can take |

A value of `env` or `headers` can name the environment of Ostra as `${VAR}`, so a secret stays out of the file. A literal secret typed in the console goes to the encrypted registry, and the file holds the text `${ostra_secret}` in its place (`SAVED_SECRET`). The function `is_literal_value` finds a literal: a value that is not blank, is not `SAVED_SECRET`, and has no `${`. The function `expand_env` returns `ExpandError::Unset` for a variable that is not set. It returns `ExpandError::Refused` for a variable that holds a credential that Ostra keeps from MCP servers.

### Name and timeout limits

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PREFIX` | `mcp__` | Start of a canonical tool name |
| `SEPARATOR` | `__` | Splits the server from the tool. It is safe because server names never contain `__` |
| `MAX_SERVER_NAME` | 24 characters | Longest server name |
| `MAX_BARE_NAME` | 52 characters | Longest bare tool name. Harnesses add the prefix `mcp__ostra__` (12 characters), and providers cap a tool name at 64 characters |
| `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS` | 600 seconds | Highest `timeout_secs`. The lowest value is 1 |
| `SAVED_SECRET` | `${ostra_secret}` | The text in the file in place of a stored literal value |

The function `is_server_name` accepts a name that has 1 to 24 characters and starts with a lowercase letter. It checks each character, and each character must be a lowercase letter, a digit, or a dash. Thus the function accepts any run of dashes, for example `a--b` or a trailing dash. The validation message says `lowercase letters, digits, and dashes`. A server name never contains `__`, because an underscore is not an allowed character. The name `ostra` is reserved for the own MCP server of Ostra.

### Three spellings of one tool

The tool `create_issue` of the workspace server `github` has three names:

| Spelling | Value | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare name | `github__create_issue` | The MCP server of Ostra. Its own tools never contain `__` |
| Harness name | `mcp__ostra__github__create_issue` | A harness CLI that reaches the tool through Ostra |
| Canonical name | `mcp__github__create_issue` | The native loop, the policy, and permission rules. It is the spelling of Claude Code |

#### Flow of bare_name

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["bare_name(server, tool)"] --> B{"Tool uses only letters, digits, _ and -, and the name is 52 characters or fewer?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Return server__tool"]
  B -- no --> D["Replace each other character with _"]
  D --> E["Cut the tool part so that the whole name fits in 52 characters"]
  E --> F["Return server__tool_hhhhhhhh"]
```

The 8 characters `hhhhhhhh` are hexadecimal digits of an FNV-1a hash of the original tool name. The hash makes sure that two tools never share a bare name. For example, `docs` with `search.pages/v2` gives a name that starts with `docs__search_pages_v2_`.

### What happens when

- **A server sets both `command` and `url`, or neither.** Validation reports the entry.
- **A local server sets `headers` or `oauth`.** Validation reports the entry, because both apply to remote servers only.
- **`agents` names an unknown agent.** Validation reports `<name> is not an agent.`
- **Two servers share a name.** Validation reports `Server name <name> is used twice.`
- **`timeout_secs` is 0 or above 600.** Validation reports `Use a timeout from 1 to 600 seconds.`

## Global config.toml catalog

The global config holds machine-wide choices. `GlobalConfig` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs` is its typed form. A missing key takes the default in the table.

| Key | Type | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tool_enforcement` | `disabled` or `enabled` | `disabled` | Whether guards check where tool calls read and write. See the note below |
| `providers.<name>` | table | `anthropic` and `openai` | Where Ostra finds the credentials of a native provider |
| `tiers.<table>` | table | `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy` | The model for each tier, per executor table |
| `harness.<kind>` | table | one per harness kind | The command and arguments that start a harness CLI |
| `permissions` | table | `deny = ["Bash(rm -rf /*)"]` | Global allow, ask, and deny rules |
| `server` | table | see below | Listen address, port, and allowed host names |
| `sandbox` | table | see below | The sandbox profile for agent commands |

A workspace can replace `tool_enforcement`, and the sandbox `mode` and `network`. The workspace function `enforces_tool_calls` returns the workspace value, or the global value when the workspace sets none. With `disabled`, an agent can reach files by any route, such as one script that edits several files. The secret-read, git-metadata, state-ownership, artifact-ownership, and no-tests guards still apply, and so do the workflow gates, the permission rules, and the sandbox. With `enabled`, Ostra adds the write scope, the report path, self-protection, and the shell and interpreter checks behind them. This is Rule G1. [Policy engine](policy-guards.md) explains each guard.

### Providers

Each `[providers.<name>]` table has five optional fields.

| Field | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `api_key_env` | The environment variable that holds the API key |
| `auth_token_env` | The environment variable that holds a bearer token. Ostra sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` when no API key is set. Gateways and proxies use this form |
| `keychain_service` | The OS keychain service to read the key from when the variables are not set |
| `base_url` | Overrides the API base URL for tests and proxies. It wins over the variable and the saved URL |
| `base_url_env` | The environment variable that holds the base URL, used when `base_url` is not set. It wins over the URL that the user saved in the browser |

The default `anthropic` provider reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. The default `openai` provider reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`. A credential that the user enters in the browser goes to the registry (`SavedCredentials`: `base_url`, `api_key`, `auth_token`), not to `config.toml`. The variables named in the provider table override the saved values. The `Debug` output of `SavedCredentials` masks the key and the token as `***`. [Native executor and model providers](native-executor.md) and [Server security](server-security.md) explain the lookup and the storage.

### Default tier tables

A tier name in a model route resolves through the table of the executor that runs the agent. A route to a tier with no entry in the table is a validation error.

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

### Harness commands

Each `[harness.<kind>]` table has `command` and `args`. The default `command` is the kind name: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`. The default `args` list is empty. Ostra adds `args` to every launch. The function `harness_command` returns the kind name when `command` is empty. [Harness executors](harness-executors.md) explains the launch.

### Permissions

`[permissions]` has the lists `allow`, `ask`, and `deny`. The only default rule is a deny rule for `Bash(rm -rf /*)`. Ostra merges the scopes in this order: global, workspace, session. The lists of the scopes concatenate.

### Server

| Key | Type | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `server.port` | integer | none | A fixed port. None means that Ostra picks a free port |
| `server.bind` | string | none | The listen address. None means `127.0.0.1`. The values `0.0.0.0` and `::` listen on every interface, for remote access |
| `server.allowed_hosts` | array of strings | `[]` | More host names that the browser can use, such as the domain of a reverse proxy. Ostra allows each local interface address and the machine host name by itself when it listens on all interfaces |
| `server.use_ip_host` | boolean | `false` | Signs in at `127.0.0.1` in place of a private `*.localhost` name, for a browser that does not resolve `*.localhost`. The session cookie then reaches every other port on the machine, because cookies are not scoped to a port |

[Running Ostra](running-ostra.md) lists the matching command-line flags.

### Sandbox

| Key | Type | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sandbox.mode` | `auto`, `required`, `off` | `required` on Linux and macOS, `auto` on Windows | Whether agent commands run in the sandbox. Windows has no sandbox backend yet, so `required` there refuses every execution |
| `sandbox.network` | `none`, `allowlist`, `public`, `host` | `allowlist` | What sandboxed programs can reach |
| `sandbox.allowed_hosts` | array of strings | `[]` | More hosts that the egress proxy allows under `allowlist`: `host`, `*.domain`, or either with `:port`. A listed host can resolve to a private address |
| `sandbox.upstream_proxy` | string | none | An HTTP proxy in the form `http://host:port`, for a machine that reaches the internet only through one |
| `sandbox.extra_writable` | array of paths | `[]` | More paths that agent commands can write. Use absolute paths or `~/...` |
| `sandbox.extra_hidden` | array of paths | `[]` | More paths that agent commands cannot see. Use absolute paths or `~/...` |

The fields `loopback` and `blocked_ports` of `SandboxConfig` are never read from `config.toml`, because they are workspace settings only.

The network values mean this: `none` gives no network, but a harness CLI still reaches its own model API. `allowlist` allows package registries, source hosts, the model API of a harness, and `allowed_hosts`. `public` allows any public address and refuses loopback, private, and link-local addresses. `host` uses the host network without a filter. Each choice except `host` gives each sandbox its own network namespace, and traffic leaves only through the egress proxy of Ostra.

The loopback values apply to macOS, where every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. `open` allows every port except the blocked ports and the port of the Ostra server, so tests reach the servers that they start. It applies under `allowlist` and `public` only. `listed` allows only the loopback ports in `allowed_hosts`. On Linux each sandbox has its own loopback, so the value changes nothing.

The function `SandboxConfig::for_workspace` merges a workspace into the global config. The workspace `mode` and `network` replace the global values when the workspace sets them. The workspace hosts join the global hosts, and the merge skips a host that the global list already has. The workspace `loopback` and `blocked_ports` apply unchanged. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) explains how each backend enforces the profile.

### Credential variables that agents never see

Two constants list environment variables that Ostra keeps from agent processes and MCP servers.

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | The variables that the default providers read |
| `BRIDGE_ENV` | `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_HARNESS` | The variables that give a harness or MCP child its own execution identity. A child inherits them from Ostra only by accident, so Ostra drops them and sets them again |

The function `credential_env_names` builds the full set. It joins `DEFAULT_CREDENTIAL_ENV`, `BRIDGE_ENV`, the `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, and `base_url_env` of each `providers.*` table, and the `oauth.client_secret_env` of each MCP server. Empty names do not count.

## Save-time validation limits

The function `validate_workspace` returns every problem that it finds, not only the first. It sorts the issues by path and message and removes duplicates. Each issue has a dotted `path`, such as `routing.model.byAgent.plan`, and a `message`. The checks below run when the user saves settings.

| Path | Check | Limit or rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | The workspace has a name | Not empty after trimming |
| `projects[i].key` | Valid and unique | Pattern `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*` |
| `projects[i].path` | Absolute | A rooted path counts |
| `projects[i].stack` | Plain text | 64 characters at most, no control character |
| `projects[i].code_provider.timeout_secs` | In range | 1 to 120 seconds |
| `projects[i].language_servers[j].languages` | Known ids, each id in one server | The 16 ids of `NAV_LANGUAGES` |
| `routing.executor.byAgent.<key>` | The key is a route key or a retired agent | `judge` must not appear. Validation reports `Judge calls always run natively; remove this route.` The judge is an engine call and not an agent execution, so `resolve_executor` always returns `native` for it. `quick-answer` must be `native`. Validation reports `Quick answers run on the native executor only; remove this route.` for any other executor |
| `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` | The key is a route key or a retired agent | Each route key resolves on each complexity |
| `routing.effort.byAgent.<key>` | The key is an agent or a retired agent | `judge` is not an agent here |
| `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity.<key>` | The agent runs per phase | `implementer` and `write-test` only |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | At least one | 1 or more |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | A finite dollar amount | 0 or more. 0 means no limit |
| `mcp_servers[i]` | See the MCP part | `timeout_secs` from 1 to 600 |

The route check runs each route key on each complexity that applies. It then adds two machine checks. A route to a harness that is not installed is an issue. A native route to a provider with no usable key is an issue, except for the `mock` provider. A native model that does not have the form `<provider>:<model>` is also an issue. Validation reflects the machine at save time, so a harness or a key that is gone later can still fail a spawn.

## Path constants and derived paths

The module `crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs` derives every path of Ostra. A reader and a writer of the same state both call it, so both resolve the same file. [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) shows the folder layout in context. [Storage](storage.md) explains the files.

### Constants

| Constant | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RUNTIME_DIR` | `.ostra` | The runtime folder of a workspace and of a project |
| `SKILLS_DIR` | `.agents/skills` | Where Ostra writes each new project skill. It follows the cross-harness `.agents` standard |
| `LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR` | `.ostra/skills` | A skills folder that Ostra still reads and never writes |
| `SKILL_DIRS` | `.agents/skills`, then `.ostra/skills` | The lookup order for project skills. `find_project_skill` returns the first match |
| `INSTRUCTION_FILES` | `claude.md`, `agents.md`, `agent.md` | Instruction files at a project root. Ostra matches them in any letter case and returns them in this order |
| `ARTIFACT_PREFIX` | `ostra-` | The prefix of artifact file names |
| `HOME_CREDENTIALS` | A list of paths under `$HOME` | Credential stores and personal data that no agent reads |
| `RESERVED_NAMES` | Windows device names | Names that open a device. See below |

### Derived paths

| Function | Path |
| --- | --- |
| `global_config_path` | `OSTRA_CONFIG`, else `<config dir>/ostra/config.toml` |
| `data_dir` | `OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, else `<local data dir>/ostra` |
| `registry_db_path` | `<data dir>/registry.db` |
| `workspace_runtime` | `<workspace>/.ostra` |
| `workspace_toml` | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml` |
| `workspace_db` | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` |
| `sessions_root` | `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions` |
| `upload_staging` | `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads`. Uploads wait here until a session or an addition claims them |
| `session_root` | `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>`. Cross-project artifacts live here |
| `session_uploads` | `<session root>/uploads` |
| `session_project_dir` | `<session root>/<project key>`. Per-project reports live here |
| `session_state_dir` | `<session root>/.state`. The engine owns it and no agent writes there |
| `harness_execution_dir` | `<session root>/.state/harness/<execution>`. It holds the hook config, the MCP registration, and the terminal transcript |
| `terminal_transcript` | `<harness execution dir>/terminal.log`. The raw PTY bytes, kept so that an ended run can be replayed |
| `project_runtime` | `<project>/.ostra` |
| `project_inventory` | `<project>/.ostra/INVENTORY.md` |
| `project_profile` | `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` |
| `project_skills_dir` | `<project>/.agents/skills` |
| `project_memory_db` | `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` |

### Report file names

The module `paths::report` names every report, so that later stages can predict each name. Here `N` is a phase number.

| Function | File name |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer` | `ostra-implementer-phase-N.md` |
| `implementer_progress` | `ostra-implementer-progress-phase-N.md` |
| `epa` | `ostra-epa-phase-N.md` |
| `write_test` | `ostra-write-test-phase-N.md` |
| `docs_request` | `ostra-docs-request.md`. The engine writes it when no implementer ran |
| `docs_parts` | `ostra-docs-parts.json`. The engine writes it for the architecture agent |
| `prompt_gen(n)` | `ostra-prompt-gen-<n>.md` |
| `completion` | `ostra-completion.md` |
| `test_request` | `ostra-test-request.md` |
| `session_context` | `ostra-session-context.md`. It holds the request, every artifact path, and each feedback round |
| `review_ledger` | `ostra-review-ledger-phase-<v>.md` when the phase value is `N` or `N-tests`, else `ostra-review-ledger.md` |
| `security_sentinel` | `ostra-security-block.json` |

### Owner-only files and folders

`ensure_data_dir` creates the data folder, or tightens an existing one, to mode `0700` on Unix. The folder holds the registry with saved credentials, and SQLite creates its `-wal` and `-shm` files world-readable. `create_private_dir_all` and `create_private_dir` create folders with mode `0700`. `private_file_options` creates files with mode `0600`. `restrict_to_owner` sets `0600` for a file or `0700` for a folder. On Windows a new folder or file inherits the ACL of its parent, which under the profile of the user grants only that user, SYSTEM, and administrators.

### Credential paths that no agent reads

The policy refuses tool calls that name a path in `HOME_CREDENTIALS`. The sandbox hides these paths, and Grep and Glob skip them. The function `secret_paths(home)` adds the data folder and the file in `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`. Each entry is relative to `$HOME`.

| Group | Entries |
| --- | --- |
| Developer tools | `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `.azure`, `.config/gcloud`, `.kube`, `.docker`, `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `.config/hub`, `.cargo/credentials`, `.cargo/credentials.toml`, `.pypirc`, `.vault-token`, `.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json` |
| Linux desktop | `.local/share/keyrings`, `.password-store`, `.Xauthority` |
| Browsers on Linux | `.mozilla`, `.config/google-chrome`, `.config/chromium`, `.config/BraveSoftware` |
| macOS | `Library/Keychains`, `Library/Cookies`, `Library/HTTPStorages`, `Library/Safari`, `Library/Group Containers`, `Library/Containers`, `Library/Messages`, `Library/Mail`, and under `Library/Application Support`: `Google/Chrome`, `Chromium`, `BraveSoftware`, `Microsoft Edge`, `Arc`, `Firefox`, `com.apple.TCC`, `Code/User/globalStorage` |
| Windows | `_netrc`, `AppData/Roaming/gcloud`, `AppData/Roaming/GitHub CLI`, `AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Protect`, `AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Credentials`, `AppData/Local/Microsoft/Credentials`, `AppData/Local/Google/Chrome/User Data`, `AppData/Local/Microsoft/Edge/User Data`, `AppData/Local/BraveSoftware`, `AppData/Roaming/Mozilla/Firefox`, `AppData/Roaming/Code/User/globalStorage`, and the PowerShell history file `AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/PowerShell/PSReadLine/ConsoleHost_history.txt` |

Five entries belong to a harness CLI. The `harness` field names the one program that can see the file, because that CLI signs in with it.

| Entry | Harness |
| --- | --- |
| `.claude/.credentials.json` | Claude Code |
| `.codex/auth.json` | Codex |
| `.grok/auth.json` | Grok Build |
| `.gemini/oauth_creds.json` | Antigravity |
| `.gemini/google_accounts.json` | Antigravity |

### Windows device names

`RESERVED_NAMES` lists the names that open a device under any extension and in any folder: `con`, `prn`, `aux`, `com1` to `com9`, the superscript forms `com¹`, `com²`, `com³`, `lpt1` to `lpt9`, the superscript forms `lpt¹`, `lpt²`, `lpt³`, `conin$`, and `conout$`. The function `is_reserved_device` returns true when the last component of a path has one of these names as its stem, for example `COM1.txt` or `lpt1 .log`. It returns false for `NUL` and always returns false on Unix.

### Path helpers that guards use

| Function | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `normalize` | Resolves `.` and `..` in the text of a path and does not touch the file system |
| `resolve` | Resolves a target against a working folder in the way that the kernel does. It follows each link before a later `..` applies, so a link cannot make a path look inside a root when the write lands outside it |
| `is_inside` | True when one path is the other path or lies beneath it. On Windows the compare ignores letter case |
| `fold` | The form of a path that guards compare. On Windows it folds case, separators, and the `\\?\` prefix |
| `strip_verbatim` | Removes the `\\?\` prefix that `canonicalize` returns on Windows |
| `windows_path_problem` | Names why a path is not a plain drive path: an NT object path, a device path, a share path, a drive-relative path, or an alternate data stream. It returns none on Unix |
| `dot_dot_after_link` | True on Windows when a `..` follows a link, because Win32 programs and Git Bash resolve it differently |
| `from_msys` | On Windows, turns a Git Bash path such as `/c/Users/me` into `C:\Users\me`, and `/tmp` into the temp folder |
| `link` | A symlink on Unix. On Windows a junction for a folder, and for a file a symlink, else a hard link, else a copy |

## Pricing constants

The module `crates/ostra-core/src/pricing.rs` computes `Usage::cost_usd` from a price catalog. Until the server installs a catalog, every cost is 0. [Workspaces, projects, and settings](workspaces-and-settings.md) explains the catalog refresh and the session budget. [Reference: server, code, store, and notify limits](reference-server-limits.md) lists the refresh timings.

| Name | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MODELS_DEV_URL` | `https://models.dev/api.json` | The source of prices, context windows, and output limits |
| `WEB_SEARCH_USD` | 0.01 dollars | Cost of one server-side web search, on both providers |
| `FIRST_PARTY` | `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `mistral`, `deepseek` | Providers whose listing wins when resellers list the same model id at other prices |
| `CATALOG` | A shared `RwLock` that holds the installed catalog | `install` replaces it. `price`, `context_window`, and `max_output` read it |

All rates are dollars per million tokens. The struct `Rates` holds `input`, `output`, `cache_read`, `cache_write` (5-minute writes), and `cache_write_1h`. The catalog fills missing values with these defaults:

- `cache_read` defaults to the `input` rate.
- `cache_write` defaults to 1.25 times the `input` rate.
- `cache_write_1h` is 2 times the `input` rate for Anthropic. Other providers have one write lifetime, so it equals `cache_write`. This is because models.dev lists only the 5-minute write.

A model can have context tiers. A tier replaces the base rates when the prompt has more tokens than the tier size. The prompt size counts input, cache reads, and cache writes. The compare is strict, so a prompt of exactly 272,000 tokens uses the base rates when the tier size is 272,000.

`Catalog::price` finds a model in three steps. It accepts an id with or without a `provider:` prefix.

1. Find an exact id in the hinted provider, then in each `FIRST_PARTY` provider.
2. Else find the longest first-party id that is a prefix of the model id and is followed by `-`. A dated snapshot such as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` then takes the price of its base id. The id `claude-opus-50` does not match `claude-opus-5`.
3. Else find an exact id in any provider, in sorted order of provider name.

The function `cost(model, usage, web_searches)` adds the parts of one response. The block below is a simplified form of its arithmetic, and it is not the source code. The real function reads `usage.input_tokens`, `usage.cache_read_tokens`, and the other fields of `Usage`. It casts each field to `f64` and divides by a local value `m` of `1_000_000.0`. The block writes `1e6` and short names for the fields. The arithmetic is the same.

```rust
let r = p.rates(input + cache_read + cache_write);
let write_1h = cache_write_1h.min(cache_write);
input * r.input / 1e6
  + output * r.output / 1e6
  + cache_read * r.cache_read / 1e6
  + (cache_write - write_1h) * r.cache_write / 1e6
  + write_1h * r.cache_write_1h / 1e6
  + web_searches * WEB_SEARCH_USD
```

`input_tokens` excludes cache reads and writes. Each provider and each harness transcript reader normalizes usage to that form before it calls `cost`.

### What happens when

- **No catalog is installed.** `price` returns none and every cost is 0.
- **A model is not in the catalog.** Its cost is 0, so the session budget does not count it.
- **A model lacks an input price or an output price.** `Catalog::from_models_dev` leaves it out.
- **A model lists a context window or output limit of 0.** The catalog ignores that limit.

## Git constants in core

A repository `.git/config` is written by whoever controls the folder, and an agent can write it. The module `crates/ostra-core/src/git.rs` therefore overrides the config keys that make git start a program. Without these overrides, a planted config could run code when Ostra lists files, shows a diff, or stages a file.

| Constant | Value | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NO_EXEC` | `-c core.fsmonitor=false -c protocol.ext.allow=never -c core.askPass=` | Every git command that Ostra starts. It blocks the fsmonitor program, the `ext::` transport, and the askpass program of a repository |
| `AUTOMATIC` | `NO_EXEC` plus `-c core.hooksPath=<empty folder>` | Git commands that Ostra runs without a request from the user: status, listings, diffs, and staging during review. It also turns hooks off |
| `AGENT_CONFIG` | `core.fsmonitor=false`, `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, `protocol.ext.allow=never` | Git commands that an agent process runs, such as the shell of a harness CLI or an MCP server. Hooks stay on, because agent commands commit with the hooks of the repository |
| `FILTER_QUERY` | `config --null --get-regexp ^filter\\..+\\.(clean\\|smudge\\|process)$` | The `git config` arguments that list the filter drivers that a repository names |
| `LFS_DRIVERS` | `git-lfs clean -- %f`, `git-lfs smudge -- %f`, `git-lfs filter-process` | The standard git-lfs drivers. Ostra keeps them, so that LFS files do not all look modified |
| `MAX_FILTER_REPOS` | 256 | The most repositories that `blank_filters_of` reads for `filter_overrides` and `submodule_filter_overrides`. The cap bounds the git processes that Ostra starts, because each repository starts one or two. `git ls-files --stage -z` runs for every repository that the walk reads. The `git config` filter query runs only when Ostra blanks that repository. The submodule overrides exclude the root repository from the second query |

The empty hooks folder is `/dev/null` on Unix. On Windows it is the folder `<data dir>/no-hooks`, because Git for Windows reads `/dev/null/<hook>` as a path on the current drive, where any local user can create folders.

```rust
pub const NO_EXEC: &[&str] = &[
    "-c", "core.fsmonitor=false",
    "-c", "protocol.ext.allow=never",
    "-c", "core.askPass=",
];
```

### Filter drivers and submodules

The function `blank_filters` turns the output of `FILTER_QUERY` into `-c <key>=` pairs for every filter driver except git-lfs. A blank driver starts no program. The function `filter_overrides(root)` blanks the drivers of `root` and of every populated submodule that git enters from it, at every depth. The function `submodule_filter_overrides(root)` blanks the submodules only. Ostra uses it for commands that the user asked for, so the own filters of the repository, such as git-crypt, still apply.

The overrides must reach submodules because a status, `add`, or commit runs `git status` inside each populated submodule in the index. That child process reads the own config of the submodule, which can be a repository that an agent created and staged.

The function `config_env` adds config pairs through environment variables. It writes `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>`, and `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n>` after the entries that the parent already holds, so both sets apply. A `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` that is not a number counts as 0. The function `agent_env` returns `config_env` of `AGENT_CONFIG`, appended to the count of the Ostra process.

### What happens when

- **The walk reaches 256 repositories.** `blank_filters_of` logs `stopped reading submodule filter drivers at <path>: a status there may run one` and stops. A status in a repository after the limit can run a filter driver.
- **A `git config` query fails.** The query returns empty output, so Ostra adds no override for that repository.
- **A repository has no submodules.** Ostra reads the filter drivers of `root` only.

## Other constants in core

These constants are small, but a reader can look them up.

| Name | File | Value | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_STACK_LEN` | `slug.rs` | 64 characters | Longest project stack. `stack_issue` tells the user which rule failed: a control character, a length above 64, or an empty or untrimmed value |
| `CREATION_FLAGS` | `proctree.rs` | `CREATE_SUSPENDED` and `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`, on Windows only | Starts the child suspended, so that the Job Object holds it before its first instruction. It also stops a server that has no console from opening a console window for each command |
| `FOUND` | `shells.rs` | A `OnceLock` of the Git Bash path, on Windows only | Caches the Git Bash lookup. `bash()` returns `bash` on Unix and `bin\bash.exe` of Git for Windows on Windows |
| `NO_GIT_BASH` | `shells.rs` | A fixed text, on Windows only | The tool error when Git Bash is missing: install Git for Windows and restart Ostra |
| `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES` | `api.rs` | 65,536 bytes (64 KiB) | The largest console layout document that the server stores. `GET` and `PATCH /api/workspaces/:ws/ui` use it |
| `SUMMARY_CHARS` | `api.rs` | 120 characters | Longest `ExecutionView::summary`. `summary_line` collapses whitespace and cuts the text with an ellipsis |
| `KEYS` | `api.rs` | `file_path`, `command`, `pattern`, `url`, `path`, `query`, `skill`, `notebook_path` | The argument names that `tool_summary` tries, in this order. The first one that the tool call has gives the summary, for example `Edit src/lib.rs` |
| `HARNESS_AGENTS` | `api.rs` | `implementer`, `write-test` | The agents that a harness routing preset moves off the native loop |

Ostra looks for Git Bash by absolute path on Windows. The first `bash` on `PATH` is often `C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe`, the WSL launcher, which runs the command in a Linux VM with a different view of the files. The function `git_root` asks `git --exec-path` first, then checks `%ProgramFiles%\Git` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git`. The functions `powershell` and `cmd` return the Windows PowerShell 5.1 and `cmd.exe` paths under the system folder. [Native tools and their limits](tools.md) explains the shell tools.

## What these settings do not guarantee

- **Registry settings protect against a file, not against a user.** A person who can use the console can change them.
- **Validation reflects the machine at save time.** A harness or a key that exists when the user saves can be gone at spawn time. The engine then refuses the spawn.
- **The credential variable list is finite.** `credential_env_names` covers the default providers, the `providers.*` tables, the bridge variables, and the OAuth client secrets of MCP servers. A secret in any other variable is not on the list.
- **The credential paths are fixed.** `HOME_CREDENTIALS` names known locations. A credential that a tool stores in another place is not on the list. A person can add paths with `sandbox.extra_hidden`.
- **The git overrides name specific keys.** They block the keys in the tables above. They do not review the other keys of a repository config.
- **The filter walk has a cap.** After 256 repositories, `blank_filters_of` stops, and a later repository can run a filter driver.
- **Cost is an estimate.** It depends on the catalog and on the usage numbers that providers and harness transcripts report. A model that is not in the catalog costs 0.
- **`tool_enforcement = disabled` is the default.** Write scope, self-protection, and the shell and interpreter checks are off until a user sets `enabled`. The sandbox still limits what agent commands can write.
